So, Torchlight II is the continuation of the Torchlight series released back in 2009 by Runic Games. This game is a sequel to the first Torchlight game made.
Plot: The story is pretty simple and easy to follow, it was pretty memorable, it had memorable boss fights and references to other games that they put in such as Vyrax's tower and the Dragon Shrine, which is a huge reference to The Elder's Scrolls IV: Skyrim. The game in my opinion is quite entertaining, although it could be a little too short for some hardcore RPG players as looking at other games for example the Diablo series and so, but personally I also agree that the story itself is a little too short, even though there are things that allowed you to just continue playing this game over and over again.
Gameplay and Multiplayer: With multiplayer added to the Torchlight universe compared to the first game that didn't have any elements of multiplayer, really did open up new windows for people to really play this game. Also with the addition of the games being mod-able, multiplayer has been as fun as ever since it is also a drop-in/drop-out type which does not affect the storyline whatsoever, but with more players in the game the hostile enemies will get a little tougher which could be hard for some people, but in general it does not affect the single player gameplay at all.
Visuals: One word-- "Polished". The game looks great and really amazing. It was detailed, beautiful and fun to look at even if they were cartoonish and not as realistic as many of the games out there, they are really well done. As for the cut-scenes, they still hold back the elements from Torchlight 1, which retained the uniqueness and credibility of Torchlight, which I believe this game is perfect for most audiences that enjoy games that maybe aren't too realistic.
Audio: The OST is made by Matt Uelmen, the composer and sound designer of the Diablo series, also joined with Max Schaefer, the same people who made the music for the first Torchlight game. Although the soundtrack really differs in theme from the soundtrack of the Diablo series, they did a really amazing job of implementing the country music themes which gave it a distinctly different sound from the "Tristram" them of Diablo which made it great. They also did an amazing job in this part as they recorded over 200 live takes using a twelve string guitar alongside with many other instruments. The voice acting in this game casted many veteran voice actress and actors such as Lani Minella and so on who performed many of the voices in-game.
Reception: This game scored slightly more than the original Torchlight, which most of the reviews received were very favorable. On review sites such as Metacritics, this game attained an overall score of 88 out of 100 based on many reviews from 65 professional gaming critics worldwide which is an amazing score. Would you buy this game? Many RPG players would probably think that this game will just be like the first Torchlight and therefore result in a quick 'hiatus' from playing the game due to the repetitive nature of the game, however this is different. The developers themselves released tools for the players to be able to mod the game as they please, and people who join any multiplayer servers with mods on them will be able to access the mods freely, which leaves the game always moldable and playable in its own unique manners all the time.

I've played Craft The World twice, in two sittings, the two of them equal the playtime you see with this review.
What the hell was I doing? Why is this review negative?
I got roped in, I got sucker-punched with the all too psychologically powerful allure of mobile-game design.
I understand that phrase is considered an ill one in the gaming community, it smacks of tedium, tasks drawn out to the most painful extent possible, and constant, tiny, new goals that move you a modicum forward for dozens of minutes of effort.
That's really what it is. I mean, what's here is done fairly well.
Your dwarves are automated little cretins with terrible AI who go out, collect resources that you assign them to collect, build what you want them to build, and come back to sleep in their shelter when their health is low, or eat food after they've exerted themselves and built up some of them good old munchies. The game works, it's relatively bug free (I had one crash, and sometimes dwarves get stuck trying to get out of water, that's about it), the mechanics are fluid, and the game is generally competent. Whoopee.
At first it's impossibly addictive. This game is deceptively simple, and what I mean by that is that there's a great illusion here of this game having a lot to it at first, you look at the fairly large tech tree, the needs and behaviors of your dwarves, the monster waves with the promise of "tower defense" style strategy, and mechanics like farms and being able to husband animals in them.
It's fairly cool at first look, but everything here is surface level. There's very little automation of tasks, you can't instruct your dwarves to automatically sheer sheep, or plant, harvest, and replant wheat, or automatically build and rebuild structures. I'm kind of stretching here, but with games of this type, I expect a certain amount of ease of use features to make it more fluid to play, but like I said, this is a mobile-style game, meaning they WANT you to perform as many actions as possible to drag out the playtime.
That basically means doing every little simple thing takes a very large amount of button presses, if you want to craft something, you first have to manually arrange the recipe yourself, then craft it, then drag it to a hot bar, then place it, then wait for your dwarves to put it down, after they've dropped it off at the stockpile, then picked it up, and finally gotten on their way.
It's that kind of maddening tedium that somehow becomes addictive for a brief period of time, and in my tiredness and desire for something completely mindless to distract me it did its job, but when I finally finished the first level, I felt a profound sense of disappointment and a total lack of feeling of accomplishment when the endgame portal appeared with a ludicrous green "EXIT" sign above it.
There's not much to get out of this game, moment to moment it will suck the minutes away from you as you fiddle away with its time wasting mechanics, but the game isn't difficult, it doesn't require much thought, the combat is mindless and so is defending yourself against the hordes of enemies that appear. I felt tired after playing this game (yes I know I spent an insane amount of time in single sittings on it).
Honestly I really don't know what was going through my head, it must have been my profoundly apathetic mood at the time, but somehow I slogged through this game twice a year apart.
I'm still completely confounded by it. My soul drifts through the aether looking for answers it will never have.
I don't recommend this game. If you want to waste your time go play Skyrim or something, or hell, play Dungeon Keeper or Terreria or anything that has an actual sense of accomplishment.

Tl;dr;
Not a bad game, but somewhat slow en tedious on the crafting level. Darf AI isn't too great either with them getting stuck or just left clueless often. Multiplayer is a true grief-fest, but what did you want? Fun to play if you can live with its flaws.
----------------
So it's all about crafting a world for you dwarves. They have opened a portal which only had the power to transport 1 brave pioneer into your playfield and depend on your guidance to prosper and thrive. That is, if you can hold off the forces of evil that come out every night and every 45 minutes (the Devil sure is punctual).
To do so you need to gather resources by clicking on them. After that your eager dwarves will mine or hack away and carry the stuff back to the stockpile where it can be used to craft new items/base decorations/fortifications/food/...
Sadly not all dwarves are born with an Einstein level intellect so you will be wondering why 1 of them (let's call him Toby) is always doing the exact opposite of what you want. Be prepared to bail Toby out a lot with portals, scaffolding and ladders.
Building the actual shelter is pretty basic and not too refreshing. The only real notable thing is the aura of the "Totem". The more comfort you give the dwarves, the larges their base will become. Which in turn gives you more space for more dwarves.
You get new darves by leveling up through crafting, completing tasks and combat. It somehow makes it feel too much like a mobile game by doing this, but then again every other comparable game does it... Leveling is pretty fast in the beginning but slows down incredibly after lvl 10, however the monster waves don't.
So you day to day management will be:
-  gather resources
- craft what you need for new technologies
- give dwarves new items
- expand base
Sounds like a lot of fun? Well it is in the beginning... but after a while you need to craft 100 fancy chairs just to be able to pass on to Steel armour. It makes no sense to me, uses up a lot of resources and especially slows things down dramatically. The first "easy" world will take quite a while to complete, even with cheats...
And then there's multiplayer... for the love of God or Buddha or whoever you wish to believe in, do it with friends or alone. Chances are random players will screw you over beyond belief sending you right back to your tedious crafting without any reward whatsoever.
So all in all I want to really like the game for its ideas and just because I love the genre, but I'm stuck just barely liking it because some things can be too frustrating. If you can get it on a decent sale then don't doubt, otherwise there are better alternatives.

Just going to enumerate some points that are making me, personally, lose interest in the game.
- Team stacking. Clans with experienced players storming a server and playing all on the same side even after several maps of 8-0, 8-1, 8-2 etc. I understand people want to play together, but if one team just rolls the other over and over because a cohesive group of experienced players decide to group and not correct the imbalance meanwhile it's not exactly "just having fun with my friends", its knowingly trashing the game for everyone else. And if you try to reason, the usual answer is: "match balance is not my problem". I guess it's up to the Devs to restore official servers match balance forcefully because the "community" can't. And I say community in quotes because these clans never have a public server running, an open bar, where they give the example on how to receive players and have a good time so people return. It's always about trashing other bars around.
- Votes. Scramble never works. People votekick others for very very petty reasons and becomes a bullying tool. Its the most coward empowering thing ever, since the voted person doesn't know who is trying to kick, so there's not even room to reason with him/her.
Every time Red Line, Hospital, Slums, Coldfront, etc comes next, there's always "that guy" that casts a vote for Inner or Downtown and the tyranny of the majority kicks in again. Plus a lot of people cast map votes while others are still playing and worried about better things.
- Game is cluttered and somewhat dumb. AA2 was hard and fun, AA3 was hard and not so fun, AAPG is just easy which amounts to very limited fun.
Americas Army lost its simulation touch, with reasonable mechanics and overall clean sight. Now we have bad 3D tags everywhere, that clutter the view and makes you feel like you're using Whallhack, as you watch your teammates moving through the walls. A Kill Feed that gives away TOO much information, which paired with voicecoms it's just a torrent of intel about who killed who, with what and where: (A:"Ok, I got the guy in dark" B:"No, that was not the guy that shot me down, there's another one, look out").
Shooting is only the closing act of a kill. Measuring odds and gathering intel to improve those odds is very important and the game just neglects that. First with poor sound in previous versions and now with the displayed info.
People still dance like crazy with no aim penalty, I quickscope with the M24 at ease all day, while shooting someone 2 meters from me seems impossible at times (for a proficient marksman role).
Incap state is just dumb. You can't interact with incaps, but they are still relevant to the game. Like if I incap a player in my sight line and I know he saw the flag carrier or anything that compromises my team's plans. I'm not going to walk to him and put a little plastic bow around his hands. It's crucial I stop him from sharing that intel. On the other hand incaps always ask for "Grenade my body, x number of guys here" and some teammate sends a frag to its teammate body killing enemy players without affecting him.
Easy revives, easy self healing. I mean... The game it's easy, too easy...
- No Army lore or sense of mission deployment. Just have to compare the marketing videos with the actual game-play. For now training is not mandatory so there's no context to the game, the missions are solely build around corridors, small and feel like a training facility not actual deployment. More over the servers are not dedicated to one map by default as before so maps with little majority traction have little chance to be played with good number of players. AA2 had many servers with niche maps with good amounts of people playing in them.
Heck, raise your hand who ever liked to do E&E in AA2 or the medical training in AA3. But they not also rewarded you with something to use/do in-game but you also would get information out of them and a notion of what is taught in the Army.
Hospital without VIP, A bad Urban Assault revamp (2 times). Maps so small people say grenades are overpowered...
Inner Hospital is a plague.
- Bad excuses to ban. I made a second account because I play every day against a similar pool of people , some already know my play style and where I'll be lurking, so tried to catch those off-guard. On 2 private moderated servers I was banned (after I told it was a second account and they even named my first account) because I had an IP linked banned account in BF3 (!). I guess some folks in the US never heard of dynamic IP, or are just looking for a reason. One of the times I was playing the whole time on the clan owners side, with them even congratulating me when I clutched rounds; they spectated me more than enough.
- To me it seems recent, but maybe it has been like that for a while in AAPG. Top of the head kills are extremely annoying. They were a constant thing in AA2, where you would have someone behind a wall or proned behind a thick frame and you would only see the tip of the helmet and they could shoot you at ease, so they have unfair odds. I understand there won't be parallax in the game so you can't have a view point and a separate exit point, so at least make something in between or balanced so both players are bringing leveled risks to the fights.
The game of course has a lot of positives, but those are not the ones that make you let a game go and play something else.
AA2 remains my most played and most enjoyed game, but something like Insurgency even with different mechanics seems to honor it more, than AA Proving Grounds. First time I opened it I thought it was Combat Arms game...

is a fast-paced team oriented multiplayer shooter co-developed by the US-Army as a recruiting tool. (does that even work?) The previous games opted for a challenging simulation shooter style whereas this game borrows over elements of both counterstrike as well as call of duty making for an interesting blend of competitive tactical shooter.
Proving grounds is a game that requires teamwork and strategy, much like counterstrike. The scoping, sprinting and prone options feel more like call of duty as well as adding its own unique features such as reviving teammates securing fallen enemies and healing yourself. The modes center around capture the flag, team elimination, and bomb planting.
Its very much a hardcore shooter in that you can die very quickly if you are reckless, and it is very rewarding when you manage to help your team or work together with your clan. If offers 6v6 and 12v12 maps for servers.
+ Nice blend of old and new features
+ Server browser and dedicated servers
+ Can be very competitive
+ Not an unbalanced, money grabbing, korean FPS.
+ Most of the players are older, more mature & very friendly.
+ Free to play
- Hardcore difficulty might not be for everyone
- Is a drastic change from the earlier installments
- Occasional bugs
- Relatively small userbase
If you like competitive team-based shooters like Counterstrike and Insurgency consider giving this one a try, its free anyway. As always, please like if you enjoyed the review, thanks!

I had always wondered about this game when I saw the mostly negative reviews I thought to myself, it can't be THAT bad. Sure enough, it was. There are major issues in the game that are simple fixes but haven't been changed probably because of pure laziness.
This game is nothing more than a cash grab. I understand it's a F2P game and they have to make money some how but the way the game is designed it almost forces you to buy veteran or spend an insane amount of time in game that really no one realistically has. If you don't play a good amount of hours then you are going to be very behind and that will result in a rough matchmaking experience.
That raises another issue, the matchmaking system. Plain and simple it's just a match maker tool. There is no formula, there is no balance, nothing!
Huge groups of experienced clans or premades can go up against brand new players with stock guns and they just don't have a chance. And it's not like it happens every so often, it's literally 8 out of 10 games consist of veteran players vs brand new players. In my 50 hours in the game (at the time of writing this review), I'd say about 5 of them were actual close games. The rest were mostly my team stomping new players or my team getting stomped by vets with everything unlocked.
But wait, there's more!
The majority of my games my team would be down in players. I had a TON of games where it would be something like 8 v 12 since the beginning of the game and nothing changes. We don't get team mates, get stomped all game and it's over. And on the flip side the same thing occurs, my team would have 10 players vs like 5-6 and the games aren't even close. Do you see a pattern forming here?
TL:DR The game is NOT balanced in many different ways (matchmaking, guns, tanks, etc) and will result in a poor matchmaking experience the majority of the games you play unless you either spend money or spend an INSANE amount of time grinding and grinding.

[Recently announced changes promise to remove my largest issue with SNOW (grinding to unlock spawns). I'll update this review once I've had a chance to try it out. Until then, take this with a pinch of salt]
I do recommend this game, but it's a grudging recommendation...
The good:
* The scenery is stunning
* Going off-piste is fantastic
* It has bags of potential
* Pretty damned good simulation (especially since the latest update, still a few glitches but generally OK)
* Excellent music
* Great fun to relax and unwind with (I prefer free roam to doing events)
* Lots of features being added / improved
* Dev team seem committed and I see no signs of vapourware
* I haven't personally had any performance issues (although I've seen post from some who have)
* Rift support!
The bad:
* Microtransactions (At least they're currently cosmetic only)
* If you want to get to the good spawn points, you have to grind XP
* Features keep being removed
* Updates are a little slow and there's no target 1.0 date
* Controls could do with a tweak (especially moving the camera in 3rd person)
* Grinding XP (worth mentioning again, especially when wiping out costs unbanked XP)
Perhaps I was spoiled by playing very early versions of this game, but I loved if because it left me alone on a mountain to explore and go where I wanted. Now, however, if you want to try the best bits of the mountain, you need to grind XP which is still insanely slow in Free Roam mode.
I may be wrong but I get the impression that once the game is Free2Play, the devs are worried people won't hang around long enough to spend money. Unfortunately, it's turned a fun, relaxing game into yet another slog.
I do still recommend it, just. It's beautiful and worth playing, but IMHO it's worse overall than it used to be.

I think my biggest complaint is literally that. The game is quite stiff. I could also complain about the apparent 'multiplayer' since it's technically not the traditional kind, but I guess the game doesn't really feel like it would work as traditional online co op anyway. Regardless, I don't care much for the competetive multiplayer portion. How you do multiplayer in this game is that you play singleplayer and you build a teleporter that then lets you and one other person teleport to a neutral area in a cave and you both just try to gather as many resources as you can really. After all is said and done you go back to your singleplayer world. I don't really think it's fair for me to complain again because I didn't get a chance to do it. In fact I kinda avoided it because I didn't like the way it was implemented.
But yes, everything else in the game is solid. It takes a bit to understand how to do certain things, like putting food on tables and getting your first house to function properly, but it all does function. I also like that there is more than one level and that enemies are a constant threat.
So I mean the game certainly has a little stiffness to it, but it's not bad, in fact I'd say it's good. I'd encourage you to check out a gameplay vid of the game if you're on the fence about getting it so you know what you're getting into.

Excellent game.
This game has a very steep learning curve but is well worth the time investment.
I would recommend that you start by watching youtube videos of the mechanics because of the lack of a good tutorial involved with this game.  The next step would be to play some skirmish against the AI to get a feel of the game.  From there you should probably venture into 4v4 or 10v10 games.  I personally don't like 10v10 games as they are nothing but arty spam fest.  As for game mode, Conquest is my personal favorite.
As for the community, this is where the game needs help.  The main game chat hub is not moderated at all and is filled with nonsense.  It really needs to be cleaned up but it is what it is right now.  The other problem is that finding good, balanced games can be tough sometimes.
The developer for the most part is really good, I just have a slight problem with the recent DLC Nation Packs.  My problem with them is that they feel more fleshed out then the OG Nations of the game and I would like to see these Nations balanced against the new Nations of the game.  Overall though, they do a good job keeping things fairly balanced.  I do wish that the series would have stayed in the European Theatre.
Lastly, I really wish that this game was looked at for competitive gaming.  It has all the tools to get there, just needs a couple things.  The first thing is to clean up the community and get rid of the cancer.  Secondly we would need a few maps that offered a balanced match, so maps that mirrored each other on each side.

TLDR: This game is basically a more serious, online version of borderlands, and that's not necessarily a bad thing. Its free so it's definitely worth the time to download and have a play around.
The main problem i have with the game could be summed up by a description of one fight. I was doing a story mission, running around a ranch shooting raiders. so far so good. I then saw a miniboss on a nearby rooftop, so i pull out my sniper rifle, and shoot him in the head. his health bar stays the same but the damage readout says 4000 damage. i empty the rest of the clip into his head. not only is he still standing, his health bar is almost full. So, skip to the sixtieth headshot i get on him, and i've run out of ammo. i pull out a light machine gun and close in. five hundred rounds later, he's at 60% health. i'm not quite out of ammo but he has been spamming grenades all around me and now there's nowhere for me to go that doesn't have a detonating grenade. i get one-shot and go into bleedout. i revive myself and run behind a building.i see an ammo crate, refill my ammo, and ~150 headshots later he dies.
So my problem is that enemies are far too bulletsponge-y. A basic, unarmoured bandit, with no helmet, will often take two, three or four headshots from a sniper rifle, or dozens of point blank headshots from an assault rifle, SMG, LMG etc.
This, combined with the fact that enemies will just keep spawning faster than you can fill them with bullets means tht the gunplay is a bit of a letdown. quite a big problem, as a lot of mission objectives involve 'interact with this object for five seconds without taking damage' objetcives, meaning you either cheese it with cloak, or you spend 5-10 minutes in the same area just mindlessly killing the same enemies over and over again until you've got a five second window. Fast-spawning mobs would be fine, if they died quickly. bulletsponges would be fine if they were finite, which wouldn't really work in an MMO. sadly, this means that you can snipe everyone in an area, walk up to the objective and find that there was really no point because the enemies have respawned already and you're stuck in the same close quarters battle anyway.
Aside from that, it is a good game. the fact it was originally not free to play means that the microtransactions aren't built in from the ground up to be 'necessary', vehicles are actually vehicles, not mounts, and you can do some fun stuff with the jet-booster quadbike you get half an hour into the game

Let me start by saying THANK YOU for not creating an SSX.  But...
So far, this game still isn't at par with most simulator type skiing\snowboarding games that have already been on the market.  The character is stiff, weightless, and too obviously procedurally driven.  It looks and feels like you are controlling the skiis not the rider.  The controls are very binary when they should take advantage of modern analog controllers. For instance, regardless if you tap the steering controls or hold, the character drops right into the extremity of the turning poses.  Same for grabs and any other feedback coming from the character.
There is no sense of speed unless you are in the trees. The levels feel wide open, flat, and tricking opportunities are sparse. The jumps in the parks feel dauntingly huge and are seemingly too big for the lack of speed even at max speed.   The physics feel just as binary as the controls and don't work well with the level design metrics for the terrain or park obstacles.  Rails riding is quirky and the rider looks dorky. Halfpipe riding is frustrating and it's nearly impossible to get any speed\air.  The radgoll is just broken, and bailing in any game other than EA Skate isn't fun. It's punishing and wastes a players time.
The best parts of this game are the jump on the right thumbstick (thank you EA Skate) when it works and doesn't give you an awkward emote instead. As well, a huge plus is having the generous ability to customize the ingame camera.
This game has a long way to go before Beta.

This review is only for a short play of co-op.
Everything feels really Trine-ish from the menus till the game starts. Meaning, positive vibes, nice graphics and relaxing gameplay.
However, things go wrong at least in the co-op mode quickly. The graphics are really unclear, it's hard to distinguish between the scrolling backgrounds, the active platforming area, and the player characters. You never really see who's who, you or your friend. Sometimes the camera zooms automatically in a way which just somehow screws up your vision and brain. I haven't had any problems with any other game in my 25 years of gaming. There's just _something_ wrong with the game, visually. It's more subtle than I make it out to be, but it's there.
The level design didn't seem to help, either. For a simple platformer such as this, requiring a map feels silly. You do need the map because everything looks a bit same and messy, so without the map you will be stumbling upon already visited areas. There's also a world map - out of which neither of us could figure out anything at all. Even after the first boss fight, we didn't even know in which world we were on the map.
Then there's the co-op play in general. Each player has their own money in game. The client's controls will be lagging badly. When another player is shown a message or a menu, another player just sees a prompt to quit the game, which will, if accidentally pressed, quit both players. Some of the game mechanics are basically broken in co-op: for example, there are moving platforms of two different colors, and you can step on one depending on which color you are. Or, in the case of co-op, depending on which color either of you are. This means that platforms that shouldn't be landable, in fact are, provided the other player is of the correct color.
After a good one and half hours of gameplay, I didn't know what was going on with the story, and didn't even care anymore. The animations are nice, sounds are nice, and I guess the single player game is technically fine. So maybe for a single player game you could give this one a shot. I just feel there are better alternatives, such as the Trine series, Shank etc. For co-op, find something else.

Played it for a couple of hours and found things I quite liked, and other things I found to be complete mistakes.
The game itself caught me off guard with its initial flow. Its reasonably fast, and wall jumping feels very fluid and nice. The only problem is, when the game places you in tight corridors, or in chamber of lazers with tight movement, you end up hyper-speed launching into enemies or lazers when you only want to tip toe carefully through an obstical.
Visually the game has very nice artistic direction. There's a lot of unique environments and sort of "light box" elements to the levels. Visual clarity needs some work though. With dark backgrounds, seeing completely black platforms is a nightmare, this is particularly bad in the second boss fight.
Enemies and hit boxes range from being completely crisp, such as in the warrior enemy, to being completely un-clear like with the flying bird/dragon enemy. Certain enemies also have a lack of telegraphing attacks. By the time you hear or see a "telegraphed attack" you're usually already hit.
The main mechanic of Light and Dark is fun, but when you enter a room with both blue and red overlapping, its just easier to run head first into the room, take the damage, and keep moving forward, because you're going to get hit anyway. This mechanic does not mix well with enemies + platforming, as they can hit you despite your color state, but you cannot hit them. Between enemies, color disco guessing time and platforming, dying in such a way is not so much "oh man, that was a tough room, I need to think this out" to more, "Wow, I have no idea what's going on" (thus the 'rushing through the level' strategy rears its ugly head).
The environments are nice, the enemies are a bit bland. There's story, but it didn't catch me and felt pretty dry. Voice acting is decent. The boss fights were tough, but still sort of fun.
For the price i'd say, despite some of the mild shortcomings, its quite worth it! Give it a shot if you like short tough platformers, but get ready for a few moments of bad enemy placement, and a cool mechanic that is sort of lost to a weird clustered design mess.

One of the best RTS' around. More tactical and slower-paced than a traditional RTS, you have to think harder before commiting your units into battle. Building your own deck from over 1400 units is fun in its own way. 10v10 multiplayer battles are spectacular and commanding air, land and sea units simultaneously really make you feel like a commander in a real war

Wargame is back! This time though, You won't be shelling German towns or sneaking in Scandinavian forests, You'll be burning poor asian women and children with napalm one more time! Thats right, The Wargame Theatre of War is now Asia!
The game controls the same as EE and AirLand, but the folks at Eugen have added another layer of tactical micromanagement- Sea battles. The units never cease to amaze me how one second I can be applauding their perfect executions of my plans... To wondering how such braindead soldiers even understand the concept of breathing.
Nevertheless, The game still proves it is fun, challenging and intellegent even if it feels like AirLand battle with the prototype date pushed back to '95. The addition of the new counties is always welcome, and Japan, China, North and South Korea, and Australia fit perfectly in the numerous factions. The addition of coalitions and the reworking of deck types makes building and customizing decks an extremly fun pass time.
But newcomers to series be warned: THIS GAME HAS A LEARNING CURVE THAT RIVALS EVE. That's right, don't expect to drop in and beginning distributing letal doses of freedom, and the tutorials aren't worth jackshit. Still, If you got the balls and are willing to sick it out, the game is immensely fun and satisfying.
Absolutely Exceptional Real Time Strategy Game. Would recommend to anybody who wants to get lost in a world of complex mechanics and thrilling action.

This
piece of art will redefine the way you see modern battle. This is a true modern war simulator. Nothing else I have ever played comes close to immitating the amount of scale and realism that this piece of software is capable of. Every single jeep, truck, tank, helicopter, plane, warship and lone infantry squad are modelled accurately with their own statistics and individual ordinance package. The infantry is always mechanized. The tanks can get stuck in mud. The fighters jets have dog fights. The various warships have CIWS which can shoot down certain missiles heading towards them. And the best part? You can choose to zoom in on any particular unit, and follow them throughout this chaos at ground level at any time.
This is really a worthy successor!

I put over 200 hours into this game. I played through the story thrice. I've messed about with mods for countless hours. GTA itself was a masterpiece of a game, but with mods... GTA itself was just a box. It was just a container for the infinite possibilities of mods. That's what made me pay $60 for a game I already paid $120 for on two console generations once it arrived on PC. Mods were the most important part of the GTA V PC experience.
At least, until Take Two Interactive issued a cease-and-desist order to the team behind OpenIV, the software that permits all substantial modding for GTA IV and V. It's been running for nearly ten years undisturbed... until June 14, 2017, when it had to shut down because Take Two declared modding effectively illegal despite tolerating it (and even celebrating it) for nearly a decade.
Because of that, I can't reccomend GTA V on PC. Don't get it. If you're getting it for a proper game, don't. You can get it on console, but I can't reccomend that because it supports Take Two Interactive. If you're getting it for mods, don't. You'll be disappointed. There is nothing to reccomend about GTA V PC any longer. Unless and until Take Two reverses this decision, this negative review will stick and the rest of the reviews will continue dropping. In honor of the OpenIV devs, "recent" reviews will reach a low of "Overwhelmingly Negative." That'll get some press attention and it will certainly get Take Two's attention.

As someone who has put thousand of hours into rct 1 & 2 over the years, this game has managed to reignite that lost addiction which is nice.
While ride and scenary options are limited, even with a limited selection there is a ton you can do. Scenary has no space restrictions so you can just overlap and create anything you mind can imagine. Even a coaster that just strolls through a couple boulders for the fun of it. Its very refreshing to see there be no limits on place scenary like rctw, or even rct2 for that matter. Some scenary items are scalable also which is awesome. Id defiantly say the scenary is the strongest part thus far.
Coaster designer is miles better then rct2 but slopes on very tall hills can still feel a little unnatural, like curve -> straight slope for a while -> Curve out at bottom. Perhaps adding another slant between the steepest and vertical would help greatly. Fury 325 for example has 81 degree drop, not quite vertical. Also some elements are limiting, 45 degree turns cant be used on slant, half loops are straight only which made making x-flight ingame impossible. Small Gripes but i enjoy recreating real parks so its mildly annoying for me.
UI and all that is basic but it functions perfectly, staff screen is a bit clunky but overall cant complain considering its EA.
The cons would be there is no tutorial or any kind of handholding at this point in devolopment, you just have a sandbox to play in basically. So if you really have no past experience with rct or would give up in confusion quickly then sure, avoid till it has tutorial.
Overall ive enjoyed every minute so far and look foward to the future updates and feel it was worth every penny thus far. Devs seem very involved with the community and the game so i have high hopes it will actually reach release given no monitary issues.

I remember when I first heard about this game I thought it sounded like a normal "gimmick" (I don't mean that negatively, per se) indie platformer where you controlled two characters at the same time with one gamepad. But the game is a lot more... the scenery is surprisingly beautiful, the controls are unique and sometimes tricky (when the brother controlled by the left joystick is on the right side of the screen) but the gameplay is varied enough to keep it fun and fresh, and the character and emotion in the game is palpable and well done.
Honestly I did not expect this game to deal with such mature subject matter, such as loss, death, guilt, despair, but it also pulls of the sense of family, love, trust too. I was honestly stunned such a short little game could be this interesting to play through.
I beat it in about 2 hours but I'm sure i'll play through it again. The achievements are all secrets-related, not progress-related, and the few that I found were neat little "easter eggs," which could be one way to put it.
All in all, a game definitely worth experiencing. Well put together, fun, crisp gameplay experience for the most part, and some touching emotional moments, both sad and happy.

The gameplay is so simple and basic: you can move, jump, attack and change power between light and dark,  and it makes the game so accesible and simple to play.
The Story:
A man started experiencing dreams and visions of the past. He attempts to take medicine to stop it, thinking that this was a medical problem, but the medicine was ineffective; something larger was at play.
The man decided to find a shaman to find out what the problem was, what these dreams and visions meant, and to cure him of them. However, the shaman told the man of the ancient stories of a battle 30,000 years ago between a great hero and the two Sisters of Chaos - one who controls Light from the Sun, and one who controls Darkness from the Moon. The Sisters were imprisoned after the battle, but the hero had perished in the process. The shaman informed the man that he was the hero's reincarnation, and that the Sisters of Chaos have apparently escaped their imprisonment. This man was now the only one who could stop them, and so he went forth on the journey.
Nothing of special, but still a pretty well plot, enough to make the player going on the journey.
Visuals and level design are great, probably the best part of the product.
Outland is a must-have game for all the platform lovers, recommended.

Pretty much trash. I love the Final Fantasy series, but this is lacking everything that makes Final Fantasy games great.
Gameplay:
No joke, literally all you do is fight monsters. There's no towns, no exploration, no nothing. There's a world map, and you click a level, and in the level you fight a few waves of monsters, then you go back to the world map, and repeat. That's it. You might think I'm exaggerating, but it's honestly so boring and monotonous. By definition, this game is a grindfest.
Battles:
Again, no joke, literally all you do is either click the enemy, or click a skill. Final Fantasy games are turn based, and I'm totally fine with that, but this is terrible. All the attacks feel basically the same. There's dozens of these cards (which represent your abilities), and they're all pretty much the exact same thing. There's next to no strategy in it, you really just click the bad guys and watch them die.
You do have to manage your character, although there's very little to that as well, even though the system looks VERY complicated, it's extremely simplistic when you figure it out. Like I've said, everything is the same, all the way through. It looks like there's lots of content and stuff to figure out, but it all boils down to the same old boring thing over and over again. It's seriously boring.
Story:
The characters are completely forgettable. When addressing this problem, fans defend it by saying, "the main character has memory loss, there's suppose to be nothing to his character!" While that is true, it's really boring. So far I've seen about five characters. All the voice acting is bad, and there's nothing really interesting about any of them.
The actual story seems really simple and boring too. You wake up not knowing who or where you are, and you run around killing things trying to fulfill a prophecy to become the messiah (very original btw). There's absolutely no motivation to play it.
I'm really sad this is such a disappointment, but with Square games, I'm not really surprised (remember FF-X2, FFXIII, etc.). This game is an obvious money grab, which they spent very little time planning.

I think the biggest "nope" in regards to this game is the price. But let me explain. This game is one of those games that fit into the category of "it's bad, but bad in a good way", though it doesn't fit it very well. As awful as the controls are, I feel it's hard to rate this game based on that because really, that's where part of the enjoyment is. This is a game that's "funny".. something you and your friends can play, and laugh at each other while doing so. The main reason this game got Greenlit, and got so much attention, is because so many popular Let's Players on Youtube played it and linked to it on Greenlight.
For a game that was a student project, it is impressive in that regard. I think it probably would have been free if it weren't for all the LPers and the like. All the people watching thought it was hilarious to see someone play this game and rage/mess up/etc.. and while that was entertaining, it just gets pretty old after the first 15 minutes. This game actually reminds me a lot of Happy Wheels, which is a game that has that funny, over the top gameplay that's fun to play or watch someone else play. Happy Wheels has thousands of user created maps (though there are a lot of users who just post the same type of map over and over again), a dozen or so characters to choose from, and a lot of entertaining and unique moments. All of that is free. However, for this.. you're spending $10 on a game that revolves around one main focus of trying to be funny with having bad controls while trying to perform surgery. It has an extremely small selection of "maps", the gameplay is rediculously repetitive as it's pretty much the same objective each time, just with the "map" looking different in each one. Heck, they have so many tools you can use in the game, yet most of them end up working just the same, so there's no real need to actually use more than two tools (for the most part).
Bottom line is.. This is a game that should have been free, or 2-3 dollars at the most. It's not a horrible game, and is fun for a little bit.. but honestly, unless you find it on sale for two dollars, I really don't recommend it. All and all, it honestly just feels like because of the huge attention and hype it got from so many large name Youtube Let's Players, the developers "finished" the game and cashed in.. charging a decent amount of money for something so very small and lacking.

The following is written from the point of view of a longtime content-creator for varying train simulators, with Microsoft Train Simulator having been my "primary" since 2005. I have been building routes since I first picked up the simulator, and have written innumerable blog posts or forum guides about my experience. As such, I won't be talking about it from a gameplay perspective, but rather from a content-creator's view with what could be considered "inside baseball" terminology mixed in.
Now, of all the platforms I've worked with, Train Simulator 2014 is by far the best. It's got the versatility and learning curve of the Trainz-series world editors, while still being as robust as the SDK included with the granddaddy of all modern 'sims, Microsoft Train Simulator. Its stability is remarkable, too, allowing for a multitude of complicated signaling systems or scenery-rich worlds either of the aforementioned simulator programs would balk at. For full effect, though, I would recommend downloading the Railworks Community Asset Pack, which contains some of the most detailed, versatile “interactives” available for the game, as well as a wealth of other assets.
By far the biggest advantage the World Editor has on any other simulator SDK out there is the "Loft" system and the tangent / arc placement. I frequently refer to a copy of C. Frank Allen's "Railroad Curves and Earthwork" handbook, and from what I have seen the TS2014 editor follows its curve-design algorithms to a T. In need of a bridge or an embankment to run underneath a section track? Any lofts--be it a third-party product or one of RSC's finest--can be snapped to the curve to match its radius precisely. You don't have to wrestle with splines like in Trainz or master quaternion algebra like in MSTS, just a few simple clicks and the chasm is spanned!
Another advantage the World Editor has to be the smooth interface--you can toggle a Google Maps overlay (provided you create an API key, which is fairly straightforward) on and off in the editor, eliminating any need for creating placemarks beforehand. Its DEM importer is also within the SDK, which I think is a first for ANY train simulator (Trainz requires Hand of God, MSTS requires DEMEX) and processes the data in a way which leaves no skew. Likewise, it's also easy to jump between the world editor and the game itself, meaning on-the-fly adjustments don't entail the ordeal of copying down latitude and longitude coordinates for some snafu in the scenery. Rather, one series of clicks or a key command and you're in the editor, and then upon fixing the snafu you can resume driving.
That's not to say there aren't pitfalls, such as the lack of compatibility with certain DEM types. RSC has provided us routebuilders with a powerful in-editor DEM importer, but only accepts derivations of the egregiously low-resolution SRTM data, sampled at 90 meters between data points. In building mountainous regions I have found this resolution of SRTM data yields landscapes which are dramatically "smoothed out" and thus bear no semblance to the original landscape, in some instances damming up narrow canyons or reducing jagged peaks to rolling hills. Comparably, I can get a sheet of 10m-resolution NED data into MSTS which renders every hill, dale, and manmade earthwork in the tri-county in impeccable detail, albeit in a more roundabout means than TS2014. The fix for this issue is quite rudimentary--all that is needed is the ability to parse GeoTIFFs--a near-universal DEM format which many freeware DEM programs such as MicroDEM or VTBuilder can convert to—through the DEM importer.
No doubt about it, I definitely recommend Train Simulator 2014 for any train-simmers interested in diving into the world editor and making your backyard line. In fact, Based on criterion I devised from what I've experienced, read, and written about what makes a routebuilder's "perfect simulator", TS2014 clinches a solid 92.5%, well more than the benchmark 80% that MSTS scores by the same algorithm. Like any "young" simulator, TS2014 still has to grow into its boots, to overcome a few shortfalls, and for the community to learn its nuances. However, from what I have found, it boasts the most powerful suite of content-creation tools on the train simulation scene, something which holds a wealth of opportunity for the future of train-simming.
Happy routebuilding, and keep 'em rolling!
-Master Craftsman, SLS Team-

It's a shame that GFWL is being put to rest because this game and Halo 2 were the big powerhouses of GFWL. Blacklight Retribution is a fun and expansive F2P game but this was a great kickstart to the series. Very minimal First-Person gunplay combined with a small but unique story while all being focused on a convincingly real futuristic world of electronic warfare. If you have $5 to waste; Instead of going to spend it on a meal at McDonald's, spend it on this here game. Even though you won't be able to play much (if any) online games, I promise the single-player missions will be all the fun you're looking for in a small game like this. The missions are short, but they have a decent replay value and I find myself running through them every few months just for nostalgia purposes.

In short, if you're looking for a neat little sci-fi shoot'em-up, you've found one for quite a good price.

Got the game on steam winter sale and had it in my library for a bit before I finally got around to playing it. The game is surprisingly interesting with unique controls (you control two brothers simultaneously), beautiful environment / visuals, and an ok story. The controls however, set it apart from any game I've ever played, and I've played a lot. Although there have been games where dual coop is a must (army of two for example), you never really control players simultaneously as this game, which makes it stand out. Def worth $4 I paid for a unique gaming experience.

Brothers' doesn't require you to have a controller, but it is strongly recommended that you do. Small nuances such as rotating wheels by rotating your thumbstick gives an inviting sense of playfullness that I haven't encountered in a game in a long time. The gameplay consists of you controlling each brother with his own thumbstick and button, navigating and interacting with objects in order to solve puzzles. The puzzles are not very complicated, but the unique controls provide you with enough of a challenge to solve them.
What I noticed above all in this game, was the attention to detail, the creator's could have not put in interactions with the townsfolk for instance, but they did. In one example, when you interact with a townsfolk with the older brother, he will take their broomstick and help sweep the floor. If you tried the same townsfolk with the younger brother, he will merely play around and do tricks with the broom, at which the townsfolk will not be amused and beckon to give the broom back.  In fact, the two brothers interact differently with people and objects, which really adds a sense of character that cannot be accomplished with dialogue. This seems necessary if the game has no dialogue, but in this case, it is not a handicap. Characters speak an incomprehensible gibberish, yet you still understand the gist of the story because of it's simplicity and the characters' gestures.
The world is also very detailed, it is colourfull and vivid when you are in the countryside or forest, and appropriately monotone when navigating a barren wasteland. There are a few moments where environmental effects change the gameplay. In my opinion, there are too few of these moments, or their effects are not strong enough, or do not last long enough. But since the game is so short, the designer's seemed to not want to pad the game with unnecessary filler.
The plot of the story is simple, and the game is short, but it still filled with quality experiences that managed to make me feel emotionally invested in the brothers. I recommend this game, especially if you have a PC compatible gamepad with two thumbsticks.

First and foremost, the single-player-co-op idea is simply marvelous. I can't recall ever having played anything like it, and Starbreeze does a great job of varying the experience and keeping the idea fresh. It never tires.
I admire a story that can be told compellingly without needing any words. Brothers is one such tale: all speech in this game is effectively Simlish. The gestures of the characters provide you all of the instruction you'd need, from a practical point of view. Eliminating dialog and focusing on the actions and interactions feels like a welcome edit of an unnecessary distraction.
Brothers is a game that focuses on interaction. There are hot spots everywhere to interact with. Many times, there is no purpose to these interactions other than the boyish fun of doing so - which is kind of the point. These interaction points aren't advertised by littering the field of play with immersion-breaking icon; they're there to reward an explorer's curiosity the same way the boys' would be.

This game was an experience like no other. I loved this game mostly on an artistic point of view. I really suggest this game.
Soundtrack: I loved the soundtrack. Each theme matched the environment and tone of the area or scene. One complaint with the soundtrack was that the boss fight music never changed and the final boss music was just a more epic version of the same song. Not many complaints with the theme itself but I like it when there are unique themes for each boss in a game.
Presentation: The art style was the best part of this game. The vibrant colors really complimented the static terrain and backgrounds. The FPS of the game was very smooth and each area in the game had very unique art in the terrain such as vines or chains in the ground or trees and rivers in the background. This game really paid attention to detail and it came out magnificent.
Gameplay: The controls were awkward at first but the characters and enemies flowed extremely smoothely. In terms of difficulty this game was off the charts difficult. We're talking dark souls difficulty at times. The final boss took me over 10 tries to beat it was insane. The difficulty was a good thing though. I thoroughly enjoyed the challenged this game posed on me. Combat system was simple yet quite fun. It was so fun in fact I would stop at each enemy and fight just for the fun of it. Level design was great. Very labrynth-like with switches, doors, obstacles, enemies and bullet hell spread out perfectly. I have a huge complaint though. The levels were very repetitive and I found myself trudging through the same patterns and trials over and over again with slight changes each time. I did like progression throughout the game with the option to buy hearts and energy and being given new mechanics and skills. One of the boss fights wasn't that fun to me and it felt like a terrible version of shadow of the colossus where you could beat the boss with silly tactics instead of skill and determination.
All in all this game was one I will cherish forever. I adored playing co-op with my friend and trying to make my way up the leaderboards in arcade. Great gameplay, amazing art and great soundtrack.
I would give this game a...            8.5/10

If you want a cross between Terraria and a super simple base building game (like say Gnomoria), I recommend this game, although you might want to check out some gameplay vids to see if it matches your preferences. I enjoyed my time with the game a lot.
You control a squad of Dwarves, you "research" tech by completing earlier tech, and you get spells to cast. Waves of monsters come at night so you have to defend your base. Underground digging can unearth dangerous monsters too.
Don't get it for multiplayer. I read about how to get that working a couple months ago, I gave up before even trying. No saves and it requires an advanced single-player game structure or something.
High points for me was enjoyable digging/exploring experience, fun managing a group of guys (something I enjoy a lot, as opposed to singular direct control ala Terreria), building infrastructure like elevators and railroads, building up a base structure.
Low points include tedious craft UI, fun techs come late in the tech tree (railroads come after you've had to build a ton of infrastructure already), low variety of enemies, night-time enemy waves get annoyingly strong eventually.
I'm glad I played it and I do recommend it for fans of the genres mining and base-building.

Overall a pretty good game but a lot of things let it down.
I am a massive train fanatic, I have always liked trains since I was a little kid, and have even had a few model train sets however my parents soon got fed up of derailing trains crashing their coffee all over the place so this game was the next best thing I could find.
At first sight this game is everything you could want, it comes with a few routes and each of these contain a decent amount of scenarios which are mostly interesting and vary in difficulty. The graphical fidelity of this game is decent but this is 2014 and using 2D trees which rotate to look 3D in this day and age is pretty awful, overall pretty good however soon enough you will have done everything in the base game... so what next?
Well one thing you have to praise is the workshop which lets you download additional routes, scenarios and some other bits and bobs from other owners of the game which are free, and to be honest if this basic feature was not in the game there is no way I would be so positive up till now, so you have to give credit to all the people who have worked hard and given up their time making free content just to make the game more enjoyable, because the developers are too busy making the next stunningly accurate DLC to sell on the store.
Eventually you will want some new routes / locomotives to play around with so you will inevitbale consider paying some hard earned money for some extra DLC which you would assume will be a reasonable price.......... Unfortunately the prices are extortionate and paying £12 just for a locomotive in my oppinion is far too expensive and this is where the game starts to go downhill for me, the DLC is far too expensive and some of the DLC I have taken the plunge on has been very dissapointing. The GEML London - Ipswich Add - On is missing popular stations such as Southend Victoria and Clacton yet I paid £25 near half the price of the game for one route.... for this reason I don't recommend their DLC as you may be surprised to see parts of the route you want are not there!!!
(P.s. the £12 class 90 add-on didn't even have a passanger view??? I am dissapointed by this as other DLCs do have the passanger view, and you don't clearly detail what is / is not included.)
Carrying on, the parts of the route it does include are pretty well done but the platforms on this particular DLC are too short at a majority of stations along the line and whilst I don't expect a 100% replica if your going to take the time to model each station atleast make the platforms the right length? my next issue is that whilst there are very good powerful features to  create / edit routes and scenarios the tools are moderately good but very buggy and will crash often or create errors with little debugging information which is just rediculous and makes these tools somewhat obsolete. I assume this is why the DLC is so expensive?? Not to mention a lack of documentation on how to use these which is a shame, engine-driver is one of many places to find some tutorials however the next part of a tutorial usually never shows up.
To sum it all up, this game is not a bad game, I have played some awful games and as a rail fanatic this game has done a good job of keeping me satisfied, however DLC pricing is out of touch and extortionate, usually not 100% complete or lacking fearues I would consider mandatory personally, the tools they have added to let the average joe create scenarios and improve routes whilst promising and fairly decent are tarnished by their incompleteness and are sometimes at best rather tempermental and require extreme patience. It is for these very reasons I can't recommend this game and I won't be buying any more DLC unless it is dirt cheap.

The game is a wargame, the 'spiritual' successor to World In Conflict, I think mainly because its set in a world in conflict, but its balls harder.
There's a whole bunch of systems you'll never master, let alone grasp. Recon is the game. Its never explained. Units have lines of sight you cant manage without a minor in abstract trigonometry. You'll routinely lose units to hostile recon you cant see, even with your own recon. Infantry is just a matter of how many guys you'll lose to his infantry until you give up on infantry, and then an airstrike will make sure you tell your kids to avoid the ground. AA has a tendancy to miss or annoy, rather then kill and destroy (Unless its your own aircraft). You're required to build a deck for the game, the cards being the different units you can bring in.
Is this explained? Sort of. Are there any hints and tips for it? ♥♥♥♥ no. The idea is trial and error. A trial of your patience as you make countless errors that you had no real way of foreseeing. Its a steep learning curve that lacks all forgiveness and anything on top worth climbing for.
Your basic games are broken into two types. Noob stomps or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Spam tactics work because the game cant handle fifty plus hind D's coming at you. Its the third game in the series, so there is a strong, devoted community that will spare no expenses in murdering you like a South African paralympians wife while your teammates hurl insults at you.
As of right now, the Navy is designed, built and commanded by Poseidon, Lord of the sea. Anything near the coast tastes the might of his wrath. Anything in the water is an afront to him, and thus shall be swept from his sight.
Just walk away. There is no joy to be found here. Just. walk. away.
Campaign is pretty cool, though. Sort of like a Modern Total war kinda. Maybe if you spent fifty+ hours with it in skirmish and were tutored by Clausewitz and the reanimated corpse of Scipio Africanus you'd probably pull something out of this.

This game has one of if not THE greatest destuction engines I have ever seen, and for some...that may be enought to buy the game, and it certainly is a highlight of the game, but the game has more to offer than just that. If you enjoy the Saint's Row Series you will likely enjoy this game, seeing how it uses many of the same mechanics. You are Alec Mason, and you are sent the task from your brother of leading the revolution of Mars against the evil EDF. Though made by different people, I find this game to be a lot like Just Cause 2, in a good way. Just about anything you see is destrucible, and you can shape the play of the game depending how you use your suroundings.
For an example, I was being surounded by EDF in a tall tower, I let them chase me upstairs, I placed many detonatable bombs across the building supports, after having almost every EDF troop a floor under me while I was on the top floor, I blew up the stairs stoping them from getting to me. I then jetpacked off the tower and detonated the bombs, I heard a slow creeking noise beneath me and eventully the bottom of the tower was no more, forcing the upper tower to fall down on its own weight. Things like that are what seperate this game from a "generic 3rd person shooter" and make it MUCH more.
If you ever played Battlefield 4 you will notice that this system is almost like the "levelution" events, only with those they are set cutscenes, in this game it all happens live in game, and it can be different depending what has already happened to the building.
Alltogether this is a great game and as of now it has a free weekend and is on sale for 3 bucks, I HIGHLY recommend that you buy this game, you will enjoy every moment of it.

Brothers begins with a boy named Naiee paying his respects at his mother's tombstone, who drowned at sea while he tried to save her. His elder brother, Nyaa, calls him to help their ill father to the village's doctor, who in turn tells them the only way to save him is by collecting the waters from the Tree of Life.
The adventure to save their father reminded me of Homer's The Odyssey as the character's are put into unique situations at each stunning locale which defines a level.  Going into further detail might spoil your own journey, so let it be safe to say that their is more to this game than what meets the eye.
While you may have heard that the fundamental mechanic of the game is that the two brothers are controlled with the left and right controller thumbstick and the left and right trigger respectively, how that mechanic manifests itself with different contextual situations will surprise and most likely impress you.  The game despite its simplicity is extremely fun and engaging.
This is one of my new favorite games, however, the only problem I can see for potential purchasers is that the game is short.  Also, upon completing the game, I have no interest to dive back into it.  Otherwise, I highly recommend this game.

Anyone who hates on this purely since 'X Job will cost me a fortune' or 'The gacha system is cash-grabby'... Newsflash, It's a Japanese game. A country who evolved the slot machine to add an extra random element over if you'll even get to spin the wheels each time you take a gamble.
Anyway, As a game, it's a breath of fresh air compared to most F2P role-playing games, in that the only time you'll pass anyone else on the road, they're not out to attack you or steal your kills. They're just another Warrior Of Light walking the seemingly endless road to attempt to make sense of a vague Prophecy that practically no-one has a real idea of how it will be resolved.
In this age of PvP and kill-stealing, where the 'best' players are the guys who have power-levelled themselves off the bloodied backs of the rest of the game's player base, Mobius Final Fantasy is a humorous and fun parody of the whole nature of the role-playing game... in that you begin being told that your role is the Hero, and constantly go 'Sure, But WHY?', with even the initally helpful Vox going silent after a bit, replaced by Echo, a literal exposition fairy who is just as fond of lampshade hanging the tropes of your situation as your character is.
The best piece of advice with it, though, is to turn Auto Battle on at the earliest opportunity, and have a good book available. You'll get more done that way, since the Auto Battle is a better player than most people.

At its current stage in devlopment, Parkitect is a very promising theme park game.
It is very similar to the Rollercoaster Tycoon(RCT) series of games, it feels like a hybrid between RCT2 and RCT3, taking the best bits from both.
The rollercoaster editor/creator in this game is brilliant, it works like the one in the RCT games but has additional features such as the ability to change the size of a track piece.
Because the coaster editor is similar to RCT it means you can't make exact replicas of real coasters but you can get really close with the help of the new additions.
The scenery/decoration editor is solid and very easy to use, just like in RCT2.
The animations on flat rides are absolutely gorgeous, they are realistic and so smooth.
The graphics are what you expect for this sort of game, they are vibrant and simple.
The interface to this game is very simple and looks nice and sleek.
The current selection of available attractions is small but the attractions that are available are fantastically made and look as good as they can.
Now on to the less than great things (All of which will most likely go away as the game is developed):
Not enough attractions, there needs to be more content to make a full sized park.
Not enough coaster types, again there needs to be more coasters.
No career/scenarios, currently there is only sandbox.
(really nitpicky) Not stable, obviously with the game being in alpha the game isn't that stable, if your park becomes large and popular, there will be lag.
So all in all this game is currently pretty good and so long as the devs don't do what most Early Access devs do it'll turn in to a legendary game.
Now stop faffing around reading reviews and go buy it.

First of all: Don't buy this game yet if you expect a finished or bug-free product. It's in Alpha state so it's neither feature complete nor bug-free.
This said, the game is well playable for a couple of hours or even a lot more, depending on what parts of the gameplay you emphasize. There's no game-breaking bugs I've encountered or any crashes I've had, just minor stuff like visitors walking through objects or walls or a mechanic stuck in a door.
(I strongly recommend to get the free cam mod from parkitectnexus to replace the isometric perspective with a free-floating camera. This helps immensely when building objects and is overall more fun and looks better.)
You can already:
- build giant rollercoasters of all kinds
- ride those rollercoasters, thanks to a mod
- custom build houses, which your visitors can enter and you can place attractions, food stands or whatever you want in. Base game does not offer the variety of Planet Coaster yet though.
- build a nice variety of attractions, however they're somewhat limited and a park the size of the quarter of the map will likely contain all of them.
- terraform the map to your liking
- download countless mods, custom buildings, new themes, maps via
and Steam Workshop
- report bugs you find on the forums
what you can't:
-get your hand held: there's no tutorial, no tooltips. However everything is pretty selfexplanatory imo, all information is visualized somehow. You need spacebar to turn objects and controls for the camera, for everything else there's a button in the UI
- build large parks as the engine isn't optimised and will run into performance issues when zooming out with parks bigger than a quarter of the current map size (means around 700-800 visitors at once, I guess this takes 3-5 hours to achieve)
technically you can build bigger parks of course but to run smoothly you can't zoom the camera out too much.
- manage your park: you can hire personel but that's about it, I think you don't have to pay them yet and can't create zones to assign them to yet (correct me if I'm wrong though, there's a button to assign them to zones, but I can't figure out how to create them)
there's no financial challenge, the park will make plus no matter what. If you lack money, just speed up the game and wait
So, the conclusion: If you're the creative type and just want a sandbox to build the rollercoasters and amusement parks of your dreams I figure there's already dozens of hours of fun in this. If you expect a lot to manage, any scenarios to accomplish or great challenges then you might wanna pass out on this for the time being (but keep an eye on it!)
It's very early days for me so far, however I'm loving this game. It's the spiritual successor to RCT2 and I couldn't be happier with that!

tl;dr: If you like DC comics or superheroes, run through the Free Trial (Free-to-Play isn't the right term, imo). If you enjoy it, try a subscription for a month at $15. If you want the full game for free more like Tera or Blade and Soul, or if you want mostly PvP, you'll be disappointed.
I've spent a lot ot time in this game, in fact downloaded it from Daybreak directly so that Steam would stop keeping track of my hours played. So, I'm going to give my two cents on the game finally.
First, the Free-to-Play system. It's really more of a free trial, in my opinion. In some ways, levelling up to 30 is the prologue of the game. It gives you a good feel for the world and the storytelling, but more importantly, it shows you the basics of the mechanics. The maximum level is 30, but after that you raise your Challenge Rating (CR) with gear from instances. This content comes in tiers, and anything beyond tier 2 is going to be exceptionally difficult to impossible for a F2P player.
So, if you want to continue, you can start another character to try different movement modes and powers, or you can pay money to play. If the concept of Pay-to-Play bothers you, then this game will disappoint you for sure. I've seen reviews on here call the game Pay-to-Win, but I very much disagree. There may be an element of P2W at the edge of the highest levels of the game, but you're already likely a "whale" by that point anyhow.
You have two options when it comes to paying for content: piecemeal or subscription. Some people swear by the piecemeal method, but I can only see it as beneficial if you aren't a frequent player. I believe that if you want to really experience the game, shell out the $15 for a month of the subscription. It gives you access to all the content, basically everything you can buy for cash other than cosmetics and utility items.
One of my favorite things about the game is the variety of content types. 1-man, 2-man, 4-man, and 8-man instances, open-ish world content, and collections to find. Putting together your own customized costume is a fun, since your equipment doesn't at all dictate your appearance. You gain new costume styles by finding equipment, and there is a lot to find. Other than the major DC characters, including Kevin Conroy as Batman, Mark Hamill as Joker, and Susan Steinberg as Wonder Woman, the voice acting is hit or miss. Wonder Girl still makes me cringe.
Hardcore players complain about the lack of content, but I disagree totally. DCUO has more consistently put out new content than any other MMO I can think of. The mechanics of the game have evolved over time as well. The recent overhaul was a huge undertaking, and had a lot of player input--and it was actually listened to and implemented.
The game is getting older, and the graphics are starting to show it. It's not unplayable by any means, but it is something that bears mentioning. Because the game's megaserver is cross platorm between PC, PS4 and PS3, the graphics are pushed as far as they can go.
I'm not much of a PvPer, but the state of PvP in the game isn't great as I understand it. Regardless of that, being able to choose between your character and unlockable Iconic characters is enjoyable even for me. You have the option of using in-game currency earned through PvP or actual cash to buy the characters. These characters are one of the things that you don't automatically get for having a membership.

If you are a fan of even just one character like Superman, Batman or the Flash for instance, it is definitely a worth while, the flaws are there like you have to pay to get more content but it is reaaallllllyyyy fun to just fool around with and play with friends, the mission sometimes gets a bit too hard but other than that it is pretty good, 4.5 stars

Wargame Red Dragon is simply one of the best Real Time Stratigy games I have ever played. However I can tell you that it is not for all RTS players. If you like building  your massive inpenrtable bace, defened by automated turrets. Sorry but there isn't any bace building in this game. If you like having one or two sets of units wipe entire forces ten or twelve times as numerous. Again that isn't possable, because just like in real life one can only carry so much ammo and once it is out you have to go get more. Also with tanks, trucks, helicopters and transports having limited range and use up their fuel supplies that is also something you have to keep an eye on.
However even if you are put off by all of that added "realisem" (remember it's a game, not a simulation so somethings aren't all that true to real life like the scale of maps and ranges of weapons for example) I would recomend you try it. If you are good at micormangement or macromanagement then this game will have a place for you. The single player campains are well scripted and interesting to play, although I would say that the AI could use some work when it comes to attacking/defending with singular type forces.
As for multiplayer some people are amazingly good, however it doesn't take too long to become good enough to enjoy the game while being able to help your team. But as with every multiplayer game if you end up on a team (should you want to play on a team as you can do 1v1 if you desire) who has rocks for brains where as you are playing against some fivestar armchair geneails don't worry if you cannot carry the entire match. Also many of the very good players have reliced theory guides or have posted youtube videos showcasing what they do to win matches and generaily if you watch the replay of a game you lost or won you can usualy come up with the reasons why that happened. Which is one of the best features of this game in my mind, if you loose horably because of a break through attack on one flank that you weren't watching close enough or the player in that sector was unable to defete it you can see why they were able to beat you
If you are sold now, please note that the game curently has some flaws, for example some nations do not have any upgraded infentry, where as most of the others have a basic pre 1980 form of infentry than a upgraded infentry from 1985 or 1990 with better eqipment and access to more advanced transports. However it has been confermed by the developers that some of the first DLC (which would suprise me if it cost you anything) releases will address this problem.
That last paragraph has been mostly delt with, with the release of The Milionth Mile most (but not all) of the nations have had an infentry upgrade option added. Also added were land based anti ship missile systems.
