Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons seems to have been developed by a group that saw Bambi and wanted to reinvoke the feelings of seeing Bambi's mother getting shot about five times during the course of their game. The mechanics of the game are the most compelling part of this game, where your control of the two brothers is mapped to half of the controller per-brother. Having the two brothers work in tandem can feel a bit awkward at first, much like the brothers' interactions, but when you get the two of them to do to interactions at the same time it feels about as good as patting your stomach and rubbing your head at the same time. The puzzles unfortunately aren't very deep making the game just feel like an elaborate walk. The story, told essentially in pantomime since the language is made up (so far as I can tell), is mostly random and pulls cheap tricks for emotional value. The world is pretty nice to look at and is set in a nordic land full of moutains, trolls, and giants, but there is little context for what you're exploring other than you're on a quest to find the world tree in order to save your father from his illness. One would think that this quest would leave little time for dawdleing but the tone of the brothers interactions and encounters, particularly with the girl late in the game, seem disjoint from the task at hand.
The bottom line is this game tries hard to make you care, but it does so in contrived ways. Grieving over a death and the inevitability of death are nice themes to explore, but when the game decides to increase the impact of a character dieing by playing fun and adventerous music right before rollercoasting into the character's demise, the methodology of trying to pull at the player's heartstrings feels cheap.

As has been said, it's an innovative single-player-coop that's simultaneously fairly simple and lots of fun.  It's also ultra-scenic and not coy about it at all.  (There are benches all over where you can sit your characters down and observe the nicely-rendered scenery).
So far I've played my first session _without_ a gamepad (uses arrow keys and aswd), and only ran in to two places where my keyboard failed to register the required simultaneous presses.  So while it says you _must_ have a gamepad, this isn't strictly true.

The game does resort to recycling models from XI, XII, LR and XIV but the game still feels like its own world and I applaud it for that.

It's worth picking up if you're a fan of Final Fantasy and have a soft spot for the legacy games.

tl;dr - Craft the World is a well-put-together game with lots to do and many ways to play. You may get very frustrated with it, though, depending on your preferred style of play.
I'm not fond of playing castle defense games, probably because I get easily flustered under time pressure. When I first tried the campaign in Craft the World, I nearly deleted it in frustration: the waves of enemies never gave me enough time to learn how to play the game.
Luckily, you can control the difficulty (and number of waves) in a sandbox game. So for those who are more casual players, who like to dig deep into how a game works, or who aren't used to castle defense games, Craft the World still has lots of fun to offer.
The developers have put a lot of effort into the game: the graphics, sound, and music are polished, the monsters are interesting and varied, the items/recipes are extensive (and frequently even logical), and they've clearly devoted a lot of time to the dwarf AI.
The dwarf AI quality is mixed: On the one hand, the dwarves have some stupid behaviors, and don't handle large amounts of commands well. On the other hand, when I took the time to learn the ins and outs of how they act, I found their behavior predictable, and could usually find a game mechanic that would allow me to control the behaviors I didn't want.

This  game is fun. I missed all the "extreme" sports games that the consoles used to have. Games like 1080 Avalanche and Tony Hawk Pro Skater always had a nice mix of sick tricks and groovy clothing options that always allowed for a fun time. This game has both and its doing it in the right direction.
For start, this game is in early access and there are plenty of bugs. With this aside, the dev team is working hard to make the gameplay mechanics, such as the actual movement and physics, extremely polished. As of right now, the skiing elements feel as they should.
You are now wondering, "hey bruh, wut bout my snowboard?! I want to be the next Dion Blaster....errr Ricky Winterboard...." As of right now the devs are currently working on the skiing mechanics alone; focusing all their efforts before transitioning to snowboards. While this may seem upsetting, I will remphasize that the skiis are nicely done. This aspect should not deter you from giving this game a try.
The game itself is centered around a few areas and one giant mountain that people can skii around. This I feel is the best aspect of the game. Every location feels new.  Any path you travel lacks the strategically placed fallen tree or mountain face that forces you to go in any given direction. While there are paths to follow, there is nothing stopping you from carving your own trail.
The game itself looks awsome too. I dont know how hard it was to paint a mountain white, but it is incredibly satisfying to look around while skiing. With this in mind, The dev team is supporting the occulus rift, which is a step in the right direction. I often put myself in first person mood to get a better immersion while going down the mountainside and the rift will probably provide a better experience.
I guess the only "downside" to this game, which isnt really a bad thing, is that this game will be F2P. The game will charge the players for buying different clothing. Who are they to tell me that I have to wear clothes..... pff!
This will be a more mature version of the "extreme" sports I used to enjoy on the consoles. Knowing this, I cant wait to take all the skill I learned in SNOW and apply it to real skiing.....

Giving Train Simulator 2014 the thumbs down is a difficult decision, but I'll explain why I feel I am compelled to do so.
I first purchased TS2014 when it was TS2013 / Railworks 3. TS2014 is essentially an updated version of last year's game with a new menu interface and some minor patches. The same routes available prior to the conversion are compatible with the current version.
First, I'll evaluate TS2014 as a game. Graphically, it is probably one of the best looking simulators in the genre, and while the visuals are not cutting edge by any sort, they adequately represent the locomotives, rolling stock, and scenery. Some locations and trains are impeccably detailed and create wonderful scenic panoramas; others are nothing special, but still pleasing, while some models and locales are devoid of details, incomplete, or just plain ugly. Some graphical bugs present themselves, usually missing or clipping textures, but this is largely dependent on the route or locomotive. Certain assets are far more polished than others. Sounds are overall nothing spectacular. They work for the most part, and some locomotives are equipped with awesome sound packs, replete with CB radio voiceovers, the hum of the engines, and great horns and bells. Unfortunately, other trains were not given the same treatment, and sounding the horn is an anticlimactic experience when the sound is muffled or lacks an echo, and instead cuts off the second the key is depressed. Much like visual detail, quality varies with sound and is dependent on the developer of a given asset.
Gameplay is fairly standard for a train simulator; there are no interesting new features or design quirks, and let's be honest, I didn't expect there to be. The standard by which simulators are judged the most is realism, and by and large TS2014 provides a fairly realistic experience. Steam locomotives, as expected, scale in difficulty compared to their diesel and electric counterparts. You are expected to obey signalling and dispatcher orders and are penalized harshly for failing to heed these warnings. Points are awarded for timeliness and subtracted for recklessness and tardiness. There is enough challenge in most scenarios to keep you on your toes; of course, you can free drive, disable all the realism settings, and run the game like MLG PRO EXTREME TRAINZ SIM 420 and surf on rails if you wish.
With all being said, Train Simulator 2014 is a decent game. It looks nice and will engage players who are interested in railroading and simulators in general. However, it is a terrible value, and I hope to illustrate why.
In the Standard Edition, which retails for 39.99 USD, you get the game itself plus three routes (the specific routes have changed since when I purchased the game). These routes range anywhere from a few dozen km (15-20 miles or so) to 300+ km (180+ miles) and provide usually no more than 3 trainsets (some are generous enough to give you 4 or 5) along with anywhere from 5 to 12 scenarios, on average. You're paying a bit over 13 dollars per route in addition to the base game. Fair enough. Where Dovetail Games (formerly
Ltd.) will suck you dry is through the numerous DLC available for the game, and I would consider Dovetail one of the, if not
absolute
offenders on Steam in the practice of pumping out overpriced and underwhelming DLC.
Consider that the typical price of a new route add-on is 39.99 USD. I bought the base game and three routes for that same price. What justifies a ludicrous markup of over 200% on additional routes, when some are smaller or less detailed than those included with the game? Moving on to locomotives, you can purchase the Amtrak California Zephyr F40PH (a common diesel found on North American railroads) for 19.99. It comes with
livery and a few missions for a DLC that, thankfully, is now included in the base game, but at one time was a separate purchase. Even more pathetic is the attempt to sell the BR Class J74 tank engine for 7.99 with a few scenarios. But the most egregious example of how bad TS2014's DLCs can get is the listing on
for a silver livery for the PRR GG1 locomotive for 4.99. Yes, for 5 dollars, you can be the proud owner of
Locomotive not included. This is absurd.
I understand that a lot of content in this game is developed by third parties, and that they need to be paid for their hard work. Yet the price gouging set in place by Dovetail can hardly be justified, especially when the developer's quality control team has a history of overlooking minor and not-so-minor bugs in the DLC they allow to be published, resulting in a wide variation in the quality of the addons. Do they want their game to have a reputation for uncertainty? The exhorbitant prices combined with the developer's curt attitude to criticism by the fanbase drives potential players away and hurts the rating of what otherwise is a decent simulation. The Steam Workshop and the intensely devoted railfan community have the potential to improve this game by leaps and bounds if the developers understood that mod friendliness and accessibility can only help their product.
If you are a railfan and value your money, just go and build a model railway. You will meet more people, gain more useful skills, and enjoy the experience much more than if you buy this game and the accompanying DLC. After all, the cost of all the DLC combined could finance a fairly large-sized model railroad. Besides, you will have more creativity at your hands and create more lifelong memories with that than by investing that money into Train Simulator 2014.

, and there were several points where I thought the act of actually progressing through a level was too difficult to be worth it, but we pressed on and eventually managed to beat the game.
Outland succeeds at introducing a mechanic (the color swapping) and fully realizing that mechanic as the game progresses, using it for everything.  Colors can control which traps are active, enemies you can attack, platforms you can stand on, switches you can activate, etc.  I don't normally see games fully-realize their particular unique gimmick as well as Outland manages to do, and this is the primary reason I give the game a thumbs up on the Steam review system.  One downside I will mention, however, is that the game can become too much of a mess of colors, making it difficult and frustrating to navigate the visual overload on screen.
Here are some of my thoughts I recorded while I played this game cooperative with a friend:
- Difficulty slowly ramps up as you gain new abilities, ultimately getting to the point where it is brutally difficult, but not impossibly so.
- Controls feel sluggish, making the game much more difficult than it needs to be.
- Boss fights are challenging, and the final boss is ridiculous.  Figuring out how to beat the first four bosses is actually pretty fun, but that last boss was a pain.
- Coins and collectibles are not shared.  I can understand for the coins, but the collectibles?  That's stupid.  You'd have to play through the game twice for each player to collect the secrets.
- There are some really good multiplayer puzzles, but then there are also several really terrible multiplayer puzzles.  Platforming elements that require both players to synchronize their movements and swap between light and dark simultaneously are really not fun to complete.  Other puzzles were poorly designed such that one player could just stand safely aside as one color to keep platforms activated while the other player could perform the platforming elements, then swap.
- The metroidvania aspects are annoying.  Things you can't reach are constantly flaunted in your face rather than slowly discovered.  There is never a reason to backtrack whenever you get the new ability unless you want to grab the pointless collectible that was hidden just out of reach earlier in the game.  I'd rather see the game actually reuse the map rather than arbitrarily increase game time.  You can beat the entire game without ever once returning to an area you cleared previously.
- Hurray, a checkpoint!  Now let's kill ourselves so we regain full health.  Seriously... this was our strategy to beat the game.  You regain full health whenever you restart from a checkpoint, so there really isn't a reason not to die and start with full health.
- Patience is a virtue, the absence of which will surely result in death.  Not recommended for those that are easily frustrated.
- The story is pointless.

Firstly, i found the UI to be either merely acceptable at best and cumbersome at worst on the PC. Why make me click and drag to craft things for the first time? It feels like an attempt to copy similar mechanics from similar games, but here it feels much more forced.
Secondly, controlling the dwarves is extremely frustrating, as there is no way to assign particular dwarves to particular tasks or particular types of work. Designate an area to get tunneled out and it's anyone's guess which dwarf will actually get started on it. Have an enemy at the door no one's paying attention to? Well, you could click on it to tell your dwarves to attack it, but then everyone nearby will drop whatever they're doing (or carrying) and run over to attack it.
Lastly, the portals feel like a failed attempt at applying some pressure to the player. In the beginning they're not bad and maybe even a bit fun in that i get to watch my dwarves beat up some undead, but eventually they're simply something that i have to sit through for several minutes so that i can get back to business.
So why have i played it so much? Because i bought it and sometimes it
scratches a particular itch i have. That and my kids enjoy it.
But, overall, whenever i play it i just wish it were better.

This game is so addictive! I would describe it as a mix between Terraria and Dwarves. Instead of doing anything directly, you tell your minions to do the deed and they take care of it. It then turns into a base defense game when monsters attack because their goal is to destroy your base and kill the dwarves. You have to plan on how best to defend and prepare for increasingly difficult waves of them which are nicely spaced to give you a chance to rebuild and upgrade between each wave. I find myself upgrading weapons and building towers to help the dwarves.
There are definitely some boring points in the game but they are few and far between. Namely the beginning when you only control a few dwarves, as things progress slowly, especially if you give them too many instructions at once. You can easily find yourself waiting a few minutes just for one thing to be finished. Later on, when you have additional dwarves this becomes less of an issue as there are more hands to accomplish each task more quickly.

An amazing game with an amazing engine for the physics and destruction. The game pulls you in with the amazing destruction concepts and keeps you there with the intriguing storyline. A definite great game even if you haven't played the predecessors (Red Faction and Red Faction II).

The destruction aspect of the game is a bit outdated in year 2015. After completing the game, I still don't have idea about when the buildings collapse. Sometimes the illusion of correct physics of constructions works great, but more often the player regressess just destroying every wall of the building for roof to come down. There are extremely satisfying moments when for example a tall industrial chimney falls over some building complex and destroys everything in its path but for nine times out of ten it falls wrong way because of the limitations and compromisses of the year 2009 physics engine. The main defect of physics of the game today are that those don't allow precise planning of the collateral damage. Don't get me wrong, the physics of the game are a programming masterpiece of its time but they would benefit very much if brought up to date. If anyone remembers the hype Deus Ex human Revolution had about ITS destructable walls two years later than Guerilla was published, that person will surely understand the irony and the degree of the feat Guerilla achieved.
The game itself is third person openworld and resembles Just Cause 2 without green lens filter. Albeit JC2 is larger and has much more content, Red Faction Guerilla outclasses it in aspect of interracting with environment. Practically every construction is destructable and it isn't just on/off thing where there is a building or not. Sometimes driving through the areas (or buildings) player might encounter buildings missing walls or structures where there is some gaping hole (Oh that's where I shot my rocket launcher two hours earlier!).
Red Faction Guerilla was a trailblazer of the openworld games, that nobody followed... for all disadvantage of the players.

It's one of the top of the genre, if not, the top of the Snow games genre. Excellent graphics, lots of maps which are very large, especially the Mountain which has more than 10 spawn points all in different areas, with each one having so much to explore than the others. You can be a pumkin head with epic shoes doing a backflip just to land it perfectly and - just in time - take a screenshot. The optimization might not be the best, so I just put it onto medium-ish settings. And I'm telling you that if I can run Titanfall on medium, I should be able to run this on high! Wait... look at that snow, all these textures! It's so good looking! Nevermind then, if you take a closer look SNOW is very strong in the category of Graphics.

It's a beautiful game, very impressive for a game which costs this little. You might say to yourself "Heh, that's nothing. Have you Seen GTA V?" and to that I said that I have seen it and played both games, SNOW and GTA V. GTA V is a costly game which is a finished release with some updates. SNOW is a cheaper game in earlier developement with way more snow. It's just very nice to see that you can change time ingame. I love to set it to sunrise. All those pinkish colors on the snow, those brighter shadows. It looks almost like a film or as if I'm an actual Skieer with a camera strapped to a flying bot following me. An easy 9/10.
The sounds remind me of the Skate series. Skate is about skating, SNOW is about skiing. Both have magnificent sounds about their genres. The snow sounds realistic as if I'm cutting it up, which I sort of am in the game. The music is excellent, just, one of the best soundtracks, Burnout Paradise in front of SNOW by only a few points. The sounds are very high quality. A simple 8/10 for sounds.
You can pay for cosmetic items. since I have recieved the Starter Edition from the kind developers, I do not know if you start with any ingame credits.  Anyway, there's definitely quite a bit over 100 items in total that you can purchase. The average itme is around 50-70 credits. Some items cost a bit more (up to 200 from what I have seen). So you could buy a lot, trust me on this. I got an epic Pumkin Hat for very cheap. It looks awesome. You can get more credits by using real-life money.
Pros:
Excellent graphics
Cheap for such a good game
Item pricing is low enough to buy a ton for little
Updates are not too rare
Sounds are very impressive
Cons:
Not the best optimization

This Game Saved My Life.
Through many years of abuse and drug addiction, I was about to end it all. Then as I sat there on top of that bridge that day, I stared off into space and there it was. A copy of TS2014 Floating in the air. I wasn't sure if it was real. I grabbed it and opened the package. I peed myself. I ran to the homeless shelter and played this for days on the only computer. At first, I told everybody I knew about this game, including Ronald the Crackhead and Serg, the former KGB spy who slept in the bunk above me. Then one day, my copy went missing. I was devistated, and in an enraged state I ran to the nearest subway station and hijacked the train. Pleas from the command station told me to stop the train, but from my experience I knew exactly what to do. I followed all speed limits and lights, which I knew of there location from the Hamburg-Hanover Route Add On DLC. Then the train came to a sudden halt and all the lights went off. There was a knock at the door. I yelled, "Who is there?". My heart pumped faster than a LNER Class A4 4468 Mallard. The door opened. The men standing in front of me seemed familiar, and soon I realized it was Ronald and Serg, holding my copy of TS2014. I yelled, "Why would you do this to me?". Serg chuckled. "I thought you might me startled. I am afraid to tell you that I must kill you now, to cover up the fact that I stole your copy of TS2014.". It was over. All over. Then all of the sudden, when my eyes were closed, I heard a gunshot, but to my surprise I was uninjured. I looked up to see Surg's limp body infront of me. "Run." Said Ronald. I was shocked. As I stumbled out of the R160A. "Thanks, man." I muttered to Ronald. From that point on, every day, I have been playing TS2014 In rememberance of that day.
Overall, the graphics and the gameplay go hand in hand, but the configuration of the controls is a bit tricky. 9/10 Would Recomend

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons opens and closes with death. It’s a game about death. But it isn’t a game about killing. What is between the opening and closing scenes is a dark fairytale world full of mature themes, and the bond of two siblings as they struggle valiantly on a quest to save their withering father. A beautiful and melancholic journey awaits you, and a deep emotional investment will be required. And though brief, this attractive storybook adventure is as dreamlike as it is affecting.
Brothers’ appeal lies in what it doesn’t tell you. Cutscenes are used sparingly, with the world itself providing the emotional pull and story. For instance, while I was using the twin-control scheme to explore a town, I was able to steal a ball and throw it down a well, leaving a small girl in tears. The imaginary language used by the characters is universally bolstered by wonderful body language, and the affection and fears that each brother holds for the other.
The twin-control scheme is key to the game’s identity. It’s a somewhat clumsy control system, with each brother being assigned to a control stick and a shoulder button. However, Brothers’ generally requires the input of both characters, both to work together and independently, to pass obstacles. It’s a key identifying feature for the game and one that has been cleverly exploited.
The obstacles are generally rather easy, and there is only a small amount of room to experiment, with generally one rather obvious solution. The challenge comes in actually performing the actions necessary to pass. As you control both brothers at the same time, and often you need to split them up to do individual tasks, some of which can be timed, it can occasionally feel like trying to pat your head and rub your belly at once. Something that for most of us, we are certainly capable, but it does require a different type of input than we would normally use.
And these siblings will certainly have you wringing your hands. Sometimes over the controls, but mostly over their relationship with each other, and in turn, your relationship with them. The epic undertaking they’re on will have them trek over snow-capped mountains, across frozen lakes and an ancient giant’s battlefield – it’s a wonderfully realised world without exposition – it exists and feels real. The settings are as varied as the tasks required of the brothers, and the emotional pull of the game will have you powering on to see what happens next. This is not a game to be played in short stretches, and at just over 3 hours in my playthrough, I completed it in just two sittings.
The dark undercurrent of death in this world is never confrontational, it seeps into every pore of the game, and can even be missed. Shortly after leaving a small village, I passed a man attempting to hang himself. Using one brother to prop him up, and another to cut the rope, I left him sitting beneath the tree to sob like a man who had nothing left. Further ahead I found a burnt out homestead, and with the brothers working in tandem, I was able to retrieve a small music-box which seemed to help the man. This sentimental scene is one of many throughout Brothers’ that outright dealt with death in a mature and intelligent fashion, an unusual but fascinating design decision by the developers.
I suppose you could say that the true aim of Brothers’ is to make us feel. Of course, there is the adventure, and the smartly designed environmental obstacles, but this is a game where touch isn’t just an afterthought, and death has some permanence, and has some resonance. And while it’s brief, Brothers’ doesn’t outstay it’s welcome, and provides an ambitious, emotionally affecting adventure that while short, is very sweet. Memorable.

This game basically is a modern, more flexible version of RCT2. If you've liked designing and building nice sandbox parks for hours and your PC cannot handle more demanding 3D-games, this definitely is for you! A game for designers, architects, coaster-enthusiasts and - hopefully soon - tycoons!
I played RCT1&2 since 2002 and used it mostly as a creative tool for building nice theme parks, so I very early found out about this game as it is very close to the first two installments of the series and thus bought the pre-alpha.
First I didn't like the graphics and the perspective of the game, but I grew fond of them because they optimized them and added color filters to tone down the bright hues. And the view is more optimized and mods even add first person functions as well (always wanted to walk around parks in RCT2). There are still some graphic glitches (also due to being able to build so freely) but I'm sure they will be resolved.
The grid-based building process is very similar to RCT, but has a lot more freedom because you can overlay multiple objects/walls and place objects like trees, rocks and decorations outside the grid as well.
Coaster building is an extended version of the original RCT coaster builder and allows much smoother transitions and banking of the tracks.
The vanilla rides and objects are sufficient to build nice parks. There are no official coaster or ride brands in the game, but you can easily get the inspirations.
The simulation so far works quite well, I had no trouble with the guests or staff so far. I really like the feature of the delivery and the added staff-only paths and staff rooms - something that was missing from RCT. The coasters and rides run smoothly and I love how the graphs for ride intensity/speed or the guests are presented.
The menus are sometimes a bit confusing, as I found out about features only by asking about them on Reddit, so there's a bit work left to do there. But navigating in them is easy and the search object function is a plus. Cannot say much about the sound, as I'm mostly playing on mute anyways.
The workshop feature and Parkitect Nexus now are somehow split, so I hope this will get resolved somehow as there are some great custom objects, parks and mods like onride or first person camera available over there already.
For me sometimes there is not enough costumization, which I hope will be added later, especially on the outskirts of parks (parking lots, roads, hotels and a customizable entrance building).
I liked giving feedback to this project, as I have the feeling the creators (who might be overwhelmed due to the Steam release now) listen and improve the game continuously.

Not so much that it's so easy you can build anything you want all the time, but enough that it doesn't take an hour of doing nothing to be able to afford it. Updated review: MOBIUS is a polarizing game because of past paywalls and gatcha, and I am not saying that these are OK. My vote up is because there is so much this game does right. Please do not downvote just because you are upset with the game, I respect your opinion. Here is why I recommend simply giving it a chance:
MOBIUS is a mobile game at heart. There is a stamina timer, a lottery, paid item shop, card-based deckbuilding. It has periodic updates every month and a rotating set of bosses for multiplayer, 4-on-1 PvE. With all these elements you get the negative things that come with them. So why do I recommend the game? Because of everything else it does right, especially compared to your other choices on mobile.
They have taken the original artwork from the old games, and completely re-created those designs in full 3d. Storm dragon, Demon wall, cockatrice, ultros, even gilgamesh! Remixed classics from the 2d games in digital and orchestrated versions. Rebuilt classic environments in full HD 3D like midgar. The attention to detail is nothing short of spectacular. It is a joy to behold. The story takes the classic warrior of light trope and gives it a new spin with a cynical protagonist who questions the meaning of fulfilling his destiny. It's enough to be fresh and nod to the classics at the same time.
The battle system is a lot of fun. True turn based battles we have missed for years (enemies don't move until after you do). Deck building involves strategy, and not only that, you can customize your classes now with skill panels using another in-game lottery called skill coins. This costs no money, it just requires random drops or multiplayer grinding to get the currency. You can pull off some amazing stuff with some hard work. On top of that is weapon boosting. This system allows you to take any weapon in the game and increase its stats. The catch is it requires lots of skillseeds and time - sometimes days - but this timer is chipped away by the stamina you spend in game. The more you play, the faster it finishes. You can unlock some game-changing passives that can really up your firepower. This can make big difference in your build.
Let me now address two major complaints many have posted about this game. First, people hate the random luck of gatcha, or summon lottery, that requires magicite, the currency that you can either get by waiting (fills up on timer) or by paying for. Look, all mobile games have this system, and people are paying for it, so it's not going away. I don't like it either, but I have learned to deal with it. Do your homework: Read user communities, like reddit or discord. Plan ahead. Wait for mercy draws which guarantee a new card or rarity. Don't pull expecting to hit a 0.8% ultimate. That's crazy. And you don't need the ultimates to win, anyway. There is an in-game shop where they release later abilities you can buy with ability tickets, given away all the time as daily rewards or event items. The catch is they require growstars to augment, and these are rarer for the f2p (about 4/month if you buy the mobius box - which you should, always, with the free magicite you're given). Again - careful planning on what to upgrade is vital to spend your precious items.
The second major complaint has to do with the jobs. This is slightly different than regular gatcha so let me explain: When you draw you have a 10% chance of pulling a new class. Legends are even harder to pull, like ultimate cards. When they were first introduced, people raged about 75$ spending requirement to get the job (it was given with purchase). This is no longer - they have been added to the regular job pull, and we even now have a 8th pull job card guarantee. But it's still very hard to get these jobs. And the less you pull, and more jobs added, the harder it is to get the job you want or need since it's all up to luck. These are legitimate concerns. So you have to be flexible and play with the hand you're dealt. If you are dead set on a specific role, it's hard to say that you'll be able to maintain it since everything is thrown into the same pot.
So with all that in mind, do I recommend this game? Yes, I do. If you are an FF fan, I don't think you'll be disappointed. If you absolutely despise grinding and mobile lottery, it might rub you the wrong way. Either way, see for yourself. I'm glad I did.

Hey guys. Out of all the games on steam this is a hidden **gem** that has consumed hours of my time. You basically start out on a small map and your objective is to dig down into the earth to find a portal that allows you to unlock the next world. Currently the second world is a medium sized map and it takes place in a winter themed world. There are a couple of unique creatures that live in each world that act different ways which I think is nice because at least the devs aren't simply "reskinning" all the textures.
Alright, I'm going off on a tangent but I'm all about the details. I'm the type of person that thinks there should be tons of customization in every game and in this one in particular I wish there was more of a variety in enemy types. There are quiet a few monsters that come out at night but I want more. I'm picky like that. Ok, now you can't just dig down into the earth and expect to find the portal and unlock the next world. First of all it's guarded by a giant zomboid creature that's all armored up that wields a giant sword. You need to have a large population of like 10 dwarves all equipped with higher tier gear, like silver or above. There are two tiers of armor above silver and like 3 below silver. Just so that you have an idea of what climbing the tech tree is like. When you're climbing the tech tree and crafting everything you have to keep in mind that it takes time to gather all of the resources you need. But you're not just crafting armor. You're required to craft everything from decorations, stone working, weaving, fishing gear, iron working etc...
That brings me to the next topic. You don't only have to dig and harvest materials from the world but you also have to craft at the beginning and bottom of the tech tree. So just because you were super lucky to have found silver ore somehow whether it be from monster drops or mining - you can't simply craft yourself a bunch of higher tier armor. You have to craft everything in the tech tree until you gain enough experience. It keeps track of how much experience and parts of the tech tree unlock as you progrerss through. Thus giving you a steady pace to the game preventing you from cheesing the system. The pacing is nice. It is fun. The only problem I have is that once you spend hours and hours crafting an elaborate castle with a basement that goes down beneath the earth to a wine cellar then when you move to the next level it's like it was all for naught.
But I mean you can save and re-visit the world again. But the purpose is to advance through the tech tree, survive the monsters in the night and not allow your dwarves to starve to death. When your population grows enough and you have high tier armor and weapons then it's time to tackle the giant zomboid wielding the giant sword. But just because you make it to the portal doesn't mean you advance to the next level. You have to continue mining through the earth to find the hidden "rooms" and each one has a giant in it that you have to slay to get a portal piece recipe. After you find 5 of them and craft all 5 then you move to the next level. Each level from the looks of it get a little more difficult.
The multiplayer is so much fun. I'm too chicken to have tried the PvP mode but I'm sure it's a blast. The Co-op mode is super fun but we need to be able to TALK TO EACH OTHER!!! Or simply leave messages for the other person to read in the world. Shouldn't be too hard to add the capability to put a little sign down in the world that says whatever you want it to so at least you could  communicate with each other that way. Or maybe it is already in the game and I didn't realize how to utilize the system but non the less the multiplayer is a fresh take and it immediately gives you a break from your single player world as well as giving you a chance to gain a ton of extra resources and loot to bring back home with you to help you climb the tech tree.

I'm quite unsure how I feel about this game.
I knew what I was getting into. I got to the point where I knocked an orange off a nightstand and then proceeded to fall about twenty minutes of progress back - and I would be fine with this since it happened about three times already. However - I have had to restart the game twice simply because I kept getting softlocked. At one point on some cardboard boxes my cauldron got locked in place and no amount of flailing my hammer or quitting and loading back in saved me. That one I did not screenshot - but - I did capture
which I flailed around trying to get out for a total of ten minutes before I just plain quit the game. Really sad to say I didn't have the experience I wanted from this game. I wanted something frustrating but fair. However the bugs aren't the only problem - the controls are... undesirable. I feel like my hammer swings fast when I hardly nudge my mouse but when I practically run it off the pad I do the saddest of hops. There's also an absolutely awful dead zone in the middle of your character that makes controlling him more of a hassle than something to learn and experiment with. The hammer doesn't have near enough friction it feels like as well. I'm not sure if this is by design but getting anywhere is just not fun when your hammer drags across the ground and bounces like jello against walls. Perhaps other people have a better time with it - I was having a good time listening to Bennett Foddy's commentary on media and how video games spoonfeed us - but I felt that the game wasn't solid enough to make a commentary with any merit. All in all - quite disappointing. But by all means - buy it if it's your kind of thing. It probably isn't though. It's a niche market. I would at least commend Foddy for trying something new but the game has been done before according to the start of the game.

Through many years of abuse and drug addiction, I was about to end it all. Then as I sat there on top of that bridge that day, I stared off into space and there it was. A copy of TS2014 Floating in the air. I wasn't sure if it was real. I grabbed it and opened the package. I peed myself. I ran to the homeless shelter and played this for days on the only computer. At first, I told everybody I knew about this game, including Ronald the Crackhead and Serg, the former KGB spy who slept in the bunk above me. Then one day, my copy went missing. I was devistated, and in an enraged state I ran to the nearest subway station and hijacked the train. Pleas from the command station told me to stop the train, but from my experience I knew exactly what to do. I followed all speed limits and lights, which I knew of there location from the Hamburg-Hanover Route Add On DLC. Then the train came to a sudden halt and all the lights went off. There was a knock at the door. I yelled, "Who is there?". My heart pumped faster than a LNER Class A4 4468 Mallard. The door opened. The men standing in front of me seemed familiar, and soon I realized it was Ronald and Serg, holding my copy of TS2014. I yelled, "Why would you do this to me?". Serg chuckled. "I thought you might me startled. I am afraid to tell you that I must kill you now, to cover up the fact that I stole your copy of TS2014.". It was over. All over. Then all of the sudden, when my eyes were closed, I heard a gunshot, but to my surprise I was uninjured. I looked up to see Surg's limp body infront of me. "Run." Said Ronald. I was shocked. As I stumbled out of the R160A. "Thanks, man." I muttered to Ronald. From that point on, every day, I have been playing TS2014 In rememberance of that day.
Overall, the graphics and the gameplay go hand in hand, but the configuration of the controls is a bit tricky. 9/10 Would Recomend

I would be able to recommend this game if we had a time machine and could travel back to 2012, which was before the company now known as Dovetail Games removed the majority of content and made it all DLC exclusive. As a result you will have to fork out massive amounts of cash in order to get your moneys worth of the full asking price of $54.99 USD.
The basic game without any DLC comes as barebones as possible and you will almost definitely be looking at which DLC you fancy within an hour or two, and of course having you to spend much more than the already ridiculous base price of $54.99 USD.
Aside from the DLC issue, there are two other blatant problems that have not been addressed by the developer. The first is the unrealistic acceleration and braking, which makes this simulator feel much more like an arcade game. The second issue is that you will be left asking where your money's worth is going with the numerous DLC you will undoubtly purchase since the developers rarely patch or update any routes or locomotives that have bugs. You will see cars driving in the air for example, alongside the road.
Since I've bought over 50 different DLC routes and locomotive packs my copy of the game actually has a decent amount of content, but since I've had to spend tenfold on this game as I have on any other; it is simply impossible to recommend it. That said, having spent hundreds of hours on this game I can say that it is enjoyable if you have an interest in trains or trainspotting.

A review for non-wargamer types, who maybe play RTS and wonder if they might like this:
W:RD has gone to great lengths to make this 3rd iteration of the series more accessible. The new filter/sorting options in the deck building screen means the new player is no longer completely overwhelmed with 50 units to choose from. The ability to compare 2 units side by side helps as well. You now get detailed information before playing a battle in the campaign. And above all, for the first time in the series you can pause or slow down the action during the battles.
On the other hand, Eugen has made the campaign game considerably more complex. In the previous game, you had battlegroups that you moved around the Risk-like campaign map. Each battlegroup was a self contained unit with a few units in each category. If a battle took place, you could be assured that your army could more or less adapt to the enemy because each battlegroup was a balanced force. W:RD now has 3 levels of 'army' that can move around the map, Your 'main armies' now are unbalanced, and need to be supported by secondary armies with specific functions. If you're not doing a deep analysis of the situation depending on the opposing armiy's composition, you're doing it wrong. This will probably lead to frustration for new players who will probably move a bunch of pawns and figure they have a big army there, only to be countered by the enemy composition.
Next, there are 1700+ units. In Starcraft, you have one Siege Tank, with specific qualities. Here, depending on the situation, you can have 5 or 6 "Siege Tanks" available, each with wildly different characteristics. Some will blow up right away. Others can take multiple hits. Some are more effective closer to the target. Some are equally effective at all ranges. Some have secondary weapons, some don't. But they all have a little tank icon on the field. And aside from 'famous' units like the M1A1 or T80, the others will be named with an arcane series of letters and numbers you've never heard of before. For a new player, this can be overwhelming.
Eugen has given up doing interactive tutorials to teach you the game, instead turning it into a manual. Did you know that it costs 2 Initiaive points to move to a new sector? And that you need at least 1 additional point to take part in any ensuing battle? This is not made clear at all by playing, only by RTFM.
W:RD is a stunning game visually. The problem is, you will prbably never look at it that way. Like most RTS, it's best played from a zoomed out point of view, and there you will see a rectangular icon that says AMX-10 RC SB bump into another rectagular icon that says T55 AM, and one or the other will eventually disappear in a tiny pinlight explosion while you are doing something else.
I still recommend this game, just because of the balls it takes to put a game like this out. It's incredibly deep, and looks great, if you ever have time to look at it, of course. So if learning the difference between a BTR-70 ZHALO and a 2515 NOROV is your cup of tea, have at it. Otherwise, I would just stick with the Siege Tank.

Originally, I had a very negative review of this game posted up here.  I was a founder of Defiance...started playing it when it very first came out, and played it all the way up until the free-to-play conversion in 2014.  I felt the game had flaws, but by and large it was entertaining and fun and I played a ton of it (my steam time is just the time I have spend playing it via steam client...I have many more hours logged in the non-steam and Xbox 360 versions).  The free-to-play conversion was, to put it very simply, a disaster.  Very fundimental, core things about the game (that would take WAY too long to explain to someone who hasn't played the game yet) were drastically changed and altered to support the new format (much heavier monetization, for example).  The biggest problem was the inclusion of a new scaling system which dynamically alters the dificulty of open world content depending on the number of players present and their respective levels.  This system worked very well originally, but was changed significantly when free-to-play started and, to make a long story short, it ruined the game for a lot of people.  I quit playing, as did a lot of other people, and figured that was pretty much the end of Defiance.    I decided to give the game another chance about 9 months later when my former clan leader was basically  begging people to come back and give it a chance and, having played it now for awhile, I have to be honest and change my negative review to a thumbs up and admit that Trion, despite some of the stupid crap they do, did indeed fix many of the crucial problems with the game from the F2P conversion.  The scaling system, while not perfect, has been greatly improved.   The monetization system (the arkforge currency needed to keep your weapons functioning at your level) has been balanced out to where the daily income you get for arkforge is plenty to keep most of your weapons up to date.  The game still has some major issues (the biggest being the limitations on how you earn some of the end-game currency), but all in all I have to admit, it is largely back to being the game it was before the F2P conversion, and the added in content is nice as well.
If you are thinking of trying this game out, I will pre-warn you however, as an old-school player....the DLC is, by and large, garbage.  The only DLC that has any significant effect on the game is Arkbreaker which allows you to participate in open world events that you cannot otherwise participate in.  The other DLC packs add very little to the game other than new vendors who run off of specific faction currency, and that's about it.  Gunslinger Trials promised a continuation of the main storyline, but that was, frankly, a bald-faced lie.  The ACTUAL continuation of the game's main single-player content has been added to the game for free (the Silicon Valley update) and does not require DLC.   The brand new (as of me writing this) additions to the game, Alcatraz Island and the new added in perks system are also in the game free of charge.  So, apart from Arkbreaker, don't bother with the DLC.

Difficult, of course, but incredibly compelling. A meditation on failure.

Parkitect is, as many other people have already said, very much a spiritual successor to the original RCT 1/2 games. I remember playing RCT for hours a decade or more ago, and Parkitect easily scratches the same itch even in early access.
Keeping in mind that it's an early access game at this point, it's true that there are things missing. But I've been along for the ride since the Kickstarter and I have to say the devs have been extremely communicative and open to community ideas. As somebody who does community management as my day job, I am incredibly impressed by the devs' responsiveness. In fact, there are several cool little things in the game that came directly from the community's ideas, such as the fact that you can connect paths to the ride entrances/exits at 90 degree angles.
And even with the current Alpha version's limitations, the game is majorly versatile. Just look at some of the great stuff in the Workshop that people have already built. Or check out the trailers and screenshots that show off some gorgeous parks.
I've already had countless hours of fun with the unfinished game—enough that it's easily been worth twice the price the devs are asking. Even better, the devs have committed to doing a monthly update during the development stage, so each month there's plenty of new stuff to try out and enjoy.
If you can't tell from all my gushing, I very highly recommend Parkitect. It's a must-buy!

Okay, let me just say this right now. If you are expecting high end graphics, dont get this.. just yet! This game surprised me. From the reviews, i thought it really was going to be like rct2 and etc. However, i was wrong. This game is completely different to rct2... in a good way though.
Parkitect has a new feature which i havent seen in any other park simulation game, stocking your shops.  In my opinion, i thought it was pretty cool. Its new and more realistic.
To break this down, here are the con's and pro's of Parkitect.
Pro's:
- different but realistic features such as shop stocking
- allows you to place a variety of rides, shops and coasters including but not limited to:
o The Haunted House(general ride) and the Suspended Monorail (transport ride)
o The Mini Coaster
o Cash Machine and Balloon Shop
- the guests in your park aern't as picky with rides like rct3 XD
- there is a large variety of terraforming, building and scenery
- the money system is not hard to manage but still provides you with a challenge to get in the greens
- the path placer and ride queue and exists are easier than ever to place
- simple and easy to learn controls once you play it for a bit
- the create a coaster tool is simple to use
- Neat and easy to use interface :D
- The rating system with rides is different to most park simulation games which although can be confusing , makes it unique in its own way (still shows the high, medium and low rating next to the numbers)
Con's-
- Guests dont have a favourite ride (Personally this has always been a favourite in park simulation games)
- no tutorial (hard to learn if you have not played many park simulation games such as the rct series)
- not much of a variety of food and drink shops
-  guests get tired really quickly, meaning there has to be alot of seating in your park for them to stay happy
- there isnt much of a night in the  game like there was in similar park simulation games (the lights dont look any different to day)
-  Barely any of the coasters have loops and corkscrews
- when creating a rollercoaster, it can be confusing seeing it run through  back to the station while designing but after ,when testing, it wont make it back to the station
- Not many seating options other than benches..,  (I would love to see tables implemented like wooden tables)
- Entertainers only have one outift and cannot be changed (only the colour can)
- glitches when a mechanic is fixing a ride ( cant get out of the exit, just freezes there)
Overall, despite my number of cons, i still strongly recommend this game to people looking for a casual, fun and enjoyable park/business simulation game. I am confident most of the cons will be fixed by the time the finished version of the game is released. :)

While Parkitect is still in early access, it's already shaping up to be a worthy successor to RCT/RCT2! I would personally advise people to hold out for awhile but if you need your curiosity satiated you will not be disappointed.
Edit: We are up to Alpha 19 and the promise of a full campaign is on the horizon. The game is worth picking up whenever it's on sale. Still recommend it!

I had my eyes on it for some time. With the 48 Hrs blow out I jumped on it. The Simulator itself seems to be a nice addition to anyone that enjoy's simulator of this kind. The in game tutorials are very nice to the newcomer, but annoying to the more experienced. Perhaps one can shut it off and I haven't found the switch yet. The menu structure can be frustrating in certain parts of the game and are in these areas really not intuitive. For example: the world editor, once in it it will take most of us a few scratches on the head until you figure out the exit sequence. Initially, I couldn't see the "Quit" button which blends almost in with the background. Also, the world editor sucks when placing objects and you wan't to fine tune those objects to others e.g. align. I gave up a few times, cursing the editor to drop dead. On the other hand I haven't dug too deep into the editor and there may be setting, hidden like the exit sequence, that I haven't found yet.
It can get costly if you are bored quickly with the stuff on hand and you want to add more content.
It seem that a tutorial for the editor is, hopefully, in the making. At first glimbs, I believe that addon content can be created using 3D, like blender, Gimp for some modeling, the to some of us know *.dds format. At this point I have no idea what can be done and what not.
All over, the simulator hasn't disappointed me, although, I had a lock up while using the editor and I ran across the documentation (all in *.pdf) by accident. It is located within the install folder.
If you like this kind of simulator, I'd say go for it before it gets back to retail pricing.

Now, to start off with, i absolutlely love playing this game. That's uderstandable right? I mean who doesn't love speeding around the streets like the flash or beating up bad guys like batman? That being said there are some positive and negative points that any starter player should know before getting invested.
*This game is outright fun to play for any geek who wants to be a hero
*it is highly replayable with multiple story archs depending on your mentor
*the create a character screen is fun to play with and make interesting characters
*the available super powers and ingame stories are fun.
*The storyline begins to get old pretty fast, with poor voice acting it makes you feel
like throwing your headphones at the wall
*most of the game is clouded with market purchases for large and micro-transactions
(ranging from new costumes to advanced storyline)

*less than half of the abilities are available to play without a membership
*any credits gained above 1500 (on standard) are in-accessable without a membership (this
means you cannot buy higher teir gear and makes it harder to advance your character)
*the membership is EXPENSIVE at appx $15 AUD per month
*all of the packs to gain access to abilities, storyline, and costumes are EXPENSIVE with the
cost for slight cosmetic changes being upwards of $5, and ability packs ranging from $50 -
$100 AUD
Overall, though i enjoy this game i must give it a negative recommendation, especially due to the fact that in order to play the whole game (currently) there is a cost of over $200 AUD in the first year alone. This game should not be classified as "free to play", it should be called "free to pay". Unless you are willing to pay an extreme amout in in-game purchases i would advise not playing or only playing this game casually.

Defiance is good overall. The gameplay is fairly intuitve for anyone who has played a FPS or MMO. Players do not "die" in this game, so there is no risk of graverobbing like some games. PvP is bv invitation only, or in special PvP maps / arenas. The world is fairly large, and quite detailed. There is no shortage of things to do at first, but as a player finishes the main missions and side mission then it becomes like a game of solitare. A lot of the same thing. Despite the tedium of doing the same things over and over to get exp, it's still entertaining. It's something to do, and occaisonally something amazing happens, like one-shotting a boss or lieutenat that used to take one used to have difficulty taking down. A major con to this game is that despite being around for 2 years or so it's still quite buggy. I will say a lot of glitches have been solved but some remain. The game does not crash as often as it did, that was usually due to overloading of the server. The main gripe I have at this time is the variable difficulty system. The game will turn up the difficulty based on the combined level of players near by. Me at EGO level 1000 is happily rampaging on a mob with threat level 4, and then some random player drives by at EGO 5000 and then the threat level goes to 10 (the max) and all enemies that spawn during that time will be extremely hard to beat by me. They need to make it so that when the level 5000 player leaves the area that the currently spawned enemies automatically derease in difficutly.
It lacks good documentation, but there are quite a lot of forums and wiki's out there to fill that need, and many of the clan's are happy to take newbies under thier wing and teach them the intracacies of the game. Overall I like the game,  Have been playing almost since the beginning.

Welcome to Craft the World: a game that has dozens and dozens of reasons to play it, and one painfully glaring reason to never buy it anyway.  It looks good, it runs smooth, it doesn't crash, and it's a charming combination of Motherload and Dwarf Fortress.  If you haven't played those games, think of it as a Minecraft RTS.  If you don't know what that is... I can't help you.
The monsters are cool, the object interactions are neat, the tech-tree is a bit obnoxious but at least it takes you in the right direction without overwhelming you all at once.  That said, I could not recommend this game under any circumstances because the AI is flat broken.  Your dwarves are beyond mentally handicapped.  Orders given are sometimes ignored, or handed off to the dwarf who is farthest from whatever it is that you're trying to do.  Occasionally your dwarves will just wander off or stand stock still and almost nothing you can do will make them budge.   They'll walk off cliffs given the slightest opportunity, if there's a group of enemies they can wander into 1v7 then they'll find it, and they'll only rarely do the jobs suited to the skills they've got.
Trying to get these little hairballs on legs to mount anything resembling an organized defense is utterly hopeless.  Often they'll ignore the first five enemies, run into the middle of them so they can attack that one zombie at the back, and then pretty much die instantly.   The only way to work around the horrible, horrible AI is to exploit the equally horrible AI of the monsters and use terrain to contain them until day break.  Or play on one of the easier modes.  Both options suck, don't do it, don't buy it, turn and run in the other direction.

The narrator has a witty, but kind retort for any and all actions you take in the game. It is totally demoralizing and anger inducing. This voice however enchants a player into wanting to continue to climb the same obstacles over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. It inserts a sense of personal challenge, and while playing I felt the need to continue, just to prove this voice wrong.
On top of this, there is a progressive narrative that unfolds as you progress throughout the game that not only sheds light on how the game came to be, but also to explain the thought process behind creating such a simple, yet elegant game.
smooth, seamless gameplay, a simple yet poweful message, somehow dated yet modern graphics, and only $7.99
How could you not pick this game up for that?

Cons:
- Forced "following" and assistance from other players. While this is the games way of helping you expand your combat options, most of the time its 4 Rock elements and 1 or 2 Friendship/Healing elements.

Major things about Defiance: It is a free to play game and Third Person Shooter
Let me get this out in the beginning of this review: Defiance is amazing+Free 2 Play! Wide variety of weapon choices, intruiging bosses, and its a show also! The money system (scrip) isn't that hard to get, and there is a good trade system between players and stores. The 5 different rarity levels go like this: White=Common, Green=Uncommon, Blue=Rare, Purple=Epic, and Orange is legendary! And if you want to edit your gun, you can! With Defiance's Salvage Matrix, you can change your weapon in a variety of ways: If the weapon has an EGO level above or below your's by 100, you can use ArkForge to level up/down any item. You can also change your gun's mods, which consist of barrel mods (ex. Power Bore ll), Magazine Mods (ex. Radiation Converter IV), Sight Mods (ex. Telescopic Sight V), and Stock Mods (ex. Close Quarters Stock I). All of these mods also have rarity levels (white, green, blue, purple, orange). Sometimes, guns don't come with all the mod slots. In order to fix this, you must have to click "Add Mods" on the Ark Salvage screen. But beware, not all mods are for the same weapons. Defiance also has a PvP system, but it can sometimes be hectic. There are Shadow Wars and Competitve Maps. The reason I personally don't do PvP is because (a) The people are VERY good and (b) The weapons and abilities can be over powered. With that out of the way, let me talk to you about the feel of the shooting. I can't really tell you the word to describe Defiance's shooting system.................aha, it's perfect! Yeah, in my opinion, The shooting in this game is great. (ex. I am using a semi-automatic sniper rifle and I shoot. I can see the bullet trail leading to were I just was. ex. I mod my current Light-Machine gun with a Inciendary Magazine; the bullet's come out red and sometimes will light enemies on fire. And if you don't care about PvP, Defiance has a very fun Multiplayer. All in all, the only thing I really don't care for in Defiance, is the slightly bad PvP and (unfortunately) not the best graphics. What I mean by this, is that when you zoom in on a other players with a scope, you will see a blurry mess. I would recommend Defiance to anyone who likes video games.

I'll start off by listing what I like about the game because there's more of that than what I don't like, but the things I don't like are fairly major and far outweigh the fun parts to the point I felt the need to not recommend it. I also have far, far more time in this game than it shows because I played for quite a while before it was added to steam, as well as playing in the alpha and beta tests.
The good:
It's an easy game to just pick up and play for an hour or so at a time, there's absolutely nothing that tries to force you to keep playing for long stretches at a time like overly long quests or time gates like a lot of MMOs have. You can log in and do a quest or a couple conflict sites, maybe an arkfall, or just run around killing random things and feel like you've accomplished something.
There's no real "builds", once you get to around 2k ego you can easily have all 4 active skills and most of the passives all maxed out. You're also not restricted to any particular weapon based on what "class" you choose when making a character, all that does is decide what starting outfit you have and that's purely cosmetic. You can use whatever equipment you want whenever you want to as long as your ego rating is equal to or higher than what's listed on the equipment, there's even multiple loadouts where you can completely customize your character's equipment, skills, and passives for different situations, essentially creating different classes that you can switch between on the fly.
The weapon skills have been made easier to level as well, you no longer stop gaining weapon skill exp when the weapon itself that you're using is maxed out and have to stop what you're doing and reset the mastery exp for that weapon.
The bad:
There's really only a couple of things here, but one of them is big. Freaking huge. Almost game breaking even, at least in my opinion.
The in game communication sucks, most people don't even notice it's even there for a long time and even when they do almost nobody uses it because it's such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If you want to play this then get in a guild that uses voice communication because you won't get anywhere trying to use the in game text chat.
The really big thing I don't like is this.....enemies auto scale to the person in the area with the highest ego rating when they spawn. The game itself is basically an open world map where you can go to anywhere at any time with no load screens unless you fast travel, and while this sounds neat (and to be fair, it is neat most times) it can easily screw people with lower ego ratings when someone with a much higher rating so much as drives past them. Any new enemies that spawn will be scaled to match that person and you can go from taking out regular trash enemies with 1 headshot from a bolt action rifle to suddenly needing 3-5 because the newly spawned enemies came in to match the person who zoomed past on their way somewhere else. It's not uncommon to suddenly be massacred by a wave of new enemies that spawned in and are an order of magnitude stronger than what you were just fighting a few seconds before.
This wouldn't be so bad if it was only in areas like arkfalls where a lot of people are expected to show up, or in co-op instances where it doesn't affect anyone who isn't in that particular instance, but it scales like this everywhere and there's absolutely no way to avoid it unless all you do is solo re-run the story quests that have their own instances to them. The game itself is fun but it's very frustrating for new players trying to get started when they constantly get screwed over by the poorly thought out scaling system.
The game USED to not have the kind of power creep where gear gets progressively stronger as you level and higher ego rating just meant you had access to more skills/passives and a wider variety of gear with better mods, but now it's like most other MMOs where you're forced to constantly upgrade your gear as it quickly becomes obsolete. To be fair you can upgrade your current gear with the salvage matrix instead of having to get new stuff, but it's a constant thing and you'll find yourself needing to stop and upgrade far too often, and you'll find yourself having a hard time deciding whether to sell loot or break it down into salvage to use for upgrades.
If you like third person shooters with slight RPG elements and don't mind the horrible level scaling mechanics then you'll probably like Defiance, but if having enemies suddenly start spawning in with 3x the HP and damage output because someone higher level showed up doesn't sound like your cup of tea then you may want to avoid this game for now and see if that changes in the future.

Craft The World is a survival sandbox game.  At the beginning of a level, you are given a single dwarf with no skills to boss around.  After certain milestones, your population increase one by one.  This game is challenging and frustrating at the same time.  I had to fail and retry over and over just to finish the first level.  This game is not really about building but more on survival.  There are some cave explorations and boss fights to do but they aren't the highlight of this game.  Resource balancing is crazy tough and you would really have to be very frugal with how you use each one of your resources.  For instance, not all my dwarves had the best pickaxes but only the professional diggers (even though they all dug at some point) or not all my dwarves had the toughest armors unless they were melee fighters.  Dwarves running out of food or lacking sleep can easily cost you your base that you've worked hard to build up.  There is a goal to this game though: open the portal to the next level.  The parts of the portal are scattered underground and you typically would have to defeat an end-game boss to acquire those parts.  I believe there are 5 levels - all in different setting but the same repetitive task.  Overall, this game was fun because of the challenge behind it but after defeating 1 level, I don't think I'm up to do another one again.  It is much too repetitive and the dwarves move so agonizingly slow.  Getting things done is an epic pain.  While this wasn't entirely boring, I'd recommend anyone who wants to try this to buy it on sale.

Blacklight: Tango Down is an interesting futuristic shooter that has an emphasis on what technology does for an individual soldier. Rather than looking through the world with your eyes, you're seeing it through a screen painted on your helmet which can receive all sorts of disruption such as EMP grenades that require your helmet to reboot and "digital" smoke grenades that disrupt rendering in that direction.
While in reality it's a really basic shooter, the premise is enough to make me recommend it based on that alone. Combine that with an exhaustive array of customizations for your equipment (and not only just stats, but visually) and there's plenty to play around with. The only real problem with this game is the lack of a reliable community and matchmaking system.

Perhaps one way to become attached to two video game characters simultaneously is to control both of them at the same time. They rely on each other, in ways that you grow accustomed to. Ingeniuty wins out here, and one could almost wish for more of it, as the story is told over less than three hours. There is a spark contained in Brothers that is all too soon over, and if ever the consideration was to make an extended edition, I would more than happily endulge.
The moments spent in Brothers are always thought provoking. With areas that are gorgeously lit and rendered, it's easy to see why the characters rest on benches provided along the way. Eye candy galore, and an exceptionally paced transitions of environments left me wanting more. No matter the locale, everything had the undertone of a story that took place before the brothers visited it. Perhaps if I were to replay it, I would analyze the stories untold and then perhaps have a better sense of this game's world.
Inginuity makes every moment exciting and rewarding, but ultimately in the end, as it gives you a profound amount of respect for the story being told. I couldn't think of a better reason for feeling a connection to the two brothers, and I hope there are more impactful stories to come.

Firstly, If all you can find in a few minutes of scrolling are negative reviews, you gotta know something's up.
This game has very little actually going for it the way I see it. The stock game which I only purchased because it was 85% off, is very lacking, containing only three semi-decent routes and about a dozen different Locomotives. And while that may keep you busy for hours, I imagine most railfans, the audience I'm fairly certain this game is meant to appeal to, will not be satisfied. Driving a few select european trains and a few North American Diesels of the same road gets old relatively quickly. There aren't even any steam locomotives in the stock game, which is funny considering the game does clearly have steam locomotive functionality. Unfortunately for railfans, if they do get suckered into buying the game, they have to fork out another 10-25 dollars for additional content via DLC. And when I say 10-25 dollars, that isn't a package of items. It's like 15 dollars for a single locomotive. Like what gives? If you bought every DLC for this game I'm certain you would spend well over a thousand dollars.
Content and lack thereof aside, the Game itself is disgustingly overpriced. I bought it for $8.24. That was 85% off. The normal retail price of this game is $55. Unless you've got money growing out of your ears, that and the cost of additional content is enough to make anyone grimmace.
Another issue I have is that the game's sound effects are rather mediocre, the horns in particular. The engine sounds are at least half decent but none of the sound effects are very clean and  the levels are all wrong.
Now, let's be clear, it still is one of the nicer looking rail sims out there, at least in my experience. The lighting is very decent and the textures, at least for Locomotives and rollingstock, are definitely what I would expect out of a modern game. The interface is fairly easy to use and relatively clean as well, and though I've heard otherwise, the actual physics simulation doesn't feel half bad. That being said, while I'd call myself a railfan, I'm certainly not an expert in the way of train physics.
In the end, the measure of a game's worth relies upon how satisfying it is versus the price you pay, and in the case of TS 2014, It just isn't worth buying. Even at 85% markdown on the base game and 50%-60% on DLCs.

There's a lot to like about Craft the World. The art is good, the music is great, the theme and overall gameplay is pretty good.
However, you progress through the game by either chewing through the entire tech tree (Dozens of hours worth of work), or by taking out two preposterously tough creatures which require mid-grade gear to have a prayer, and high end gear to reasonably take on.
Once you beat a level, you get to move on to a different biome theme and grind the same tech tree over again until you either research everything or take out a couple preposterously difficult monsters.
On top of this, the "quests" really don't give an indication of the end game, just that you need to build seventeen flower pots to level up so you can learn the next weapon crafting so you can learn farming.
If they revisited victory conditions, and the tech trees, this would be a really pretty cool game.
As an example: Forest Biome - Accomplish 3 of the following (Create a lake of X size, Harvest a bajillion wood, Build a keep of X size, Kill supertough badguy, Complete the tech tree, etc). For the tech trees, if they split them out into Military, Resource, and Keep trees with specific recipes requiring levels from other trees (such as traps being in the keep tree, but not being available without iron weapons) it would go miles, as currently it seems like the progression is driven by a pattern rather than a logical progression.
There is a lot of good in this game, but progression is stymied by the victory conditions literally being "grind tech for ten hours to get to the next level to grind tech for ten more hours". I can't recommend this game as a result.

It's not bad. It's about what you'd expect for a game that's free.
It's got a storyline to follow and linear progression.
Heavy emphasis on type matching advantages.
Leveling system branches out in different ways, but focuses on job levels.
It's pretty similar to other mobile games of this genre, using fusion and monster card abilities.
If you play right, you should have an easy time getting through.
You get a warning after two hours to take a break, which is neat.
Battles are generic. You tap the screen to attack and collect orbs you can use to cast your abilities. Do that enough times and you can eventually use your ultimate attack. You can also absorb orbs to increase your resistance and make other orbs appear more.
There's nothing I can see that would be bad for the player experience.
It's definitely a game that takes time, and you have a limited amount of stamina for battles.
Don't expect to play for extended periods of time due to this limitation.
First timers should know that you need to press Alt + Enter to enter full screen mode. I'm not sure if there's a setting somewhere to configure this, but you won't be seeing the menu for a bit so this is the solution I used to take care of that early on. As this is a mobile game, the interface is primarily made for touch input, but I've had no trouble using a mouse.
