First a good TL;DR with bullet points:
Pros:
- Good example of a Diablo Clone (Action-RPG)
- Well-developed class system and build paths
- Nice Graphics
- Should be called "The Real Diablo 3"
- Workshop Avaible and full of amazing community content
Cons:
- No re-skill option (without modding or cheating)
- Nice story yet not so amazing
- Devs stopped working on the game a long time ago, for leaving room to the modders, yet some base update for the vanilla game would be appreciated.
Full Review:
Torchlight 2 let's begin with the basic this game should have been the true successor of Diablo 2, I will never stop repeating this. Torchlight 2 took everything good from Diablo 2: good classes with a tons of possible build paths, fast gameplay and really nice game enviroment.
The vanilla game let you choose from 4 classes: Engi, Outlander (thief/rogue), Mage and Berserker every class feels really unique also every class feels different from itself thanks to the several build paths avaible for every class (Outlander for ex. can spec into archery/gunslinger, elemental or poison build focused, necromancy/minion master; with tons of possible hybrid combination).It's also notable as the game use a unique system of spell-scroll, unique spells that you can learn only by using dropable scrolls in game, this make even more unique each build.
Differently from Diablo, T2 hasn't many randomly generated dungeons this give an easy way for re-starting a save without asking yourself "Where am I? What is this?" yet it makes replayability a bit boring since you will replay every single dungeon simply with a different class.
As Diablo this game also don't have any "reset" options for re-building your class so you will need to start a new char or using cheating metods.
Luckly every "bad" aspect of this game can be solved with a few clicks, the Steam Workshop hasn't ever been so useful, modders created a ton of content for Torchlight 2: new classes (most of them feel really unique), new animations, new companions, new skills, new areas and even the "most wanted" reset button for your builds.
So in the end if you're looking for a good Action-RPG or a God-like Diablo clone that will bring you back to the memory lane of diablo 2 this is your game, I advice to every player to play this game for your first run in vanilla mode, then just go ****deep with mods and try out whatever you would like. Also "it's dangerous to go alone" take with you a few friends and just go have some fun.

Borthers A Tale of Two Sons is providing us a unique gaming experience. It is adventure platforming game with coop gameplay that you control the big brother with your left analog (or WASD if you use keyboard) and right analog for the little brother (directional buttons in keyboard). You will control both of the character at the same time to cooperatively solve the puzzle throughout the game
Your father is dying sick, and your mother has died prior of the game. You, the two brothers, begin the quest to find the magical ancient tree that believed to have the cure of the disease. And the adventure begin. You will journey the beautiful world that's so believable. Every detail in this game is really well made, imaginative and even your adventure is short, you will still find something surprising in your journey. The story itself, it's simple, really simple that you won't struggle to understand what's going on. But not predictable and will arouse your emotion. Even they speak in "not an actual language" like how The Sims character speak and the animation is not like L.A. Noire that motion capture the expressios of the actors, you will still able to feel the emotion of the character, amazed by how the thing turned out. Playing this game is like you read very good pop up fairy tale books but with the story development that is not like usual fairy tale
The gameplay is simple, just movement, rotate the camera, and interact but can be quite entertaining. You need to do a combination of the older and little brother to solve the puzzle and do the platformer in this game. The elder brother is bigger and stronger, capable to handle heavier task like pick up a sheep or pull the heavy lever. And the little brother is smaller and lighter, so he can pass the fence or being boosted by his big brother to reach a high platform. Each character has it's role and the cooperative combination of them make an solid puzzle solving adventure. The puzzle itself is simple and relatively easy to solve but not boring, entertaining and unique in every encounter you will face. Don't expect to see a same puzzle in a different place in this game. Every stage has it's own unique puzzle and platforming
But this game has zero replayability, except you want to look achievements that you may overlooked in the previous playthrough. But despite of that, there are no reason to play it in the second time. And people who seek for challenge in their gaming experience will be dissapointed in this game. This game is very easy and not gave me a hard time at all. And off course the game is really short. Four hours to finish it including some exploring or interacting with some of the NPC's
My score is 8 out of 10. The game is short, really short but so enjoyable. Fear not, with a cheap price tag this game is worth your money. If you like some simple and emotional story with unique and easy gameplay but can be very entertaining. This game is maybe for you. If you are someone who want a challenging puzzle platformer or someone who want more complicated story telling, I don't recommend you to play this game

Red Faction Guerrilla Steam Edition is a one of a kind Military based shooter. I normally am not one that always plays shooters constantly so this game gave me a change of pace with a great level of difficulty from the very start.  The whole purpose of the game is to try to take over control points to stop this evil organization that has killed many people. In order to take control of these sections of the game you will have to bring down small and then large heavily fortified buildings.
There is little to hardly no cover system so often you may need  to shoot small packs of enemies and then retreat for a bit to get your health meter back up which automatically regenerates and then head right back over that way to finish your mission.  There is a wide variety between the tpes of vehicles you can hop in to remain safe from the opposing faction. The first consists of your normal vehicles you can only drive and have no weapon attachments. You can generally hop in any vehicle even if a civilian or the military organization your taking down is in it. Sometimes this will require you to shoot  them off the turrent based military vehicles so then you can invade control points easier.
In my own opinion wrecking crew mode is the greatest feature of all because it has no story and you just follow short  objectives like blowing up barrels to demolish buildings, using walkers to just obliterate everything standing in your way in what is known as Total chaos mode which is just a free-for-all destroy type of mode within wrecking crew.
My favorite part about this game is the use of Walkers to demolish control points if you are lucky enough to find one. There are usually a few different types but only one that has missles which is something similar to something that would be seen in a Armored core game or even generally comparable to a Star Wars AT-AT walker though smaller.
I'll give this game a solid 8.5/10.  I highly recommend you check it out. It is made by THQ which was a company that went bankrupt eventually after having games only targeting family friendly kids games, movies games and then they created fully Muture games which was primarily targeted towards adults though that did not help their downfall as a company.
All in all the destructible environments reminded me of some videos I have seen where people play the Battlefield Shooter series.
Way beyond its time.

I bought this game during the Christmas sale in 2013 and was very dissappointed, I eventually out of frustration deleted it from my PC I'm so glad I did not pay full price.
Today I saw the reduced price of 3 DLC's I had really wanted back then but could not afford, they were 50% off in the current sale and I almost bought them but, thought I would first check the Steam forums to see if there were problems / improvements with the 2014 update and I'm glad I did because they reminded me what a purely money driven bunch of bugs this game is plus, there now seems to be more problems and no attempt to solve any of the existing long term bugs.
Look at the specs, they only provide the minimum requirements 2 gig ram 512Mb Graphics card windows XP there is no mention of the ideal set up.
I couldn't play this, it constantly crashed I have a 1gig Gforce gtx 280 card 4 gig ram (32 bit Vista so just over 3 gig usable) and 2.8 quad core processor so, I assumed no problem, WRONG!
I went on the forums and met two attitudes one being, yes there is a long term bug that causes this crashing and it has never been fixed the second presumably from the games company employees or its fans was my PC was not up to the job with less than 4 gig ram which suggests you need to be runnuing 64 bit to fully utilize the software, there is no mention of this in the specs which claim it will run on XP with only 2 gig Ram and a 512 graphics card. If that is not true then the product is being misrepresented however, they are probably using the word RUN in the loosest possible of terms.
I tried turning everything down to minimum but, it still crashed with depressing regularity.
There is a lack of documentation with the game however, it is available, made by the fans fortunately there is a strong fan base that the company in no way deserves a lot of what the developers should be doing is being done by those playing the game.
Most items in the workshop require you to purchase overpriced DLC's to use them because the base game comes with so little.
I found problems with things that did not seem to work as one would expect or were missing entirely such as lights, trackside information provided too late to effectively use, commuters as dumb as ducks.
I could happily ignore all the little things and even inaccurate simulation if the game was as good as it ought to be and indeed could be especially with the available fan base plus, if a second mortgage were not required to purchase DLC's some several years old already, just to make the game more varied challenging and enjoyable to play.
I was going to spend $25.00-$30.00 on DLC's not a lot to some but, a lot to me now, I shall be spending less on something that works as it should and will not require a constant financial input.
I don't object to paid DLC's but, a game should not force you to buy highly priced DLC's just to make it playable, especially  as this game is buggy however, I suppose fixing it is not as lucrative as producing another $20.00 DLC.
The basic game is the bare minumum possible perhaps not even that, in the countries covered there are enough trains new and vintage and miles of track to provide a bigger and more varied starting package and still allow for almost endless DLC's.
The devs claim this pricing strategy is to keep the price down on the base game, I feel it is more give the buyer something so basic they'll eventually spend far more money than they would ever have been initially willing to pay to make it playable, just add up the non-discount cost of the base game and say 4 DLC's you could be well on the way to $100.00 even top games cost less than that and many excellent simulators that also have plentiful DLC's provide far more for less cost in the base game.

Alright. Defiance. Where to start? I think I'll start with basic information.
Defiance is a free-to-play third person shooter MMO. It has some basic mechanics such as vehicle use and your firefights, but there's also your MMO elements such as weapon elementals, 4 abilities each with its own unique skill tree (grid). Most of your time will be spent probably looking for some pretty snazzy loot. Or, you could take the team approach and go hunt down some "Arkfalls". More to be explained.
Story:
Defiance is set in post apocolyptic alien America, in the California region. It is based off of the SyFy show, called, well, Defiance. Your job is to locate and collect the Ark technology to cleanse the earth of the aliens who intend to, well, as most aliens do, take over the planet. (That's the jist I believe. Haven't done too much story, and haven't started the first season yet).
Gameplay:
Gameplay is exciting and is sure to keep your attention. You'll have to develop skills with your weapons (you rank up each specific weapon type to gain perks for said weapon type, e.g. Bolt Action Snipers or Pump Shotguns.) that can be used for aid in combat. You'll also want to learn to develop combat strategies for all of the different types of enemies ranging from weak Hellbug Skitterlings to massive, tanky Minigunners.
Graphics:
Graphics are surprisingly well done for a TV show game. Yes, I'm aware some aren't terrible, but I was't too impressed with a few. Defiance look stunning. I love wandering around gazing at the various sights. It's a pretty good visual to have.
Flaws:
I feel like there isn't enough depth to the co-op. Pretty much everything can be done solo, with the exceptions of Arkfalls and the major events that occur over time. Missions can all be solo'd if you have the weaponry and levels.
Another thing is the level system. This one isn't a super big issue, just felt strange, so I listed it as a flaw. It's so strange. You have these numbers that just kinda rise and fall as they're needed, aside to your permanent level. It's hard to explain, but you'll see for yourself.
Overview:
In general, Defiance is a solid game. Free to play, everything that can be done with real money can be done with IN GAME currency, so there's no need to spend your hard-earned cash on some shiny new weaponry. Unless you're impatient, of course. The gameplay feels solid, and I enjoy playing with friends despite the somewhat visible push for co-op.
Based on my experiences with a lot of F2P games and how Defiance stands out, I rate Defiance a solid 9/10.
Was enjoyable, but endgame wasn't all that great. If you have the money, go with Skyrim or something.

Craft the World is a nice mix of Tower Defence, Base Building and Resource Gathering / Management and after 200 hours of play I can safely say that I have gotten great value for money with this game!
You are constantly moving forward one way or another. With a vast tech tree to work through, there is always something new to craft, new weapons, new tools and new decorations are plentiful. Ever increasing waves of an enemy horde will keep you on your toes, complete with a countdown so you know how long you have left to bolster defences and get ready for the pending invasion. Also the main aim of the game is to build a portal and move on to the next new land, for this you must find and defeat the boss creatures hidden in the depth of the world, be careful when digging deep though and more than 1 surprise awaits in the far depths.
You are never left bored, not only are you mining to find the Portal (and to gather resources) while waiting for the invading horde but enemies will spawn in unlit areas and the day/night cycle will bring a small horde of enemies to your door each night.
There are plenty of tools, weapons and armours for your dwarves to choose from ranging from stone and wooden stuff to mythril, do you go for style over functionality? will your dwarves be melee warriors, archers or mages? finding a balance that suits you can mean the difference between success and failure when attacking strong enemies.
Building a home for your dwarves is also important, keep them happy by giving them good food (and maybe a nice little something to drink ;) )and a nice place to live, there are loads of choices in this department, from various walls and floors to fish bowls and comfy chairs. So much to choose from keeps the game fresh.
This is a game I always go back to and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes tower defence or resource management games.

Craft the World is a simulation crafting game with population management. It mixes elements from Gnomoria, Terraria and Dwarf Fortress.
Good:
The game has a nice overall feel. Graphical design is pleasant. It is not the usual retro pixel art. There are many things to explore and craft. Options related to unit customization are good allowing multiple skills to be learned and gears to be acquired and used. In addition there are various spells like teleport and fireball that can be used via mana. These features add some depth into the usual simulation.
Bad:
Audio design is varying in quality. There are some nice sounds and there some really terrible ones. Minimap often does not synchronise to the actual view screwing up map movement. The interface is made for mobile use which means that there are limited number of keyboard shortcuts and the ui elements are too big. Leveling is slow paced restricting capabilities throughout the progression. Shelter limits are also buggy at times connecting non-existing walls. Unfortunately, the biggest and ultimately fatal problem of the game is the AI which did not get much better during the last 2 and a half years and still doing horrible things. Pathfinding issues resulting in units falling and get stuck. Terrible combat system without any kind of control, fleeing people everywhere resulting in a chaotic mess. There are some stuff which tends to help in these situations like the instant scaffolding block and the horn spell but these are limited and sometimes not even work.
Overall, the game has a nice base with clunky UI but the AI which controls things is broken and is working constantly against the player.

With the surprising lack of hype for bannerlord, I thought I aught to review this, given that when bannerlord comes out there will probably be some kind of sale on this.
Warband doesn't change too much from the original mount & blade: same factions (with one added) similar map, ect.. However, these seemingly minor changes completely change the game experience, making it far more varied and interesting. While there are some factions that have an easier time than others (swadians always seem to get wiped out quickly due to their positioning, unless the player allies with them), you can certainly win as any faction, and each has a unique fighting style with different strengths and weaknesses. The somewhat unique combination of strategy, RPG and FPS/3PS lets you play the game how YOU want; be it as a trader, benevolent or evil lord, or even King/Queen of your own nation.
As one final note, there are plenty of amazing mods for this game, from minor graphical improvements to complete gameplay overhauls. For any lover of medival games, this is a must have.

I'm not going to surprise anyone, I guess, by saying that I recommend you play this game. No matter who you are and what kinds of games you like, you really should give this one a try. It's a must-play.
The game's biggest asset is the story and how the mechanics are interwined with the story. The game never offers too much of a challenge, but its innovative "each-stick-controls-one-character" approach is, at times, challenging enough to get used to. Once you get a hold of that, the puzzles are unlikely to stump you. This is a relaxing experience, which is there to be seen and played by yourself, while focusing on what's going on. Watching a playthrough of this short game is doing yourself an unimaginable disservice.
Pretty much everything else also works incredibly well in this game. The art direction and design proves to me again that video games do not need anything more than the tried-and-true Unreal Engine 3 - they "just" need imagination, and vision. Sure, it's easier to say that we need more detailed graphics and lightning effects to convey emotions and atmosphere, because that doesn't demand any artistic input in the game's style... well, Brothers is proof that this standpoint is plain wrong, and if a game has a boring visual design, not even next-gen graphics are going to make it look better than Brothers does. The game is gorgeous, and each of the different locations you'll visit is uniquely attractive, while conveying the theme in a near perfect way.
The soundtrack also helps a lot in building the game's atmosphere. It is one of the best I heard in recent years, and definitely unique in its own way. This is the first time I heard an OST so dipped in northern-european themes. The vocals do most of the heavy lifting to establish this feeling, but not a single track sounds like it doesn't fit into the overarching goal of the music. Not only a spot-on supplement to everything else in this game, it is an achievement on its own. You can buy the OST over at BandCamp and I highly recommend you do that.
What more is there to say? This may not be the best game of all time, or even the most moving one, or the most influential one - but that doesn't change the fact that it is a must-have.

Couple of days ago, i would have wrote a great review about this game. Unfortunately, this became more and more frustrating. I will give out the good and the bad.
The good :
Dwarves AI
- I've read a lot of people complaining about the *AI* of the dwarves. I'm sorry people but even if this is partly true, it is a challenge that as a true gamer, i kinda enjoyed. Yes they aren't totally polished. The logic behind their behavior ain't flawless, but in the end, YOU need to give orders or adapt your gameplay to this obstacle. This is not the *easy to play* type of behavior which is fun in the end.
Skill tree
- It is great to have a skill tree to refer to. I hate the fact of games like Terraria that you obviously NEED a wiki page for recipes. It gives you a good idea of how to progress from early to end-game. Don't be fooled tho, this is going into the bad to.
Biomes
- It has a couple of biomes which is interesting for its difficulty. Without spoiling, there are monsters which you might not want to encounter to soon. But the challenge is still fun.
Being a god
- You control dwarves, they do your bidding. How come you couldn't have fun doing it? Enjoyable, truely.
The bad :
Bugs and more bugs
- Be careful, i ain't talking about bugs as monsters. I am really talking about in-game bugs that shouldn't be in a full release. Those are beta bugs! How come you would release a full version of a game which has so many bugs??? At least FIX them. For example, (SPOILER, DON'T READ IF YOU STILL PLAN ON BUYING!), 4th map, Takmak is supposed to be pleased, but goes in ragemode for no reason(was blue colored), Plants grows with missing sprites. Yes you read it right, missing sprites. Some players already reported those but it's worth mentioning again. Killing a boss drops a scroll. If it drops in lava or in the ocean, you are doomed to restart your WHOLE game. If it were 1 hour games, i wouldn't mind a little bug, but this is a GAME BREAKING bug. Those kind of bugs shouldn't be present in any full released game! One game could take from 10 hours to X hours above that depending on your abilities and knowledge of the game. There's more but i think you get the point.
Dwarves AI
- Yes it was in the good part. Why is it in the bad too? Simply that sometimes, the AI just go nuts. Dwarves freezing, walking left to right to left and so on on one block. If you have multiple dwarves working close to each other, this tend to happen a lot. And since you will probably have this situation to happen frequently, so are those bugs.
Skill Tree
- It doesn't make any sense how it has been built. When you start a new game, i shouldn't feel like FAR behind for more than a couple of minutes or even one hour. It is VERY frustrating to be weak for a very long time with waves of monsters spawning every 45 minutes and monsters spawning each nights. I'm not complaining about the difficulty of the game. I passed the first three maps rather easily because of dropping gifts(i suppose it was for christmas because i don't receive them anymore at the 4th map. This game should redo it's whole skill tree to make more sense out of it.
Monsters - Bestiary
- It's fine to know how dangerous a monster can be when you discover it, but there is no way to see how strong it is untill you actually encountered it. Bosses, cave goblins and so on, are insanely strong and you don't know that untill you fight them, I get that. But there are no stats available, and since the dwarves AI is rather stupid, most of the time you do understand that too late and dwarves gets killed. Which this is my next point in the bad.
Lack of information
- There is almost to none informations in-game. What to do, how to do it. How can i resurrect a dwarf, how to i heal my dwarves beside sleeping in beds. How come it is so slow. What's the point of having a totem. Wait, what is the totem??? SOOOOOOO much informations that should exist which doesn't. Even the WIKI lacks informations concerning mechanics of the game.
That's about it. What i suggest, buy it when it is below 10 bucks. I'm glad i bought this during christmas because at 20.99$, it's far too expansive for what it's worth. But at full price, this game is a no go, there are better games on the market to waste time in it than this one.

This game is very slow paced. It took me 16 hours to beat level one. But it's so addictive. Mining, mining, mining. Building, building, building. Setting up your defenses and preparing for the next invasion. Upgrading your gear to take on the underground bosses. It's slow and methodical, and strangely very relaxing.
I ran into a glitch about 5 hours into level 2. Something went wrong with my shelter, and the algorithm that checks if your shelter is complete buggered up. I had all my doors and walls intact, but it was still saying it was incomplete and the only hole that was flagged was right beside the stockpile. There wasn't even a door there. So my dwarves wouldn't rest and they got slaughter in the next battle. I'm guessing this bug will be patched at some point. As near as I can tell it happened because the monsters beat my door in, and I replaced it in the middle of a fight, with the monsters still inside my base. Not sure why this should mess things up, but that was the situation.
Other than that, I've lost so much time sunk into this game. It's so much fun just giving orders and seeing the little guys get things done. People are complaining about path-finding issues and such, but I'm guessing they just don't know how the game mechanics actually work. I had no problems at all with the path-finding once I figured out portal spells. It all makes logical sense, unless you're a dummy who gets easily frustrated.

Long time RTS player here, going all the way back to the Close Combat series.  I'm always keeping an eye out for strategy wargames that focus on *realism* - engagements taking place at real distances, where terrain matters, etc., but are still FUN.
After Close Combat there was one hell of a drought--for years.  Combat Mission was good, but (sort of) turn based and the visuals were...lacking.  Later, Company of Heroes looked promising, but ultimately played just like Starcraft.  The Men of War series was probably the best thing in realistic wargaming for a while until this series got wrapped up in its impossible campaigns and petered out.
Wargame (this one AND the prior one) has a huge (but not overwhelming) scale, realistic scope, meticulously detailed units.  Infantry movement isn't at the level of detail of a Close Combat game, but that's acceptable given the scale.  This game is brutal, but the community (the game launches to a menu with an already-active chat window) is helpful and entertaining.  Honestly, nobody is very good.  This is the sort of game that you'd probably need a stint at West Point or Quantico to be truly great at.  But that's the fun: the multplayer games are a satisfying length of slamming around the map hoping (if you're like me) that someone on your team knows what they're doing more than you do.
It's hard, but the menu isn't too complex.  Your units go, they stop, they land (if they're a helicopter).  It's not "Micro" that makes you good, it's deploying them intelligently...
You'll spend as much time customizing your army "decks" as you do playing, and you'll enjoy every second of it.
Last note: this game takes truly amazing screenshots.  And yes, it DOES look that good, but in the heat of battle, combined with dubious camera controls, you'll rarely be looking at your units that closely.  Wish the camera was snappier so you could zoom around and see those amazingly detailed units up close more often.
Last last note: The second Wargame title (Air Land Battle) added airplanes, which the first game didn't have.  This one adds boats.  They're nifty and look great, but they're expensive so it is very sad when they sink, which they will.

Outstanding quality RTS that any military nut would enjoy.  Will also stress out your grey matter, too.  If you aren't familiar with the Wargame series, it's a borderline strategic simulator more than an RTS. No base building, no real resources (besides point income from holding sectors), and every unit has morale, health, ammo, and fuel that needs to be tended to carefully with supply lines.
The scale is unlike what most other games in the genre offer.  It reminds me almost of the original Supreme Commander in terms of sher volume of units on the field and map size.  Every unit you take into battle will never come back alive once destroyed, and you need to make your own decks of units to take into battle, which is almost a kind of game in itself...finding the right unit combos or roles to take.  One of the major reasons I recommend this game is because of that.
The army variety and unit selection is also awe inspiring.  You can pick from about 1,500 units, all modeled correctly to their real counterpart and act like the real one too.  Nations to build from include the US, Canada, France, UK, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Poland, Russia, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, China, and Best Korea (I mean North Korea).  There's an army for everyone's taste and they all feel and play unique.
Naval battles need some work and balancing, though, but it also may be just the nature of modern warfare on the ocean.  It revolves around who makes the biggest ship blob and has the best radar gattling gun screen to stop incomming cruise missiles.
Overall if you wanna work your brain a little in an RTS and focus entirely on the war and not the bases/economy, this is the thing for you.

After a few contemplative moments and a nagging uncertainty as to whether Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons would be worth picking up in it's Fable-istic graphics, I was finally talked into it by one of my friends during the flash sale. It's neither the longest game nor the smoothest running controls to boast. However it's possibly one of the best uses of storytelling through interaction & tone than almost every other game I have played to date.
I won't go TOO in depth about the story, but while the premise seems to be about two brothers focusing on trying to get a healing regeant for their father it's truly focusing on the brother's relationship with one another. The emotions portrayed through body language are superior, and the tone of their sub-common speech is well executed.
There is very little action, some incredibly grim scenes, and this nagging background tone of hope through the storyline. Don't go into this expecting a fighting game, but you should come in expecting a story and a (simple but concise) puzzle. It absolutely delivers and is worth the money expended unlike many games that seem to forget that games are a form of storytelling. Grab this game, enjoy the ride, and DON'T SPOIL IT FOR YOURSELF.

I'll admit I had pretty low expectations going into this game having not looked into it too much before trying it out. However it was surprisingly enjoyable.
It helps that I am a fan of match-three style puzzle games, which HuniePop is. I also tend to be a fan of dating sim games, particularly of the yuri variety so, check and check. (Thank you for giving the option to switch main character gender!)
Voicework was surprisingly good, and while it took me awhile to get the hang of the particulars of the game like what to gift the girls and when, it was fun once I started getting into it.
I liked that the game didn't punish you for pursuing the entire cast in a single playthrough, though I can't help but feel like there was some missed opportunity there perhaps for some replay value, but it's arguably the same difference and so my point is pretty debatable or potentially moot. Either way it was nice to not be too restricted by the game.
The main frustration I had with HuniePop came in the form of the UI and window sizing. I had the seemingly common issue of the phone's graphic staying on the left side of the screen all the time, and in both fullscreen or window view, parts of the game screen were cut off from view, like it didn't adjust to the resolution of the monitor very well. I tried a few of the supposed fixes listed in the Steam community discussions, but they didn't resolve the issues for me and I was never able to get it to work as you would normally expect a game to behave in fullscreen or window views, so there were times when I had to switch out of fullscreen mode to view my current money and hunie amounts at the top of the screen (which hid from view important UI elements on the bottom of the screen instead), and I learned to just deal with the extraneous visible art elements that I'm sure were normally intended to be invisible until needed.
I think this same issue is likely also what caused my more frustrating difficulty from a gameplay standpoint where the mouse cursor would seem to go out of synch with the UI elements. The center of the screen area seemed to work fine, but go further out towards either edge, especially the left side for me, and they started going very much out of synch. You would have to move your mouse cursor much further to the side before the item you were trying to interact with would register as having the mouse cursor placed over it. This made completing some of the puzzle sections quite difficult, especially the time sensitive ones, because you would have to move your mouse cursor 2 or 3 columns further to the left say, than you intended, in order to grab the token you wanted.
It's worth noting that I tried playing HuniePop on both my Windows machine and my Linux one and the issues persisted on both machines, so it wasn't even an OS or hardware specific problem which is the strangest part. I can only conclude it was something the software did not like about perhaps my screen resolutions on both machines, or some other aspect shared between both my computers that I couldn't guess gave it trouble.
I should also mention that I did not have this sort of problem with my short time playing HunieCam Studio, a later game from the same developers, so something must have changed or improved between this game and that one on that front, or perhaps I was just unlucky with HuniePop in particular in this regard. Either way it was something I learned to work around and once I got used to the quirks, the game was still plenty playable and enjoyable despite the interface related issues.
As far as the gameplay mechanics of the puzzle portions themselves, I liked having different tokens that gave more or fewer points depending on the girl's preferences. The player pitfall aspect of the broken heart tokens was good too. It definitely added some strategy to the experience.
Though I do wish some of the reactions from certain characters when you accidentally matched the broken heart tokens were a bit less...abrasive. I don't think the player ever intentionally matches those tokens, so hearing the date get so upset about it and sometimes curse at you was kind of disheartening, at least to me anyway. It suggests you as the player were offensive or rude or downright crass with your date by how strongly some of them reacted, and it would have been nicer I think if it was toned down in intensity a bit for some of the more expressive characters. Likewise for some of the failed date responses. It's not like the player is ever trying to fail them. No need to kick them while they're down.
At first the points goal seemed to ramp up to an unfair level quickly, but then when I found out the importance of gifting and building up traits it made the going a lot more fair. Traits were a feature I quickly forgot about in the early part of the game unfortunately...probably because they were hiding in the phone menu rather than somewhere more front-and-center like the shops or the profile pages or most of the rest of the main game's content when you visited a girl. Pro tip: level your traits, it's essential to progressing in the game.
Gifting date items was a fun system too because it sort of allowed you to play out your favorite strategy, or tailor your approach towards each girl's specific personality. It took a lot of trial and error to find my favorite combination of items to bring along too but once I did it made most dates more enjoyable to navigate the puzzles without feeling like I had zero chance to succeed at it just because of RNG on what puzzle pieces ended up dropping next.
I believe at the time of writing a sequel is in the works, and I am definitely looking forward to playing that one, with as much fun as I had with HuniePop. I was not expecting it, but I can't deny that it was an enjoyable game. I'm looking forward to seeing more of this type of content with HuniePop 2 in the future.

I am impressed with this Early Access game, and recommend it to RCT 1&2 fans. It has loads of shops and rides for you bulid and play around with, and its a proper tycoon game with loads of micro managaing.
I don't want to compare it to Planet Coaster as they have both got there strengths and weakness . As both games are decent Theme Park games in ther own right, so it worth playing/owning both titles as they offer different experiences.
As for RCTW thats just a shambolic mess at the moment, which won't be fixed.

As a game, Parkitect is great. Attention to detail in music, graphics, gameplay and controls really pull the whole thing together into a quality product.
What really makes Parkitect stand out from the rest of the Early Access swarm is the level of passion for the community and the history of the genre that we've seen from the devs.

If you liked rollercoaster tycoon 1 and 2 this is definitly a game you should consider buying. Obviously the game is not perfect due to it being early access. But the dev's have brought this a long way and continue to update it. For the price I would say its a good deal at the moment. Plenty of shops, coasters and flat rides to choose from and build your park. Not to mention a lot of different scenery objects.

If you loved Roller Coaster Tycoon then this is the game for you. It has expanded upon the basic gameplay from that, thrown in a hint of the Sims and released a great piece of work. This is only day 1 of the early access and it has ablsolutly blown me away. There is a large selection of rides and scenery with more promised to come in future updates and from the community. I am still learning the interface but it is easy to pick up.
The gameplay needs a few balancing tweaks here and there but I am very impressed with it for a Day 1 early acess release in Alpha. The sandbox is a great way to just play around and learn the game with few restrictions.
The soundtrack is amazing. It is very relaxing, yet upbeat and fun. There are enough songs so that they do not get annoying having to listen to the same song over and over again. The caroucel is actually several recorded clips of music from a Wurlitzer 162 organ which is a real nice touch.
I love the artwork as well. It took me a few minutes to get used to it but now I love it! It was made even better by ramping up the graphics. I have a GeForce 750M 2gb card in my laptop and it ran  beautifully on max settings except for a few seconds of initial stutter.
I am very excited to see what the developers bring to this game. It is a solid product worth $30-$40 as it is right now. I can't wait to see how it grows!

You have three Rollar Coaster tyccon games coming out, Planet Coaster, Rollar Coaster Tyccon World, and Parkitect.
If you enjoyed RCT 1 and 2, Parkitect is really great. It has simple graphics defualty in a semi isometric view (you have four view angles by defualt) but is very modable. Even in its pre alpha stages it paid attention to even the small details like being able to choose how much cheese, condiments, letus is on your burgers  how much soda and how much ice you put in your soft drinks effecting the overhead cost at the cost (or improvement) of custermer satisfaction. You can set your ride A to only start its cycle when ride B starts to have your rides in sync (which could mean doing some really awesome things with two coasters that always start together at the same time).
Planet Coaster in pre alpha is shaping up to be a pretty great game if you where more into RCT3, it looks beutiful, its got that fine level of control when it comes to construction to the point where the vendor stands are all fairly generic designed to allow you to build and decorate them how you want them themed, same goes with the rides as well. The lighting engine is great, you can make your park look amazing when the sun goes down and your lights come on. It currently lacks the ecconomy (or atleast it did last time I played it, maybe it got added in a recent build) but reguardless is a great game even with how early it is.
RollerCoaster Tyccon World, well just don't touch that with a 10 foot poll, it is a horrible mess compared to the other two and was basicly Atari trying to make money off of the title alone.  The customization is horribly lacking, looks great in screen shots but runs sickingly aweful, and it to the RTC series is like THPS5 is to the THPS/ THAW/THUG series, a atempt at a cash grab with no care or effort put in.
Pick up Parkitect, pick up Planet Coaster, pretend like RTC World doesn't exist and you will love both games.

Once upon a time, wannabe-Hope Estheim was transported to the world of Palamecia, which used to be its own Empire in Final Fantasy II, but I guess up and took over the world after the heroes won.  I bet you feel dumb for playing through that game now, don't you?
Mobius Final Fantasy is a mobile-to-PC port of a single-button RPG, that is actually pretty good, and is a game I find - oddly - that I like.  As always, I'll talk about
,
, and the
about why exactly I've thumbs-downed a game that I claim to find good, and claim to like.
First, the game systems, even with the mobile micro-pay bulls@#$, are actually pretty good.  People who played Final Fantasy XIII might recognize some - this game uses a reasonably modified version of the Crystarium system for job growth, except that each job's 'skill panel' is tied to that line of jobs, and instead of spending generic Tech Points, you spend elements gained by fighting battles with certain cards equipped.
Next, the general production value.  The in-engine cutscenes are good, the sound designs are great.  The story, while cliched to hell, puts a twist in having a hero who has common sense, for once.  "Explore this endless desert, doesn't this sound like fun!?" asks the obligatory annoying Moogle.  "No, it sounds foolish" says your character.  That's right, wannabe-Hope Estheim actually has a brain, unlike some JRPG protagonists I know of.
Lastly, the micropay setup isn't extremely onerous.  It's easy enough to get Crystals to advance job lines through regular play.  Cards level up and become powerful through in game systems.  Even the Stamina system is forgiving - my first play session only ended because I ran out of Phoenix Downs in Chapter 2, not because I was barred from continuing due to low Stamina.  Sure, you can pay to speed the process along...but the game doesn't make you pay, and is an OK RPG to boot!
Minor gripes come first.
First, ladies, you don't get a character model.  You get to be wannabe Hope Estheim, voiced by wannabe Cloud Strife.  Guys who want to play as girls?  Same.
Speaking of gender confusion, wannabe Hope Estheim is a big fan of the 'backless' style.  The Knight 'skin' for instance, has minimal chest armor - a really bad idea - well-armored arms and legs, and everything laced neatly up in the back.  I'll say one thing for wannabe Hope Estheim - the boy is
in his sex appeal, and apparently never went to middle school.
More serious things.  The UI is...nonstandard.  Commands are hosted on the sides of the screen, instead of corners, as is more typical for PC games.  Some of this can be attributed to the fact this is a mobile port, but if you're going to make a PC version of a game, why not make your UI not break interface?
While the micropay system isn't annoying, the game is shot-through with mobile bullcrap to the point where it's an immersion breaker.  For instance, you can't get to a configuration menu for the first hour of play, because it's all forced tutorials that never let you set screen resolution, fullscreen/windowed, or much of anything else.  This is particularly annoying, when the game A) assumes full screen resolution, but B) puts the game in Windowed mode, which
moves certain things off-screen in Windows 10.  Because a few pixels of certain buttons were clickable, I was able to soldier past the tutorial; this was close to being a game-breaking bug, but fortunately fell short.
Once again, we have an Obligatory Annoying Moogle, who you meet early in the story.  Other than to have intra-party racism once the fairy joins (Moogles know the fairy as a selfish trickster, while the fairy is just flat-out racist against moogles), and speak in an annoying high-pitched voice, the moogle is just there to facilitate the story, and does little else of value.
Also, the game features "Exploration" segments where you can freely move about by holding the mouse button down and moving the mouse.  While this seems neat, in actuality, it's very seldom done, and very seldom effective.  Instead of needing to explore a ruined castle to find a teleport stone - said exploration being an entry bridge, a big room, and a remnant of a room just off that - why not just show a cutscene?  We're already full-linear in this game; it'd serve it better to stick with that, especially since the story is, if not awesome, at least reasonably engaging!
Lastly, and worst, is the RNG.  The game works by attacking, to generate element orbs.  You then use element orbs to power special attacks from your equipped cards, or you can use the 'Element Drive' to gain element resistances or restore your HP.  There's cases you will find where you need to restore your HP...and you don't get Healing Orbs, because they're generated semi-randomly.  These lead to needing to use a phoenix down, through no fault of your own, presumably to make you micro-pay.  Yes, I see through the charade.  No, it's not amusing.
I spent an entire night considering my rating for this game.  On the one hand: there is a good game in this.  There is a good story.  The production value is good.  That being said, the thumbs-up, and thumbs-down buttons aren't under any of those questions.  The question is "Do you recommend this game?"
The reason I do not, is because this is a phone-to-PC port, but I don't disrecommend it on principle alone.  The reason I disrecommend it, is because if Squeenix had taken about a year or so to really think this through, and exorcise all the micropay and RNG-ey elements from this work, then post it to Steam and just have us pay around $9.99 or so for this game, this would be a much,
better title.  As I've said before - there's a good game in this, I genuinely enjoy it.  The mobile micropay stuff constantly breaks immersion, though.
That being said, I doubt this game will stay installed on my system for more than about two weeks.  The novelty of 'a good phone RPG' will wear off, because I'm playing on a PC; I have other, better games that are developed with PC gaming in mind.  In about that time, there'll be something I want more.  To make room, this cellphone game will be deleted from my PC.
Squeenix, if you want my money, give me something to buy.  This game is genuinely good, and you've almost got a good PC RPG in this.

This game might be the best game I ever wished I hadn't played. The gameplay is just fantastic, the graphics are beautiful, the world is enchanting, and the story is heart wrenching. I am not exagerating when I say this might be the single saddest game you will ever play.
I'm sure if you're aware of this game, that you've heard all the reviewers say "It's an emotional game." Even knowing that going in, you won't be prepared for what this game has in store for you.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons might be the most powerful game ever made. Everything from the puzzles to the controls are carefully crafted to feel the rollercoaster of emotions that was written by some of the most wonderful and sadistic people.
I'm not a very "emotional" person, so with that in mind... If I ever meet the creators of this game, I will straight punch them in the face for how emotionally stirring this game was. You've been warned, play at your own emotional risk. But please don't listen to me and play this game anyways.
The only complaint I think anyone could make about this game is that it's too short. Personally, I don't feel it is. When the game was done, I was satisfied and it felt like I had been playing all day. The pacing of the game is perfect, allowing the range of emotions to play out naturally and makes sure the game doesn't overstay its welcome.

I have over 5000 hours clocked on my Steam account across a variety of genres.
The 3 or so hours I spent playing Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons were some of if not the most captivating and incredible hours I've spent consuming any form of media.
However I look at this game, it blows me away.
The graphics and aesthetics are outstanding. Every area in the game is lovingly crafted for gorgeous views. The animations on the characters are top notch, which is very important because there is no real dialogue in the game - they speak a form of gibberish but through the context, tone of voice, and body language you can generally understand what they're saying.
I'm a heavy book reader, but the story and environment in this game rivals some of my favorite works. The feelings that this game invokes put to rest the debate on whether or not games can truly be an art form.
The gameplay is very novel and innovative and quite fun also. It's not lacking at all in that department - as a puzzle/adventure game, it goes where no other games have gone before and for that alone is worthy of being played.
This may not be my favorite game of all time - I may not be able to sink loads of time into it. I've got thousands of hours in Counter Strike, nearly 700 in Dark Souls, etc. But dammit this is definitely up there, and one of the most important games you can play this generation.

The story, while linear, is brilliantly told through some outstanding gameplay set to a wistful soundtrack. Perfectly paced and long enough to feel fulfilling but short enough to not feel as if it's dragging on.
Level design is impeccable with lovely touches like benches situated at various vantage points as if there hint to the player to stop and take in the amazing surroundings. What you expect to be interactable, is interactable. The puzzles while simple, suit the game; it's a story game more than a puzzle game.
I enjoyed every moment playing Brothers and for once didn't feel like I wanted to rush to the end. I can't recommend this game enough to anyone wanting a true adventure game with a touching and compelling narrative.

Coming from a studio that has developed a number of action-heavy games, Starbreeze Studios has created a beatuiful world in a story-driven game. Despite its lack of dialogue (or rather dialogue in a language I do not understand), the story development remains coherent. The story is very basic, which at its core is an adventure story centering around the quest to acquire a rare object; however, the developers have managed to create an intricate world that conveys a epic scale, while grounding the story in the relationship between two brothers. With the help of a filmmaker, they have captured a cinematic story that does not overstay its welcome, yet remains engaging.
In the current state of games, many games strive for graphical realism. Contrary to this current trend, this game opts for an aesthetic that has soft features but still able to show us a beatiful world full of intricate details. Unfortunately, due to the use of the UE engine, there will be texture pop-ins during texture heavy areas, but it was very infrequent in my playtime.
Last but not least, the most interesting part of this game is the control feature. While you can play this game on a keyboard, I would highly recommend playing on a game controller (360 controller). Using both control/analog sticks to control each brother respectively and triggers to control actions, it is perhaps the simplest control scheme I have ever used. Not only that,  it is a creative use of a controller that utilizes a co-op approach to play a single player game.
Due to the creativity and its general aesthetic of the game, this game has become one of the most memorable games I have played recently. A basic story that takes place in a beautiful world of trolls, humans, griffins, and more. The developer has also set "vantage points" to admire their jaw-dropping set-pieces. All in all, I would be very interested in seeing what Starbreeze Studios puts out next because this game has put this studio on my radar.

I generally don't notice music in video games too often, but HuniePop's soundtrack is an absolute masterpiece. The songs fit their environments perfectly and are rotated enough that I never grew tired of any one track. I can still hear the songs in my head months later as clearly as if I played it yesterday.

Once upon a time, wannabe-Hope Estheim was transported to the world of Palamecia, which used to be its own Empire in Final Fantasy II, but I guess up and took over the world after the heroes won.  I bet you feel dumb for playing through that game now, don't you?
Mobius Final Fantasy is a mobile-to-PC port of a single-button RPG, that is actually pretty good, and is a game I find - oddly - that I like.  As always, I'll talk about
,
, and the
about why exactly I've thumbs-downed a game that I claim to find good, and claim to like.
First, the game systems, even with the mobile micro-pay bulls@#$, are actually pretty good.  People who played Final Fantasy XIII might recognize some - this game uses a reasonably modified version of the Crystarium system for job growth, except that each job's 'skill panel' is tied to that line of jobs, and instead of spending generic Tech Points, you spend elements gained by fighting battles with certain cards equipped.
Next, the general production value.  The in-engine cutscenes are good, the sound designs are great.  The story, while cliched to hell, puts a twist in having a hero who has common sense, for once.  "Explore this endless desert, doesn't this sound like fun!?" asks the obligatory annoying Moogle.  "No, it sounds foolish" says your character.  That's right, wannabe-Hope Estheim actually has a brain, unlike some JRPG protagonists I know of.
Lastly, the micropay setup isn't extremely onerous.  It's easy enough to get Crystals to advance job lines through regular play.  Cards level up and become powerful through in game systems.  Even the Stamina system is forgiving - my first play session only ended because I ran out of Phoenix Downs in Chapter 2, not because I was barred from continuing due to low Stamina.  Sure, you can pay to speed the process along...but the game doesn't make you pay, and is an OK RPG to boot!
Minor gripes come first.
First, ladies, you don't get a character model.  You get to be wannabe Hope Estheim, voiced by wannabe Cloud Strife.  Guys who want to play as girls?  Same.
Speaking of gender confusion, wannabe Hope Estheim is a big fan of the 'backless' style.  The Knight 'skin' for instance, has minimal chest armor - a really bad idea - well-armored arms and legs, and everything laced neatly up in the back.  I'll say one thing for wannabe Hope Estheim - the boy is
in his sex appeal, and apparently never went to middle school.
More serious things.  The UI is...nonstandard.  Commands are hosted on the sides of the screen, instead of corners, as is more typical for PC games.  Some of this can be attributed to the fact this is a mobile port, but if you're going to make a PC version of a game, why not make your UI not break interface?
While the micropay system isn't annoying, the game is shot-through with mobile bullcrap to the point where it's an immersion breaker.  For instance, you can't get to a configuration menu for the first hour of play, because it's all forced tutorials that never let you set screen resolution, fullscreen/windowed, or much of anything else.  This is particularly annoying, when the game A) assumes full screen resolution, but B) puts the game in Windowed mode, which
moves certain things off-screen in Windows 10.  Because a few pixels of certain buttons were clickable, I was able to soldier past the tutorial; this was close to being a game-breaking bug, but fortunately fell short.
Once again, we have an Obligatory Annoying Moogle, who you meet early in the story.  Other than to have intra-party racism once the fairy joins (Moogles know the fairy as a selfish trickster, while the fairy is just flat-out racist against moogles), and speak in an annoying high-pitched voice, the moogle is just there to facilitate the story, and does little else of value.
Also, the game features "Exploration" segments where you can freely move about by holding the mouse button down and moving the mouse.  While this seems neat, in actuality, it's very seldom done, and very seldom effective.  Instead of needing to explore a ruined castle to find a teleport stone - said exploration being an entry bridge, a big room, and a remnant of a room just off that - why not just show a cutscene?  We're already full-linear in this game; it'd serve it better to stick with that, especially since the story is, if not awesome, at least reasonably engaging!
Lastly, and worst, is the RNG.  The game works by attacking, to generate element orbs.  You then use element orbs to power special attacks from your equipped cards, or you can use the 'Element Drive' to gain element resistances or restore your HP.  There's cases you will find where you need to restore your HP...and you don't get Healing Orbs, because they're generated semi-randomly.  These lead to needing to use a phoenix down, through no fault of your own, presumably to make you micro-pay.  Yes, I see through the charade.  No, it's not amusing.
I spent an entire night considering my rating for this game.  On the one hand: there is a good game in this.  There is a good story.  The production value is good.  That being said, the thumbs-up, and thumbs-down buttons aren't under any of those questions.  The question is "Do you recommend this game?"
The reason I do not, is because this is a phone-to-PC port, but I don't disrecommend it on principle alone.  The reason I disrecommend it, is because if Squeenix had taken about a year or so to really think this through, and exorcise all the micropay and RNG-ey elements from this work, then post it to Steam and just have us pay around $9.99 or so for this game, this would be a much,
better title.  As I've said before - there's a good game in this, I genuinely enjoy it.  The mobile micropay stuff constantly breaks immersion, though.
That being said, I doubt this game will stay installed on my system for more than about two weeks.  The novelty of 'a good phone RPG' will wear off, because I'm playing on a PC; I have other, better games that are developed with PC gaming in mind.  In about that time, there'll be something I want more.  To make room, this cellphone game will be deleted from my PC.

Mount and Blade: Warband has more upsides then it does downsides. Though the graphics are not that great and the game may experience some lag even on large beastly computers, its all worth while for the experience you recieve from this game. The everlooming knowledge that you are not immediatly on top, and are of small stature to the world around makes you feel small at first, but that more you play, the more you make an impact on the people, kingdoms and world around you. Warband gives a great sense of medieval warfare and can really immerse you in a harsh, unforgiving world.
-The game's combat engine may not be new, but is impressive, sometimes allowing for 150v150 matches with AI as well as online players.
-The modding community posts some really good mods on the worshop as well as ModDB and the Nexus.
(I reccomend, Gekokujo, L'aigle, Parrabellum, Perisno, and the Third Age)
-The learning curve for Mount and Blade is not too steep, but still offers a challenge. Think of it as easy to learn, hard to master.
-The diplomacy in the game is fleshed out enough that it is enjoyable, but not extended enough so that mods may take their own toll with the in game diplomacy.
-A lot of customization for you, as well as companions you meet within the game.
-Kingdoms vary a lot from each other, so playing experinces will be different from your last. An example being if you play as the Sarranids, you may use horse units a lot more, but if you play as the nords, archers become your friends.
-Online play offers variety as well as duels to test your skill against friends, bots or random opponets online.
The DLC (Napoleonic Wars) is totally worth the 10 dollars, and changes the game completely. This new DLC adds new gamemods such as Commander (Lead AI Troops against other players in the style of the Campaign), as well as line battles between online groups of regiments if thats what your into.
-The start game is really fun, and can really become a time consumer if your not careful.
(Though the game is relativly old, I still have to remark of the graphics).
-The graphics are good at best on ultra. The game is relativly old and this shows with how the faces look on people and how building's textures look within towns. If your looking for a good graphical game like Mount and Blade, wait for Mount and Blade: Bannerlord to realease, as it seems a lot better in its state of graphics.
-The endgame can become boring. After you have conquered the whole entireity of the game's large map (May take a while). The game seems to get boring, and repetative after you have completed everything. This can be fixed though with mods and different playing styles.
-Glitches in the game can overwhelm you if your not careful. Using mdos comes with its own risk, especially outside of the steam workshop. If you mash too many mods together, you may experience a pile of steaming garbage, being a waste of 20 dollars. So please tread at your own pace. Thankfully, most of the Glitches are not game breaking, and wont cause crashes.
-Unless you have a beast of a computer (Which I dont, I just wait through the lag) You will experince a lot of lag, especially in 150v150 battles, sieges or conversational screens (If both parties have more than 1800 troops at guess). This can be countered by lowering your graphics settings, or how many units on the field.Note that lowering your graphics settings will make your graphics experince a lot worse, and maybe at sometimes look downright ugly.
Certain features can be counted as good and bad.
-Unforgiving World: If you spend a lot of training a unit up from start to finish, so that they are the best unit in their class as well as faction, they still has the chance of dying and never coming back. You can lose all of your army, and sometimes a lot of your Denars (in game gold) because you lost a battle, got captured, or were ambushed. This gives a sense of challenge within the game, and can sometimes make you feel frustrated.
-Prejudiced AI: Starting the game as a woman can make your time and experince a lot harder, as women were not given the same rights of men during Medieval Times. This may or may not be a good experince for you. If you wish to have the hardest experience possible, starting out as a Women Farmer, is your best bet. Know that the Kings of the land will not see you as a rightful ruler, bescause of your sex. Marrying into a high ruling family can increase your changes of Stweardship, but this is very unlikely. This prejudice option can be turned off however.
-King Harlaus wont stop giving feasts: King Harlaus is the King of the in game Kingdom of Swadia. One flaw with him is the fact that he hosts feasts in the most strange and insane times. Feasts can be good, but may also distract you, as well as other AI Vassals, especially in a time of war. Feasts can be used to improve relations with other lords, talk to the King in Private, or look for a lady to marry/Husband to marry. But if I must attend another feast within the spand of 3 god damn minutes, I Will flip.
All In all, Mount and Blade is one fo my favorite games, and I do solely reccomend you buy it, especially if there is a sale on Taleworlds games.

This game is kind of a mixed bag. It either nails something or flops completely.
Pros:
Highly Replayable, There are lots of weapon options and movement options.
Tons of Customization, Every outfit has multiple colorations (You create the coloration) Also there are an absolute load of costumes and weapon styles in this game, including ones that allow you to look like your favorite DC superhero.
Varied Quests, While they do get a little repetitive after a while, there are still different enemies and bosses.
Movement types are fun to use and varied, adding to replayability.
Roleplaying (I don't personally but it gives you vague enough character decisions it works out pretty well).
The closest thing to a justice league game with modern graphics that isn't injustice.
Cons
MIcrotransactions are forced down your throat from the beginning. The game is playable without them, but upgrading to premium enhances gameplay a little with more inventory storage and whatever you bought it with.
While the game advertises a lair and you can get one for free in game, you need to pay for the lair system which is five dollars and actually makes having a base practical. Same with any non main story DLC and the utility belt upgrade. Upgrading to a membership allows you to have more than 2000 dollars in your inventory at a time. This is fine early on but gets annoying later. This really cripples what would otherwise be a fun and innovative game.
I have to say as well that the voice acting is absolutely abhorent earrape for some characters. Others are completely fine however.
I also must say that PvP is basically unusable until you are level 30 (The max level in the game) and have top tier gear (You do not have to pay for top tier gear in my experience) because there is no level or skill matching unfortunately.
The community in my experience is a mix of helpful and questionable but I haven't gotten too involved beyond accidently joining a guild.
In conclusion this game is a 6/10. It's a shame that it couldn't be more enjoyable because of constant requests for your money. To better this I think they could easily have just a pay for premium after you've played an hour or two as a suggestion. Upon opening after you've played a bit they show you like whats hip and new in the market and that's fine. The Lair System and Utility belt should just be included honestly or have both in a five dollar package if they really insist on their current price point of 5 each. Aside from bad competitive statis and paywalling, I've had a lot of fun screwing around in the game and using the character customizer to model drawings and characters. The paywall however takes it down a solid 3.5 points and competitive a 0.5 as I don't get too into competitive stuff but I also would like to fight a villain as my cool characters at any level.

WarGame Red Dragon. 8/10
I love RTS. My favorite to date is still Company of Heros because of the story driven theme and it's a good RTS in general.
Wargame Red Dragon is next up. While there is little personality to the game, I love it anyway because I am also a sim junkie. This is what would result if World in Conflict got A-10 warthog Flaming Cliffs pregnant. I really like the scale, the terrain, the Era, the models and the depth of comand. Just creating your own special decks for multiplayer is fun, and is perfect for satisfing your mico manage OCD.
While many people complain about balance, I do not. I would rather try to come up with clever stratagies to bring an underdog up. We have played using the worst OPFOR decks we can create and still win (more so than with a premium Blufor deck). Some features I personally like.
1) When you are playing a multiplayer game, you are sort of stuck watching the battle from birds eye view so you can keep an eye on the field which isnt that cool, but when the battle is over, you can replay it and adjust the time. Now you can watch the battle from any angle, even from a units shoulder. Those who make epic vids will love this.
2) While the scale isn't "realistic" it is scaled very well.  Well enough to give you some feel for actual stratagy. This is why I say it has a nice SIM feel to it.
3) VARIETY. You can create the deck you want to play! It's not a matter of caping an "AMMO" dump so you can afford tanks. You get what you bring, you bring what you want. Great for team play.
4) I LIKE THE NAVY! This notion of one Navy being better than another is false. It's all about your deck and how you use it. If your enemy showed up with a better navy than you, then chances are your Air Force is better than theirs. Every battle is an excercise in knowing what is your strength and thier weakness is this vast combonation of units.
5) I like friend chat and invite features. You dont need to tab in and out of Steam to invite friends to join game.
6) Choke points are only partially important.  As a result there is always a way around a fortified position, it's just time consuming and risky. Not a mindless meat grinder that devlopes the same area each instance of the map.
7) The best and really only modern arms grand command simulator! If you like games like Total War Napoleon for the battle instances, you will like this one.
That leads me to what I wish the game had.
1) A grand campaign like the Total War series. Then you could bring other units into it like ICBM, spies, satalites and diplomacy. Have populations and national rescources.
2) Combat enjineers who deploy bridges across rivers for battles.
3)Anywhere but enemy territory placeable FOBS that dont run out of supply if in a friendly zone but can be placed in a neutral area.
4) A topigraphical overlay. I love the importance of LOS and elevation, It would be even better if it was easier to see from a distance.
5) Better concealment for infantry in forrest. Some AI behaviors for them. Like running away from napalm, taking cover automaticly under fire from heavy weapons.
6) Navy divers that can swim unseen and Marine units that can forde rivers on foot.
7) Loss of communication to units if all your Command units are destroyed.
That about sums it up. I don't subtract from the game for the things it dosn't have, because it's unrealistic to expect everything. I giive it high scores because it aproaches RTS in a way I always wished they would, and I like the theme that so few have tried to do, and the Few that have tried were not this good. I.e. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is definitely unique in its mechanics, as well as graphical design. It was a great pleasure to play though the story, and as other reviewers have mentioned, 'experience the emotion'. There are many unique and quirky elements to this game. The environments change dramatically as you progress through, and the other 'characters' you come across are plainly awesome.
I personally found the controls to be annoying to deal with, though. It reminded me of childhood memories, of messing around with two controllers for the sake of it... trying to control two characters alone. It felt gimmicky in this regard, and it would've translated to a co-op game MUCH better.
In terms of puzzles, this game is fairly simplistic. Everything jumped out at me within moments of viewing the area - and as such it was a very easy game. If you're looking for a harder challenge, looking elsewhere might be your best bet. In terms of storytelling, and something new and unique... this is the go.
The above aside, I would recommend this game... but only at a sale price (around $5). It's a quirky and very enjoyable experience once you look past the gimmicky control system (and stop feeling like a lonely person, trying to play a co-op game alone).
Even though this game pretty much requires a controller, the story more than makes up for it. It's only around 3 hours long, but well worth playing. Give it a shot!

I understand if you are reading these reviews as you are sceptical on whether to buy this game or not.  I was once like you.
I originally witnessed this game release on Xbox LIVE Arcade on the Xbox 360 and soon after a media storm ensued - praise was given everywhere from nearly every major gaming outlet.  I still didn't bite.
Roll around Steam Winter Sale 2013, I buy Brothers for £3.  Yep, £3.  Possibly the best £3 I have ever spent, on anything.
To truly experience this game you will need a controller as this is a "Single player co-op" experience, you will be controlling the two brothers on the one controller - One brother using the Left analog stick and trigger and the other brother using the right hand side.  It is difficult to get used to, it is very unfamiliar, at times uncomfortable and it is absoloutley incredible. The way the controls are mapped and how they are used in gameplay tell a narrative that you are probably thinking is impossible, especially when the characters speak a kind of "Simlish" language.  Without spoiling anything, these controls are mapped in an EXTREMELY smart way - Please think, if you play this game, why each brother is mapped to that specific side of the controller. Hint: It was not done on accident.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons takes so many conventions we have become used to in gaming and completely flips them on their head, and then some.  Take nearly everything you know/have learned about modern games and throw it away before heading in to this.
The audio is great, the visuals are near perfection.  I can not say any more without spoiling this experience... Just buy and play this game, It will be like nothing you have ever experienced.
I highly recommend this game. A must play for all gamers. The story is something worthy of a Hollywood blockbuster told in a way that can only be done through video games. 10/10

Simply brilliant adventure-story telling game.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons offers a unique experience of its own and delivers it thru incredible graphic details. When you journey, you'll see the intrinsically beautiful game world and level designs. The OSTs just add more to the awesomeness, so atmospheric and fitting.
Gameplay is quite simple as you only need to move around and solve simple puzzles. There's a bit annoying boss battles but it's nothing anyway if you play many more of challenging games nowadays like Bastion. Though, really, the major strength of the game lies not in its gameplay but in its storyline - despite the voice actors speak in made-up language (no English caption sorry!), it can convey the story with the body language and display. Following the story is also another great experience. You'll see the value of your sibling, or brotherhood, through how the two brothers here work together and lend a hand to to each others. Sometimes we forget about that siblings are wonderful gift, eh?
Checkpoints are scattered throughout the game so suppose you die from accidental glitches - yes, happened to me - or die in boss battles you don't have to retrack your steps too far. The game offers chapter to chapter selection so you can easily replay the chapter you want to rewatch.
While the controller is recommended (xinput based works flawlessly while dinput requires x360ce to play), you can also use keyboard to play the game. Heck, you can coop using gamepad for first player and keyboard for the second player, though it's a bit awkward to play coop in a game like this. That said, controlling two brothers using gamepad, which is recommended, can be a bit awkward at first as usually we use the right stick to aim or shoot not to move.
If you want to have a perfect achievements, it's not hard. Basically everything can be done in one playthrough - and that also makes the game quite limited in replayability. zero reason to replay the game unless you just want to remember the story.
