Installed this yesterday evening and have clocked up 9.5hrs.
~When you first start it seems a bit low-budget and a bit like a B movie, I wasn't so sure at first, it just seemed a bit thrown together, but, if you stick it out until you've done the first few main story quests and stumble upon some public geared events you may well start to enjoy it.
There's plenty of players online that you bump into, random side quests and lots of public events you encounter when just travelling to and from your objective. In that respect it's been a fun few hours.
If I had to describe the game it's Mass Effect meets Destiny meets fallout with some RIFT style random events you get caught up in. Playstyle is very much like mass effect, it's third person offset camera, with basic run and roll / dodge but lacking the cover system. The way you run around dispatching enemies in various environments and zones reminds me of playing mass effect vs destiny, the hud animations when you collect items and interact are similar too.
There are quite a few similarities to Destiny whilst on that note. So if you are looking for a sci-fi fix of that type then take a look at this. I think Bungy had quite a bit of inspiration from this. I played Destiny from beta and release, leveled up a Hunter to 30 with all legendary and exotics, did all instances / strikes and put in a hell of a lot of playtime (then got bored and sold it along with the PS4) so I have seen all of it.
The environments the art style and post-apocolyptic battle of Defiance much like the (rather poorly explained) battle of the traveller and environments. Certain mobs look very much like the Knights and others (and raiders look nearly identical to some of the enemies on earth, mutants with swords charging at you very similar in idea to the vandals concept).
Scenery is of a very similar style, certain outfits and gear look similar, the HP system and hail-of-bullet style play and mob encounters are similar too. Even down to the rocket / thrust system on mounts and the way mounts are summoned and an AI 'ghost' style entity guiding you. I have the cloak ability and building on other specs similar to the hunter style play. There are certain things it does better too, like the fact that it IS open world, and not just some crappy restricted zone or 'patrol' style small planet map. The actual social aspect that was heavily lacking in destiny is in Defiance. I could actually see me getting more play time from this.
I'm not sure of the longevity of this game at the moment, there is a very big map and several continents to explore, I have travelled to quite a few zones already but I am still discovering places, I feel the combat may get a little tiring, but there are plenty of weapons and a lot of modifications that you can do to them (you can modify the stock, barrel, scope and ammo / magazine type).
There are a ton of micro-transactions, the store has a lot of gear you can purchase, but they have to make some money somehow since it's gone F2P right? The servers won't run themselves! I haven't found yet however that I need to buy anything, quests do the standard MMO thing and reward gear, be it weapons, outfits or shields / mods, so there is plenty to keep you going while you assess whether you really do like the game or not. And if you like it, why not buy a weapon or outfit, it's cheaper than a pint of beer...
Some good and bad points so far:
+ Graphics are very pleasent - nice effects, nice level of detail and terrain looks very good, models look good too
+ Well designed environments
+ High FPS - even on highest settings performance seems very good, never dropped bellow 60fps once, even with about 100 players on the screen in a total frag-fest
+ LOTS of action - if you like unleashing a hail of bullets and projectiles into enemies you will enjoy it
+ Lots of gear - Weapons, modifications and equipment available even without buying from the store
+ Zero server and connection lag experienced thus far
+ Good sound FX
+ Open world - no real set path, do anything you want and at your own pace
+ No leveling system - as such, this is a postive I believe, new players can instantly join in with veterans and have fun
+ Skill trees with lots of progression
+ If your into the series, this links in nicely and has episodic content that carries over to the game
+ Fast travel if you want to get somewhere in a hurry
- Widescreen users may experience 'vanishing' textures and objects on high settings - after some play time (memory leak?) although the game still looks great on medium and this problem will go away
- Story is a bit bland - not very well explained, not engrosing or that interesting in game
- Music - gets very annoying after a while, the combat music is limited to one track that really gets on your nerves, at least you can turn it off
- Some enemies have way too much hp - and not in a good way, IE in certain quests the mob won't kill you, you won't be worried at all but you will roll around shooting him for about 10 mins getting very bored with his never ending HP!
Overall if you have a few spare minutes, are bored and fancy just trying something new, then for free it is really worth a shot.

For those who are tired of the same whining reviews about a free to play game: Here is an honest review: The sections called "Conclusion" are teh TL;DR versions of the section.
1> Yes, the devs want money, we all want money, there are many convienances to paying into the game.  One of which is Content, Not the whole game is accessable as a non-paying or non-subscription player.  Free to play does NOT mean the whole game is accessable.  It means you CAN play it free.  You can get right to max level free, and a mid to mid-low CR rating for free.  You can get higher for free with a little hard work (And repetitive.) but in general.  if you pay for the subscription, or pay for the unlocks in the real money market - the whole game can become accessable for you.
Conclusion: Free? Yes, Whole game accessable for free? Not really.
2> Revamps and alterations to the game when you just get comfortable to what was originally there for you.  Yes, they updated the system, made changes to the numbers, and put a challenge back into the game.  Some people like the new and refreshing way the game now works, some people don't.  You'll get that with -every- game.  How many times has WoW revamped and changed things?  How many times has Diablo revamped and changed things?  Look at dev logs and see all the changes.  DCUO is no different, things change sometime - either you like it or you don't.
Conclusion: Did everythign change?  Not everything, but some things did.  and it was mixed received like any other change.
3> Gameplay and controls, Well, honestly.  I think they did a marvelous job with the game play and controls.  Nothing really seems clunky or awkward.  it's an ARPG, (Action RolePlaying Game) Meaning that it's not turn based, or cooldown dependant like WoW would be.  You click your mouse, your hero does a basic attack, you right click, your hero does a basic ranged attack, and then you can use various combos of these two buttons when you unlock new combos.  You have your "Superpowers" on your hotbar, 1-6 with 7-0 being items and utility items.  Yoru powers are on cooldowns and/or charges that you recharge through various other attacks and actions.  so there is a slight learning curve to combos and rotations - but it's a very gentle curve that can grow to be very advanced and powerful.  Easy to learn, fun to master.
Conclusion: The game play is pretty nice, good for newbies and veterans alike.
4> Story.  Wow.  This is one thing that I'm surprised to say that the game excels at.  The story is very rewarding - and though some parts are extremely poorly voice acted (Giganta and Wondergirl scene comes to play >.<) the story itself is really nice and imersive.  If nothing else, I recommend you take a character from 1-30 just to listen to and watch the story unfold.  The full game is voice acted, meaning you don't need subtitles.  Some of the combat voices can get annoying and repetetive (That stingzzzzzzz) but all in all, it is SO worth the play through if you're a DC Comics, or a superhero fan in general.
Conclusion: The story is imersive and well written with very few instances of poor voice acting.
All in all, I have to recommend this game.  No, you won't get the full content as a free player, no, you won't be able to spend more than $5,000 of ingame money at a time as a free player, but come on.  If no one spent a dime into a game this massive, there would be no game to play.  It's not fair to those of us who can't afford to pay to play the game, but it is not pay to win.  You can't buy power,  Why people say it's pay to win is because people who subscribe, or people who buy content can get their CR (The Combat Rating after you reach max level) higher because they have acess to more content.  And you only feel the burn of that in PVP.  The game is worth it for just the Solo content, let alone finding a group to play the more challenging free content with.
Conclusion: It's not pay to win, it's pay for content, I hope that you try it for just the story itself - although I could understand someone being frustrated with the Free to Play limitations of content.  I hope to see you in game!

Ah yes, Surgeon Simulator 2013. There's a reason why it is NOT called Surgery Simulator, mainly because the operations in this game is extremely wacky and way off the standard protocol. (Surgery without gloves? Blasphemy!)
You control a faceless surgeon who apparently has only one hand. (Which might also be the reason why he isn't wearing gloves, because how on Earth would someone put on gloves with only one hand without assistance from others?)
Operations include heart transplant, double kidney transplant and brain surgery (which are the only ones I've unlocked so far, I hear there are secret missions that can be unlocked besides the TF2 crossover). Each operation can be repeated in a different setting other than the usual operating theatre, such as in a speeding ambulance and in a zero gravity environment.
The controls are.......unique, as the keys are mapped according to which finger is used to tap each key. This means you have full finger control (finger gestures abound). But, full control does not mean simplicity, as you have to control the wrist and arm movements with the mouse. Therefore, to say the very least, the controls are very tricky, but once you have played several sessions you'll have some degree of mastery with it.
Overall, it is a game with a quite steep learning curve, but the satisfaction gained when completing an operation is immense. 8 out of 10.

Short Review:
If you like to literally die within 3 seconds of the round starting then this game is for you.
Long Review: TL:DR is at the bottom
This game is just bad overall. Good enough for a F2P game, and best yet, no P2W no payable DLC's or skins or anything like that, just gameplay. Every gun is free and unlocked as soon as you get into the game, as well as all the attatchments and equipment too. Other than that, this game is literal trash compared to it's previous versions. Let me go into depth on this.
Guns - 5/10
There is only 6 guns in this game at the time of this review, but that isn't the problem at all. It actually keeps balance between the two teams as they both have the same loadouts. There is two assault rifles (m4 and m16) a shotgun (remington 870) an LMG (m249) and two snipers (m24 and mk14). The worst part about guns? Literally everything else. When you fire a gun it feels like you're just holding a toy gun and doing fake recoil in a pretend world. It may as well be a pretend world too because there's no bullets tracers (That I have seen). It feels like I should be screaming "PEW PEW PEW!!1! HEY I SHOT YOU, YOU'RE OUT JIMMY" over mic and that I would expect a "NUH UH YOU DIDN'T HIT ME I DODGED IT" as a response.
Gunplay is mediocre too, it bascially comes down to whomever sprays the most. No seriously, I watch people play this and when they see an enemy behind cover they just spray at them and get a kill. It's boring af.
The good thing about it though is that when you aim down a red dot sight or a scope, it renders the stuff outside of the scope too, and I think that is cool.
K00L GRAFIX - 7/10
Game looks good and runs pretty well overall. It's basically what you would expect from a F2P shooter on Unreal Engine 3. Also no crashes as of yet.
Maps - 4/10
The maps in this game are horrific. In all of the maps everyone spawns at their base that they can move freely around in until the red wall decides its time for you go play cops and robbers with your friends down the street.
As soon as the red wall dissapears GO RUN IT'S CALL OF DUTY : PROVING GROUNDS, WHOS GOING WHERE IDK JUST SHOOT EM', and as soon as you take no more than 10 steps you're getting shot at by the enemy. The maps are that small, which is rediculous considering when you fly around the map before a match starts you can plainly see that it is 20% playable map and 80% scenery and ambience on the outside of the tiny warzone you're plopped in. Honestly, my 6 year old nephew could design a better map.
Gameplay - 4/10
Oh my god, I don't even want to review this. As you've seen in the previous parts of this review, the gameplay consists nothing of spraying and getting to the OP peaking spots first.
But I have to go in depth of this, so I will.
Let me start off with saying that this game had a ton of potential, but it fell way short. As mentioned earlier, gunplay is mediocre and it feels imaginary. Movement is claimed to be "fast paced" but its really just a super small map, and you actually run kind of slow. What's cool about it though is that running affects your accuracy, so the more you run, the less accurate you'll be and vice versa. You can even "be quiter" by pressing alt and making your character move slower(?) which does basically nothing as people can hear you through concrete walls anyways. The grenades are cool, you can carry two of these combos in a loudout: (m67 frag) (2x flash) (2x smoke) (2x fog(=smoke???)). They actually feel nice to throw as you can throw them right away at the push of a button or you can pull them out and cook them if you like. Unfortunately, the only useful grenade in this game is the flash, which by the way is very well crafted. When one explodes next to you it affects your vision (during the flash and after the flash dissapears), movement, accuracy, and sound, just like a flash should. If you get shot, you lose health (obviously), but the system works different in this game. You have bandages, but they don't heal you. they only stop the bleading and your health will only fall to a certain percentage when bleading. For example, I have 100% health. I get shot. I take immediate un-healable damage of 8%, leaving me at 92% health. I then continue to bleed down to 76% health unless I bandage and stop the bleeding. It's way more easier to understand than I am making it sound. You can also revive "dead" teamates unless the enemy team has "secured" them or they have been shot in the head.
I'm starting to drag on in this so I'm just going to end it with this:
The movement is nice, you can sprint, crouch, prone, vault, lean, prop your gun on stuff, climb, and even slide into places. Gunplay is aweful. Maps are aweful. Grafix are decent. Sounds are decent. just a meh game overall.
TL:DR
Play this if you're too poor to buy COD.

A complex game with many different facets and choices. There is no storyline as one would normally think of it, but the game has such a detailed and fleshed out world that you will very easily end up creating your own epic tale.
You can be a trader, a governor, a warlord, a loyal knight in service to a king, a mercenary captain, a slaver, a bounty hunter, a bandit, a vigilante, pretty much anything you want to be. You can conquer towns, seige castles, raid villages, ambush caravans, rescue noblemen from prison to gain favor with them and their families, compete in tournaments to gain wealth and renown, help a claimant take their rightful (or not!) place on the throne, there really is so much to do.
This game can be as easy or as hard as you like it, having the option to reduce damage done to yourself and allies if the game is too difficult for you or if you want it to feel like a movie (victorious hero defying the odds and all that). You may also adjust the size of battles to make them feel as epic or as personal as you'd like (Although the game does play better with larger battles, in my opinion)
There are also a multitude of mods for this game, ranging from simple tweaks, to complete expansions, to total conversions. Alternate maps, historical maps, Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, I think there's even a Star Wars mod being developed.
At over 400 hours at the time of this review, this game is one of my all-time favorites, and Taleworlds have certainly earned a loyal supporter for life.
TL;DR This is one of the best games I've ever played, and certainly the best open-world RPG type game I've ever experienced.

Just Cause has a grappling hook.
Red Faction has a sledgehammer.
You'd think the victor would be clear, but, no.
Play Just Cause to blow up and leap about diverse islands.
Play Red Faction to smash up and truck about gritty Mars.
Both games seem to have odd camera-handling (on a controller at least).
Just Cause takes some serious getting used to, but it is possible.
Red Faction has strict control configurations; you can't have your mouse at the ready to do the turret sections without going into settings and changing it from controller to KB+M. There are sensitivity settings for both, but changing it on controller only seems to affect Mason, not the camera absolutely (I had to quit after failing several times to tap the camera just so in a turret section).
Also the driving isn't all that tight, but that might just be dependent on the vehicles.
I played this game on... 360 or PS3, I forget. Sunk tens of hours into it; was the first Red Faction game I played and it appealed to my "Destruction for a good cause in a sandbox" needs. Indeed, I
Guerilla broke ground in debris physics.
Red Faction: Guerilla is a very fun and awesome game; six years after release (not sure if it has been on Steam that whole time, though) and it is still being updated. Several people, at one time, could not get the game running(?) - I had zero issues.
That was for while it was heavily discounted.
The combat isn't the tightest. As I said in mentioning the turrets and having to "tap the camera just so"; same is pretty much true for standard firefights too.
The cover system is very finnicky; what YOU think would constitute good cover might not be.
Holding RB to bring up the weapon select, you then push one of the face buttons (YBAX) to choose your weapon. The RB menu stays open for a split second, but often long enough for you to switch weapons instead of reloading or interacting with something.
Why we have to use RB to switch weapons when you can only carry 4 in the first place and they are arranged in such a way that to not allow us to switch weapons with the D-Pad makes no sense AT ALL (unless there are some sort of Follower Commands or something I've yet to see (I don't remember much of the finer points)).
Driving suffers from the same (")problem(") as the combat. X is your handbrake - sometimes you have to hold it, sometimes you have to tap it, usually you'll end up spinning completely around. Trying to destroy the towers when the Red Faction escapes from the starting area -- the mission that most stuck out in my mind. Because I failed it a-numer-tous times. Because I would end up driving up the side of a cliff to get a tower planted right at its edge because Mason wouldn't turn the wheel as fluidly as I'd want.
I'm pointing out faults in Guerilla that I find as such because my frame of reference has been (of late) comprised of incredibly tight experiences like GTAV.
Really, because of that, I'm inclined to be more lenient than I'd usually be and go ahead and write off the "faults" in Guerilla as consequences of it being... arcade-y.
You cannot aim with the trigger. You have to click the right stick. = The ultimate proof of this (Just Cause is the same way and the driving also seems a bit delayed).
EDIT 2: Playing on Hard, the game isn't hard. It's just unfair. If you are in territory that is
run by the EDF (enemies), and you're trying to do a challenge, say, Transporter (race a vehicle to a destination); you will no doubt fail it. The roads are so serpentine / there are so many terrain features / there are too many constructs in your path. So you hit Retry. You are immediately blasted by hordes of enemies.
I don't know if you're meant to beat the game and then do challenges - if beating the game would erradicate the EDF - but it doesn't matter. If you're able TO do those challenges regardless, you still have to tangle with gratuitous enemies.
If you're in hostile territory, say, trying to destroy a building, you can clear all enemies, continue demolishing, turn around and literally watch seven enemies spawn right in front of you.
At the moment, driven by rage, I must change my review from positive to negative.

This game is really something special. Even though it's 5 years old, it's still ahead of the times. The main draw of this game is it's physics engine that allows literally EVERYTHING to be destructible in realistic ways. Tear down entire buildings with a sledge hammer and watch them collapse in a realistic manner. Plant remote charges on weak points and try to take down a building in one blast. Drive a semi truck, through the support columns. In later stages you even unlock a gun that makes entire portions of structures melt away.
I heard that when the developers first created this engine, all their buildings initially collapsed under their own simulated weight. They had to study architecture and learn how to make buildings that would stand-up, so that you could knock them down. That is a testament to how cool their destruction engine actually is.
On the downside, the graphics aren't awesome, but are definitely passable. The game-world seems very small despite being gigantic. That's because the map is very sparsely populated, and buildings are not everywhere. There is definitely a good amount of stuff for you to destroy, but every building you destroy stays knocked down for the rest of the game. So the story is that you are trying to save mars from an oppressive earth military, ironically, by knocking down every single building on the planet. Don't ask questions, just blow stuff up.
The shooting and driving in this game are ok but not great. There is a small selection of vehicles and guns, and missions can tend to get kind of repetitive. But the destruction engine more than makes up for it, as knocking down buildings in this is insanely fun.

Heroes & Generals is an multiplayer action tactical WWII FPS game published in 2014.
This game is like Battlefield 1 with lower graphics, and for free.
Its an OK game to play. You can play it by yourself, or with friends, and its a lot of fun. Although its a bit hard game. Comparing to CoD, where you are really fast, and feeds are always filled with loads of kills, in this game its different. You respawn at your spawn, get on bycicle and cycle into the frontlines of war, where your main goal is to take over points.
What makes most people (including) mad about the Multiplayer are the tanks. If you are an infantry, and you go to a point, and there are like 3 tanks on it, your chances to survive are minimal. Its hard to destroy them with mines, although with a bit of luck and accuracy, you can destroy them with rocket launchers.
Arsenal of weapons and equipment in this game is really awesome. You can upgrade your weapons, although its not visible on the outside, it just makes the weapon better.
Arsenal of vehicles although isnt that good. There are 3 basic vehicles, on which you can only put boxes with ammo or health.
Every gun, attachment or vehicle can be purchased with earned money, but it takes a long time to earn such value. If you have spear money, you can buy gold coins, which you can use on weapons you dont even have unlocked.
Overall, I rate this game 6.5 / 10. Its definitely the best game for people that want to play Battlefield, but cant afford it.

Brothers has a haunting beauty about it, a slow, quiet pace, which delivers its story with subtlety. Its environments are brilliantly presented, and vary significantly as the game progresses.
Challenge is minimal, with puzzles providing pacing, rather than barriers; the few occasions where things were slightly less straight forward were never cause for frustration. Despite this, there is a real satisfaction here. Stepping back from the main goal, and poking the world around you will reveal situations which aren't necessary for completing the main story, but which leaving unresolved will feel wrong. In other cases you'll just be rewarded for your curiosity, with a small moment you would otherwise have missed.
But the main strength in Brothers lies in the way it builds itself over the course of the game, something which results in one of the best integrations I have ever seen between the control system, and the story itself. Ludo-narative resonance if you must. Without these sparks, the game would have been a pleasently enjoyable experienced, and worth playing for anyone who enjoys good world design; with them I think we have something a bit more special.

It's fun, and difficult, but the way the game interprets your mouse inputs makes it way harder than it should be. Cursor is relative to position of head of the hammer; there is a massive acceleration curve, which makes it so that if you make so much as a tiny twitch of the hand, it'll throw you off and cause you to lose all your progress immediately. Beyond the acceleration curve, since the game tries to keep your cursor on the hammer itself, if your cursor happens to cross the character's body, it is interpolated or thrown immediately to the other side of the character, which brings the hammer with it, along with your progress.

This game is a lesson in human psychology and game design.

The game is pretty interesting, and often challenging. It is a F2P game with microtransactions, but not the usual cash grab most of F2P games have.
Stamina (the thing you consume to start battles) is decently sized and refills pretty quickly, and you keep getting elixirs (things that recharge your stamina) all the times as in-game loot or as login gift, so there is not really much artificially stopping you from playing.
You also receive summon tokens and ability tokens relatively often, so you can try your luck a couple times per month without spending and upgrade your own cards quite fast.
There is a "monthly premium" thingy as well, which gives some amazing value (summon tokens, ability tokens, extra skillseeds, and some pretty useful items), surprisingly it costs 3000 magicite and  you earn about 150 a day for free with no effort, so you can keep it active just by logging and collecting it twice a day, and you have also some spare change to upgrade your inventory.
I've been playing "free" since the release, and I got pretty far in the game. There are not many games that allow you to get free "premium currency", especially not by just logging in. Of course you should not expect to compete in top ranks on the leaderboards this way, but the game is pretty enjoyable if you don't set too high expectations.

Torchlight II has an abundance of re-play value and considerable depth. Good fun to play.
8 / 10

The "true" sequel to Diablo 2, it improves upon the good old hack, slash, and loot formula by a factor of ten. Streamlined leveling and looting allows you to wade right into the thick of things with gleeful abandon. Enemies crumple, pop, explode, and sizzle before a variety of interesting spells and abilities. Within only a few hours, you can easily destroy hundreds of monsters and around 3-7 bosses (with the epic loot associated for them).
So! For $20, you get this game. It's fun, it's cheap, and an improvement on the ARPG formula on every level. You have offline solo play, LAN, online co-op, mods, character customization, and even a bit of PvP.

Torchlight II would be amazing if there was more of an end-game to speak of. The multiplayer is a huge step in the right direction, but Runic's not there just yet. Gimpy PVP is a non-factor and a low item diversity means every character of a given class is shooting for the exact same gear at level 100. Game modifications and saving character files locally is a double-edged sword; while it is nice to have community contributions, it also makes cheating a breeze. Difficulty scaling is rather uneven through New Game Plus 2 and beyond, and characters that have advanced that far are unable to join games or play with those that are not on the same stage of NG+ progression. While I wish there was a broader meta, this is still the best loot-'em-up I've played since Diablo II.

Defiance. Have you watched the TV series? Cool, you'll probably be one of the people who understands why that's the name of this game, because there are suprisingly few allusions to it in the game of the same name. That's fine with me, but if I hadn't have watched the show I guess I'd still be wondering if it was one of those gritty, angst-ridden titles that never really lives up to what the Dev's have delivered. Don't get me wrong, I have really enjoyed the time I've put into Defiance so far, and will continue to put in because I am keen to see how it all plays out, but this is a game that definitely has it's great points and also areas where it deserves more work.
I have a realtively shallow background when it comes to MMO's, so I was pleasantly surprised to find one that for the most part felt like a single-player with other people running around going about thier daily lives. Being free-to-play is what drew me in in the first place, as I'm currently fascinated with what kind of stuff people consider to be worth absolutely nothing at all (a strange concept considering the amount of work that goes into making a game), and quickly fell victim to the (obviously successful) not-so-micro puchase system. I blame one of my mates who I convinced to play with me, as I probably wouldn't have bouth the DLC if he didn't, thinking that maybe it would have unlocked other territories or given me extra loot capacity, and I was very dissapointed when that was not the case for $20 (AT HALF PRICE!) worth of investation. Yeah I got extra missions and daily currency, but it basically amounted to sweet-♥♥♥♥-all in the grand scheme of things.
On the upside though, cutscenes in one-off co-op missions is very enjoyable, especially when they are often funny (in a Borderlandsish way), and they don't seem out of place with the main missions so you start getting a real feel for the characters. In short, Defiance is worth the 14GB download just to play the series missions if nothing else, but I doubt you'll be able to help yourself from getting out and about if you go in with that intent...
Key bindings were pretty easy to configure to suit my usual play style, although I'm yet to find a better place than Alt for dodge because I'm not used to being spoiled for choice, having both dodge AND jump. I haven't really played around with in-game voice, but Raidcall seems to be the common theme amongst the clan I hooked up with. That's also something worth a mention - there are good bonuses to being in a clan and having friends. Being able to teleport to them any time you like is the one I have used the most, but you can also recieve boons just from being in a clan. I found this to be a novel concept, and the navigation thing helps get bulk numbers fast for the good instances.
There's probably heaps more I could waffle on about, but the main things are that it's a 3rd person shooter with a pretty straightforward RPG system (the most intense decision you'll have to make is what outfit shows of your characters boobs the best), basically troll-proof, and it's free. Why not eh?

Brothers has a haunting beauty about it, a slow, quiet pace, which delivers its story with subtlety. Its environments are brilliantly presented, and vary significantly as the game progresses.
Challenge is minimal, with puzzles providing pacing, rather than barriers; the few occasions where things were slightly less straight forward were never cause for frustration. Despite this, there is a real satisfaction here. Stepping back from the main goal, and poking the world around you will reveal situations which aren't necessary for completing the main story, but which leaving unresolved will feel wrong. In other cases you'll just be rewarded for your curiosity, with a small moment you would otherwise have missed.
But the main strength in Brothers lies in the way it builds itself over the course of the game, something which results in one of the best integrations I have ever seen between the control system, and the story itself. Ludo-narative resonance if you must. Without these sparks, the game would have been a pleasently enjoyable experienced, and worth playing for anyone who enjoys good world design; with them I think we have something a bit more special.

I'm not entirely sure what I'm supposed to say here. I have a bunch of thoughts, but they're not coming together as a whole.
The game feels like a folktale, but not a modern Disney version with all the ugly or scary bits stripped away so all that's left is singing animals and a happy ending. On one level it is a fairly straightforward story of the quest that two young boys go on, and it's a very, very old tale which anyone of any age will be familiar with, but the most meaningful parts of it and the way it's told will probably resonate the most with adults, not children. There's adventure and courage and family and loss and all sorts of stuff going on if you let yourself become part of the experience. It's not a happy story, but it does have moments of happiness and joy here and there, and it's not really a story about sadness either, even though there are some tragic things that happen. I suppose that would make it bittersweet, and it certainly goes through a variety of contrasting feelings in a few hours.
It's also aesthetically very satisfying. Everything looks great, and all the different areas you travel through have their own distinct personality. A lot of effort clearly went into bringing the world and the characters and creatures you interact with to life, and every single detail just seems...right. Whether it's the charming village full of flowers you start near or sweeping vistas in the mountains, everything feels like it belongs. The music also does a lot to set the tone, and while the not-quite-language the characters emote to each other in was a little weird to me at first, I grew to like it after a bit, and it's rather expressive.
It wouldn't do not to mention how the game plays/feels too. The controls are simple but effective for what you need to do, with one analog stick and trigger for each of the two brothers (you can supposedly play it with the keyboard, but it was very obviously designed with a controller in mind, and that sounds like it would be very awkward). The stick moves the character, and the trigger interacts with whatever they're standing next to. It seems pretty basic, but when you're controlling two characters simultaneously in real time, that's plenty to keep track of.
In fact, if one of them gets hung up on an object in the scenery and the two of them ending up swapping sides on the screen, it can descend into complete chaos until you stop and move them back where you expect them to be. That isn't really a problem when you're just running around talking to people or solving puzzles, but when the game decides it briefly wants to be an action game for a few minutes a couple times (which is a poor decision in my opinion), it really isn't suited for it, can turn into kind of a mess, and tends to break the flow of the rest of the game (the same issue I had with the puzzles in To the Moon, which I thought would've been otherwise perfect if they'd been removed).
That's my only real substantial complaint about the game though. In general, the dual control scheme is used in clever ways, so I'm mostly willing to overlook the ways it doesn't quite work, and getting used to it pays off in the end with the things they do with it and the way it gets you attached to each of the characters.
If you dont mind using a controller,get this no questions asked.

There are plenty of fun, action packed triple A games out there, and a nice selection of story oriented RPGs, and the indie game market has been booming. But 'Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons' has something very unique about it. There isnt a word of english in this short little story, but it's controlls are extremely simplistic, yet unique in their own way. You control two characters simulaneously with both analogue sticks. The game itself is very short, but it has one hell of a sound track, and a suprisingly emotionally empacting story considering there is not a word of english to be found in th game. You start the game and think 'This is a little odd, and slow, not sure if I like it really.' Well, that's the though process I had at the time anyway, but giving the game a chance, I soon found myself becoming immersed in the beautiful world of 'Brothers'. And I played it in one sitting until finish. And was very suprised at how much I ended up loving the game. It's really something that you must experience yourself to fully understand the appeal, but I do highly reccomend playing this game at some point in your life!

I have tryed many other recording softwares before, including, but not limited to: fraps, dxtory, bandicam, litecam, camtaisia, and camstudio. But this, by far, out performs them all in almost every way.
Action! - Gameplay Recording and Streaming Software is a fantastic peice of software and does a great job at what it does.
Options:
First off, the option to go with two different versions of the sofware depending on what you're using it for (available on the website) is a nice touch for those who know what they need and don't want any extra expenses. Of course the only difference is the licence, so the features are consistent between versions.
Customisation:
Action! comes with a plethera of options compared to many recording softwares out there. A breif overview is this: What you record/the recorded region of the screen, what format you use, audio and visual type and quality controls, save destination, live streaming options, webcam recording and/or previewing, keyboard shortcuts and remote options, benchmarking, screenshots (and any related settings), launch options, language settings, HUD adjustments, exporting options, auto splitting, and optimisation settings for Action! itself. Each of those has a more in-depth explanation as well, which I will go over in the future on my channel and post a link to below when it's ready.
Quality:
The overall quality is outstanding to begin with, even on slightly lower quality settings; and the hardware acceleration options are a nice touch for decreasing framerate loss in game. The audio is also good quality for both system sound and optional microphone settings, although that really depends on your microphone if you have a mic set to record, and also has hardware accelerated options. Another thing with the audio is that you have the option to record the mic to a separate audio track, making it easier to edit later on.
Usability:
One problem a lot of payed recording softwares have is that they are too complicated or confusing for most new-comers to the software. Action! does not have that problem, as it is very easy to use despite all the settings you're given to play around with. Everything has a clear name or description available to you, and they are catagorised in the menus of the program in a logical and easy to find way, accompanied by fitting icons as well. They also provide plenty of helpful information on the website if you do get stuck and need the help.
Overall I cannot recommend this software more if you are looking into making high quality videos. I hope this review helped you make a decision.

An inferior update to the venerable Wargame: Airland Battle. Red Dragon takes a lot of the worst aspects of W: ALB and magnifies them ten times - point & click artillery and airplanes are vastly superior to conventional ground forces, the maps are so large now that moving tanks and other ground vehicles across the map is impractical because they require micromanagement and extra resources just to ensure they have enough fuel to move halfway across, and the game is still missing many quality of life features like the ability to reconnect to a game (the netcode is even worse now than in ALB) or a ruler to measure distances. The community has devolved into nationalistic tribalism, and the developers do not take substantive and researched criticism into consideration.
Red Dragon is a quick and dirty cashgrab compared to Airland Battle. If you want a modern RTS that isn't StarCraft, I heartily recommend ALB.

The best game I know for commanding a medieval army while participating in the battles yourself! By default you can set the battle size to 150 men at a time, but if your PC is decent you can adjust it higher in the config file to fight with 200 men, 300 men, 500 men, or whatever you can get away with.
There's a variety of weapons to use instead of just the usual swords and bows in most medieval themed media. I particularly find the horse combat addicting. It is just so pleasing to ride by and slice an enemy from horseback.
Outside of fighting the game is an RPG in which you level your character, manage your party, buy and sell things, side with a kingdom and make a name for yourself, protect your feifs, etc.
Don't forget to check out the plethora mods that change the game to take place in all kinds of settings from historical wars and fantasy shows. Because of the modding community you can be a samurai in feudal japan, a European knight going on crusade, or a commander in Middle Earth. There is also the DLC's Viking Conquest and Napoleonic Wars.

The game revolves around two brothers' quest to save their sickly father. The 'shtick' to this game is its unique control scheme, which also necessitates a controller. A keyboard/mouse would be nigh impossible. You, the singular player, control both brothers simultaneously with one controller. The left stick moves the older brother while the left trigger initiates his interactions. The right side does the same for the youngster.
The game is made up of simple, with occasionally tricky, puzzles involving both brothers. Environments are some of the best I've seen in recent memory. ENORMOUS amounts of detail and creativity abound. The surprising settings the brothers find themselves in evoke feelings of a magical journey. The true accomplishment of this game is the emotional response it created. Had I played this in one setting (easily done within about 2-3 hours) by myself, I almost assuredly would have been in tears at the end. This is only made more poignant by the fact that the 'twist' moment near the end of the game actually happened to the primary developer. He literally put his own life experiences in the game. This is a must-play game.

This is an update to my review as of August 25th 2017.
I had hoped to modify this review to be more positive, but Rockstar Games has again take moves that are abjectly anti-consumer.
Rockstar has made "adjustments" to the in-game account balance of its players. THis is fine as an anti-cheat measure if:
1. Applied accurately.
2. Applied in a timely manner.
The fact of the matter is however R* is applying these adjustments to players as punishment for events out of their control. In January 2017 I was sexually assaulted by a Neo-Nazi in-game. I am not exaggerating - this player was tattooed with Nazi symbols and his crew embled was the Nazi flag. He literally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me by using mods to force certain animations on our characters while raining money bags.
Now I'm not a sensitive person so of course I laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off while taking screenshots before moving along with my life.
The story is to point out how immensely flawed Rockstar's online service is and the inherently faulty logic of adjusting a "victim"'s account SEVEN MONTHS after an incident occurs. Suspiciously, right before the release of what will undoubtedly be the most expensive DLC ever.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Get your hands off our mods you dirty apes.
Seriously though, Rockstar's actions relating to GTA:Online have been a downward spiral of anti-player changes. From its inception two major issues have plagued GTA Online: Matchmaking and cheating.
The root cause of these issues is the P2P nature of the online service. The poor matchmaking and reliance on the connectivity of 3 - 27 strangers leades to the game's reputation of "loading screen simulator". Rockstar has not taken any steps to prevent online modding ("hacking") instead preferring a punative approach by banning any user that signs in to GTA Online with modded files. With no ban appeal process there "coincidentally" also leads to increased sales.
Thanks to allowing rampant in-game "inflation" Rockstar has continuously pushed the monetary cost of new content introduced in DLCs. This has lead to a viscious circle where a user has the choice to benefit from a modder's "generosity", spend literally hundreds of hours repeating the same task or purchase Rockstar's "Shark Cards" which had NOT scaled up to the increased cost of items. A single car in GTA Online can now cost 80 USD. Every development decision is keyed towards selling Shark Cards.
Now, I refrained from posting my thoughts in this venue because as the unwilling beneficiary of illegitimate money I was still able to enjoy my time in GTA Online. But Take Two has just issued C&D letters against the developers of modding tools for GTAV. While I don't use these mods myself I strongly support open community development. It is unacceptable to litigisously attack independent mod developers whose work only enhances the game experience and ultimately drives sales.
Shame on you Take Two and Rockstar.

Still wouldn't reccomend.

An inferior update to the venerable Wargame: Airland Battle. Red Dragon takes a lot of the worst aspects of W: ALB and magnifies them ten times - point & click artillery and airplanes are vastly superior to conventional ground forces, the maps are so large now that moving tanks and other ground vehicles across the map is impractical because they require micromanagement and extra resources just to ensure they have enough fuel to move halfway across, and the game is still missing many quality of life features like the ability to reconnect to a game (the netcode is even worse now than in ALB) or a ruler to measure distances. The community has devolved into nationalistic tribalism, and the developers do not take substantive and researched criticism into consideration.
Red Dragon is a quick and dirty cashgrab compared to Airland Battle. If you want a modern RTS that isn't StarCraft, I heartily recommend ALB.

Please don't let the Negative review fool you- Craft the World can be a really fun game when it wants to be. I bought this game after Terraria, Gnomoria and Dwarf Fortress were feeling a little stale, and after reading that from the Store Page that it draws so much from similar games, I thought "Well, this is the game for me!"
CtW does a LOT right- it has a great allocation of resources, a Tech Tree that rewards the player (though still in need of a good bit of work on some of the later technologies), graphics that inspire a friendly and positive player experience, and a great base-building simulation.
So why is it a Negative review?
Because it's a Mobile game. Everything about CtW reeks of "The App Store is our major goal". No key bindings, a crafting menu COMPLETELY designed around touchscreens, and even a big Dwarf holding an iPad when you load up the game just ruins the experience for me. Despite it's initial release on Steam, Craft the World makes PC users feel like an afterthought. Everything is dragging, everything is awkward, and you'll need to head to the wiki if you want to figure out any Hotkey shortcuts. However, my overall negative review comes from more than a moral standing-
The game fails to deliver on population management completely. If you select an enemy, ALL of yours Dwarves will drop everything they do to fight it. If you mine a tunnel, you're going to have a conga line of Dwarves picking up resources in the LEAST sensible way possible. If you start a task, cancel it, and restart it, you're going to have a Dwarf standing around while another Dwarf, often from the other side of the map, comes to handle the task for some odd reason.
The Evil Portal event feels like an artificial restraint on my fun, making me have to pause everything I'm doing for a night while trying to herd my Dwarves into their home quick enough to survive, and the zombie waves are just a lot of "keep smacking them until they go away(win)/until they break your door down(lose). The Goblin events are frustrating at best; I don't know how the developer thought putting in a random surge of enemies without ANY warning would be a great idea, but it's still more fun than the Evil Portal event.
A lot of mechanics are frustrating to deal with and calling them unintuitive would be a major complement. Selecting a single space and having four different options for that space pop up makes me think "How much better could this have been if they'd put effort into making it better for Mouse/Keyboard users?"
All in all, Craft the World is fun. Sometimes. Every time I play this game, it wants me to have all the fun in the world, right up until it trips over its own shoelaces and falls face-first onto the floor. When Dekvoir makes a release better tailored for PC users, I'll gladly change my review. Until then, don't pick the game up until it goes on sale.

WOW! I mean seriously! WOW!
Impression
This game is just simply amazing! I bought it while it was on sale, however, I would gladly have payed full price. The game is currently in early access phase. Sometimes, with early access there is definitely some bugs or some issues with the game. This is true at this point. But the issues are minor enough that I really don’t mind a lot. I’m sure they will iron them out and if they don’t, the game is still amazing and I would still pay full price.
What is it?
This game has some definite parallels to popular games such as Terraria. That isn’t a bad thing either. The success of Terraria is undeniable. I have played many hours of that game myself. This is NOT a terraria clone however. This has similar features and gameplay models but it is far from the same. In this game you are more of a dwarf god in that you tell them to chop a tree down and they go to work. You don’t have one character to traverse the world with, you control multiple characters to tell what to do and watch the magic. Still want that control of being a character? Don’t worry, they got you covered. You can individually control the dwarfs as well. There are also a lot of great twists on old enemies as well as some spectacular new ones. Did I mention there is also experience and reward as such? This is great since nothings is worse then the same old dwarf with the same old abilities. You can also outfit your cool warriors with armor, weapons, tools, fishing poles, and so much more. The goal is to survive and thrive into a great dwarf community. I have over 5 hours of play time as of now and that’s what I know so far. I’m absolutely amazed at how good this game is.
Buy or Fly?
The ultimate question you’re probably asking yourself is, “Should I buy this damn game or not?” Well, if you like boring straightforward cookie cutter games with absolutely predictable gameplay, then don’t buy this game. If you like fun, new and creative ways to play a mix of genres, then this is a MUST BUY! I would absolutely recommend this game.
This game is on iPhone and iPad?! Buy or Fly?
Silly question. YES! I bought it on both Steam and my iPhone/iPad already! It’s the same game on both but a slightly different experience. Either one is worth buying but I say buy both!

As someone who's played many music games before, this doesn't feel like one of them. It feels more like a tool to make music with predetermined beats and melodies, and while that's appealing to some, it's not quite the rhythm game I expected it to be. If you like an ambient experience, then Sentris is pretty cool. If you're looking for something akin to DDR where timing is everything, I'd skip it.

It's not a game nor is it a creative tool.  It gives you rules to "pass" each level which along with the poor samples restricts your creativity, but conversely it's easy to pass levels and create a loop that sounds bloody awful.  Before you buy this, have a look on YouTube and see whether there are any shining examples of good loops that people have made, and that includes the trailer for the game.

Sentris is an outstanding way for a person of any level of knowledge or experience to approach making music. It translates aspects of musical theory into a set of simple visual cues that match with the audio to convey ideas without need for words, which is a truly impressive achievement. The level of guidance offered by the simple puzzle mechanics serves to push the player along while also leaving ample room for experimentation. The early portions of exploring the game are limited in such a way as to make it difficult to produce anything that sounds bad, but always with enough of your own creative decisions included to make the end result feel like the product of your own effort. As one digs deeper there is a fantastic amount of freedom and depth to be found and new concepts to be explored.
My time with Sentris was fun and educational in a way that I've experienced with few other games in my life.

I walked away feeling embarrassed that I had failed to 'get' Sentris.
The tutorial in the release version immediately got me on the right track and removed my doubts about this game. Within five minutes I was creating funky loops that went beyond the tunes the game was feeding me and I felt the thrill of composition that I know the designer was aiming to inspire. There is a real satisfaction in building loops layer by layer and it is especially cool to see how the sound evolves as later layers start to push earlier ones out of the loop. The way the progression of songs helps you learn what the game has to offer in terms of depth is almost perfectly executed, the only thing that I struggled a little to figure out was how to change octaves in freestyle mode (you have to climb or descend the scale to reach the octave you want to play in).
I have now worked my way through all of the 'puzzles' that the game ships with (excluding one, Kentucky Fried Chernobyl, that seems to be broken) in their default forms and started to mess with the remix function, which lets you change the BPM, key signature, scale mode and instrument set for any track, and the endless random mode. There is a lot of room to experiment using these tools and although I don't think I will be using Sentris for serious music composition I definitely see myself regularly dipping back in to this game for short jam sessions.
Sentris is not without flaws; I would have gladly played through two or three times as many puzzle songs as the game shipped with or made my own with a level editor, freestyle mode being a face-button toggle rather than a shoulder-button hold makes the controls a little clumsy at times, and the game never gives you control over the length of the blocks you are placing even in the remix and infinite modes, although I suspect that this last 'flaw' was a deliberate design decision to force players to experiment and compose rather than reproducing tunes or beats they already know.
I would recommend this game to anyone, even if you do not think of yourself as a musical person I think you will be pleasantly surprised by what you are able to create in Sentris.

I love TS2014 in general, but I have some reservations about some recent add-ons.  Specifically, the "NEC: New York-New Haven Route Add-On."
The product description also says that the expansion includes "Metro-North Harlem Line and New Haven Line."  This is only partially true.  It only includes the Harlem Line stops which also happen to overlap with the New Haven Line.  The description is misleading.  Even though having Metro-North, Grand Central and the New Haven Line are wonderful additions to TS2014, I was also hoping to have the full Harlem Line, so I was disappointed to find this description was somewhat misleading.
I was also disappointed to see of a reference to "the Yankee branch, which serves the New York Yankees Stadium on baseball match days."  If the game designers and/or Steam's product writers had taken more than 10 minutes to research Metro-North, they would know that Yankee Stadium is located along Metro-North's Hudson LINE.  It's an entire line itself, not just a branch.  In fact, Metro-North's track mileage and diagrams consider the Hudson Line to be the main line -- the Harlem and Hudson Lines branch off from the Hudson, not vice versa.
{UPDATED} Originally, I had complained about not being able to see the full cab controls of the Kawasaki M8 cab.  It had been awhile since I played TS2014, and I forgot about being able to right-click and drag to alter the point of view.  After having taken a few runs, I tried the tutorials for the heck of it, and the tutorials reminded me of this.  So, I apologize for my ignorant complaining earlier this evening.  However, I stand by my criticism that the M8 cab's monitors fail to realistically show the names of the stations (as the real-life train cabs do) and the lack of automated PA announcements.{/UPDATED}
Hopefully the game's designers will read this review and take some of these comments into consideration.  I realize it would be a tall order to expect them to add the rest of the Harlem Line, but at least remove the reference from the product description so other customers aren't misled.

I've seen a lot of reviews - especially early on, before updates happened - complaining about a multitude of "bugs" in this game. I personally didn't find that many, and certainly none of great note. White Day's main problems, in my opinion, lie more in the realm of questionable game design and story.
The latter of these two is as bat-turd crazy as one would expect from an Asian game heavily influenced by anime and manga cliches. Early on, your character witnesses a "janitor" slowly bludgeoning a kid to death with a baseball bat; and shortly thereafter another character observes that if the janitor catches you sneaking around the school he gets "very angry", and the punishment he metes out is "harsh". Phew! Glad I went to a namby-pamby AUSTRALIAN high school, where the worst they'd give you is "the cane", and even then only with your parents' permission (and I don't even know if they're allowed to do THAT any more)!
There's also the usual ludicrous "cute teenage girls" antics, in which your complete doormat of a male player character runs errands for pouty females, who either deride him or all but give him a blowie upon completion of said task. There's also no end of "let's split up" and "you can find your own way out of here, I'm going this way" scenarios. Logic doesn't exactly loom large in the developers' minds.
Now for the game design. I'll save the worst for last.
The atmosphere is quite, quite excellent. The sound, in particular, does a sterling job of keeping you constantly on your toes - you'll come to dread the jingle-jangle of key chains by the time you're done, believe me - and the employment of jump scares is infrequent but generally effective.
Puzzles. There's some quite good - if sometimes rather obscure - ones. Despite the game having been translated into English, however, there's an absolute corker of a puzzle which REQUIRES YOU TO KNOW CHINESE NUMBERS AND MATHEMATICAL SYMBOLS in order to solve it. (Hint: just Google a walkthrough. Or learn Chinese.)
Maps. No complaints here. The creepy, abandoned school buildings would be quite a pleasure to explore were it not for the mother-♥♥♥♥ing JANITORS.
Ooooooh, yes...THE JANITORS.
What can I say about the janitors? They very nearly ruin the game, in my opinion. They're far too persistent, seem to pinpoint your exact location WAY too easily, and linger too long even when you've found an effective hiding place. They are a constant and ultimately tiresome pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥♥which ensures I won't be replaying this game any time again in the near future...despite how much I enjoyed most other aspects of the game. They also have a tendency to appear precisely between where you are now and where you need to get to, requiring you to spend a good deal of time backtracking and hanging out in toilet cubicles until they move on elsewhere. Not much fun, I'm afraid.
Oh, and the "no running in the school corridors" idea? Fun on paper, maybe. Tedious as all heck in practice.
The 2001 version of the game - notoriously hard to find, and even harder to get to work, on PC at least - has garnered quite the reputation over the years. And while this would appear to be a by-and-largely competent remake, it's possible that White Day's "time" has passed. It's an enjoyable enough walk down Memory Lane for those of us who grew up with clunky old survival horror games, but for those weaned on the likes of Outlast and Alien: Isolation, it's definitely dated some. Irrespective of which of these two categories you fall in, I would only recommend this if you're willing to approach it with patience. Arrive in a grumpy mood, and you're likely to leave even grumpier. But for those willing to be tolerant, the rewards just might outweigh the frustrations.
Oh, and as a final comment: there's a similar Korean high-school horror game - no doubt inspired by the original White Day - called The Coma: Cutting Class. Of the two games I would recommend that first, unless you're specifically in the market for a first-person game. The Coma is much the same thing but with cartoonish 2D, side-scrolling graphics; and has, I see, just enjoyed a revamped re-release which presumably renders it all the more superior. As always, though, each to their own...and if you just can't get enough of Korean high-school horror, I'm happy enough to recommend both.
Verdict: 7.5/10.

The first time I have played this game was actually on a friend's PS4 and I really loved it. Once I noticed you can get it on Steam aswell, I was rather shocked to see what kind of a bad reputation this game got on here. Mixed? Honestly I can understand where certain people are coming from with their opinions.
White Day is a first person korean horror survival game, sort of like Fatal Frame and even DreadOut.
You play as charming, yet not very talkative, transfer student Hee-Min Lee on the day before White Day (Basically Valentines Day). What was a simple premise such as giving the girl you like a box of candy, quickly turned into a dark and twisted night of horror. Fighting is no solution, all you can do is run and hide.
Now ever since Clock Tower or games like Amnesia, people were all over this sort of gameplay mechanic of running instead of shooting everything, and many still love that, but for some reason this game gets a lot of unreasonable hate.
Everyone says the Janitors (one of the main enemies of the game) are stupidly difficult to avoid, but that is not true at all.
Like every enemy in every game, they have a pattern, they have weknesses and the difficulty also plays an important role in this. On Hell they can hear a fly fart in the other building, while on very easy they couldnt even hear you if you shout directly into their ears. And yes, it may be a little unbalanced or unfair sometimes, yet still, play it on easy first, know the tricks, save frequently and be patient just as you would be in real life or any other game. It really isnt that difficult if you get used to it.
Some tips:
- Doors slow them down such as stairs
- Keep the main lights off, use your lighter
- Dont run if you KNOW he is near you
- Listen to his whistling and keychain
- Hide behind thing or the toilet
- Close doors to rooms but keep the ones in the hall open if you arent in it, they will close it on their way through, showing you they are nearby
- Be patient
- Cutscenes or characters with you will reset or remove them for the time being. They also wont respawn, untill you pick up the next token.
If you are patient and take your time to fully explore and enjoy the game, the story and every tiny little secret in this game is more than worth your time. Even with its tiny flaws, its still a great game with a high replay value.
The only thing I dont like about the game, is the fact you have to pay for each aditional outfit, but this is optional.
I would give it a 7/10

Specially recommended for those who played the original, but the game itself is pretty good, though you have to ignore some flaws in it. I'll clarify what I mean.
I'll start with the negatives:
>The AI is, sometimes, pretty broken. Will it destroy your experience? Possibly, but for sure it will make you say pretty bad stuff for the janitor and I doubt you won't get angry somewhere in the game. That's not a completely bad point since you have your difficult choice, but still, when you are in the third floor and know that the janitor is on the first floor, so you open a door and here he comes, running like crazy, because somehow he heard the door opening.
Yes, that happened to me. Many times.
Of course you have places to hide and everything, but it's really annoying because it can waste pretty tedious and unnecessary time on your gameplay just waiting for him to go REEEEEALLY away. And, while you're waiting, there's my second point;
>The jumpscares. Oh, the jumpscares...
So, do I like horror? Yeah, I love horror. Do I like jumpscares? Well, it depends a lot on the buildup and the AMOUNT of jumpscares, 'cause if you have many, it loses the "fear" factor. And, if you're playing on hard mode (basically, that's like the "right" difficulty to play White Day, there's many more stuff in hard), there's A LOT, A REALLY BIG FREAKING LOT of jumpscares.
For example, there's this (pretty present on the complains about the game) Head Ghost (or Hair Ghost, I think). This little princess roams around the school and sometimes, it "finds" you (on hard, it appears almost every time you go to another floor, except if you don't stay much time on the floor, that's something I noted but can be wrong). Well, that's pretty cool and expected, since you're in a haunted school and everything, a ghost roaming around and finding you must be pretty scary, right? It should be, if it didn't pop up a ♥♥♥♥ING PICTURE OF HER FACE SCREAMING LOUD AS HELL ON YOUR EARS!
Frankly, this, let's say, "americanized" jumpscare destroyed this ghost. On the original, it appears and when it hits you, it only kinda whisper something (in korean, I have no idea what it says but it's scary as hell) or laughs in a chilling way. Here, she does the laugh, but after screaming in your face. It worked the first time, but then on I simply removed the headphones or lowered the volume when I heard her noise.
Also, when the game was released, this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ also did you DAMAGE when it hits you! But thanks god, the devs actually care for the players and removed this terrible part.
I won't go with much more on this topic, but I'd like to mention that the jumpscare they added in the girl writing on the chalkboard (that math girl there) also let me down. The original, you only hear her writing on the chalkboard when you enter the room, but here you see her (not actually any problem with seeing her), and the bad part is, when you get close, guess what? Yup, SHE SCREAMS IN YOUR FACE! :D
Yes, many things scream in your face in the game (specially on hard mode), so be prepared.
>Last negative, but something that could make me cry for so much disappointment but not really a flaw in the general game, was the first time you encounter the hanging ghost. I won't go in details to prevent spoilers, but in the original, it was one of the most remarkable horror scenes I've ever seen in horror videogames, because it was dark and you only see the ghost when the thunder lights the place, causing a giant sense of fear and danger (as your mind starts thinking what the ghost will do to you). Well, here, the whole place is actually bright and you can see everything, including the ghost moving, removing completely that sense of fear and danger that the original had.
Now, to the positives, I'll try to be more direct:
>Storyline is amazing. That's basically what I have to say. If you want, you can even avoid getting through the troubles of playing on hard/normal and just play on easy/very easy, just to enjoy the wonderful storyline that this game have.
>Atmosphere is pretty good. Even though the jumpscares are kind of a let down sometimes, the atmosphere in general is really good, even when you want to go out and punch the janitor's face (which you will want, eventually), there's always this sense of danger and some points that can get you at least uncorfortable (the manikin and the noises around the school for example).
>A very good variety of difficulties. There's basically a difficulty mode for everyone here, to the most "let's enjoy the ride" to the most hardcore player, and I must say, the game does a really good job managing the level of difficulty (please ignore the broken parts of the AI).
>A very good variety of endings, too. I mean, A REALLY ♥♥♥♥ING GOOD VARIETY of endings would be proper to say, because if you want 100% of the game, you have to finish it basically 55 times.
Yes, 4 girls, 3 of them have 3 different endings (good, mid and bad) and one has 2. For a 100%, you have to finish EACH of this endings in every difficulty. But don't be scared, you can get all endings in basically three new games.
One for all So-Young endings, one for Sung-A, you load and get all Jy-Hyon and another new game for the new girl endings, but you'll load your game a lot of times to do that, and you'll probably need someone to guide you on your choices to get all in just three new games. Considering that, you won't really need to go through the whole game 55 times, just something like 15 or so.
>Graphics. At first, I thought it wasn't so good, but as the game went on I noticed that the graphics are actually pretty nice and also, unique. Characters specially, they are really nice, if more anime-based games went with graphics like that, it would be pretty good. Yeah, you don't have that "wuw so much details brah" like a new Call of Duty of something like that, that you can see details of even a scar on the side of the face of a character, but the graphics here still nice to look at, and in my opinion, I actually prefer that style.
>Ghost stories are awesome, just that. Really awesome.
>Sounds is also really good. Even I prefer the walking sound of the original, it's not bad in the remake. But well, soundtrack is amazing, the sound of the ghosts are really good (even the screams are well made), janitor walking works well and his whistling always sends a chill down my spine. The credits song is AMAZING btw, specially in korean.
>Voice acting is also very good, characters have distinct voices and it's really good to listen to (except that new girl's voice, I want to strangle her every time she says something). Though, some parts are better in korean, like the bathroom ghost's voice when she appears (that one when you're hiding in the last one and everything), in english is actually kinda cute, not in a scary way, but in korean is pretty damn scary.
>Last point, puzzles are amazing. I don't know many games that made me actually go and learn morse code to progress. I love that, I could actually learn things playing this game, how awesome is this?
I also learn a bit of chinese in the, for some reason, polemic chalkboard puzzle. About that one, frankly, if you complain about "bad localization" just because you don't have the whole answer on your hand, maybe you should go to other games, something more "light" (not offensively, I just don't know if that's the type of game to you, really).
Final words, yes, the game has some flaws that may be a problem on the experience, but with many positive points too, so I don't think those flaws will completely destroy the whole thing, specially if you are capable of ignoring them (even if just for the sake of enjoying the storyline). I don't think the game should have so many complaints for things like "I couldn't get through that puzzle" or "the AI made me die", honestly.
Even though I think the original was better in many things, this one is still pretty good, too, and I give it a 8/10.

Having played through the Android version and now playing through the PC port, I can recommend White Day to fans of old school survival horror games. Old school being the key words here.
I am not a big fan of the original game. It was playable, but inherently silly, badly written and with underdeveloped gameplay mechanics. The remake is exactly the same, just with "better" graphics.
However on a market over flooded with hundreds of modern horror titles, White Day feels like a breath of "fresh" air. It truly is an old school survival horror title in the truest sense of the word... despite being a modern remake, the game transports you to the early 2000s with it's bactracking, obtuse puzzles, awkward translation, so-so voice acting and inventory management. If you cannot stand any of these things, stay away from White Day.
The environments are well designed and, in a classic survival horror fashion, look and feel like real places. The maps and room placement make sense. Again, modern horror games often try way too hard, throwing over the top environments, level design and... well... everything at you. It is good to play a horror game that takes place in normal, not over designed environment. Not that there's anything bad with that, but like I said, the marked is over flooded.
If you play on Normal difficulty or above, be prepared for about 3-4 puzzles and situations that are hard to read and require trial and error to figure out. Again, this was normal in early 2000s, not so much now.
What really might put people off playing this game however is the absolute silliness, non-sense plotting and anime hysterics during cutscenes. This is a Korean horror so silly plot, characters not behaving like human beings and "subtext" not being a subtext at all but being hammered into your head 24/7 are pretty much given. What makes matters worse is the anime style of the characters, who are animated and act like in a third grade anime Saturday morning cartoon.
However if you can swallow all this, you are in for a refreshing old school horror gaming experience. With all it's faults.

200+ hours down the drain. I don't even need to say much about what's wrong with H&G; any other reviewer has said enough already. I love WWII, and I love FPS, (especially when it's free!) Hey, at least if you are a masochist, this would be perfect for you.

After throwing in a few more hours, I can say this: it still sucks. In fact, it sucks even more because it's a game where pistols cost as much as (or even more than) tanks, anti tank weapons are handed out like candy so using tanks make me want to smash my computer now, and god-awful internet issues, where some games are (kinda) smooth, while some games I've reached (no joke) 10,000 ping! The "spawn protection" allows the enemy to spawn camp even harder, and the "balance" amounts to hoping you don't get matched with Americans in light tanks, Germans in medium tanks/tank destroyers, and Russian pilots. The whole point of an SMG, is that it's an easy to wield, compact MG basically. What has been Reto-Moto's response?
"Oh, let's add some more vehicles, and make our maps slightly different!"
