Pretty cool little game.  Graphically one of the best you will find on the free to play idle market.  There is even a decent story to follow as you play along.  It's nothing like you will get from a paid release from the FF franchise but it's the best when you compare it to other idle games.  I don't see these 2 aspects being out shinned in the idle genre for the rest of the year as of 3-21-17 when I write this.
So yeah, this is an idle game.  To an extent.  You move forward to the next battle and can go afk while this battle is being completed.  But it won't take more than a couple minutes usually.  So you bring the game back up, listen/read some dialogue and go to the next battle.  Rinse and repeat.  You are limited by stamina.  You spend a little for each fight and it takes about 5 minutes of real time to regenerate a point of stamina.  Battles can absorb small amounts to a select few that will absolutely drain your play for a long time.  Whenever you level up however not only do you get stamina fully restored but you get bonus stamina caried over.  Nothing is wasted.  I do however recommend burning through bonus stamina asap.  When the timer is not running to regenerate stamina you can view this as a waste.
That said, starting out is fun.  You level up like crazy in the beginning and find enough elixers (stamina refills) that you can sit and play this a large chunk of the first day and still maybe not have eaten through the bonus stamina.
Each class can use about 4 abilities.  The abilities are in the form of cards.  So 4 cards slots per class with each class having certain restrictions on what types of cards they can use.  I won't go too much deeper into this as part of the fun and the only thing to do when waiting on stamina to regenerate is figuring out the card system.  Difficult and overwhemling at first but simple and easy to understand once you've played a little.
So, how are these people going to try and take my money?  Well, being a ftp game they are indeed going to try and yo money.  Magicite (the premium currency in the game) is very rare and  hard to come by.  You earn about 100 every 18 hours if you can make it on every 18 hours you can start to come out ahead a bit.  But if you are only getting on every... lets say 24 hours on the dot you may fall behind or never get ahead.  Let me esplain, Lucy.  for 3000 magicite you get a special bonus each days and better rewards.  Also buffs to upgrading your cards.  It's kind of like subbing to the game for a month.  So every 30 days, at a rate of 100 mag per day, you are able to sustain this.  Buying bonus magicite is incredibly expensive; way overpriced.  There are actually some things, nothing I have seen thats required or gamebreaking though, that require you have spent x amount or bought x amount of magicite.  But really encourages spending real money.  But if all your magicite is going to keep your sudo subscription running you not going to have any for anything else.
Also, new players may feel a bit bad as there is a lot of content that is limited time.  Cards that are simply no longer obtainable.  This also pressures existing players to buy the magicite to try and earn these limited time only spell cards because remember, all your magicite is going to the monthly sub.
Everything about this game is good except the business model.  They are asking for your money so strongly.  It's like being in a theme park but not being able to ride anything because you had to give em all your money to breath the air inside the park.
That being said I still had a great time with the game without spending a dime and got decently far.  So it's worth a try.

Sentris is a fantastic game with novel ideas on music creation. Whether you are a veteran of the music game genre (harmonix fans I am talking to you), or you simply have an interest in making music, Sentris has something fun and engaging for you to discover.
The most intimidating aspect of learning to play an instrument or learning to write music is finding out how different sounds come together in collaboration to create an interesting complex whole. What makes Sentris so intriguing is the way it brings players into music creation without judgment. Players are invited to solve musical puzzles without harsh critique. This allows players to follow the game's progressive musical structure or completely deviate from the game's pre-set suggestions without negative consequence. The results can vary from being an only slightly coherent cacophony of noise to surprisingly deep melodies and rhythms that are uniquely authored by the player.
Samantha Kalman may be a relatively new name to video game players, but her work on Sentris gives me hope that we will see more excellent indie games from her and her company (Timbre Interactive) in the future.

Sentris is definitely worth looking into if you have any interest in creating music. It reminds me of my days playing with software such as FruityLoops, but puts its own unique spin on things. I’ve enjoyed playing through the provided songs and am starting to create my own unique setups (as well as attempting to emulate some more widely-known music too).
"What is Sentris in 2 Minutes?" Video:
Overall the game is a lot of fun, and quite a versatile tool once you get to grips with it. That said, there are a few features I would love to see implemented going forward. Primarily these are just additional expansions for added versatility when creating songs. It would be great to be able to select notes outside the standard scale that I choose, and to apply effects (such as reverb or echo) to specific instruments during remix.
Nevertheless, the initial offering (at time of official v1.0 launch) is a joy to play around with. When you hit upon a riff that catches your ear and develop it into something you love, it really brings a smile to your face. Whether you're smashing notes together until something sticks (or doesn't!) or meticulously crafting a pre-meditated loop from scratch, Sentris is really unique and wonderful take on musical creativity.

I suppose, if you really need your superhero fix, this game might work.  I haven't been able to enjoy it for a long time.
Pros:
- The cities are very well designed, famous locations to be found all over Gotham and Metropolis.
- Coming across a supervillain or hero in the world can make for a thrilling battle, especially if there are a number of decent players nearby to help.  Brawling with Bizarro, for example.
- Graphics are nice, with powers well animated.
Cons:
- No matter how hard you try, or how powerful you get, you will always be a second tier hero.  The major characters such as Superman or Enchantress always being more important than you.
- Community isn't helpful at all.  Asking a question will get you ridiculed and mocked.  I had one player actually claim to have been born knowing how to play when confronted with the fact everyone was new once.
- Powersets, while well designed, are a bit limited.  Once you've seen a set, there isn't much variation from that point.
- The game is focused on endgame play, and gear oriented grinding.  While, yes, many comic book heroes have gear of some kind or another, they rarely focus on it.  This game makes it a necessity.  Grind to get the best gear you can get, so you can move to the next tier and grind for the next level of best gear.  That's it, that's the entire point of endgame.  No story, no plot, no worthwhile resemblence to DC comics of any era.
- While not a bad thing to a large portion of players, I find the functional lack of role playing to be a huge con as well.
- PvP is rampantly broken, being available anywhere except inside certain buildings.  It is extremely frustrating to be working a mission only to have some idiot OP player 12 to 15 levels higher than you drop out of nowhere and stomp you into the ground repeatedly.  The pay gear allows these same players to easily overpower you even if you are the same or higher level.  I have been PvP beaten by characters 8 levels below me simply because I didn't have the best paid gear.
On the other hand, the voice acting is superb.

Craft the World is for want of a better term "My first Dwarf Fortress". It's Dwarf Fortress made accessible to the market, and it's about time someone actually got around to -doing- this. Initially released in Early Access, this title has been something of a rough gem that has, over time steadily been sanded and milled into a shining diamond, just waiting to be plucked from the dark underdepths by grubby, stubby hands and long, curly beards.
Dwarf Fortress is a very "marmite" game, because in part it's one of those games that requires the kind of in depth understanding of all the systems and sub-systems that go into it that usually come along with multi year degree courses. Not so in Craft the World, no, whilst the Dwarves do exhibit elemental stupidity in buckets, much like their DF cousins, they are quite able to follow simple instructions and they are able to manage their tasks in a vaguely dwarfish manner. Those skilled in their jobs will prioritise things accordingly, and the dwarves with weapons will actually kill things, as opposed to stabbing themselves in the foot. There's none of this "Fey mood" malarky either, thank dieties. Instead you'll be dealing with nightfall bringing undead knocking at your door and ghosts who wreak havoc with your stockpiles.
Whilst the tech tree was "servicable" to begin with, now it's a monolithic thing that requires time and effort to unpick, with dwarves being forced to live in fairly basic digs with leafy beds before they are given homes suited to their dwarfly status. The game systems now support farming, fishing, and a full complement of other activities, so provided you can keep your dwarves alive, you can eventually have a busy, thriving little fortress, able to stand up to the worst that the world throws at you. Well, most of the time...
Throw in trading with the locals when you acquire precious gold coins, skill books which teach your dwarves such vital skills such as how to climb without plummeting to their doom and a simple RPG-lite system of skill building and you've a recipe for quite entertaining gameplay. It may not have the absolute depth of Dwarf Fortress, but it certainly will slake the thirst of anyone wanting to get -into- the DF genre, and in that, it serves as an excellent introduction.
The graphical style is well thought out, opting for a very cartoonish and well furnished design that uses sweeping colourful flourishes and a wide palette, ensuring that there's always something interesting going on, and that the dwarven holdings -look- the part. Furniture goes from being something that shames you to being something that shines. Enemies range from comical looking skeletons to nasty beholders and trolls and goblins, all well thought out and whilst not perhaps going to win awards for animation, they -do- look well designed and everything in the world is consistent.
The sound? Well. I'll be diplomatic. If I hear dwarves snoring one more time... *eyetwitch*
It's "My First Dwarf Fortress", and it's a very good place to start, there's been other efforts, and those have done pretty badly in comparison, this one however nails the mark, striking a good balance between being accessible to the newcomer yet offering enough of a challenge to keep experienced players at the whetstone long enough that they should feel suitably stretched out enough to consider graduating to the 'real' Dwarf Fortress, if that so pleases them.

If you're a fan of previous Wargame installations, Red Dragon is a must have. However, if you have no prior experience in the Wargame series but still insist on getting the game; be warned, the online learning curve is very steep.
Wargame is a unique kind of Real-time Strategy game, differing from well-known RTS games like C&C or StarCraft in many aspects. Typical base building -- or rather, base building at all -- is absent, as are typical economic systems (i.e money, different resources and all that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t). The latter of which is replaced by a single, universal "resource", to which you use to bring units in from off screen.
Wargame also incorporates more realistic mechanics into the game. Units will react to situations more realistically, for example, a tank company being bombarded by artillery or caught in a napalm strike will freak the ♥♥♥♥ out and try to escape from combat, disregarding orders in the process. Most units also have limited fuel and ammo, which will need to be resupplied to them. And projectiles act like projectiles would in real life, having chances to hit or miss a target, with factors like an obstructed line of sight coming into play.
Now, as much as I love this game, I find that the naval combat -- one of the selling points of the game -- is unredeemably bland. As beautiful as it looks, there's almost no depth to it at all; it's a simple matter of "huck enough missiles at the bad guys to kill them". Unlike the aircraft mechanic which plays a pivotal role in the game, the naval combat's role is minor at best, but more commonly is downright trivial.
Overall I give Wargame: Red Dragon a 8.5/10, Eugen definitely has not disappointed with the beautifully detailed battles that we've come to love from the Wargame series, but the not-so-subtle lack of depth from the naval combat is hard to overlook.

GENERAL GAMEPLAY
The main gameplay is through war battles, as either of 5 troop types you can play as:
Infantry, Tank Crewman, Paratrooper, and Recon
Other than the obviously explainable, recon is your sniper, and infantry is the all-around soldier, and suses whatever necessary to win.

Do I recommend this game?
Tenative yes - it honestly depends on the person.
This game is good for those who like an asian style atmospheric horror game. There are ghosties and jumpscares, but a majority of them are hidden unless you play on hard or higher difficulty (and even then a majority are optional). The other main strength of the game comes from the story. It's very well done and has an immense amount of lore behind it (with more lore being hidden behind secret optional puzzles) and it is thoroughly enjoyable.
The reason I say 'tenative'?
The janitors are easily the worst part about the game. The two janitors VERY QUICKLY go from being 'spooky' to downright annoying. They are the near constant 'threat' that only exist to waste your time that could be used to solve puzzles and look around. The AI itself is very finicky (either too aggressive or extremely passive) and often seems broken (my hell mode playthough was easier than my normal mode playthough - janitors extremely passive for a majority of the hell mode run)
So in the end: It's a very good atmospheric horror game with a great mystery and lore to it, but if you get easily annoyed with stupidly designed AI, you're better off watching a playthough on YouTube or Twitch.

I've been a fan of White Day since I played the original version ages ago.This is a korean survival horror game. You play as Hee-Min Lee, a high school student who gets trapped along his schoolmates inside Yeondu High School, a haunted school which is home to lots of ghost stories. You'll have to solve puzzles and even face some of the ghosts in order to escape.
Pros:
-Multiple endings: The ending is determined by how you interact with the characters (whether you are nice or mean to them).
-There's a new playable character (Ji-Min Yoo): She didn't appear in the original or the mobile versions. When playing as Ji-Min, you can get two new endings (depending on Hee-Min's choices when meeting her).
-Graphics: The game is similar to the mobile version, but it looks much better.
-Music: the music is great and fits the game perfectly.
-The school: you'll be able to explore most of this creepy school and learn about its past through various documents.
-Ghosts!: There are 20 ghost stories you can collect around the school. However, you'll have to play on Hard or Hell modes to see most of them.
Cons:
-The janitors: they are the main threat in almost every phase of the game. They're very frustrating in harder difficulties.
-The story is a bit short: You could complete the game in 2 hours or so (even less if you speedrun or don't look for secrets/documents).
-Some of the ghosts are just jumpscares. Not scary at all.
-Other minor bugs.
Despite everything, this is still one of the best horror games I've played and one of my favourites. I'd recommend it to any survival horror fan.

Sentris, in its current state, is hard to recommend based on the twenty dollar price tag.  The menu, if you can call it that, is extremely bare bones.  There’s no in-game option menu that would otherwise allow you to adjust audio volumes and the like, though the Unity Engine does feature a separate pop-up on launch that allows you to adjust screen resolution, graphics quality, and full screen.  There are no instructions or tutorials at present, plopping players into an environment that they’ll have to figure out on their own.  I do praise the theme behind the project and would really like to see what it’ll be like when it’s officially done.  I’m giving it a “thumbs up” on the idea alone, but if you’re strapped for cash, I’d wait for a few more patches / content updates.  It’s an Early Access game, so it goes without saying that the above opinions are subject to change.

Brothers- A Tale of Two Sons is an example of vivid, impactful storytelling through the interaction of yourself or myself with the characters of the game. I felt more attached to the seemingly made language spouting brothers than i did to booker dewitt in bioshock infinite. Although a very short game, only 5 or so hours long, it created an atmosphere that begs more. I bought it on sale, and played it to cap the night, and BAMN 5 hours later i got out of my chair saying "holy sh*t what did i just experience," Brothers is a perfect melding of mechanics, visuals, music, storytelling, ambiance, style, drama, and comedy. Every single scene evoked questions and evoked answers to previous question. Each and every cutscene aided the story  and gave respite to the sometimes tedious gameplay mechanics. Truly a marvel of interactive storyrtelling. I give it a as near to perfect rating 4.9999999/5 stars and highly recommend it to anyone of any age or skill level. If there is a type of video game that is not just a cutscene/interactive movie or a nasty mess of mechanics but still evokes a drama and evokes emotions then this is it. This is something beyond a video game, the emotions i felt were so rich and the connection i had with two brothers whose names i dont even know is so profound that not to call this story art would be a travesty against the very notion of art. If what this game makes someone feel is not art, than no movie or book or painting can rightfully be called art..... jeez This game is so good I start making philosophical arguments. Seriosuly amazing!!! -OB

It's not often I've liked a game so much that I've actually been willing to press even
buttons to tell the world how awesome or potentially life-saving something is. Well, I don't know about the latter, but
is indeed
some. Every scene and every image may induce awe-inspiring, jaw-dropping gazes upon its on-lookers thanks to fantastic art direction by Starbreeze Studios. Who'da thunk the makers of The Darkness and The Chronicles of Riddick games could make something so bright and colorful? But then again, maybe we shouldn't assume too much about Starbreeze's new-found love of color just yet. Even in the span of the game's three-hour playtime, there are several instances of “dem feels” to be had.
may also wreak havoc on your thumbs and cranial wiring thanks to its unique control scheme. Each brother is assigned their own analog stick and trigger allowing them to move and carry out context-based actions independently of one another, leading to some pretty hilarious moments. I can't count how many times I've let go of the wrong trigger while one of the brothers dangles precariously from a ledge or chain, only for him to meet an untimely demise. The worst is when you have the brother controlled by the left-side of the controller on the right and vice-verse. It's a bit like trying to do a math problem upside-down. I dunno know, though; I'm pretty bad at math.
All these eccentricities of game design culminate into what is one of the best ending sequences in a video game to date. This is one you just have to experience for yourself, so I'll leave it at that. This is the kind of story-telling that the medium has been striving for the past couple of years thanks to a booming indie scene. If Siskel and Ebert were here today, they would have said, “Thanks to a severe case of carpal tunnel, we can't help but give

”

You must, I repeat, you MUST play this game. This title is another fine example of how the indie genre is creating a big, if not huge, name for itself in the gaming industry. Ok, where to begin. The visuals are absolutely stunning, quite possibly the best showing of video game art that I have seen in my many years of gaming. Not to mention that the game sounds just as beautiful as the game looks, offering one of the best soundtracks of the year. The story line is beautifully gripping; the game itself will only take you a couple hours to complete, but man those few hours will become almost non-existent as you make your way through the fantastic storyline that Brothers has to offer. The controls may seem unfamiliar at first using both joysticks to control each character separately, but this doesnt break the game even in the slightest; the control scheme will become second nature as you progress. In short, the game is the complete package and you can expect what truly is one of the best titles of 2013. Even at the $15 price tag, the game is absolutely worth it; to get it for under $10 is a no brainer. 10/10

I bought this game when it was still in its early stages of development, almost a year ago. The game was fun back then, but it clearly needed a lot more work put into it, so I left it for a while and decided to come back to it once it had been updated a bit.
Almost a year on, I decided to give the game another blast and see what had changed. The answer to that was, not a lot!
It's a very slow paced game where you need to craft various items from basic house furnishings, to weapons and equipment. The recipes need more and more materials to create them, so you need to venture deep into the earth and explore the wild around you to find them. The problem is, this slow pace is almost halted to a crawl as the AI of the dwarves is absurd!
The dwarves often stand there "path finding" when they are stood in the middle of an open area, with nothing around them which could be considered an obstacle. Often even a simple jump takes 20 seconds of calculations to work out how to do it.
I revealed an area with some pretty tough monsters in it. A guardian whom can summon skeletons and is only vulnerable to mithril (which will take you some time to research due to the afore mentioned problems). After realising he was too tough, I cancelled my command to attack him and wanted my dwarves to go back to what they were doing. The problem was, once I had cancelled the command, this did NOTHING to stop my dwarves repeatedly running and trying to attack the Guardian. Even using the "call to fortress" feature was useless as that would cause them to stay in one place and do nothing, then once I cancelled this order, they would run straight back to the Guardian to try and kill him!
In the end my dwarf I had skilled up to be my main warrior was killed due to his own (and the games) stupidity. After this, I decided that the time and effort I put into getting to where I did had been wasted.
I would not reccommend this game unless the developers revamped the entire AI system and made the game actually playable. Until then, it's not worth £14! I would pay maybe £3 for this game, but would much rather see it offered as a flash game on some website for free!

Avoid this "game" like the plague. From the videos and screenshots it looks like a mix of Terraria and user-friendly Dwarf Fortress. It's not.
This is a mobile game masquerading as a desktop game. There is no content here past "leveling up" and that feels like a hollow and pointless experience.
Probably the worst part of this whole game is the "Tech Tree" which seems like it would be a feature. Instead it's your chains. Do you want to craft a single wood helmet? Do you have the wood? yes? TOO BAD. Instead first you have to craft  5 ladders first because.... you wouldn't know how to make a helmet without first making ladders. You want a wooden door? Do you have all the required materials for it? yes? WELL TOO BAD you still have to craft 10 "Locks" first. I'm not kidding. This ruins the game as even if I have the materials for things I can't craft them until way later because of the tech tree. The prerequisites for items don't even make sense.
The one upside of this game is that it's fairly well polished. It's pretty, has decent music, and runs smoothly. Unfortunately the downside is pretty much everything else. Save yourself the money and more importantly those hours of your life that you cannot get back. Avoid this game.

Train Simulator 2014 basic review for new comers.
Mixed bag, certainly not the worst simulator around, but not the best either.
Good points;
*Scenery excillent quality with plenty of expance and features.
*Loco and rolling stock details very good and accurate, both inside and out with more or less all cab controls functional.
*Good variety of add-ons, both scenery and rolling stock.
*Includes feature to allow customised variety of wagons to make up train consists behind loco.
*Includes a route/scenery editor to create or edit features of routes.
Bad points;
*Accurate/precise control (throttles in particular) from good to poor, varying from unit to unit, particularly with the Class 43 HST which requires constant 'feathering' of throttle to maintain a, roughly, constant speed, particularly at low speeds.
*Very unrealistic feature whereby in some missions track points have to be changed manually by player, often while driving   the train which can be a source of frustration by causing distractions and, naturally, can lead to failed missions due to accidents.
*Sound FX could do with a little fine tuning, especially with some horns which sound just awful.
*Only includes one very vague tutorial on using the most basic diesel loco controls and no tutorial for steam locos
*Though mentioned in the Good points, the route editor is not the most user friendly.
Conclusion: Overall a decent game, if you stick to the easier missions, harder ones can be hugely frustrating with the driver operated points, the only real way for new players to learn how to drive properly is through trial-and-error in quick drive mode (as the tutorials are not up to much other than the very basics) and stick to the easier missions, only try harder ones if your the kind of person who isn't easily frustrated. I do recommend this, but not to a huge degree.
p.s Although train driving certainly isn't something I've ever tryed in real life, I get the strong impression that the developers of this game made little effort to consult actual experts in this field (other than for loco/cab detailing and control layouts), in particular actual train drivers. This really is something they should try out before releasing any future editions of this game, get REAL drivers to try it out and give advice for fine tuning before making it available for retail.

Edit: Since recommendations have apparently been converted into reviews I thought I should elaborate a bit.
First off: TL2 is not as good as Diablo 2. After playing it for a bit again, 70 hours or so, I tried D2 again and the better gameplay and design choices just felt really immediate. I went on to go for Patriarch again. That said TL2 is the best of the "clones" I've played. It's not worthy as a successor but as with some other genres it seems that the pioneer will always remain the greatest.
Regarding graphics. At their best, the graphics look fantastic. TL2 in 60 FPS is really something that must be seen to be believed. Unfortunately the graphics are unusually heavy, and most computers will find it hard to keep the framerate high, especially in big battles. Said big kerfuffles also bring to light another problem regarding the visuals. They're very busy. So busy in fact, that in the multiplayer each player has a column of blue light emanating from them so that you can identify players in the mess. This is not a good thing, relatively I say that D2 still has better graphics, not because they're flashy with advanced effects, but because they're concise and serve the gameplay. Freeze, poison, curses and auras, other important spells etc. are easy to identify in D2, in TL2 not so much. The overabundance of various effects and the subtlety of others makes the graphics not serve gameplay so well.
Thematically, TL2 is obviously a big deviator when it comes to comparing to D2. If you can get over it, the visual design is occasionally pretty stunning. However at times it feels somewhat generic, as "cartoony á la WoW" has become the go-to fantasy style over the past ten years or so.
The gameplay is a mixed bag. The skill system is simpler than D2's all across the board, but the attributes are done differently. One of the usual complaints in D2 is that other than the mandatory Strength and Dexterity points, all points for all characters go in Vitality. In TL2 all attributes are useful for every character in some fashion, but optimal distribution is usually just stacking Strength or Focus, as those are the attributes that increase damage by a percentage. Vitality is not as useful as in D2, as the HP increase is not as important and because the other bonus granted from it is block and armor increase, which tends to be useful for shielded characters only.
Dexterity gives minor things like critical change, dodge and fumble recovery. Fumble is another mechanic new to TL2, instead of missing, characters can Fumble their autoattacks which makes them cause reduced damage. The reason for this seems to be making the combat feel more satisfying, as characters missing with attacks is a common complaint with action RPGs. However it usually seems to just make it more frustrating, at least for me, as Fumble just makes it look like your character just barely scratches the enemies with his autoattacks, with no clear reason, as fumbled attacks look the same as normal ones.
The constant fumbling combined with relatively powerful active skills makes builds involving large amounts of auto-attack rare and/or not that useful. In comparison to D2, most every melee attack utilized auto-attack attack speeds, life leech, etc. but in TL2 very few of those kinds of bonuses apply to the active skills. And because the actives do much more damage and other things, relying on auto-attack and utilizing the bonuses for it is seldom a sensible option.
Regarding skills, as mentioned, the system is not as robust as Diablo 2's. Skills are divided into three "trees", but you don't need to invest in prerequisites, so they're more like categories instead of trees. There are no synergies, so builds come down to using skills that work well with each other, or just spamming the most overpowered skill possible, like the Engineer's Emberquake. The skill scaling is different: instead of diminishing returns like D2, TL2 goes with flat increases every rank, as in rank 1: 9% dodge, rank 2: 12% dodge, rank 3: 15% dodge, etc. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand skill increases stay meaningful all the way to the end. Some skills in D2 hit diminishing returns hard which meant that there wasn't really a point in spending more than a few points in certain skills. On the other hand, especially at the start, the skill increases feel petty and unimportant. For instance: would you rather spend another point in the skill to gain 2% more damage, or buy a new skill altogether that does good damage with just one point in it, and even scales (a new feature in TL2)?
Scaling is another point. Most skills scale in damage with level, generally with skills that do flat amounts of damage instead of weapon damage. Weapon damage is another problem in itself. A disproportionally large amount of skills rely on weapon damage, even the Embermage's and Outlander's more spell-like abilities. In addition to it not making much sense, it also makes your weapon, and its DPS to be more precise, overly important. Some builds in D2 relied more on weapons, and usually it was regarded as a weakness. In TL2 most builds need weapon damage which makes the DPS the focal point of gear. The other bonuses aren't that important, especially considering that several weapon enchantments only activate on autoattacks, like mentioned.
Gear as a whole is not nearly as well thought out as in D2. Because it's the only real source for HP, most every item choice on Veteran and beyond is decided by the amount of health on the item. In D2, most characters got plenty of health from Vitality, and life on gear was relatively rare, so it wasn't that important. In TL2 you MUST stack health to stand a chance on the harder difficulties. This combined with the underwhelming bonuses of the other usual enchantments meas that itemization is  banal and pointless. Adding to this problem is the fact that most uniques have boring, nonsensical or otherwise worthless bonuses that make them unique only in the sense that you'd have to be a real hipster to ever equip them, most of the time. Their drop rate is overly high too, and some bosses even drop guaranteed uniques, most notably the last boss which always drops two. Sets are done a little differently. Set is more like an enchantment instead of an item rarity, and two of the same set item can be worn and it will still count towards completion. This makes them much more common and more viable for non-twinks, but causes them to lose their uniqueness quite a bit. The aforementioed health stacking is also a limiting factor regarding sets, as some just don't want to spawn with HP on them.
The inclusion of multiplayer was something that was highly anticipated. Unfortunately it works in about the same manner as Open
in D2, which makes it pretty worthless for anything serious. There are rudimentary anti-cheating features in place but with local saves anything resembling ladders or an economy is just a futile effort. Another pretty big blunder is the unbelievable amount of player separation. D2 had realms, ladder and non-ladder and hardcore and softcore. TL2 has Casual, Normal, Veteran, Elite, NG, NG+, NG++, etc., hardcore and softcore, so maybe you see my point. The player base gets splintered into so many sections that it really hurts the ability to play with others. So mainly the multiplayer is only good for playing with friends. Also, the loot is instanced, depending on point of view this is a good or a bad thing.
It might seem like I'm complaining about everything but I feel like I'm just scratching the surface, but my point is that it's not as good as Diablo 2, but an OK clone on its own, and fun for its own reasons. Recommended if you want to play solo or with a friend for a bit for fun, but not if you're looking for the next greatest aRPG/dungeon crawler/hack'n'slash/click looter/diablo clone/whatever. For that we have D2 still.

enjoyed this game. For the most part. But let me start with the most obvious thing that I hated about it. The janitors.
The janitors are not scary. The janitors are not fun. The janitors are annoying as ****. This game would be infinitely more enjoyable, interesting and scary without them. The only purpose they serve is to artificially prolong the gameplay time, because they stand between you and exploration, scares, story. If anything, I think they actually ruin the atmosphere of this empty creaky haunted school. You know, when you are exploring the dark corridors, about to **** your pants because of creepy music, something knocking on the window of the fourth floor, stepping on creaky floor... and then suddenly a guy with a flashlight and baseball bat shows up, limping towards you, whistling with his whistle and you have to run to the nearest toilet (since it's the only place you can reliably lose him)... the only thing missing is Benny Hill music. And you don't think "oh no, so scary, he's gonna catch me", you think "Oh ffs, again? I was literally 2 meters away from objective and now I have to crawl through all this AGAIN?".
Not to mention that on harder difficulties their ability to hear and see you becomes just absurd, with them hearing you open doors 4 floors away.
Sure, there are a few creepy moments involving them and they are nicely integrated into some cutscenes. But it doesn't really justify their presence, in my opinion. They are simply annoying.
OK, with that out of the way, let's actually talk about the rest of the game. I have never played the original myself, so this was my first experience with White Day. And I loved every second of it (that did not involve janitors).
I consider myself rather desensitized when it comes to horror genre. Seen too many movies, played too many games, so it's pretty hard to find something really scary for me.
Well, I stopped playing this game after the first 10 minutes to go and turn the lights in my room on. Because holy ****, the sounds are so creepy. The atmosphere overall is creepy as well, but it can vary, depending on situation. But sounds are always there. Just some random static, some footsteps in an otherwise empty hall, something knocking on your window, something screeching, something whining... the sound design here is absolutely amazing.
The ghosts are great. Just don't forget that you have to play on hard to see them all.
One thing I've noticed about a few "let's plays" of this game that I've seen - people often skip ghost stories they find and don't read them. HUGE mistake. These stories are amazingly creepy and add immensely to the atmosphere. So do yourself a favor and read them.
And then, of course, the ghost design itself is awesome. But hey, what did you expect from Asian horror? Their ghosts are always top-notch.
Could, maybe, use a bit less of jumpscares. The ghosts and their sounds are already creepy enough without this cheap trick of popping and screaming. Actually, my single favorite ghost in the game is the one that just stands in the room doing absolutely nothing. Scares me deeply and much more than the jumpscare ones.
Exploration is fun (when the janitor doesn't stand in its way). I love finding some obscure things and figuring what to do with them. This game has a lot of these tiny missable things and it's pretty cool for completionists. Also has around 10 different endings, so the replayability is great.
The puzzles are... how do I put it... it's not that they are difficult, in fact, I only had troubles with one of them. But you need to have a certain way of thinking to figure some of them out. I'd say the game would benefit from giving you just a tiny bit more info about what it wants you to do. But then again, maybe I just suffer from being a modern gamer and too used to games holding my hand all the time.
However, there are things that are stupid. To solve certain scenes you need to have certain items. However, you can not know that you need them until you encounter these scenes. So, you die, then you search for more items, play through the section again and then you win. Which can be frustrating. Especially because - yes, you guessed it - the janitor who doesn't let you explore every room in peace. Thankfully, even on hardest difficulty (where you can not save) the game's autosaves are placed smart enough not to put you into dead ends. So even when you die, you usually start relatively close to where you need to be. So it's not a big gripe. Besides, it's always fun to see your hero die in a new way.
All in all, I think this game is great. It's scary, it has replayability, it is visually pleasing (which is one of the reasons I bought it in the first place, I just LOVED characters' animations and facial expressions, huge props to people who worked on them). It is an Asian horror and an Asian game through and through. Which means it involves creepy lore, creepy sounds and music and unfortunately, a certain amount of wasting your time. If you've played many Asian games, you probably know that for the most part they involve a f-ton of grinding, text
reading, random unavoidable combat or clunky UI. It's just part of the course. Thankfully, this game has none of the above. Instead it has the janitor who slows your progression, makes you run in circles, replay bits of level over and over again if he catches you or spend a huge chunk of game sitting in the toilet, waiting for him to leave your floor...
But if you think that you can deal with this part, the rest of the game is very much worth it. Honestly, it's an easy recommendation for anyone who loves horrors.

A pretty good sandbox game, with a mediocre The-Moon-Is-A-Harsh-Mistress-esque story. The really interesting thing about this game is that you are essentially a terrorist fighting the powers that be: the EDF. I, at least, would constantly go around with bombs strapped to my vehicle with a specific target in mind. Success wasn't surviving the attack; it was destroying the target. Even on medium difficulty, when the EDF came in force, it is very hard to survive long. I would have liked this game to be a conversation on terrorism and guerrilla warfare for a good, but extreme, cause. The ambivalence of destroying a civilian structure that probably-- but not certainly-- was a base of operations for the enemy would have been wonderful, and would have made this into a great game. Instead it is a ham-fisted, "the EDF are killing innocent civilians, they are evil tyrants, you must stop them" kind of a deal.
Anyway, this open-world, physics-based third person shooter is a fun diversion and it's worth the twenty dollars they're asking. And, yes, seeing that building stand for a split second after most of its supports have been destroyed, then seeing crumble absolutely is one of the most satisfying experiences in video games.

This is a fairy tale of a game. There's nothing terribly complex or unique about it, but at the same time there's something endearing to it. It's a brief experence, to its benefit, and no part of the game overstays its welcome, I feel. Mechanics that utilize the two-character controls are introduced and dropped before they get stale. The general "plot" is pretty unremarkable, but like any fairy tale I wasn't really expecting it to be super special.
The artstyle is pretty simple but the landscapes do look pretty great. There's little benches strewn about that do nothing but pan over the vistas, but you'll find youself wanting to sit in them for a bit anyways. The music is also pretty good, especially during chapters 3 and 4. but by the end of the game I found myself wishing there was a little more variety to it.
Locales are kind of connected together in a way that doesn't seem terribly cohesive, but the variety in types of places that you visit, especially for such a short game, it pretty nice.  I also like that the achievements are just little extra/optional things that you'll find yourself doing in the world naturally without searching around corners and stuff for game-y collectables or something.
Not too much of a time investment to experience and no frustration. I suggest everyone willing just gives it a playthrough to wind down after work one day or something.

This game is an excellent example of how class oppression has existed throughout time, even in the feudal era which preceded our especially oppressive modern capitalist era. As you play as a feudal lord, traipsing around and attacking your fellow lords, you get choices such as attacking and looting villages and forcing them to give you cattle or food, their very means of sustenence. No remorse is shown by your character or others in the game, and yet you lose "honor" for such petty things as fighting another lord over a woman. However, as you explore the map and talk to the various peasants and workers, the predecessors to the modern proletariat, you get a real sense of what it would have been like to be a common man in that day and age, deprived of even the modest "freedoms" that the bourgeoisie have granted society today in order to appease the proletariat's hunger for liberation. You also see the heroism of many pre-proletariat workers fighting for material equality in the form of "bandits" and "looters," obviously derogatory bourgeois terms created to make us consider standing up to feudal oppression to be "theft" or "murder." However, when you make an effort to see through the haze of lies crafted to make us look down on the proletariat and the forces of social change, you see a truly remarkable recreation of the forces that eventually toppled the feudal system to give rise to the modern bourgeiosie and the system of capitalism as we know it. You see the merchants distributing the ever increasing supply of goods to different cities and you see the urban workers slaving away day and night to produce more and more goods to satisfy the bourgeois' hunger for profits. You see the foundations of the means of production being built, the foundations that bourgeois have used to achieve their position in the world, and the foundations that will be used to topple them. If you want an in-depth, if slightly propogandized, look into what the world was like before the oppressive system you live under today, it is worth putting a few more dollars into the pockets of the businessmen who funded this game to get it. As you will see, the workers have nothing to lose but their chains. Workers of the World, Unite!!!

This game has a solid foundation, but has several major design flaws. Since the game already has a lot of positive reviews, I'll focus on why mine is negative.
First off, it's extremely slow paced. It requires a lot of micro management, so you can't just set orders and go do something else. But it moves so slowly that you'll be sitting doing nothing for a minute or two after assigning new orders. Set some blocks to mine, trees to cut down, animals to hunt, then open portals near those places. Now wait 2 minutes while your dwarves finish those tasks. Then repeat. In order to play at an engaging speed, I actually used an external program to run the game at triple speed, which improved the game significantly.
Second is the crafting "tree". All items, weapons, equipment, decoration, supplies, etc are bunched into groups of 4-5 items. In order to unlock a new group of items, you have to craft a certain number of items from the group (or two) that lead up to it. Crafting a lot of only one item from that group has diminishing returns, so it is best to craft 2-3 of each item in the group. The problem is, it isn't laid out in a tree. The next tier of armor might have furniture and glassware as prerequisites (as an example, I don't remember exactly). But each of THOSE requires 1-2 other groups first. So you can't rush to the items you want: you have to make EVERY ITEM IN THE GAME a few times to progress. This just compounds the first problem, slowing down the game. Even though you could easily just dig down and get mithril to make the best gear in the game, you can't actually craft those items until you've made every single other item in the game several times over. Imagine if in Minecraft, even though you can easily dig down and find diamonds in 10 minutes, you couldn't actually make diamond gear until you've spent 10 hours gathering materials and crafting every other in the game 20 times. Or if in Civilazation, there were no tech trees and you just had to research every single technology, in the same order, every game. That's what it feels like. There's no choice. It gets boring and tedious after the first time.
Third is the lack of real progression from level to level in the campaign. There are four "worlds" in the campaign. Beat one, go to the next one. Here's the problem: each world only has a few new items to make. You play world one, get your dwarves decked out in the best gold and mithril gear, and then move on to world two... and you're back collecting sticks and leaves. World two lets you build four "ice" versions of other items, which are only better in that using ice doesn't waste the more valuable resources. Then you go through the whole crafting tree, taking forever to get enough resources to get up to gold and mithril again, so you can go on to world three and start all over again. World four finally adds some new weapons, which is nice, but they aren't a huge improvement on the same weapons you've been using since world one. It just doesn't feel like you're progressing. Normally in a campaign, when you move on to the next world you get access to stronger gear and the like. But in Craft the World, you work through the exact same progression over and over.
My overall conclusion is that the game has potential but is poorly designed. A major overhaul could make it really good. Increasing dwarf movement speed so you don't have to micromanage portals for transportation would be amazing. Sorting the tech tree by item type would be a big help. Iron armor -> silver armor -> gold armor, instead of iron armor -> glassware -> fabric dying -> whatever -> silver armor or whatever the progression is. This would let you focus on what you want/need at the moment, instead of wasting your time making items you don't need first. When I need better armor so my dwarves can survive the next invasion, I don't want to have to make a ton of armoires first. The last major change would be changes to the scope of the campaign worlds. World one should be shorter, with iron as the only available metal, and weaker guardians that only require that iron gear to beat. Then world two is slightly larger, with silver added and guardians that require silver to beat. This way, the player actually feels a sense of progression from world to world. As is, it's just painful and quite frankly STUPID to go from mithril right back to wood, and then have to work back up to mithril. Also, don't make me unlock all the crap again in world two, three, four. It's a 100-200 hour game, with only 10-20 hours worth of content.
Of course, for a lot of people it isn't just a game where you rush to beat the campaign. Like Minecraft, it's about building your vision of the perfect home. But in Minecraft, when you have a new vision you start a new world and can quickly have everything you need to start building again, but in Craft the World the tech system means that if you start a new world, it'll be at least 10 hours before you start to see your vision take shape.

Though not a Game of the Year by any means, Craft the World is a fun game that will keep you entertained in short bursts.  It can be best described as Terraria if it were an RTS where you were in charge of a tribe of dwarves instead of just your hero and, of course, there was significantly less content to discover.
Your tasks in the game include gathering resources, feeding and caring for your dwarves, researching technologies, building defensive structures, and digging deeper and deeper.  Each and every dwarf is an individual with skills that can be learned and improved and equipment that can be upgraded as you develop the technology and acquire the neccessary resources t ocraft it.  Though it was exciting to acquire new technology, it was often tedious working through the previous tech to fill your research bar as you are required to craft the same three or four items many, many times.
Though it is enjoyable and I believe that it is worth it at a sale price under $10, the game does grow old rather quickly and, if you're anything like me, you'll find yourself burning out toward the end of the first of five worlds.  I recommend this for fans of resource gathering and building games (Terraria/Minecraft), though, as stated earlier, it is more of an RTS as you are in charge of several dwarves at a time.

Grand Theft Auto V offers a great single player experience, assuming you don't want to expand the life of the game via mods. Grand Theft Auto V was a great game that was made even better through modding, until it wasn't. Rockstar has previously reassured players that mods are totally fine, provided they do not alter online gameplay, but it seems like that has been changed by Take-Two.
The shutdown of OpenIV seems to be a blatant attempt to force players to access new content through Grand Theft Auto Online, rather than modding. Prices are high for in-game content, and players must either grind constantly or purchase Shark Cards in order to access any of the new content. In addition, it seems as though Grand Theft Auto Online moderation has become lazy. There are modders in nearly every session, and many of them set out to ruin the online experience for other players. This has progressed since the release of Grand Theft Auto V on PC in 2015, and legitimate players are turned away because of it.
This move is yet another attempt to prolong the life of Grand Theft Auto V and charge players to access additional content, all while providing an unsatisfactory online experience.
If you want to enjoy a great story without the intention of using mods or having a great online experience, then go ahead and spend the $59.99. Otherwise, save your money.

Pros:
+Routing is very dynamic; choices have significant changes in who you interact with and each lead to a unique ending.
+Pacing: your character is fast, and controls are solid, so movement is very fluid.
+Graphics: for a port of a mobile game, everything looks crisp. Besides some awkward animations (the janitor pivoting on the spot while running to turn around, running through doors, etc.) it looks very good.
+Puzzles: the puzzles aren't particularly difficult, but just intuitive enough to add a reasonable challenge.
+Music: the soundtrack is superb, and the variety in different areas and situations is fantastic. I'm particularly in love with the doppelganger fight music.
+Voice acting is solid.
Cons:
-Five patches have updated the janitor's AI, which speaks to the game's biggest problem. You're going to spend a LOT of time running in circles from an unloseable AI. Like exploring? Reading notes? Looking for clues? You can be found anywhere at any time (even during cutscenes) and that gives you the choice to run across the map and back a few times losing him (after which he'll patrol between you and your objective) or simply reload a save and start your whole quest over. The game's ultra-simple but ultra-aggressive AI programming makes the main enemy rip all of the game's good aspects to shreds on all but the easiest difficulty.
-At least one forced death on your first playthrough: later in New Building, a cutscene will inform you that you have to set a condition to deal with a ghost... but as you approach the area to meet that condition, you'll be killed after some QTEs. On subsequent playthroughs you have to deal with it ahead of time before you're supposed to know about it. For your first time, enjoy that forced death and the backtracking it forces.
-They added pseudo-random jump scares with the floating head ghosts. While out and about with your business, a barely-noticeable floating head can float up to you, and on hit you take damage but also a full-screen jump scare.
-QTEs at unnecessary random spots during some cutscenes, which just give an insta-death. Sloppy and a totally lame tack-on.
-Menus lag; the game seems to have issues scrolling through menus, and some buttons and options will "stick" until tried a few times.
-A minor complaint, but cutscene skips are slow, only fading out after a few seconds of forced watching. Very annoying on mutiple playthroughs, which this game is centered around.
-Not too hot about the $50 of day 1 DLC when the product itself was SUPER buggy and messy, but that's up to the player I suppose.
Verdict: Ignore the harder difficulties unless you have the game thoroughly memorized. Play on Very Easy, and if it still isn't fun for you, return it, because it doesn't get better. On the easier settings it can be a satisfying horror experience, if buggy and unpolished. But, I wouldn't recommend it at its current price for how many poor design choices really bog down the experience.

Having not finished the original, I looked forward to this game. But it was delayed. Again and again. I know it's been available for mobiles all this time, but I wanted to experience it properly. For two years of delays, this game has way too many bugs and unpolished issues, however most of them make the game actually more enjoyable than the realistic approach many horrors tend to stick with now.
The gameplay is a survival horror classic. You lurk around a certain location, find notes contributing to the lore, items to help you save and buy heals, avoid a patroling enemy and many different ghosts haunting the school, get jumpscared (which I know is a cheap scare, but it fits with this game) solve puzzles (which sometimes might seem very weird, but most of that is due to translation difficulties really) and proceed to the next location until you beat the game. The AI is extremely simple and does simply what it's meant to do - be a nuisance to your progress. The best thing about the gameplay is that it actually feels like a game: the first time you play it you're confused and terrified of the unkown, but after some time you start to see its mechanics, you learn about all the ghosts and their behavior - you start mastering the game and "survival" in "survival horror" starts to take priority.
The story, and specifically the characters might often make you question their ingelligence, but given some time you grow attached to them as more of their background is revealed (although still at a little weird pacing). The game features multiple endings and sort of different routes. The general story and course of action you'll take will not change, but the cutscenes and bits of story/lore that will be shown to you differ. If you're a completionist, then you're up to some time consuming challenge, as the game requires you to get all endings on all difficulties which leads to having to get 35 endings plus extra (i.e. simply die at some point and also some secret endings). But you don't have to replay the game entirely for each one: sometimes a simple save load is enough.
All in all, White Day is definitely a good experience despite its many bugs, issues and countless delays. If you like classic survival horrors like the old Resident Evil or even the newest installment which tries to go back to its roots, you'll most probably enjoy this game.

Action! is a really well-made piece of recording software that is quite comparable to the likes of Fraps, PlayClaw, and all other big name softwares. Action has its own .AVI codec, FICV, so don't plan on raw uploading to YouTube if you don't record in MP4 format. Supports game, active window, and region-based recording. Can record videos at the same framerate as the video, which is kind of gimmicky in my own opinion. Also supports time limited recording, meaning you can set it stop recording after X amount of minutes, hours, etc. Has built in streaming support with a free 14-day trial, after that, you have to pay $7.95 a month, which is actually quite cheap. Also supports audio recording, and FPS benchmarking. It can make use of AMD APP hardware acceleration. Supports webcam overlay in a screen recording.
Overall, this software offers a lot, and I could easily recommend it to anyone. Records some of the smoothest and high-quality videos I've seen - especially for their size when compared to the likes of Fraps. Honestly though, I use PlayClaw for my goto recorder, simply for the MJPEG .AVI codec, as I prefer to do raw uploads to YouTube as I don't do any video editing.

Before you get into this game, note that it's a Final Fantasy title in name alone.
Combat is done solo
using basic attacks to draw orbs and using said orbs to use ability cards. It sounds simple but it's actually tons of fun with 900+ cards to collect.
You can also level up the cards both in rarity
and in battle to gain more HP\Strength and overall character level.
That said the combat is still more of a traditional turn-based style, you get a certain number of attacks per turn and you can do even more using support cards
and leveling up your job class.
Honestly, this is an oddity.
There's plenty of music within the game, yet the majority of it only plays when certain conditions are met.
An example, if you pull the
class you'll get FFVII music during battles.
If you pull
you'll get the FFX battle theme during battles.
Those are Legendary Job examples, but each of the standard jobs also have their own theme songs.
Sound-wise, there's plenty of fanservice but nothing too grand, the attack & ability sounds are decent enough depending on the skill.
This being a port of a mobile F2P game, means there's a
that slowly goes down per battle. Many see this as a negative, but it doesn't really matter in the long run since you get all your stamina back every time your account level's up and get +1 on the max total stamina.
The game also give's you plenty of ethers which refill your stamina instanty upon use. Not to mention login bonus's and special event's that also give you more items.
I would recommend visiting the
before starting and checking the wiki section for details. It's really important not to screw up in the beggining since that can make or break the game for you.
With that said, It's still a great game. With enough time you can get mostly everything without spending any real-life currency on the game.
Enjoy.

In Mount&Blade:Warband you are a person in 1st person or 3rd person which tries to survive.
Here is no magic, only steel.
You can have people following you, these people will get better through fighting or if you or your companions have the skill "training" by just being in your party.
The fights are intense, the maps for the fights are multiple and very different.
You have soldiers which do melee or ranged fighting from with our without horse.
If you deploy and command your troops in an intelligent way (not complicated) then you can crush superior forces.
There are personal skill which allow each person to be better in something, like being able to use bows which are stronger.
There are leader skills which only apply if the leader (you) has them.
There are party skills, where the highest skill in the party is taken and if the leader has it too, the skill gets a small bonus.
You can trade, the logic for trades is ok. Certain areas produce certain resources, so they are there always cheaper.
You can create businesses which use these resources to create wares and sell them automatically.
You can join a faction and wage war.
You can attack caravans and sell the loot.
You can have cities, town and fortresses.
You can ride into battle with 40 knights in heavy armor and lances behind you.
You can create armies which consist of the best ranged troops there are and rain dead from above.
You can wade into the thickest of the combat and ... die. Not so smart.
But you can use melee weapons, shields, 2-handers or throwable weapons like throwing knives, , throwing axes or whatever you find in the many shops of the world or as loot.
There are so many things you can do here, but to be honest, the most fun is for me always the battle. Riding into battle with knights is a great thing.

-the bad-

Uninspired name (craft the world... Come on!!!)
-the ugly-
Click drag, click drag, click drag, click drag, click drag, click drag, click drag, click drag, click drag, and finally... CRAFT. After over 270 hours of play over the course of this games development I've finally decided, this deserves a review. Before pros and cons; Craft the World is sold as a sandbox strategy game but some may find it to be somewhat linearised by the tech tree system in campaign mode. Don't let this give the impression of restraint because, once you get past it, this really is a lovely indie game which developed dramatically with input from an involved community and provides ample room to exercise your creativity. The artwork, 2d platform and atmosphere I find quite perfect and the game is incredibly engrossing.
The concept of the game is that of a dwarf colony strategy sandbox in which you control a group of dwarves mining ever deeper for riches and plunder, whilst building a defensable home defined by your creative style. I would say it takes a patient and meticulous personality to get fully hooked (both good traits to have); if you enjoy a relaxed process of developing a base/fortress and a group of characters then you should be into this.
Some people have complained about the control of the dwarves being clumsy but you just have to learn how to do it and the way they behave, then it becomes routinely easy. Additions and AI updates have gradually taken away much of the real problems anyway and it is now great fun doing what you want to do with the game.
Pros:
- Relaxed gameplay that nonetheless provides plenty of interest and excitement
- Huge scope of construction options and possibilities in base building
- Great mining style and game mechanics with an excellent range of resources to gather
- Plenty of cool enemies to test your dwarven mettle against
- Good possibilities for dwarf development; not level ups but skills experience and equipment
- Attentive and involved developers with a great community
Cons
- Minecraft style crafting mechanic
- Some eventual repetitiveness, can say the same for all games really
- Linearisation through tech tree, sandbox mode available
If this review has resonated then buy it and call me a c#£@ if hope turns to ash of disappointment.

An interesting MMO and very enjoyable for the first 50 hours. Surprisingly for being free, the game does not have any pay-to-win aspects, like at all. I'm serious, you can do anything without paying. There are "boosts", but are completely optional.
For those not familiar with the setting, Defiance takes place after a human-alien conflict, and the accidental activation of many terraforming machines resulted in Earth being shapeshifted into something new with the old. The game is set in California, with most of it being submerged. The game's map extends from Mount Tamalpais to Silicon Valley, making it an impressive size of about 15 kilometers.
The only few problems I have with the game is some of its acting, and a lack of side activities to do if you're going solo. The real serious problem to me is the mission layouts, as it's always a "defend the person", "navigate interiors and kill a dude", or "mass assault a location and kill a dude" series of scenarios. Pick a card if you do a main mission, as it will most likely be one of the three I just listed.
I'd say you should download this, it's pretty fun with a group of friends.

Look, I got this game when it was free, and I feel like it was worth the "price" of admission. But, I do have my fair share of complaints with Outland. And maybe these are just personal gripes because of my experiences with platformers, or maybe they're legitimate issues with the game's overall design.
I have died in this game more times than I can count. So much so that it's gotten ridiculous, to the point where I've considered uploading a "death compilation" to my YouTube channel. However, the point is this - Outland is hard, even with two players. My friend and I had a lot of issues getting through the jungle level, which in my opinion...is just too long for a first level. It really needs some trim work, maybe stopping the level before <spoiler>, and then making <spoiler> the start of the next level.
While yes, checkpoints are a thing, it's daunting that my friend and I have sunk almost an hour and a half into this game, and we're still not done with the first level. If this was Mario, we'd probably be done with the game by now. Not to say length is inheritedly bad, with all the things the game has thrown at us in the first level, it feels like it just goes on and on, without the scenery really changing all that much.
The gameplay itself is good for a platformer, and there's some neat concepts thrown in for good measure. The online seems somewhat shallow, but it's good for what it is. It has a story, which is decent enough, probably phenomenal by the standards of the genre.
While it hasn't been my cup of tea, I should still recommend it because of its interesting aesthetics, and the fun factor you can have yelling at your friends for repeatedly dying.

Before you get into this game, note that it's a Final Fantasy title in name alone.
Combat is done solo
using basic attacks to draw orbs and using said orbs to use ability cards. It sounds simple but it's actually tons of fun with 900+ cards to collect.
You can also level up the cards both in rarity
and in battle to gain more HP\Strength and overall character level.
That said the combat is still more of a traditional turn-based style, you get a certain number of attacks per turn and you can do even more using support cards
and leveling up your job class.
Honestly, this is an oddity.
There's plenty of music within the game, yet the majority of it only plays when certain conditions are met.
An example, if you pull the
class you'll get FFVII music during battles.
If you pull
you'll get the FFX battle theme during battles.
Those are Legendary Job examples, but each of the standard jobs also have their own theme songs.
Sound-wise, there's plenty of fanservice but nothing too grand, the attack & ability sounds are decent enough depending on the skill.
This being a port of a mobile F2P game, means there's a
that slowly goes down per battle. Many see this as a negative, but it doesn't really matter in the long run since you get all your stamina back every time your account level's up and get +1 on the max total stamina.
The game also give's you plenty of ethers which refill your stamina instanty upon use. Not to mention login bonus's and special event's that also give you more items.
I would recommend visiting the
before starting and checking the wiki section for details. It's really important not to screw up in the beggining since that can make or break the game for you.
With that said, It's still a great game. With enough time you can get mostly everything without spending any real-life currency on the game.
Enjoy.

If you're a fan of Final Fantasy, then I recommend you download this game.
It's Free to Play, and usually that means Pay to Win, but that isn't true in this case. I haven't paid anything and I have two decks of rare cards that are maxed out for my current level. I also have been finding plenty of Crystals in chests which are necessary to make job advancements.  Your Stamina (which is needed to progress on the map and fight battles) regenerates fully everytime you Level Up, and that happens very frequently early on.  You also will find many Elixirs in chests which can be used to fully recover your Stamina.  If you use an Elixir to recover your Stamina, then you end up Leveling Up the next battle, your Stamina will actually over-lap itself and allow you to keep the original and new value.  This means for example if you have a Max Stamina of 50 and it's nearly full when you Level Up, it will show as something like "Stamina: 45 (+50) / 50"
There are no big down-sides to this game.  The only problem is you might enjoy it so much and keep playing for so long that you actually will wear yourself out, and the gameplay may seem repetitive.  Since there's an abundance of Crystals, I suggest trying different play-styles (different Job types) and experiment.
Right now I favor Warrior-type Jobs and switch between Dark Knight and Samurai for their different element expertise.
My advice for how to use your Magicite is to only spend it on Job Card Summoning.  There are extra Job Cards you can get that way that allow specific specialization into a single Job, like Dark Knight for example.  Normally, Dark Knight is a sub-Job of the Onion Knight (Warrior) Job-Tree.  When you get the Dark Knight Job Card itself, you're able to unlock advanced versions of the Dark Knight and have more Stat Specializations that go beyond the Onion Knight basic tree.
Every 16 hours or so you're able to automatically harvest 100 Magicite so it isn't even necessary to pay to save Magicite.  The only reasons to pay is to:
1) Support Square-Enix and specifically the MOBIUS team
2) Get what you want right away instead of saving up for weeks (depending on chance of what you pull from summons)
I love Final Fantasy so all the Jobs and references and crossover events are fantastic.  I like how it's a new version of the Final Fantasy I story, it's twisted and mysterious.  New events and story arcs come out all the time.  New Jobs and abilities and cards are released frequently.
As of writing this, the Final Fantasy VII event is happening, and I'm making my way to earning the maxed-out version of Sephiroth's Masamune.  We're also able to get a Legendary Job Class that is basically called Soldier First Class, and uses Cloud's costume and Buster Sword.
I played this game on my phone when it released on my Birthday (August 3) and it was amazing but didn't have much at the time.  After coming back to it on my PC for the Steam version, it's packed with content and I'm so glad it's brought to PC for a greater and more worthy experience.
Check it out and thank you to Square Enix.

This game is constantly improving and I have had it about 4 years. It keeps getting upgraded and there is no subscription fee. So for all the negative criticisms about this simulator, I think it has really grown into such a realistic Train Sim and nothing else can touch it.
As a Diesel (GE and GM) expert I would like to see the ICE panel screens accurately reflect the real thing like Flight Simulator X (FSX) does with its payware addons.
It is improving so maybe in the future or a private developer like Precision Manuals for FSX will come along (not saying it will be PMDG just an example) and develop it.
The European (German mostly) scenery and equipment is exquisite, it is polished (no screens but the sounds and visuals are realistic 95%!!!) and if you do buy it you will be getting a very decent sim.
I highly recommend it and this coming from an experienced diesel operator. As I said its not perfect but it is the best available and is getting better with heaps of addons and updates.
EDIT: The screens I was referring to are in the General Electric Locomotives. Also appropriate to simulate is the Air Brake system which takes up to 90 seconds to apply on Westinghouse Air Brake trains which I believe is not properly simulated right now.
The SD 40 has some commonality with the Equalizing Reservoir but I am disappointed there are no gauges in the ES44s (on the screens) showing your air pressures and such as. This will be the next thing to implement.
Then there is the Electronic Air Brake System which applies brakes simultaneously.
I would like to see realism in doing a Pressure Test on non-electronic air brake trains which is manual and there is automatic tests for Electronic trains. Also an end of train monitor can be attached to normal air brake trains as well giving drivers opportunity to make emergency brake application from the rear. That would be wireless but the electronic braking system is wired normally but there are several versions. An electronic/electric cable must be connected (and driver to turn it off or into shunt/switch mode before ground staff can disconnect or connect them when attaching or detaching rail vehicles/cars) for it to operate. Then the locomotive does a setup of the electronic brakes on its computer system. All this is not simulated so I am unaware of which air brake system is being used. It is like the flight simulator coming out with basic set ups (not authentic in real world) that let players get in and fly/drive without having to do months of study.
One difference I really like between this and Micorosoft Train Simulator is this has sound effects for everything. Every notch you put the diesel locomotive into it has the equivalent sound effect. the sound effects on this platform are well done, at least 9.7/10.
Add to this the route builder which is quite easy to use and easy to learn unlike Unreal engine map creation, you will be entertained and enjoying trains for years to come.
I give Air Brake realism 4/10 on this although a caveat. It does brake trains reasonably realistically.
Microsoft Train Simulator on my last trip had quite realistic handling and physics. The physics for TS2014 has improved well to my liking. I even managed to overshoot some passenger platforms myself.
Overall I give TS2014 an 87% score.
I would say the first step if they want to bring authentic air brake operation (without using ECP which would take a lot of work to simulate) into it is to adequately simulate the time it takes to exhaust air from the Brake Pipe (BP) and for individual wagons to operate as well. I believe older wagons (cars/vehicles) would be slower, due for maintenance and noisier........thus making the simulation authentic. sparks from wheels.....fires...
So it would take a minute or more for a car at the rear of the train to apply the brakes and then it would be a run in effect and the locomotive would feel it is being pushed from the rear. A run out effect happens when the brakes are released and can cause a train to part, a buffer/knuckle to break.
The SD-40 has exhaust ports with mufflers but can be heard. The ones without mufflers are very noisy and you hear every bit of the air leaving the brake pipe.
And then there is charging the brake pipe with air. When cars are attached and the rake is of some length, the locomotives will not move unless detached. The air brake prevents it until a certain pressure is reached. But if the cars have been left there for some days and there is no air, hand brakes are released, it is possible to roll the locomotive but safety systems prevent power being applied until a safe pressure of around 70PSI minimum is reached, thus enabling a successful brake application.
