If this were a month ago, I'd give it a thumbs up. Now? No.
The latest update - the "Beta" update on March 10th completely changed the game from something good with lots of potential to.. something that feels less like a game and more like a cash grab. They've added microtransactions for any sort of cosmetic item. Anything that one could originally use on their character for free in the Alpha has been put behind a paywall. As of now, you can only get these items through purchasing a "credit pack" and getting them that way.
The developer says that they will eventually add ways to earn these items in the game, but to release a major "update" with the microtransactions in-game for people like myself who already spent money on said game is a red flag. I know that the developers need to make a living and game development isn't cheap. On their forums, a developer has said that it was economically unwise for them to charge $15 or so for the base game and have everyone unlock the gear from the start - thus the microtransactions. However, I fail to see why exactly this business model has been adapted - it would have been much easier to just increase the price of the game accordingly - instead of adding a microtransaction system.
Again, I realize that the developers need to make a profit. That's fine - but the current business model is not the best way to go, and if a drastic, negative change took place from Alpha to Beta, it makes me skeptical about what the future holds. Only time will tell. However, as of now, the game does not appear to be something worth investing in.

This game has me quite torn. It has so much potential to be a really awesome game but just a few things hold it back, I think.
I really like the base mechanics of the game. You don't control your people individually, but rather tell them what to do and they'll get to it eventually. This can lead to annoyance as things can become high priority to you and your people continue to do the other 'housekeeping' tasks you've set. I could be wrong, but as far as I know, there's no way to increase priority of tasks. That's definitely a problem.
The other thing is that even on the 'fastest' setting, the game gets boring waiting for your dwarves to complete their tasks (even if they immediately jump on them), especially early on when you only have 1-2 dwarves and basic equipment. I know it's kind of supposed to feel like that early on, but this is too much. I'm just staring at the screen waiting far too often.
Also, there is a time box constantly counting down. Every 30 or so minutes (15 I think on the fastest setting), a large group of mobs attack your people. They aren't generally too difficult to defeat, but it does absolutely require your attention. I like the feature, but not ALL the time. This is a crafting game, primarily, and the demographic that likes crafting and building usually doesn't like constant distractions. We want to build our giant god damn usless-but-purty constructions and landscapes.
Lastly, the non-sandbox modes are brutal. Even if you have the materials to craft something, you can't craft it until you reach enough experience in the prerequisit tech tree research. I find myself crafting 14 'dyes' or 8 diving helmets or whatnot just to get enough experience in that tech to be able to craft further. It's infuriating at times. The crafting isn't all that streamlined either. Everytime you craft something new you must drag each ingredient from your inventory to its proper place. That would be forgivable IF you weren't required to craft nearly 100% of what's possible to craft to get to the end of the tech tree. One or the other. Absolutely not both.
Like I said, this game has so much potential, and as it is, it was still fairly fun for me for at least the first time through. However, now when I play I just end up frustrated every time. It's like the designers are too concerned with 'what makes sense?' and not enough with 'what is fun?'. Streamline menus, find a new crafting/tech system, speed the game up, realtime 'increase priority of task', and don't have the mob attack timer on constantly. Maybe a mob attacks only when you steal a rune or something underground so you can choose the time.
It's mostly a solid game, and I'm sure some people will get a lot of enjoyment out of it. Make note of the date of this writing - perhaps they will update it and fix some issues. I want so badly to like it but sadly it isn't there yet.

I would like to review TS2014 from a recent perspective, especially with the NEC: New York-New Haven Route Add-On as well as the Metro-North Kawasaki M8 EMU Add-on.
i started out on TS2014 somewhere in December 2013 as a gift from a friend. He brought it for me because he knew that i was a train engineer (unlike a 'driver', as this title is known in the States, i am a train 'repairman' engineer), and a big thanks to him.
The graphics, at a high setting, were consuming on my graphics card. The standard (i prefer not to call add-on) routes like London-Faversham High Speed Route gave an original feel to train driving. Not having visited the States (i hope i would soon!), i find the Donner Pass route a little bland, which was reflected in which route i spent most time on; the United Kingdom one.
When it comes to TS2014, i could not agree with the difficulty in coming to timeliness. Having played the Japanese train simulator Boso View Express (BVE, freeware) for eight years now, from version 2 to the latest version 5, i could say the Japanese do better job at making you squeeze every ounce of power out of a train when it comes to 'catching up with the timetable'.
From here, i discovered that TS2014 offers something different for a train simulator; scenery. Driving the train in TS2014, i no longer stared at the timetables, instead i spent time looking out of the 'windows' and catching a glimpse of the 'scenery' as it sped by, taking screenshots 'on the platform', watching the bogies (or trucks you call them in the States!) turn as the train goes over a switch. These are things that i have never done with any of the versions of BVE. And i would seldom be late to my schedule even as i engaged in these auxiliary activities, for this, i thank the developers of BVE.
After half a year on this game, i found the DLC (the Metro-North Kawasaki M8) that i was waiting for; a Japanese EMU, or at least, majority of it had originated from the Land of the Rising Sun. It was a notch above those i had experienced before, the same could be said of the route add-on (the NEC: New York-New Haven) that it runs on. i had no problem adapting to the percentage (%) control of the EMU (for eight years, majority of EMUs in BVE have notches for power and brakes). The information screens (known as TIMS on Japanese stocks, for Train Information and Management System) lived up to their name, although the sensation of not being able to adjust the HVAC/sub-system settings was a little irritating. The train performed well, and i wasted no time in completing the two career scenarios for the pack (with full points). It was simply exhilarating to have a EMU that handles just like a (Japan) domestic stock running on the busiest rail line in the States (and its timetable is still not tight enough for me!).
After all the accolades, i have to give my frank comments here.
i noticed that putting stocks with incompatible power supply (like the M8 on London-Faversham, on the third rail sections) is allowed, you will be able to move the train with practically 'no power'. For my XBox360 controller, i have to hold the throttle button to make this happen, once i release it, it will go to coast. If you are a 'simmer' bent on realism, this is one step-back.
Many modern EMU rolling stocks have regenerative brakes, this basically converts mechanical energy from the motors to electrical energy when braking and feed them back to the grid, the power supply (3rd rail or overhead catenary). The heavy-haulage locomotives in the States have them too, where they are called dynamic brakes, which unlike EMUs, feed to a large bank of resistors to be burnt off. When braking from high speed, this action will cause a rise in line voltage, over a certain point which the grid will no longer be able to safely receive the power and the on-board resistors will have to 'burn-off' the energy, while the pneumatic brakes take over, a process known as brake-blending. This sadly is not replicated on the stocks; you will always get regenerative braking as long as you are in the right settings for brakes. A year 2003 PlayStation 2 release of Train Simulator by a Japanese train simulator development firm 'Ongakukan' could replicate this condition, especially when you brake a 10-car EMU from 110 km/h and another EMU brakes at the same time into the same power section.
i shall not be nitty-gritty on the small details like wrong speed restrictions that made me feel as if the train was to fly off the tracks while negotiating a switch (but hey, alas it stayed on the tracks!), or (very) frequent bugs that other users have also rated down in the previous comments. They are right, this game has its fair, and sometimes, unfair share of bugs.
i had a good time with it, and i would continue exploring DLC maps that allow the M8 to run on, albiet with correct voltages, please!

Grand Theft Auto V offers a great single player experience, assuming you don't want to expand the life of the game via mods. Grand Theft Auto V was a great game that was made even better through modding, until it wasn't. Rockstar has previously reassured players that mods are totally fine, provided they do not alter online gameplay, but it seems like that has been changed by Take-Two.
The shutdown of OpenIV seems to be a blatant attempt to force players to access new content through Grand Theft Auto Online, rather than modding. Prices are high for in-game content, and players must either grind constantly or purchase Shark Cards in order to access any of the new content. In addition, it seems as though Grand Theft Auto Online moderation has become lazy. There are modders in nearly every session, and many of them set out to ruin the online experience for other players. This has progressed since the release of Grand Theft Auto V on PC in 2015, and legitimate players are turned away because of it.
This move is yet another attempt to prolong the life of Grand Theft Auto V and charge players to access additional content, all while providing an unsatisfactory online experience.
If you want to enjoy a great story without the intention of using mods or having a great online experience, then go ahead and spend the $59.99. Otherwise, save your money.

This is one of my favorite games of all-time, played for dozens of hours outside of Steam. Bought it again because it was on sale and I was too lazy to look for the CD.
It's very similar in basic game design to Grand Theft Auto 3+: Third-person view, missions that start with some job that needs done, a map to reference a waypoint, jump in a vehicle, and head to the objective. But with fully destroyable buildings, piece by piece. Sandbox-like in that regard (it's not actually a sandbox game), but how you place explosives, shoot rockets, or swing your super-hammer is up to you. Watching a tower fall after you blow up the base is just awesome. Or watching it fall after you crash a truck through it. Or watching it fall after an enemy accidentally drives his armored car through it. You can't dig through the terrain, but destroying structures is much more fun. The action is non-scripted and the physics engine leads to some highly entertaining events - I shot an explosive canister that was next to a garage. When it blew up, it tore a hole in the side and the armored car inside was lauched forward, over a steep hill, through the air, and fell through the roof of another building that I needed to take down. After a moment, it exploded. It was like some ultra-violent Rube Goldberg contraption. Completely unexpected and I doubt I could ever reproduce it.
Some missions have you steal a vehicle, others will have you defend a building, or rescue hostages. Most will have you destroy something. Plenty of optional missions. Or you can just pick a high-value enemy target and take it out to help lower their level of control of the sector.
The storyline is kind of predictable, though there are a few twists here and there. In the original Red Faction, the fairly-evil Ultor mega-corporation is brought down, with the help of the Earth Defense Force. In this game, the EDF has become the cruel occupiers of Mars and they killed your brother.(Not a spoiler, it happens 5 minutes into the game.) Nothing overly creative. And, like too many games these days, there's someone talking to you over a communicator while on missions- Someone who you'll want to find and punch in the face. Guy gives me a mission to rescue some hostages that are about to be executed. I accept the mission and about 4 seconds later I jump into my truck and he starts screaming "Mason! What are you doing? People are DYING!" Holy crap old man, keep your pants on, I haven't even started the truck!
But, these a minor issues in light of how fun the game is otherwise. Highly recommended.

In Mount&Blade:Warband you are a person in 1st person or 3rd person which tries to survive.
Here is no magic, only steel.
You can have people following you, these people will get better through fighting or if you or your companions have the skill "training" by just being in your party.
The fights are intense, the maps for the fights are multiple and very different.
You have soldiers which do melee or ranged fighting from with our without horse.
If you deploy and command your troops in an intelligent way (not complicated) then you can crush superior forces.
There are personal skill which allow each person to be better in something, like being able to use bows which are stronger.
There are leader skills which only apply if the leader (you) has them.
There are party skills, where the highest skill in the party is taken and if the leader has it too, the skill gets a small bonus.
You can trade, the logic for trades is ok. Certain areas produce certain resources, so they are there always cheaper.
You can create businesses which use these resources to create wares and sell them automatically.
You can join a faction and wage war.
You can attack caravans and sell the loot.
You can have cities, town and fortresses.
You can ride into battle with 40 knights in heavy armor and lances behind you.
You can create armies which consist of the best ranged troops there are and rain dead from above.
You can wade into the thickest of the combat and ... die. Not so smart.
But you can use melee weapons, shields, 2-handers or throwable weapons like throwing knives, , throwing axes or whatever you find in the many shops of the world or as loot.
There are so many things you can do here, but to be honest, the most fun is for me always the battle. Riding into battle with knights is a great thing.

Initially, dropped in the game world alone with little instruction and no mandated direction beyond a short tutorial quest, by your ten or twentieth battle you might feel like you have already seen it all.  But then you assembled your first 50-man crew and started feeling cocky.  You ambushed a foreign Count and next thing you know you're rotting in a dungeon stripped of your invaluable scale mail, stolen in defeat as a war trophy.  It takes every coin you've earned to pay your ransom and now you are back where you started, alone and broke, only this time all but naked with nothing but a righteous fury-fueled lust for revenge seething in your core.
Before you know it, from this ignominy, you've defended castles with a Thermopylean skeleton crew of elite men each adorned by raiment stained by the blood of untold dozens of your foes.  You've fought off the last ten men of an army of hundreds while near death and alone, your army littered and broken about you, to narrowly escape capture with your injured and your life.  In time administering your own fiefs, castles and capitol cities across multiple provinces; collecting vast wealth of which you once only dreamed such that your old stolen scale mail has become mere petty gutter trash.  At some point you have begun to feel like a Vaegir and look down on those clod-kicking Khergit scum.  You spring Artimenner from prison and are delighted to see an old chum and in reconnecting, instantly forgive him for throwing that nit fit about Klethi and quitting your crew hours before a crucial siege; telling him so, out loud, to your computer screen.  You'll discover a sinister smile on your face, one that manifested itself from some dark place inside you you never knew existed, when you throw King Yargolek into his own prison where he once held you just weeks before.  Along with the traditional and familiar taste of victory and sting of defeat you'll push the far rarer stone of Sisyphus and, rarer still, taste the bitter milk of Pyrrhus and know them utterly.
You can create a dozen characters, ask a friend about their characters, or watch a let's play on youtube, and see an entirely different story told of a unique citizen of Calradia play out in an infinite variety of ways.  Not only have I played hundreds of hours of Mount and Blade (the original and Warband combined), I've watched hundreds of hours of other people playing it.
Mount and Blade and Dragon's Dogma (and their updated forms, Warband and Dark Arisen respectively) are two games I consider very special in an age of stale game design.  They both don't appear to be anything special on the surface and upon closer examination only shine their flaws more brilliantly.  But as the old alchemical proverb holds, "From the vili figura springs the water of life."  If one takes the time to experience these games in their fullness, one finds an experience beyond that offered by their contemporaries.
I cannot recommend them highly enough.  They are, in a word, sublime.

Do you want to know what's so incredibly sad about reviewing this game? Mechanically, it's great. I've grudgingly come to accept DLC as an unfortunate fact of the industry, but nickel and diming customers once you've already squeezed $60 out of them isn't just a♥♥♥♥♥♥move. It's inexcusable. The game is very polished for an MMO type of genre, but there are some pros and cons (warning: a little extensive based on all time spent analyzing it):
+ Lots of replayability and interesting group quests/raids you can do with others
+ VERY good customization (colors and styles) with loot drops and pretty much every cosmetic that can drop through mobs defeated or whatever you find in event maps
+ Pretty easy hotkeys to set up and mix and match with other skills (although each class is separate but hybrid in a way)
+ Lots of people still playing on each platform (I played on both PC and PS4 for quite some time, although the Steam version is not reflective of my old client progress)
+ Game is pretty optimized for low end PCs/laptops (I own a laptop and have had little issues with graphics most of the time, and only a little bit of lag here and there)
+ Both Heroes and Villains have their own hideouts and bases and what not; lots of variety and diversity through characters you can make and see in others
- A little lackluster and repetitive campaign mode for every Hero or Villain created
- If your friend creates a faction opposite of your own (e.g., you pick Hero and they pick Villain), they CANNOT meet you in person since the campaign quests are aligned to both factions differently... in other words, game prevents you from meeting each other because of story missions being unique for each side
- Chat and social seem a bit rude at times (only got a few people to truly help me end game without hearing complaining half the time... sometimes I even got crickets as a response)
- Hard to really group up with people manually (like through text chat), only other option is to just matchmake anyways
- Speaking of matchmaking, queue times are pretty LONG at times and makes it feel like an eternity just to raid with others
- Most end game content (DLCs especially) are driven by paywalls and loot locks; you can only roll loot from those types of missions once a week or once per month (only a few are daily ones)
- A freemium model apparently separates half the community from those who "pay to win" and so on, giving them extra benefits and incentives over f2p players (e.g., inventory space, trading/brokerage, etc.)
- Half the cooler powers and abilities for those customizing at start are sorta locked behind a paywall as well (making you invest more just to start over or do anything else)
- Once you beat the game maybe one time, you'll wish you had some friends to play with on regular basis, otherwise you start feeling left out or bored
All in all, give it a try, maybe it's for you... or maybe not!

The very first thing you might ask is why a lot of people that gives negative reviews, actually have more than 100 hours invested into the game. This is firstly because of the compulsory upgrade of the game that the developers push, so a lot of people you see with 600 hours when the game released last year, owned the previous version of the game and invested a lot of hours into it before it became TS2014.
In regards for myself, I started playing the old Microsoft Train Simulator and invested hundreds of hours into driving the Japanese fast trains and enjoyed that game fully. When Railworks released, I downloaded it through other means and played some of the older routes with the diesel engine on the UK maps which combined with the broken game was kind of boring.
When TS2014 released, I actually believed that it was of course the same developers as Railworks, but that the engine was completely new and that the only reason there was so much DLC to download and buy was because of backwards compatibility. Jokes on them for doing such an excellent job marketing the new version of their game and dibs on me for digging through 70 EUR worth of DLCs just to come to a boring conclusion about the game: It is not complete.
If you start out by buying the steam version of TS2014 with the UK, German and US standard routes, you'll be amazed at the nice graphics and 3D cockpits as well as the scenarios. But when you've beaten all the scenarios on expert mode with golden stars or 990+ XP and you are only 6 hours into the game, you ask yourself why a big sandbox open ended game with unlimited potential, only have 6 scenarios for each route and approximately 3 scenarios per vehicle.
So here comes the hook: You are the missing link, you are the missing developer. They expect us to learn how to use the editor (which you can't even exit using the ESC button) and has lots of illogical and unintuitive controls. It is not only frustrating when you have to spend 10s of hours on youtube watching 13 year old German kids explain the editor in broken English (Zumindest nehmen Ihre Zahnspange aus, wenn Sie sprechen.); at the end finding yourself with a perfect scenario where each train goes and leaves in perfect timing. This is where you press the fast forward button, make all the trains move from their starting locations and then press the "Test Scenario" button. What happens when you do this you ask? The scenario will save itself as if the current time stamp was the beginning of the map and you have to remake the whole scenario from the beginning, because the editor automatically saves over your scenario without you having to confirm a save.
But the Steam Workshop will add the missing link between the missing content and the customer developer. It gives the users the powers to upload their glorious expert scenarios to the cloud and can easily be subscribed to by the click of a button. This is of course if one of the customers get past the initial learning curve of the stupid UI in the editor and after at least 3 hours of testing and time table experiments gets a mission working, he uploads his contribution to a filter based browser that gives us much more content. Out of the 30 subscribed scenarios I've downloaded on the UK London-Faversham high speed route, 2 of them worked, and this is why:
So  you downloaded the DLCs for a route and got all the trains included? Great, that means you can now actually drive the route too. Because without the engines and the carts, the scenarios won't work and you will just get a big blob of a message saying: "Content 123_Cart_Livestock is missing from content". You can then choose to edit the scenario and try to find the cart in question and replace it with a cart you have or just quit back to the menu. Even more interesting does this incompatibility become when you have 20 or more of this missing carts that you don't even know what they are, because some guy with that extra DLC of that Northeast corridor route from TS2012 has and this is how the whole Steam workshop is right now.
Other games shows you mod and expansion incompatibilities or at least lets you have them downloaded but not use them, but no, TS20XX requires the actual DLC on your computer to enjoy a scenario. So until editors of scenarios knows what DLCs they are using (because there is no way to tell the difference between trains and what DLC they comes from), most of the scenarios you can play are from those people who have the exact same setup as you.
It becomes even more frustrating when you go online to find solutions for the bugs you find because according to rumors of many reviewers and people writing in the steam discussion, every time the game is reupdated with a new name, all the threads and discussions in the steam discussion disappears as the "old" game cease to exist and a "new" game gets a new created steam discussion forum. So a lot of information on how to resolve bugs, workarounds in the editor and scenario editor is simply gone from existence on the discussion pages and that had a huge group of experienced veterans of train builders leave the scene completely.
And then we have the game elements of course which are completely disturbed. Passing a red signal doesn't give you penalty points, it will abruptly end the game with a nice pop up saying: "You passed a red signal at danger, game over". Great, I understand the level of simulation that goes into a train drivers career for making such a huge mistake, it is one of the reasons many modern railways uses an Automatic Warning System to make sure a train does not go past a red signal without emergency breaks applied. And the only reason you want to try to pass a red signal is for fun of catching up with the train in front of you and watch the red lights of it but the game will not allow you to pass a red signal. So what is the problem?

At the time of this writing, I am only at about ninety minutes of gameplay, roughly. Within the hour of this game I have already found that the controls are sluggish, not due to the fact that the game was poorly designed, but because the designer likely made you want to feel like you were climbing a ♥♥♥♥ing mountain with a sledgehammer like the god damned animal you are.
This was genius, along with the accompanying quotes or music that would play if you just lost a lot of progress. The whole game has this tense, yet relaxed atmosphere to it that makes success almost monotonous, while failure is absolutely crushing. There are people in the reccomendations who whine that the game is too hard and you shouldn't play it unless you like 'bashing your head against a wall,' but I disagree. I think this game is good at teaching a lesson, and that lesson happens to be the opposite of bashing your head against a wall. This game will teach you that with every fall, a mistake was made, and you have a choice afterward; to either get angry, and continue to make the same mistakes you have been for the fifteenth time in a row, or slow down and try to figure out what you have been doing wrong, even if you think the tactic you've been using this entire time is sure to be the only tactic that should work.
All in all; I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who wants to be entertained, frustrated, and have a lesson hammered into them at the same time.

I'm going to review this game with the premise that it one of a few games that could be categorized as Dwarf Fortress like, and will refer to DF throughout the review. The game has some major flaws, but overall it's a great game and is well worth the price. I'll start with the negatives. The AI is not great. The dwarves have a strange way of prioritizing what needs done, so you can't queue up too many task at once, or it will take forever for the important ones to get finished. They also path terribly sometimes, ignoring nearby warp portals if was built after they decided to go somewhere. They will also walk into a hole another dwarf is about to fill to pick up dirt, and will just stand there deciding what to do next, rather than realize they will be trapped. Also wood is far too important for building for not being able to reliable plant it yourself. You end up using the portal spell to send your dwarves out onto the fringe of the world for a few trees all the time. The tech tree is also very poorly implemented. The order in which the dwarves research things is very strange, with seemingly easy things towards the end of the tree and hard things at the beginning. It also forces you to make countless items you'll never use, simply to advance the tree. Combat can also seem kinda clunky, as dwarves will sometimes waltz away from a monster wave simply because none of the monsters are marked for combat. The lack of a profession system is also very irritating. In DF and many DF like games, you assign your dwarves/gnomes/goblins/etc a job, and they perform that job. Such as smith, miner, logger, etc. In this game all dwarves do everything. There is a skill system (dwarves gain up to 3 skills in things such as logging, swimming, archery, etc), and I've read that a job is done by the dwarf with the highest skill in that task, who is currently not doing anything. While I'm not sure if this system even works, it is a bad idea to begin with. The game can also begin to be repetitive. At 21.6 hours I've beat the first world and have moved onto the second world. You simply begin back at square one, with one dwarf and an empty tech tree. The only difference is that the world is harder. I can easily see how other people with more hours and who have gotten to further worlds say that by world 5 the game is boring.
Now to the good. The side view 2D is an interesting perspective, and fresh from many of the other top down view DF like games, or any city builders in general. The fortress defense mechanic is very fun. Although the nightly skeleton/zombie hordes do not get any more challenging, the hourly monster raids do start to get harder. This is until all your dwarves are equipped with mithril weapons/armor, at which point the game becomes fairly easy again. The tech tree, while overall being badly implemented, can do a good job at driving you forward to research new items. There are several types of metal to work with, which leads to a nice flow of upgrading your weapons. There are also several types of walls/roofs (once you finally research them), so you can make cool looking forts. Although the game does discourage making individual bedrooms (by keeping interior doors until well into the tech tree) and this does detract from making interesting looking forts. Once you also get farming (well into the tech tree, this is another negative) you can make interesting looking fortresses with attached underground farms. This is always one of my most fun parts of DF like games. The spells are nice too, and make you feel much more involved than many DF like games. Dwarves getting tired of eating certain food too often, forcing you to take advantage of the different types of food available. While I love Gnomoria, I hate knowing I can just grow wheat and my gnomes will never get tired of eating wheat bread and drinking wheat beer (in fact spamming wheat in it is to your advantage). Overall, the thrill of the first 15-30 hours is great. You want to explore just one more tunnel before you go to sleep, and the portal spell makes exploring the fringes of the world much more accessible. If you don't mind spending 20 dollars on a great 30 hours, and then (from what I've heard) an "eh" another 20 hours before the game is just too repetitive, then this is a great game for you. If you are a fan of a DF and are looking for something less intense and requires less time and energy, this game is also great for you (or if you are too scared to jump straight into DF but want to play a fortress builder).

with it being f2p it's hard not to recommend it: I'll break the game down best I can by catagory.
Story: This is the toughest part, it's like they took a really good story and tossed it in a blender with a crappy fan-fiction of that story. The result is a decent storyline as far as MMOs go, but it could have been so much better if they hadn't done things like insist on replacing the word &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; with "shtako" and other such ham-fisted attempts to blend Voltan and human culture.
Gameplay: This aspect of Defiance is actually pretty damn good. It basicly plays like a 3rd person RPG (think Mass Effect without the cover system) with players aiming for themselves and activating 1 of 4 abilities as the situation calls for it. The number of abilities might seem limiting, but there's plenty of passive abilites to equip to tailor your build to your play style (if memory serves you can equip 10 passives at a time).
MMO Staples: there's no dungeons in the traditional sense, instead there are a multitude of community events (Arkfalls, sieges, ect.) that randomly take place on the world map. These events can be joined or left at will with no need to formally group up with anyone else. Rewards are based on earned point scores from the participants which, among other factors, are determined by damage dealt, times died, players revived, and damage healed. No matter if you're a noob or a veteran, these community events have something for everyone to do.
Character Customization: The character models look pretty good, but the level to which you're able to customize them kinda falls flat; not saying you'll look like everyone else but given the limited options you'll probably be left wanting in this department.
F2P vs Pay to Play: Defiance shines here for damn sure. In terms of playing the game, you won't really be compelled to the cash shop for any gameplay mechanic - related untill you get near the end game. Even then it's more a matter of saving time, not "P2W".
Overall Defiance is worth a look,

I've had it for a while now, and I can say that while it has it's flaws, it is definitely a solid recorder. It can record games at 1080p if you want (and can). I will mention that there is an original option in the quality options, which is for recording at a resolution that isn't 1080p, 720p, 480p, 360p or 240p. It will not record higher than 1080p though. If you are playing a game at 1080p, and you set it to record at 720p, it will only record at that resolution. This is a fantastic feature because, while it may look a bit blurry (and i mean a TINY bit), it will come out as a much smaller file. Which is good if you don't own a very big hard drive or want to upload something to Youtube in your lifetime. This recording option can be done in any of the listed resolutions. This feature is lacking in several big recording softwares, which force people to manually compress the files.
The UI is fantastic, and way more straight forward than most recorders that I have used before. The recording options are easy to reach, and yet they seem to do a lot without being confusing. There are SO many features that I love about this software that I can't find in most recorders. There's a window option, where you can record a certain part of your screen, which is very handy for windowed games. There's a facecam option if you have a camera. And of course, it has the usual voice recording options.You can choose for it to limit your frame rate while you are recording, which is good if you don't want lag or just simply want to record at a certain FPS. Action also performs WAAAAYYY better than FRAPS. The recording quality is definitely grainy, but it's worth it for the better framerate, and while some people may want to go for the recorder that records a tiny bit better, Action won't dive on the frame rate.
When I used FRAPS to play a retro game, I got about 5 FPS, and the game even FROZE at times. Even when I wasn't recording, having it open slowed the game down.  With Action, the game ran like it did when I wasn't recording. It was incredible how fast it ran. One complaint I have, is the FPS options I mentioned earlier. You can chose to limit your frame rate at 60, 50, 30, 25, 24 (yes 24), 20, 15, and 120. Why are the options so random? Why is there a 25 and 24 option? There's no difference! And yet there's no 40 FPS option. I actually really like limiting my frame rate at 40. So why am I stuck with using 25, 24 and 15? Get rid of 24, as a single frame difference is NOTHING, and add 40.
EDIT: After a long time of use, I have noticed how much of a lottery it is when it comes to audio. Sometimes the recording has tinny, echoing sound, which really sticks out like a nose unless if you mask it with music in editing. Other times, however, it records perfectly fine.
IMPORTANT: To do live streams, you need a subscription. It comes with a free subscription when you buy it, but I can't remember how long it is. I have never streamed using Action, so don't ask me how it performs. I really want to emphasise that there are programs like OBS (Open Broadcaster Software) that can not only record games, but also stream them FOR FREE. Not to mention you can also add on screen pictures and messages in real time on OBS. So if you want to do live streams, seriously consider something else.
If you want to see it in action (joke intended), check out my Youtube channel at
My videos are mediocre, but I have a lot of fun making them :).

I've been a great fan of America's Army 2 for a number of years - when AA3 came out, I was less than impressed - now Proving Grounds has, in my eyes, addressed some of the biggest issues from AA3.
More than anything though - modern FPS games have become far too tech focused and, as a result, have moved away from realism.  This game IS far more tense and stressful than you expect, because it is still well within the realms of realistic.
You crouch behind cover that's barely big enough to offer adequate protection, with long lines of sight that a sniper could be staring down their scope at you through, trying to decide if it's the right moment to move - you pop your head around - just for a moment.  Nothing happens.
You peek again - even faster - trying to spot a telltale sign of movement.
Nothing happens.
You look across at your team mate, a few feet away - and indicate them to go whilst you cover them.
They jump over and start running for the next bit of cover - you pull your weapon out and look over the top.
It all goes dark and then you find yourself watching the match from the sidelines.
The sniper wasn't in front of you after all - he's behind you.
Tense - you don't know the half of it.
Recommended - Hell Yeah!
RECOMMEND

In Mount&Blade:Warband you are a person in 1st person or 3rd person which tries to survive.
Here is no magic, only steel.
You can have people following you, these people will get better through fighting or if you or your companions have the skill "training" by just being in your party.
The fights are intense, the maps for the fights are multiple and very different.
You have soldiers which do melee or ranged fighting from with our without horse.
If you deploy and command your troops in an intelligent way (not complicated) then you can crush superior forces.
There are personal skill which allow each person to be better in something, like being able to use bows which are stronger.
There are leader skills which only apply if the leader (you) has them.
There are party skills, where the highest skill in the party is taken and if the leader has it too, the skill gets a small bonus.
You can trade, the logic for trades is ok. Certain areas produce certain resources, so they are there always cheaper.
You can create businesses which use these resources to create wares and sell them automatically.
You can join a faction and wage war.
You can attack caravans and sell the loot.
You can have cities, town and fortresses.
You can ride into battle with 40 knights in heavy armor and lances behind you.
You can create armies which consist of the best ranged troops there are and rain dead from above.
You can wade into the thickest of the combat and ... die. Not so smart.
But you can use melee weapons, shields, 2-handers or throwable weapons like throwing knives, , throwing axes or whatever you find in the many shops of the world or as loot.
There are so many things you can do here, but to be honest, the most fun is for me always the battle. Riding into battle with knights is a great thing.

A good RTS game with interesting mechanics, deep tactic and challenging missions.
Actually, I bought this game because of TD tag, but i was surprised too see RTS game instead.
So, let's talk about the gameplay. You are a mercenary who delivers cargo through the space filled with pirates and asteroids. Each mission you start with an empty platform where you should place cargo . Then mission beguns. You goal is too save as much cargo as possible and make a delivery keep within a time. The sooner you finish and the more goods remain intact, the higher your reward will be.
Seems easy. Just place more space engines. And there are pirates come. Every mission somebody will try to bring you down. So, you are forced to build up your defense. But the space on your ship is not endless. So, that's the first strategy feature in this game. You need to find the balance between speed of ship, attack turrets and defensive structures.
There 2 types of towers: laser and rocket. Each one has 3 levels. Yeah, it seems not enough, but it's enough for satisfy your TD needs, believe me. Each tower (actually each building) has 1-2 active abilities which requires some money for use. For example basic laser turret has Rapid Fire ability, which increases attack rate by 3 times for 30 seconds. With this ability just 1 turret can deal an insane damage. But you must have money for it and manually activate it. There we come to the big negative side of the game.
Game requires a lot of micromanagment. Even for me, I played SC2 in Diamond league, it was tough in some moments of the last missions. Yeah, i played on hard, but I am experienced hardcore gamer, if it was hard for me, i afraid it will be almost insane for more casual players.
I will give you an example. Enemies usually come from all sides. You have about 3-5 towers at each side. So when wave comes, you need to manually click at all towers, activate abilities, then recharge the shiled when it fades out, rebuild desttoyed buildings, overcharge reactors for getting extra powers for using stronger abilities, when you need to boost your engines (if you want achieve the best score), when you need to build new towers (before building you need to plan your build order), then you need to repair damaged towers, and you to pray god for having money for all these actions. And.. after that you realize enemies comes from other side and everything repeats again, until mission finishes (usually it takes 8-12 minutes).
Pros
- Innovative mechanics with good RTS and TD elements.
- 5 chapters with minor differences in the main gameplay. You transport nuclear weapon on Chapter 2, which could explode and damage your ship and you transport people on Chapter 3 which wanted to be in the center of battle, so you need to place them close to sides of the ship
- Interesting mechanics of upgrading your turrets and ship at all.
- There are really a lot of tactics and strategy :D
- Pleasant visual effects.
Neutral
- Game requires a lot of micromanagement. For me, WC3 1v1 player in the past, it was pretty interesting. But i think, a lot of casual players will suffer :D
- The story is well written and voice acted, but I skipped it anyway :D
Cons
- The game requires to replay previous levels to get extra money for better weapons for passing harder missions. For example, i passed all levels and my ship was only 55% fully upgraded.
- If you passed the level bad you will really low amount of money.
- Usually, you need to lose mission 3-5 before you understand where enemies comes from and where you need to build your defense. It's specially important for boss missions, because if comes from the side where you have low defenses - you will lose.
A great game. I was really engaging by playing this. I can recommend this game for a full price for RTS and TD fans

I was on the fence about this game - it isn't a BAD game - it's just highly unpolished and leaves a lot to be wanted.  I picked it up for 3 or 4 bucks, and I will say it was worth that price.  That being said, I just can't bring myself to giving this game a thumbs up.
PROs:  Fun game concept - combines the strategy of a TD with some real-time elements, although one could argue the game would be better without this.  The game is decently challenging, especially if you wanted to go through and 5 star evertyhing.  A game type I haven't played before.
CONs:  Where to begin.  First off, enemies come from all angles... the reason this is, in my opinion poor game design, is that because each level has the same enemy spawns each time, it basically just requires that you play and fail a couple times until you figure out where you need to stockpile your defenses.  The game also forces you to transport a ton of junk and severely limits what you can place and where.  This gives the game a very 'cramped' feel-  On some levels I've maxxed out my rig with resources to spare only halfway through the level, and it is very difficult to place everything.  It almost feels like a puzzle game more than a tower defense at time.  For me, half the fun of a TD is finding a way to build up a huge defensive front and face increasingly difficult enemies, and this game has none of that.
Perhaps the biggest failure, however, is the fact that the game requires an intense amount of micromanaging, but is incredibly difficult to see your ship clearly or perform multiple actions at once.  This game NEEDS one of two things: 1) A way to pause the game and input decisions - so whent he game is unpaused, everything happens at once.  See Faster Than Light for a perfect example.  Or 2) If you want the game to be about real-time micro, you need to give me a way to hotkey my buildings and select more than one at a time.  As it is, it is just a click fest on hard to see buildings where mistakes are easy and the controls are cumbersome, leaving a huge disconnect between your intentions for your defense and the way it plays out.
Overall, needs a lot of work.  Has a good base concept, but lacks severely in terms of replayability and tires quickly.

Imagine a game that can be set in any time period or universe that you desire. Imagine a game where you can be in the middle of a massive medieval style siege, or on the front lines of a Napoleonic battle with 200 other players. That is this game. I bought this game back in 2012 after seeing mod gameplay of Mount and Musket. I haven't gone back since. Since that time I've fought in line battles, been the Samurai retainer to a  Daimyo, backstabbed the Lords of Westeros, fought for and against the forces of Isengard and Mordor, and even started my own kingdom in the base game. Mods are part of what makes this game great.
The game's combat is also one of the best systems of combat I've ever seen. Deceptively simple and incredibly deep, you will always have to work at your combat skills and you can only get better. In the single player you ride around with a party of adventurers that you collect and literally do whatever you want. Want to be a merchant? Be the best Calradian merchant there is. Want to be a bandit causing terror and earning spoils? Become one. Want to be a mercenary company? Do it. This game lets you be what you want to be, and its freedom makes it one of the best sand boxes out there.
Mod-wise I would recommend The Last Days of the Third Age, A Clash of Kings, Floris, The Deluge, Gekokujo, and Warsword Conquest. I've gotten hours of entertainment out of each and if you don't like a mod you simply uninstall it.
The community is also amazing, organizing battles with up to 200 players, with sieges and field battles. With the amazing amount of mod content, you can be fighting in any time period that you want. This game is really whatever you want it to be.
If you can't tell by the amount of hours I've put into this game that it is good, then let me just say this: buy this game. I still pour hours into it four years later. Experience it and then when its sequel comes out (God only knows when the devs are going to release that game), buy that too. You'll not find a better game or a better community.

It looks like a simulation, but don't be fooled. It's an obstacle course. You must build six items from group A to build 8 items from group B to build 10 items from group C to finally build something that you actually want. So you have no meaningful choices. You can run the obstacle course efficiently or inefficiently, based on how well you understand the system. And learning the system is fun for a while. But once you've learned that system, you'll play every map in exactly the same way. There's no room for individual taste or trying out different strategies. To win, you must do exactly what the designers intended for you to do.

Really good dwarf fortress-y game, very addictive.  The music is nice and context-sensitive in a way I can appreciate.  The graphics are pretty good.  The campaign feels a little repetitive since you wind up crafting mostly the same things each time to progress, but the worlds are different enough that it stays fresh enough to be fun.  Learning how to properly defend your base without outright exploiting enemy AI is fun, even in the world type where a large portion of the incoming enemies ignore doors and fortifications.
However, it feels incomplete in some ways.  The tech tree's progression is really weird, like, sometimes you have to grind out decoration objects in order to unlock better equipment, or do some cooking to unlock things unrelated to cooking.  The pathing AI can glitch out when dealing with water, dwarves jump into pits sometimes, mages waste spells on weak or caged enemies, and most noticably, cave goblins will sometimes just freeze in place once they get near your base, not even fighting back.  Cave goblins also get stuck doing tasks they cannot complete, like clearing vegetation too far away from where they are standing.
The difficulty curve is really weird as well.  The first few nights are absurdly dangerous as you have ineffective weapons, no armor, limited resources, and few dwarves.  As soon as you get even basic fortifications the difficulty takes a nosedive, and never picks back up.
Even so, the game is really fun.

The best part about this game is that even though there isn't much of a learning curve to get going, it takes a lot of trial and error to do things correctly.  In other words, this is a game you can jump right into, but it has taken several playthroughs for me to really become efficient at levelling.
At its heart, this game is a crafting game.  It doesn't suffer from the pitfalls of most other crafting games, either.  The inventory is easy to sort, and the skilltree makes it fun to progress.  There are also battles that require a bit of strategy to overcome.  There is a timer that counts down to the next major attack, and half of the goal is to make sure that the Dwarf's home is prepared to take on the onslaught of demons.  Each onslaught is slightly more difficult than the one before it.   I've found that a dwarf colony with just the right efficiency can stay a step ahead of these onslaughts until the end when it's a race to get as much mythril ore as possible to get every dwarf fully buffed.
I've played through this game several times, and I intend to play through it again.  This one was money well spent.

Surgeon Simulator is what I like to call a
game. You know, the sort of game that you buy for a laugh, play it for maybe an hour or two and then forget about it. This is somewhat unfortunate, but inevitable being the sort of game it is since Surgeon Simulator is actually a brilliant idea. It makes fun of itself with the title, it's only barely a "simulation" of surgery so if you were actually expecting Trauma Center or something then... no. It's not that. It's more like a skit on Surgery, there's no real tutorial, you're just flung into the surgery room armed with whatever you can pick up, no experience, you just have to perform heart surgery on this poor sap.
Of course, once you get into the mindset of "this is a game about having a laugh" the game instantly becomes fun, if a little frustrating at time. It all comes down to the control system which is unique to say the least, you use the A, W, E, R, and SPACE keys to control the fingers and thumb of the surgeon's hand, the mouse is used to rotate the hand and move it around the operating area. You have to literally pick up the tools you think you require to operate on your unfortunate victim and use them appropriately, be it a bonesaw, a scalpel, a hammer, whatever.
Surgeon Simulator isn't a game that I would pay full price for personally, but it's a great buy in the sales if you want a truly new experience in gaming.

While the first half of the game is great and feels like it's exploring its possibilities, the second half really feels like a chore at times. Pro's:
Sound
Sound effects are good
Voice acting is good
Music is decent (not distracting, but not really catchy either)
Graphics
Visually, the screenshots say it all, crisp and polished in general.
Units (tower modules) are easily distiguishable from one another.
Character's look like what they should, considering thier story roles and voices. They only exist in still images during story drops.
Gameplay
Not a typical tower defense, its more akin to a puzzle game with a towr defense theme. There ARE different ways of beating each mission in terms of tower setup, but its usually a difference of beating them into a pulp, or barely reaching the end. There is a lot of trial and error, especially if going for 5 stars.
Cons
Gameplay
It can get frustrating mid-late game when you're grinding for 5 stars on each level.
Upgrades tend to be active upgrades, rather than passive damage boosts (etc), so many of them feel a bit useless.
Lots of micro managing in the late game, this CAN be fun, but I put it in cons because a lot of people are fussy lol.
You don't get to customize the size/shape of your ship for each mission, nor does it grow as missions progress. This is where the puzzle element becomes more apparent, since your ship design is preset for each mission. Instead you can customize the layout of the starting components that are mission specific (fuel tanks, observation rooms, etc.)
Story
Not really a con, but if you're looking for a deep narrative, it isn't here. It's a lighthearted comedy.
Overall:
If you like TD's, or puzzle games, you'll probably like this, the more conservative you are, you might want to wait for a sale tho.

This is a tower defence game where the twist is that you move through a path rather than the enemies. Really the only difference that this makes is that there's a much smaller area for every weapon or defence system that you place. The gameplay is reasonably good fun and each level requires 5-10 minutes of concentration. However after just 5 levels I was already finding the game quite repetitive.
There is an upgrade tree, however despite a range of choices it still feels fairly one dimensional. Most of the upgrades involve giving a certain sstem a special power which must be manually activated. There is no pause feature in the gameplay as there is in Faster Than Light and so much of the game becomes time pressured micromanagement, which I do not find enjoyable. The upgrades are somewhat independent of your performance in a level. There is no real difference between limping across the finish line and dominating the level with an abundance of scrap metal, as long as you complete the requirements your reward is the same. The game wants you to spend all of your scrap each level as there is no benefit to being thrifty.

The dialogue in this game is truly terrible. Thankfully you are able to skip the dialogue and none of it has any bearing on the gameplay. Still, this turns the game into a series of individual repetitive missions as opposed to a game with any real story and progress.
There are much better strategy games and tower defenders out there.

I forgot to mention that the sex scenes have the woman moaning in pleasure as she progressively gets undressed, but you really treated that as an annoying distraction didn't you? ...and you did.

I really like the open world FPS style, and as I grew up in the Bay Area, it's great to see a terraformed landscape that I feel familar with - it really lends a sense of immersion. Graphics run well on a mid-range machine, and the music is solid. The gun combat is great. To me, it feels like a cross between an open-world version of Halo and a non-cartoony Borderlands.
There are a few flaws, such as a somewhat confusing mod interface and a significant lack of melee weapons when you begin (which really kind of sucks, as one of the main characters in the series relies completely on throwing knives). I'd also really like to have the abiltiy to play as races other than Irathi and Human (you can play as a Castillan with DLC, but those guys are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s - gimme a Sensoth already).
All in all, it feels like it has a really solid foundation that could be built into something as full as WoW. Unlike a lot of other F2P games out there, there's no sense of "pay to win", and I'm really digging exploring the game world and lore. The quests are solid and the main quest NPCs are well scripted, animated, and acted. I'd really like to see the capacity to travel beyond the Bay Area into the greater world of Defiance, but then, I haven't even made it out of Marin yet, so I can't really complain.  It's a very richly imagined world that we're seeing just a bit of - I'm hoping that Trion maintains it enough to actually build out the world all the way to NYC.
TL;DR: As a F2P game, 100% worth trying if you like the series, shooters, or Sci-Fi in general.

First thing to know about this review is that its coming from someone who is not used to first or third person shooters. Coming from DAoC to WoW, GW2 and most recently the Secret World, I grew up on keyboard + mouse, and find it difficult to navigate using a controller.
That being said, I absolutely fell in love with the game from day one. There are a few elements that, if they were different, would make this almost the perfect game, but its so hard to find a game that has everything you are looking for.
I'll go over a few of the things I've experienced.
Character Appearance - Pretty limited customization. You only have 3 races to choose from and not a whole lot of options within those confines. Your stats are based solely on your weapons, so clothing is strictly cosmetic and you only get 4 outifts to choose from in the beginning. Yes, you can buy or earn different clothes, but they are set uniforms, not individual pieces. Your appearance consists of a headgear slot and a uniform slot.
Community - The chat system is extremely awkward. But people are generally friendly and most will openly help you as you learn the basics. For me, it was even harder at first because I wasn't familiar with the basic weapon stats and what they meant, so I wasn't sure what I needed to look for. But almost every question I asked was answered and people would even offer to help show me the ropes.
Quests/Missions - It consists of a Main Story line, Episode (based off of the TV show) missions and oodles of side missions. You can only pick up one at a time but they are literally all over the place. Plus, there are Pursuits (which are like achievements) that you gain Rep with certain factions, bonus outfits, vehicles, etc...
Random Events - My favorite thing about the game is the constant random world events. Arkfalls, Incursions, Sieges.... its like a ton of fast action shoot 'em up where you race from one place to the next until all the big bads are eradicated and you are left with a ton of drops and a feeling of accomplishment. However, make sure your inventory is as empty as you can first because it fills up quickly!
Solo vs. Group - One thing I like best about the game is that when you are doing a mission, since its in an open world, people driving by can just jump in and help if they choose to, or if they're on the same mission can join in, too. You don't have to be grouped to get credit, you just have to be a part of the action. If someone higher level than you does join in, the threat level may rise according to them but since its on a sliding scale, your level effectively raises also. So its much  easier for people who like to play alone rather than group.
Content & Travel - The map is expansive. You get your first vehicle within the first Main Mission, which comes in handy as there is a lot of travel. There are also "fast travel" locations which let you teleport from one spot to the next. Another thing I love about the setup is that you can instantly teleport to anyone who is in your group, clan or even just on your friends list. (It makes stalking MUCH easier!... j/k)
Weapons - For me, this is where it got confusing because there are just too many weapons to list. I promise you'll NEVER get bored. They range in rarity from white, to green, blue, purple and orange as the highest. They are random drops and drop frequently. You can also buy weapons from regular supply vendors, or once you gain reputation with other factions (some are only available through the DLC content) you can purchase from them, also. You can attach mods to the weapons as you level making the statistics change according to your playstyle. It is a rather unique system from what I've seen, but then again I don't have much "shooter" experience.
I'm sure I'm missing a few other things, especially to those of you who co-op and PVP (I don't have any experience in that area yet). I'm trying to advance my characters before I attempt to step up to that level.
My complaints:
* Characters - You only get 2 character slots. And, again I wish there was more cosmetic customization.
* Inventory - DEFINITELY not enough inventory space for all the weapons & the mods plus your shields & other accessories.
* Loadouts - You only get 2 loadouts to start (which is where you can switch back and forth between gear & weapons) and only get up to 6 total in the end.
* Chat System - Could use some fine tuning chatting, adding friends, finding people, etc...
* Content - Although the map is huge and there is a ton to actually do, the overall look is the same from one end to the other, making it feel very repetitive at times because although you're on a different mission and in a different place, you're essentially killing the same mobs for the same things.
All in all, I love the game. My few issues are minor but again, I'm definitely more of a casual gamer and don't get into the nitty-gritty aspects.

If you enjoyed Terraria then Craft the World is the next best thing. The game features a campaign mode with 4 maps which increase in size and difficulty. The objective is to gather materials to create a shelter and equipment to allow your dwarfs to meet increasingly difficult waves of enemies who attack at night. You create everything from armour, weapons, furniture, food and potions with the ultimate goal of opening a portal to the next level. The game worlds are not as large as Terraria and the limited metals make it impossible to fully equip your dwarves in the best armour and equipment except on the larger maps.
Unlike Terraria you don’t directly control a single character but instead issue commands which the dwarves then carry out, this allows you to queue large construction projects or mine huge areas and simply sit back and watch the dwarves complete the tasks. You can construct various defences which allow you to automate your defence, I found this part of the game the most enjoyable as your hard mining and crafting is eventually awarded with a base your enemies can’t breech.
On the negative side the game suffers from strange path finding issues, sometimes dwarves stand motionless with an icon above their head indicating that they can’t find a way to get to a location. It’s understandable when the location is miles away but as you mine and create complex tunnel systems they become more frequently lost even when going a short distance. It’s also a shame that nothing carries over to the next level. You open a portal to the next map but you start that map with nothing.

Customer support for this game has been severely lacking for a long time now, clearly no longer care about individual users and the game is now just an open money grab since they attacked the modding community.

Alright, I've just finished Craft the World and I figured I'd give my two cents worth. So the game, as advertised, was a mostly fun mix of Dungeon Keeper and Terraria. With dwarves. I enjoyed the first half of the game (about 33 hours for me) immensely but after that I realized the rest was more of the same. There just isn't enough variety between levels. That's not to say I didn't enjoy the second half. I did. Quite a bit in fact. But it definitely started to drag on, especially in the last level.
The two biggest complaints I have with this game are the mana regeneration and the dwarf AI. With the way the game works you *need* mana for portals and it doesn't regenerate nearly fast enough. Running out of mana can make already tedious tasks such as gathering deep down minerals take hours instead of minutes.
Then there's the dwarfs. Dear God the dwarfs. I hate to be overly critical but these little guys have some of the worst AI programming I've ever encountered in a game of this type. They get lost constantly, stand dying in front of enemies when they've been ordered to go home, idly stare at blocks they *should* be mining because the game assigned the job to a dwarf all the way across the map, etc. They are just plain stupid and make the game far more frustrating than it should be.
It may seem that I'm complaining a lot when you consider that I *do* recommend the game. The fact is, despite it's flaws, it's still a lot of fun and the developer seems to be steadily updating it and listens to the community feedback. If you're hungry for a Dungeon Keeper-esque game or can't get enough of the survival/gathering/crafting type game, I would recommend giving it a try. But, oh, not at full price. No. I'd suggest waiting until it's $10 or under. As it stands, I don't feel it's worth $18.99.

this game is overwhelmingly epic. despite it's age, it is just as good today as it was 6 years ago. i haven't found another game like it. you get to start out with next to nothing, and over time, you can build up your relationships with the various lords of the land and the different factions while you level up and get stronger and raise an army and train your troops and recruit some companions that are like secondary characters you get to specialize as well. this game definitely forces your character to specialize in some stuff and use your companions to boost your armies stats in other stuff. if you wanna be a leader and a medic, it's harder to also be an engineer and epic warrior as well. or if you want to be a tracker/trainer, it's hard to be a medic/leader as well. you need companions for the things your character isn't good at or your army will start to suffer mid to late game.
i like that you can choose to join a faction and rise up through the ranks in that faction or just screw it all and be your own boss and try to take everything for yourself. the battles and missions in this game are also pretty fun. taking a city/fort or raiding a village are a ton of fun. you can divide your troops up into different formations such as putting the footsoldiers together and the archers together and the calvarly together or give yourself a small group of bodyguards for combat and while in combat, you can direct each individual unit formation to do different things. like hold position or charge forward hold fire or fire on my command or at will. there's a decent amount of strategy to the battles, but if you have a large enough army with powerful enough troops (almost all the troops can be upgraded and have their own upgrade paths), you can largely ignore the tactics and just stride into battle and lay waste to your foes with little to no thought put towards tactics. when you start a battle, you get a battle advantage and depending on how high or low (it can even be negative) you starting advantage is, affects how well your troops usually perform. but even beyond that, as you just play the game and build relations with lords and towns and factions, you'll also build your renown in the world and the higher your fame is, the more troops you can have in your army at once and the better advantage you'll tend to have. i love it cause it makes me feel like my enemies are sort of scared to fight me because they know my reputation for crushing enemies and armies larger than my own.
the more you build your relations with the various lords and factions, the more likely it'll be that you can convince some of them to follow you and add their troops to your own when you're striding into battle or take over some towns/forts. if you build your relationships high enough and you're already part of a faction, you might be voted to be marshall of the faction and get to control all the armies of your faction.
if you want a great action RPG that's also a semi-open world strategy game, i recommend this one. start off as a small unimportant weakling and work your way up to being a lord or king of your own nation. it takes so long to complete a game that it feels like a real campaign. i've only finished 3 games in my 240 hours of gameplay cause it takes so long. so if you don't want to play this game for tons of hours, i would suggest finding something else, cause i don't think you can win a game in 10-20 hours. it's not something you can really finish in one sitting, but i like that about it. once you start a new game, you know you've got about 40-100 hours of gameplay ahead of you before you win.

Mount and Blade: Warband is a sandbox RPG set in the fictional land of Calradia. This game is certainly in my top five favorite games of all time, and my Steam in-game hours tell that story. This game is full of nostalgic elements which make up for its graphical and other technical shortcomings.
M&B: Warband is one of a kind. It has immersive gameplay, sophisticated yet simple troop managment, a vast variety of weapons and armor, multiple factions, marriages, relationships, companions, wandering poets, belligerent drunks, great combat mechanics, tournaments, enterprises, and nostalgic, humorous dialogue during encounters with lords and bandits alike.
With so many options as to how to play the game, this game has a high replay value, you can play multiplayer, custom battles, be a wondering scoundrel, a bandit raider, an honorable gentleman, a hated vagabond, or even a lord of an existing kingdom or king of all Calradia!
This game has a few downsides however. It takes many hours to learn the game mechanics well, and hundreds of hours to successfuly conquer Calradia (if you even dare attempt it). It also lacks graphicaly and at times lacks some immersive elements that many would enjoy (mods can do wonders, however).
If you want a game with medieval lore, a great modding community (I would recommend the "Diplomacy" mod is you would like more options as a lord when it comes to diplomatic relations and such), addictive gameplay, and full of challenging economic, diplomatic, and military dynamics, look no further than Mount and Blade: Warband!

Greetings!  I’ve always enjoyed tower defense style games and enjoy any offshoot and spinoffs that are done well.  This is one such a game; in Space Run your towers are built on a ship to help defend it while it moves from A to B.  This game starts with a solid fundamental in tower defense and adds on it by requiring certain payloads, optional objectives and even boss battles.
What’s my motivation:  Really this is all just putting a good coat of paint over solid mechanics, you really don’t need to be moving down a lane as it is not all that different than staying still mechanically but it creates a good atmosphere as ships and asteroids attack you.  The boss battles are interesting as well because they might vastly change your approach to the level.  Some require very unique approaches that are counter to the way you want to play the rest of the level; especially if you are trying to get max stars.
Try Again:  The game does not require a lot of time to play; a handful of minutes per level (assume you beat it) and most levels are easy enough to live through given the minimum requirements.  I like this as it creates a game that is easy to enjoy.  The challenge comes when you are looking to perfect that level; you will find yourself pinching for seconds or creating build orders and memorizing the layout.  To be honest, I enjoyed this a great deal.
I’m the Mann:  The story isn’t stellar (hehe Buck would be proud) and kind of yawning at times but you really aren’t here for this and the developers know this.  It is told in a comical way that is so bad it seems proud of it.  Almost glorifying the grindy nature of games the story makes puns here and there as you think you are the gift to the cosmos while everyone thinks you are bumbling idiot.  Mechanically, not much wrong here either, lots of upgrades different styles; if I had to laser in (hi-five) on something I’d say the menus could use a bit of work on explaining how you blow the competition away (okay, I’ll stop).
For the cost I’d say get this game if you enjoy tower defense, even at full price.  If you aren’t sure wait for a sale, not all of us can be as successful as the Mann (sorry, I lied).  I hope you all enjoy this as much as I did.  Oh, I guess you could say there is a minor issue with replay but it’s $15…get over it.

I normally recommend games like this because I like what they are trying to do for gaming as a whole but unfortunately this really didn't live up to what it could have been. This game feels like a great attempt at a game built to tell a story but doesn't quite follow through. The story is interesting, and very dark. This clashes with the almost cartoon/Fable art style. I’m pretty sure this was intended (as it’s pretty obvious) but the clash straight up didn’t add anything to the story and the two just feel out of sync. Character development is lacking, so the emotional impact Brothers tries to convey isn't as deep rooted as it could be. I really wanted to care about the characters but their personalities were only given one or two insightful moments throughout the entire game. Only so much can be conveyed through actions which gets me to my last point. The made up language aspect was interesting but I think took away from the story. A really great narrative or script would have made this game far more impactful. It would have given the characters a bit more depth and could have made the adventure seem more urgent and dire.
On a brighter note, the game mechanics took a bit of getting used to but in the end really added to the idea of making the brothers work together. The puzzles weren't hard but they were fairly entertaining. Lastly, the music was absolutely fantastic. I would get the game just for the soundtrack honestly.
To sum up, In many cases the game mechanics helped the themes and aspects of the story, but at the same time more things took away from it. If a bit more time was put into character development I think the game would have been awesome.

It's been a year or more since I wrote the original review, and I think it's time for an update.
This game is still spendlid, but I have a slightly more varied view on Torchlight 2 than I did before.
The vanilla game is something I definetly appreciate far more now after playing with mods for 30-40 hours, and switching back.
This game has several mechanics which make it stand out for me. Things like the reputation system make it easier to upgrade your skills quicker without making you overpowered and consequently beating the mobs easily.
It also has some of the most satisfying combat I have ever seen in a game. I have not seen or played Diablo 3, but this makes me feel pretty happy as I slaughter dozens of zombies or whatever.
The effects of the weapons, abilities and armour are well made, and most are randomly generated but manage to be intersting and be genuinely nice to find.
The levels are relatively different and varied, and have a large selection of different enemies, abilities and focuses with good art design.
Just buy it whilst it is on sale!

This game doesn't revolutionize the match 3 genre, but it does bring some new things to the table. There are 37 different date gifts that do various things that affect the match 3 gameplay. One item might delete all the tokens of a single type, another might delete tokens in a 3x3 grid. You are able to carry 6 into the game with you at any given time and you need "sentiment" to use them. This causes you to decide between matching sentiment tokens to get your items ready or matching any of the 6 other tokens to boost your relationship with the person you're dating. Each girl has tokens types they prefer over another, so you have to build your items around that to get the most out of them.
Even after the initial 8 girls, there are 4 more to find, and after that, there's Alpha Mode. In Alpha Mode, the game just gets more and more difficult as the requirements to pass a level get higher and higher.
