I bought this software completely off of a gut feeling.  Never a good idea, espically when it's $50, but it gave me a pleasant surprise.
As a sidenote, before this, I used FRAPS to record most of everything I did, which tanks my framerate for one reason or annother, and always seems to output massive files.
It has a very clean and easy to use UI, and it's actually quite attractive.  It was incredibly easy to use straight out of the box, which is important to me because I really hate messing around with programs for months until I finally figure them out fully.  Even rebinding controls is fairly extensive while remaining simple to use.
It outputs in either AVI or MP4, and can record in 1080p without losing many frames at all, which is amazing, but it still has the filesize issue which could just be considered an issue with recording anything in HD.  It also has a framerate counter in the corner.
Now for what I didn't find so good...
I'm not a streamer and have no interest in doing so, but they lure you in with the promise of a streaming software and then only give you 14 days until you have to pay a monthly subscription, something that makes little to no sense beyond greed considering many cheaper programs do it for free.  That's a no-no.
You cannot use active desktop or specified area recording without having Windows Aero theme enabled.  This was incredibly frustrating for me because I hate the Aero theme and yet it still gives the recording UI making you think you're doing something when you're not even outputting a file.  I spent quite a while re-shooting a single 2 minute section until I finally closed it down, changed my Windows theme, and started up and it *finally* worked.  This NEEDS to be fixed, either disable the "ghost" UI or allow us to record without Aero on, I don't care which, I just know it needs fixing.
All in all I'll give it a 7/10, it would be an 8, but there's also a fake review I recall seeing on here (you can tell since it's written like a disclaimer,) so there's annother point gone.  I'll fully reccomend it if they fix the issue I mentioned.

I'm a youtuber, have been for a while. Granted, not a very popular one. But Throughout my time of making video's I have tested all sorts of different game recorders, from fraps, dxtory, bandicam and so on. But none of those really hit the spot, yes they gave you a simple recording, but none of them provided any excellence or standed out in some form. Mirillis Action! is by far the greatest game recording software available, you can record in both avi or mp4, depending on how you want your video, quality and how good your computer is. It's tiny file-size makes it easy to store on usb's etc, allowing you to take it anywhere. But by far, the most valuable and greatest thing I have found in Mirillis Action! is the webcam features. Everybody love's to see horror reactions, using facecam's to allow this. But no other software actually has a built in webcam interface that will automatically combine your webcam onto your video, with perfect matched timing and functionality. This is very useful, especially if you're doing horror let's plays, such as myself.
Overall this software is amazing, and pretty cheap too with the functionality you are getting.
However, with great software comes a few problem's, that I'm sure will be fixed, or features that are lacking to be added.
My main problem with this is audio, you are able to do as other softwares alike this would, use two different tracks if you want, you can adjust the ratio of system to mic audio. However, this can be an issue, as you may find some game's have very different audio levels. Because of this, it's very hard to find a ratio balance that provides good audible mic quality over gameplay, whilst ensuring you can hear the gameplay too. If you find the balance, it is perfect. But maybe, and I hope Mirillis do this, but having an auto-balancer, or a testing of somesort would deeply improve with this.
This being said, that is the ONLY problem I have had with this software, and you can get by that very easily, as long as you spend a while configuring it and testing it repeatedly.
This is a purchase worth making if you are into the YouTube community. I would Highly recommend if you are a gaming youtuber, to purchase this as it will open your recording ability to a new level. Plus I haven't even gone into the exporting and auto-uploading choices available in the software. Say's it all really.
So yes, It's good, in fact it's great! Definately worth the investment!

If you love adventure, RPG, and total war then this is your game.  I have owned this game for over four years with almost 900 hours on record and I still play it. Afterwards it get's repetitive, lucklily there are tons and I mean tons of mods that range from changing certain game mechanics like the diplomacy mod for instance is a very popular one, all the way to toal game conversions.  Some MOD's take place during historical medieval europe, japan, revolutionary war, civil war etc.  Beyond that there are a lot of fantasy mods which I enjoy the most personally.  They have a decent collection in the steam workshop, but I always went to
to get all the mods I most enjoy, but be careful, there are some mods that have not been updated or abandoned for years and may contain viruses.  Other than that, this is a game that you can use cheats and still put hundreds of hours into a campaign.  For me that is always fun, although some people differ on that.  But playing the game without cheats is just as fun.  Lastly, this is also a game you don't have a powerful rig to pay, this game can run decently on a dual core with a 8800gt and 2 gigs of ram. Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy is the new game by the creator of QWOP. Inspired by Sexy Hiking, the 2002 B-game, the challenge is to overcome a mountain of seemingly random objects equipped with a hammer only.
As simple as this sounds the game is not easy. It requires a very precise control of the mouse and a lot of training. Simply repeating actions until success, doing things faster or spending more time doesn't lead to progress in the game. Only improving this small but mighty set of skills can get you to new heights. But careful, the danger of falling down is always present. You can even fall from almost the end of the game back to the very beginning of the game. Endless struggle and terrible setbacks are an essential part of the experience.
This, along with the audio commentary by the developer featuring background info about the creation of the game and considerations about game design and our modern media culture in general make Getting Over It more than game: it's actually a study on difficulty in games, various aspects of game design such as challenges and rewards, and ultimately the experience of terrible setbacks and getting over them. And it's a masterpiece.
The fact that the game is very hard but not too hard to complete and that the granular difficulty in detail actually makes the gameplay does suggest that Getting Over It is very well-designed. It's absolutely worth a try and worth the money it costs on Steam. Try playing it in the evening, with a glass of wine, for relaxtion, approach it like zen gardening, and DO NOT RIDE SNAKE ;)
P.S.: You should never give up but if you do you can see the rest of the game in my first complete playthrough:

"Don't let it get to you." That's what the game wants. Accept you're going to struggle the first 30 minutes with the first few areas, and that you'll probably hit rock bottom a few times. Figure out how to move first, where you can plant your hammer and stay, and learn the best way to recover. Don't overextend on those either, you'll just knock yourself down faster. Be zen, and don't focus on beating it. Focus on playing it. Focus on the experience. It's a hike, not a race.

Let me put some perspective on this. At the time of this review, I have spent over 500 (261 Online, >250 Offline) hours and $450 (USD) on this game. And let me tell you, it's a labour of love. There are so many great things about this game, and yet there are so many things that also need work. I'm sure you've read a lot of reviews about this (If you're a smart consumer, at least), but let this one be definitive for you. I'm going to lay everything I've seen on the table, and hope for the best...
1.) "Why is there such expensive DLC?"
The DLC in this game is expensive because some of it is made by third-party developers, then packaged by DTG and shipped to you. Basically, you are not buying straight from the source and a are going through a middle-man (Who also has a monopoly on the products). No competition, no need to keep prices down. That being said, the product you are receiving needs to be worth it to you, and that will vary depending on the product (and your bank). Beased on my experience (and my $500), third-party locos are the best, while DTG Routes (or, more seemingly 'Worlds') will beat out anybody else's. I understand they're not perfect, but who is?
2.) "Bugs? BUGS!?"
Yes. They are there. Personally, I've been hit with script errors and other things, which will crash the game. Sometimes, the sound will not initilize on startup, frames get lost more often than they should, and couple scenarios are broken (Some fixes available).
And don't you EVEN get me started on the Editor, which freezes and crashes out (among other problems) all the time. The way the game creates and runs AI traffic is FRUSTRATINGLY idiotic, and makes it hard sometimes (well, more than 'sometimes'...) to make it do what you want. The Timetable view is nice, but horribly flawed because of the AI and how it is scripted to interact with the player (Basically, it's not allowed to in any way). The only thing that's nice to say for the Editor is that it's easy to put in assets, as long as it doesn't crash out beforehand. Trainz '12 did a much better job with it's Surveyor function, ESPECIALLY when it comes to AI.
That being said, when the game is running well you will have next to no problems. The menus look great and it's generally easy to create consists and stuff. The Quickdrive option is also nice, at times. I find the new TSX Mode (the main thing that separates TS2013 and TS2014) not worth it. The only thing it really seems to add is lighting flares, rain drops on your windows, and aliasing (which could make your game look truly stunning, if you've got the gear for it). I find a nonaliased but scenery-packed constant 30fps works best for me, but then again I don't have a top-tier rig either.
3. "Okay, how realistic is it, really?"
You're answer depends on the product. Most routes are realisitc, up to a point. You're not going to get the entire Surfliner Route, if that's what you mean. Most things you can buy are Legs of much larger real world routes, such as the British WCML from Glasgow-Carlisle or the German ICE route from Berlin-Wittenberg. There's also smaller routes, such as the Falmouth Branch or the Isle of Wight. The largest I own is the Western Lines of Scotland route from Stranraer-Carlisle, while the smallest is the Doncaster Works, which is just that... Doncaster Works....
Realism in this case is a general term, and how you use the software. If you use the game GUI and keyboard commands, it's going to feel a bit arcade; there's no getting around that. But, if you turn off the HUD, use mouse control (or even Raildriver), and actually make yourself have to pay attention to what is going on, it feels a lot more like a simulation, albeit partial in some cases. I have to say though, it's exilarating to be flying up the Brighton Line at 75mph (95 if I'm pushing it) in the A1 Tornado, while keeping an eye on signals and fire levels and water levels and boiler pressure and speed restrictions and all the other things necessary for a safe and on-time service.
Basically, it can be really hard if you want it to be; otherwise it's so dumbfoundingly easy a 5 year-old could probably get the hang of it.
4.) "Why all the Ads? I don't like stuff pushed into my face!"
Personally, I don't think it's that bad. On the start menu, you usually get two little squares (not really that noticeable) that show you the latest and greatest products that came out on release. There's an in-game store that lists all the available DLC, and will show pictures and a little info on the thing you want to buy. It'll also show any sales that are currently happening as well.
For some reason, though, the in-game store doesn't list the Bundles (usually a Route and some extra Loco(s) that would otherwise be available seperately at a higher total cost) that are on Steam, which I think is odd and unfair, especially since I could've saved a little money when I first started, until I leared the hard way. Se la vie?
Also, the loading screen in the game is a slideshow of (well taken) in-game shots of (usually new) available DLC, along with some (completely obvious and, in my opinion, glaringly derrogatory toward my intelligence) "insider tips" from the staff at DTG.
All in all, I don't mind it. If you really hate it that bad, then go Go Offline in Steam and all that stuff goes away. Literally. So why are we critisizing a business for trying to drum up some revenue (especially in this economy), when you can just turn it off? (Get over yourself, people.)
5.) "What is your synopsis? Should I buy this?"
You ask some hard questions....
All-in-all, I like it. It's challenging when I want it to be, but easy when I don't. There's plenty of content to keep you busy (if you've got the cash), and replayability is nice and high. The fan-base around it is booming, and the Workshop has some awesome (FREEEEEE) content. You can learn a lot, but have fun at the same time (Being a history buff helps).
If it weren't for the bugs, Editor, and expensive DLC, this game would be a home run. Unfortunately, the developer(s) have put a noose around the game's neck, and inadvertinently given it's product a bad name and some wavering confidence in it's future. If you can get past that, and/or if the devs finally see the light and miraculously start working out the kinks, it'll be spectacular.
If I were you, I would buy it (On sale, if at all possible with anything) and then buy all the DLC you possibly can so that way I don't feel like such an idiot (who's having way too much fun driving trains all day!) ;)
6.5/10 w/bad stuff. 9/10 w/out.
Be sure to look for my indiviual reviews on each DLC I've bought. Hopefully I can help you make some better decisions on where you should spend that $20 burning a hole in your pocket!

In terms of AI, it seems very, very limited, even in terms of trainz 2006's capabilities.
In trainz railway simulator 2006, you could use triggers and rules to append orders onto trains / trigger events and all of that lovely stuff to create more in-depth game play, whereas in rail works, it's purely an A-B method, there's no dynamics in the orders what so ever which could give real potential to how AI could be used like in trainz railway simulator 2006. (yes, I just did compare a game created in 2014 with a game created 8 years ago, although, technically, it got implemented in TRS2004, passenger service pack).
The passenger movements are all nice, but it's not that big of a deal, compared to what I've listed here, which would be core game elements.

This game doesn't revolutionize the match 3 genre, but it does bring some new things to the table. There are 37 different date gifts that do various things that affect the match 3 gameplay. One item might delete all the tokens of a single type, another might delete tokens in a 3x3 grid. You are able to carry 6 into the game with you at any given time and you need "sentiment" to use them. This causes you to decide between matching sentiment tokens to get your items ready or matching any of the 6 other tokens to boost your relationship with the person you're dating. Each girl has tokens types they prefer over another, so you have to build your items around that to get the most out of them.
Even after the initial 8 girls, there are 4 more to find, and after that, there's Alpha Mode. In Alpha Mode, the game just gets more and more difficult as the requirements to pass a level get higher and higher. Most people won't get to this point, but some might, and it's quite rewarding to see a combo of matches to line up. If you're this deep into my review, you probably have forgotten that this is a game about sleeping with multiple girls, but that's exactly what this is. It's a well crafted game, and there's more that I haven't even mentioned yet. But! That's for you to find out. If you like match 3 games, I would recommend this one, but I also hope you aren't playing with any family in the room...

Space Run is a rather unique tower defense game. You run cargo through deep space with your ship and build various weapons and defenses to protect your cargo from pirates and other hazards.
The graphics look decent enough and most of the time the game is too hectic anyway to really pay attention to the visuals.
The sound effects, music and voice acting are all pretty good.
The core gameplay is decent enough. In each level you are provided with a ship with some cargo containers and a few basic components and during the level you need to build various weapons and other components on a hexagonal grid. Completing a level will earn you credits and these can then be spent to purchase new components and upgrades.
The game does provide some interesting tactical choices with the component placement. Weapons have a limited arc of fire and shields only cover a small area. You also need to fit in enough engines to make sure you make the delivery within the time limit.
Unfortunately there are several rather questionable design decisions that really undermine this tactical depth. First of all, pretty much all the components have one or two special abilities that have to be manually triggered. This makes the game quite hectic and extremely micromanagement heavy, not something I particularly enjoy in a tower defense game. Adjusting the direction of the turrets is particularly tedious.
Additionally, all the enemy waves are fixed. In practice this means that to get a good score (and to earn lots of credits), you generally need to replay a level a few times. Personally I found this type of repetition quite annoying.
As long as you are willing to do some grinding for credits, the game isn't overly difficult on normal. However, you need decent micromanagent skills in the harder levels and this can definitely be a problem for some people.
The game controls well enough with mouse+keyboard. You really want to get familiar with the keyboard shortcuts, however.
The story is pretty much rubbish and the writing is fairly poor. You keep fighting the same two pirate captains, who keep coming back despite the fact that you blow up their ships several times.
Rather annoyingly the voice-overs often don't match the written text.
I found the game quite stable and I did not run into any major issues. The only minor annoyance was the really long loading time when starting the game.
Space Run has a nice core concept. Unfortunately the heavy reliance on micromanagent and having to replay the exact same levels several times make the game much less fun than it could be. I would not recommend Space Run unless you are a tower defense who can overlook these two issues.
Before this review I played through the game on normal difficulty. I five-starred a lot of the levels, but not all of them. This took me 11.5 hours in total.

Suprisingly good game that kept me coming back until I had completed it.  Missions are good enough to have replay value in order to try to get a perfect score. Fun tower defense type of game with nice and effective graphics and an extremely cheesy 'story'. And the game doesn't even try to be serious which makes it even more funny.
Deliver cargo on timed missions while constantly preparing for incoming astroids, chunks of crystals, opposing cargo ships, small fighters and up to some massive pirate ships. Some more dangerous than others.
Make sure to have enough engine power to deliver your cargo in time, defences like shields and ecm and of course plenty of different weapons, all with special abilities.
Graphics are nice, clean and effective.
Sound is great.
The music is a bit simple, but enough for the job.
The missions range from very easy to extremely challenging and getting them all to a five star rating, meaning you've delivered all cargo for that mission within a certain time limit, is in fact quite difficult.
Replayability comes from the fact that you have to gather enough credits and reputation points in order to buy every possible piece of equipment and upgrade which you will need for the more difficult missions. Plus getting these difficult missions to a five star rating will probably require many many retries and rethinking strategies.
Levels are always the same and the key to success is to learn the type and location of incoming dangers to maximize your result in the next try.. and the next.. and the next :)
Once everything has been achieved, there's no real need to play again though. It would have been fun if there were some more missions or maybe even some random ones. But all in all it has enough content to keep you playing for tens of hours.
Missions are also relatively short. So it's a game you can easily jump in and out whenever you want. Although at times you might not want to stop as you try again and again. Very likely with a high blood presure and lots of cursing. Victory will be sweet.
I've had a lot of fun with this game. It was well worth the money for the 40+ hours it took me to get five stars at every mission, including all the achievements.

This game is a fable.
It tells you a story, and it's a familiar one.  There's hardship in the home, and two young boys do what they feel they must.  They set off on a quest together, inseperable and interdependent.
They journey through a world they find familiar - but as the player sees more of it, the world reveals its surreal and magical bits and pieces.  The journey shows glimpses of grand scope and mysticism, but don't forget: your two young heroes have a task, and they journey on to succeed.
But... As soon as you think you have a handle on things, the game begins to test your resolve.  Mechanically, what you do isn't difficult: two analog sticks, two triggers and timing.  Emotionally? ... Well, if you feel any investement in the characters you encounter, the game might make you FEEL things.
There is no intelligible speech in the game; the inhabitants of this world speak their language just fine, but the player has no idea what is being said.  Of course, the body language/mimeography reveals just enough for one's imagination to take off and run with all sorts of meanings.
There is no comat in this game, but there is a measure of challenge.  It's a story that asks you to try in order to reveal more of itself.  The trial may be more one of morbid curiosity and courage.
While playing it, I got strong memories of Neverending Story, that same feeling of discovery and adventure, as well as the realization that every fantastical element in this world is matter-of-fact to its inhabitants and serves as allegory to something more familiar, mundane.
Over the course of 4 hours or so, I saw this story through to its conclusion, encountering a few of the side-stories within (optional activities and further glimpses into the world).  The levels are linear and well-paced, but this pace is slower; the game is meant to be savored rather than devoured.
I love this story.  It is so very simple in its idea, so old in its roots; the pace is natural and doesn't offer (nor require) handholding.  Buttery smooth and saccharine-sour, this delicious morsel is worth sampling, then pausing to savor and reflect; then, should the mood strike again, perhaps coming back for a second helping.
I love a good fable.  This is a good one. Come see for yourself.

only bad thing is (but this is the same of every sports game on pc) you need a controller.

AWESOME simply awesome. Still in development but has massive potential for multiplayer and multi winter sport event modes. Fluidity, physics and textures as well as playability has been well thought through and designed to acuratley mimic fp or 3rd person skiing experience. Hopefully will also be adaptable to occulus rift down the track. Packed full of adictive features including a great musical score, wide variety of character options, points scoring system for trick based moves (like ssx ps3) snow is a must have not only for winter sports lovers but really for anyone just wanting something a bit different, replayable and adrenaline pumping fun.

While the game isn't finished yet it is definitely fun. Getting to relax and just ski down very detailed mountains* and forests. Some mountains are more exciting than others but definitely worth play to get used to doing tricks.
*The ammount of detail in this game's level design is incredible, I have never seen any game put as much into an open world map this early into the development as Snow has. I would love to be able to treck the mountain sides myself in any sort of adventure game and be able to get a better look at the castle for instance.
There are very few invisible walls in this game and even then they are easy to get around, going beyond the laid out paths reveals a far more detailed game with small hidden cities or castles or forests beyond the visible limitations. Further getting to a point of no-return (falling off the edge of the world) is a tough as it is and takes a lot of time to dedicate to get that far.
To developers thank you very much for this game, even from early access I've had a lot of fun with it. I would highly recommend this game for others to just enjoy some winter skiing and exploration.

. I pre-purchased this game to support further development. It'd be a shame to let it die at this point.

Ah yes... The game we've all been waiting for, for a long time. I have always wondered as to why there haven't been too many "realistic" (or even close to it) skiing/snowboarding games. It has always been some sort of jumping over mountains doing sextuple backflips. Why? I don't know. I first heard about this lovely game from a friend, when I was asking him that very same question. He pointed me towards this, I watched a couple of videos and then fell in love.
This game is just perfect. It has a huge variety of tricks you can do, a huge variety of rails you can hit and just  a huge map to shred! I love the first person mode (especially with changing the FOV to 110) while riding. Riding through the woods at a massive speed is really exhilarating. The game plays really well. The tricks look cool, the park is smooth and... awesome and the epicness and softness of freeriding is exquisite. I have played the game for almost 50 hours now, and I keep on finding new places to ride and love. The level of customization is pretty neat too (even though there are no khaki pants whatsoever).
But even though the game has all that, my favorite part is the devs. I have contacted the team numerous times through twitter and they have always been super fast and helpful with their awnsers. Just the other day, I suggested that they add movable lights to the game (for street spots and such), and their awnser was "That's a great idea! We'll make sure to include that". I also remember asking them on a livestream of the game in a super early version about building kickers and stuff, and they said that they are already working on it. All this from a super small team from Stockholm!

8,5/10 (Because no khakis)
*Note* I'm a snowboarder waiting for snowboards to be implemented. The review was based on skis. Probably would've forgiven the khaki issue if the snowboards would be in it already.

I love this game.
I can't really tell what exactly makes me love it but i love it. (It's probabably the characters in the story and the grind)
Since i can't really reason why i love it i'm gonna throw in some tips i've figured out or found
(Note that these tips may have already appeared in reviews so sorry if i repeated something already stated)
Save your Magicite.
You get 100 every 16 hours and 40 minutes and you can buy a Mobius gift box for 3000 (It's worth it, trust me.) Also you start with 1000 so it would take you about 2 weeks to get the first one if you don't forget to frequently collect it.
Augment at least one of each monster card you find to 3 stars.
It's not that expensive (unless you are unlucky with material drops) and it makes it so you drop these cards already on 3 stars rarity (Makes it easier to farm skill-ups)
Use cards corresponding to your class.
It's a rookie mistake but if you can try not to use for example Mage cards on Warrior classes. If your card doesn't correspond with your class it simply won't receive "Magic" stat bonus.
(The next one isn't necessary to follow but i think it's worth mentioning)
Don't use 3 star ability summon.
It's just not worth it to pull a 3 star maxed card (for 2 tickets) since most of them can be purchased fairly cheap (with some exceptions) in ability shop.
I'd recommend saving your summoning tickets for job summon (6 tickets for a job, no chance of dupes), greater summon (6 tickets for 6 cards) or 4 star ability summon (maxed 4 star card for 5 tickets).
That's it for what i remember at the moment of writing this.
Feel free to point out if i forgot something or made a mistake. (English is my second language)

Before I get into it, let me just say that this title is actually fairly fun. It seems like a good time killer and feels like something really appropriate for your smartphone while you're on a train or taking a break at work. That is also why I am giving this a thumbs down. This IS a smart phone game lazily ported to PC. It still FEELS like a mobile game despite being on a much more powerful machine.
Gameplay-wise, there is some clumsiness in design that goes beyond the "its a mobile game on pc" thing. You upgrade skills and unlock new abilities, but the order in which you unlock them seems to be almost random. You need to build through a few tech trees before you can make basic building components like doors. These are the things you need at the very beginning of the game and by the time you can make them, you've already worked around not having them... thus you don't need them. Also some components like wool to make rope are exceedingly hard to come by and you won't see a sheep until you're further along... thus having recipes at the very start which require rope really sucks.
This game doesn't deserve the bad rap I'm giving it. Make no mistake it EARNS a thumbs down, but it really doesn't deserve it. These are things that the developer should have put a little more time and effort into to make a polished game. The graphics are otherwise great. The gameplay is very nonchalant and casual. And over all the game is very relaxing to play. These are great traits that could have made this an amazing game... but in a few key areas it just seems to fall short.
Make no mistake, you're buying a mobile game for PC here and it has enough design flaws that you'll lose your love for this game the longer you play. And I say this because this game is definitely a game that should be loved. I feel like maybe another 3-6 months of development could have made a massive difference in this game. Who knows. Sans a major content patch fixing things.. i'd say pass on craft the world unless you see it on a deep sale.

I can not recommend this software for the following reasons:
1) It can not broadcast my game.  I have to use full screen, or set up a selection window around the Windowed instance of the game.  The latter doesn't work, as the controls get permanently attached beneath the selection area, rather than staying in the seperated interface the controls began in.  Since my game is the hieght of my screen, it kicks the controls off screen, rendering them inaccessable.  There is no work-around short of short-cut keys.
2) There is no preview.  It appears that there will be one, but when streaming, there in fact is none.
3) It can not handle overlays with transparencies.  It can only use straight-up square images as they are.  No Chroma.
4) It can not handle audio intelligently.  I have Game Sounds, TeamSpeak, Media-Monkey, and a microphone.  Ideally, you could have each on a fader in a mixer with a side-chain compressor dynamically lowering all sounds but TeamSpeak and Mic when they are creating sound above a set threshold.  This can't do anything but select an audio source and/or a mic - period.
5) This software actually performed worse than Open Broadcast in my testing.  I run a modest game (DC Universe) on a Core i7 3770, 16GB RAM, Creative Labs X-Fi HD Titanium, AMD HD6890 and I have 18Mb d/l and 11Mb u/p speeds from my ISP.  Open Broadcast reliably, and repeatably, outperformed this software.
6) This software sells as though it were a "buy this and then use it all you want" title, when in fact it is actually a subscription model.  I find the sales presentation of this title deceptive.  Period.  I had no idea it was subscription based until I had already purchased, downloaded, installed, and run the program for the first time.  Once you run it, the Subscription Model is the very first thing it talks about.  Keyword = DECEPTIVE.
Summary:
If there was any semblance of a Help->Contact Us within the program, and they could be reached with this feedback and all of the above issues were resolved, it would be worth the money to buy - not to subscribe - to buy.
As it is - totally wasted my time and money on this and will have to return to OBS just to broadcast properly - which it did for free in the first place.

Playtime: about 12 hours for single player
The newly updated Red Faction Guerilla steam edition comes with trading cards and achievements since they migrated away from Games For Windows Live. It also seems to be less buggy, but this may be a coincidence. You don’t need to have played the previous Red Faction games to understand what’s going on, and if you played Red Faction Armageddon, the campaign story isn’t really spoiled for you either. The stories take place with enough time in between for all sorts of things to have happened.
You play as Alec Mason, a recent immigrant to Mars planning to live with his brother as a miner (actually a scavenger of salvage). Unfortunately your plans are ruined when you experience the brutality of the EDF (Earth Defense Fleet), the powerful military organization that seems to be in the pocket of all the major corporations keeping the working man down. Alec joins the Red Faction, which is a kind of resistance/terrorist group committed to driving the EDF off of Mars by any means necessary. So now you (as Alec) spend your time blowing things up (and collecting salvage).
Red Faction Guerilla is a third person open world game, similar to Grand Theft Auto or the Saints Row games. Since it takes place on Mars, there’s also reduced gravity though you don’t really get to fly around everywhere, even after you get a jet pack. The trademark of all Red Faction games is destructible environments, so like Red Faction Armageddon, you can pretty much destroy any man-made structure in the game, including buildings, bridges, walls, and all the crates the EDF leaves lying around. There are a few things that might give you trouble, for example some buildings have indestructible metal girders as part of the construction, but you can still knock them around and cause the buildings to collapse. It’s probably easiest to just ram your cars into the buildings though. Yes, like Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row, you can hijack all sorts of cars (no aircraft) and drive all over the map. The game world is moderately large and probably would take 15 minutes of straight driving to get across it. You can’t do that though since Mars has mountains and valleys blocking you so you mostly need to follow roads.
You can carry up to 4 weapons at a time, but one of them is locked as your trusty sledgehammer, which is decent for destroying buildings. There isn’t too much variety in the projectile weapons, and you’ll probably stick will explosive weapons in order to bring down buildings. Weapons and their upgrades are unlocked in the game by completing side missions or just picking them up from fallen enemies. Once you’ve unlocked the weapon you can restock it from any of your “safe houses” around the map. Money in the game is salvage, which shows up as shiny metal that you can pick up by walking over. Most of your salvage will likely come from completing missions, but a there’s a lot to be gained from the rubble of buildings.
Pros:
+Wreck buildings in all sorts of ways. Usually the quickest way is using explosive weaponry, which has ammo limitations, so I like to try and crash cars into the buildings whenever possible. Just make sure you have enough room to build up ramming speed (and enough firepower to survive the EDF retaliation).
+The game has multi player which I only dabbled in for about an hour. There are actually people still playing but not more than a dozen or so at a time. No co-op campaign play however, which is a shame. There are a lot of multi-player modes, but people only seem to be playing the deathmatch types.
Cons
-Unfortunately for me, a large number of the game’s Steam achievements are for grinding in multiplayer, and a bunch of the single player achievements require finding ALL of certain types of collectibles.
-The game’s side quests become repetitive after a while and by the time you unlock the game’s final area, you probably won’t be doing any of the side quests since you’ll be bored by then.
-For an older game, my computer actually heats up when I play for a while. The game uses Havok engine, which seems to appear in a ton of the games I’ve been playing recently, but the game’s graphics aren’t much better than say, Fallout 3.
All in all Red Faction Guerilla is a good game worth your weekend to play through. The campaign has its exciting points and it’s fun to go around blowing up buildings. The DLC Demons of the Badlands is included in the Steam edition (I don’t know if the GFWL version had it). The DLC is about 3 hours and includes a few new weapons to play with, as well as a completely useless new kind of collectible (battery packs that don’t do anything). At least in the main game, all the collectibles had some sort of benefit (like give you a little salvage).

Oh my goodness, where to begin.
So, like many of the reviewers so far, I found out about the game through YouTube. I would wonder why they (the YouTubers) were playing a game that they knew was going to make them rage. Was it for views? Likes? I'll admit, there were a lot of videos I watched because their rage made me laugh. I guess I'm mean-spirited in that way.
And then, a funny thing started happening. I started thinking that I wanted to try this terribly anger-inducing game myself. I started watching the videos and living vicariously through the players. Their pain became my pain. Their joy became mine. I needed to play this game. This was 2 days before the game was released through Steam.
The wait was intense and painful. I wanted this game more than any others that I can remember. But finally, the wait ended, and I began to Get Over It, with this strange bare-chested man, in a cauldron, whose only mechanism for moving through his world was a hammer.
Why did I do this? I had played it so many times in my head that the movements felt... second nature. Was it ego? Was it to see if I was better at the game than those people that I had watched? That wasn't it. Was it because I wanted to finally experience it for myself as opposed to experiencing with other peoples' motions and emotions? That wasn't it either.
With this cauldron-man standing on the precipice, between an obstacle not yet overcome and a gut-wrenching drop back to the beginning of his journey, I pause to consider my reasoning, and to write this review.
I came to the realization that what was the most exciting thing about this game was exactly what made it the most frightening. It was sheer adrenaline, pushing me higher and higher, and then all the way back. Back and down again and again... and again.
Every leap was filled with anxiety and anticipation. Every correct landing brought ecstasy. Every incorrect landing brought exasperation. Every time I thought I was going to drop that I saved whether by luck or subconscious skill or divine grace brought unimaginable relief.
This roller coaster of emotions was the one thing I was unprepared for when starting this game. It taunts me with every obstacle I overcome. It mocks me every time I fall, which admittedly is a lot. But every time I have to start all over, it lifts me up with the knowledge that I've done it before, and I can do it again.
Will I complete this game? I don't know, probably. But I will never forget it. And for that, Bennett Foddy, I thank you.
-jay

When I was 17, I decided I wanted to be a game designer. I had previously toyed with the idea due to loving video games since I was a small small kid, but the pressures of highschool and having to decide what to do with your life finally made me solidify my decision and head towards the path of game development.
The years went by. I went to university for computer programming. It felt soulless and more concerned with teaching me how to manage databases for google rather than something fun and artistic with the skill. I decided to then go to art school, but realized I couldn't draw and that most of the classes were for people who knew what they were doing and just wanted to burn money practicing. And all the while, every time I tried to do something to advance myself personally aside from institutions, I would get shot down. Every year when I would finally muster up enough energy to attempt something creative to get better at the things I love, I would fail to meet my own high expectations and fail miserably. The failures hit me so hard I would never get back up until months and months would pass.
My friends felt like they were taunting me by trying to help me out. "All you have to do is just keep doing things, and you'll get better at it". The hardest part to swallow is that I knew it was true. But I didn't know how to explain the invisible force of failure to them. For some reason when they got back up from failing, they barely gave it any attention and just moved on to the next thing. Every time I attempted an ambitious project or failed to change something I wanted to do with my life, I would feel hopeless and like I could never come back from it. Even after the bitterness of defeat and depression wore off a few days later, a wave of long term procrastination would swathe over me for months and I would do nothing but waste my time living day to day and playing video games. It isn't that I suddenly didn't want to partake in these creative endeavours, but rather they just didn't get done- I would avoid them on a subconscious level by doing literally anything else just so I didnt have to feel the pang of self defeat and absolute misery.
Then I played "Getting Over It". I bought it without any hesitation mainly because I am a huge fan of Sexy Hiking and wanted to play the spiritual sequel. The game drew me in immediately, there was that familiar damned tree at the very beginning, the way your hammer moved was exactly the same, and there were even some devious parts that I remembered coming exactly from the game itself. I moved my way up the mountain, and the commentary soothed me and provided me more information on Foddy's inspiration from sexy hiking and how he felt media was changing in recent years.
But the interesting thing was that I got back up. I would lose almost hours of progress, falling down the cliff in a way that was 100% crafted by Foddy to be devious and "hateful". But I took a deep breath, checked my phone, then got back to climbing the mountain. I would realize that once you fell down and regressed to a previous state of the game, due to your previous practice and new tactics you could get back up to where you were in half the time and frustration. I learned that recklessness is actually helpful in some situations, you can't hesitate and have to just "do it" rather than inch your way up slowly to get over some obstacles.
At one point the commentary quoted Mary Pickford, saying "Failure is not falling down, it is not getting up again". that then made me realize what I was doing. Why was I approaching my life with fear and self hatred due to my failures and this stupid game with a dude in a bath pot was the one exception? I know that video games are fun and an escape from reality, but is climbing a virtual mountain designed to put stress and fatigue on the player really that less painful than having to fail on things in real life? I was learning recklessness, perserverance, self preservation, and self esteem- and immediately applying them to a sequel of a game called "Sexy Hiking" for gods sake.
Would I get to the top of the mountain? Maybe not. Maybe one failure would finally drive me over the edge, some terrible puzzle where you could easily hit the very bottom by making a simple mistake. But it was the fact that I gave it more of an honest and long term shot than most of my attempts at being creative that disturbed me. And I knew that after playing "Getting Over It", I would go back to my regular life, letting failures keep me down for months and retreating to my hundreds of video games instead of dealing with my anxiety and low self esteem. But while this realization may make me want to scream out for help in fear and panic, it also gives me hope that maybe this journey is not as hard as it seems. Maybe all it takes is a new perspective and new way of challenging yourself to make the oppressive force of falling down not so hard on yourself.

Lag, at times, was also a real problem. Following friends they would suddenly lag for five to ten seconds. By the time they finally move they had jumped clean off the mini-map. Lag in combat, though, seemed low and perfectly playable.
The interface is poor. Very definitely designed for a console! On the PC it feels awkward to say the least. Not all the keys can be remapped either.
The chat is almost non-existent, so the game really doesn’t feel like an mmo at all. There is very limited social activity! You might consider that a good thing though!
Skill mods are great, but you can’t switch setups.
On the really positive side of things, the game deals with multi-player combat well and the gun mods are excellent.   And I think those two points are really important. Get those two right and you have a game that a lot of people are going to enjoy. Not everyone cares about the story!
So recommend or not? Sheesh. Another hard one! I think you need to make up your own mind on this one. If you want story and depth, then no, don’t bother. But if killing stuff is your thing, then sure. Why not?
I am going to say no, becuase "for me" I don't think the game has longevity. But I would at least recommend trying the game and making up your own mind. Cus it's free.

So I was recommended this game recently and it's been a journey to say the least.
First off, understand this: Surgeon Simulator is a mock of a true simulator.  It is mocking other simulators complicated, sometimes frustrating controls, and it excels at that.  It is also is also a mockery of surgery in general, kind of a bummer if you ever played Life and Death from '88.  To be fair, a true surgery simulator wouldn't be well received.  This game has you breaking out ribcages, allows you to throw organs on the floor (after you take them out you don't put them back in, save for the replacement heart/kidney/brain), and has you do so with the most ridiculous tools available.
To some, that sounds great.  Not me.  I enjoy true simulators such as MS Flight Sim, Euro Truck, and SimCity.  In those games, I don't really find the controls too challenging, so I don't really get the joke here.  I've heard of QWOP, which is essentially a jogging simulator where you control the thighs/calves separately, and must maintain balance while doing so.  Not really my cup of tea either.  So if you like the idea of frustratingly bad controls, or might find the humor in it, give it a try.  There's a free version out there (as any good sim should have) to make sure you enjoy before you buy.
It's not for everyone, but it's for some.  There are definitely some hilarious moments, such as raging on your desk in reception, answering the phone, and making all the (rude) hand gestures at the patient, but after that the bad controls lost their luster on me.
Surgeon Sim gets a 2/5.

My friend and I picked up this game, being free and all, and played it together for about an hour and twenty minutes.
This game could be called Metroidvania, but it feels very linear and your characters don't develop in a way that makes you feel attached to them, which is uncharacteristic of the genre. The story sounds like it has depth if you're a toddler. Listening to the little 'poems' or whatever you'd call them that the narrator reads occasionally is actually pretty funny (which is unintended). None of the mechanics are inspiring. The 'main thing' is switching colors to interact with certain elements of the world, however they opted to take the mechanic and add more things to make it confusing rather than keep it simple and make thought-provoking puzzles. This is like a fancier version of Fireboy and Water Girl.
The controls feel awkward. It falls victim to a problem that recurs in many platformers wherein the developers mistake slipperiness for realistic 'acceleration' of the player's running, and has many other mechanics that feel poorly executed. It often feels as if the controls are the real obstacles, not the platforms.
While it's free you might as well get it, but otherwise I would advise you not to spend a cent on this product.

Ikaruga cross with Ori and the Blind Forest even though Ori came out after this. :) This game WAS the Ori-like game before Ori was a thing.
Odd analogy aside, I got this on the PS3 a long time ago and really enjoyed it. Now I can play it on my laptop wherever I am. I've played through the game on PS3 so I'll assume the experience is the same, but I do have one gripe about it. You can't change the keybindings on the keyboard layout. At least I haven't seen how. I like WASD for controls, but the J key on my keyboards has that raised dimple and it gets on my nerves that one of the more used functions (attack) is bound to this key. I generally shift IJKL bindings to OKL; and I can't do that with this game.
Other that that one little issue the gameplay is tricky to get the hang of. You start out as a "neutral" guy and gain the power of light (blue) and dark (red) to avoid certain attacks and do damage to enemies. There are four or five (I can't remember how many) bosses that are pretty challenging at first and unlock new abilities when you defeat them. There are collectables that reveal themselves on the map after gathering a certain number of them to help you get the last few. You can upgrade your health and energy too. The final battle is pretty hard.
The graphics are really nice for as minimalistic as they are. Most things and objects are black or very darkly shaded except for blue/red on the enemies and player to indicate their alignment. The backgrounds are bright and colorful. The animation and projectile movement is very fluid at 60 fps. It's a bit "bullet-hell"y in spots, sometimes requiring you to spam the alignment shift button rapidly to get through a section. Some enemies are pretty hard to beat. The guards in the last section always seemed a little too strong to be as numerous as they are, but you'll never fight more than two at a time IIRC.
So yes, I recommend it. It's good fast paced exploration fun!

This is a list of Reto's policies that negatively influence game development and public opinion:
Whenever something game changing is about to get in game, nothing can stop it. At the very best, devs make a public test server available 1-2 days before launch without reflecting complaints. This results in unfinished and disliked features in game which take months to tweak in the actual game! If the feature needs so many tweaks to be working properly, roll back the live servers and do the tweaks on a separate (preferably public) server, dont punish your regular players.
Devs dont consider forum polls representative no matter how many votes there are just because its a fraction of the playerbase voting. They also refuse to solve their percieved lack of representativeness by implementing in game polls because they "dont want polls". Nextly, they take silence as agreement, which is wrong. Silence is neutral, its not agreement nor disagreement. They keep referring to vocal minority and silent majority as if these were constant values. They somehow dont understand that if they implement something vocal minority wants and silent majority doesnt, the silent majority will become vocal majority and devs will see what the opinion in the community really is and can roll the change back.
Having trouble with constant eye strain and very limited visibility, both of which are getting worse by the build and both of which can be easily fixed by rolling back/editing a few values? No problem, we will put it into pipeline and maybe in 3 years you will have a fix....
Let me demonstrate this on 2 examples:
spawncamping/mining - Instead of editing a few lines in game rules (prohibiting this behavior) or using the vehicle ghost mode system that they developed for skirmish battles, devs decided to fix spawncamping by working on a set of requirements all new maps must meet to (probably) prevent spawncamping. Needless to say that its more difficult to make maps because of it.
teamwork/special AT limits - Instead of using special AT limits like in the past (for example 3 tanks per battle max) and instead of using already working squad system, they decided to make a whole new system and connect everything (related or not) to it. That took about 90% of human resources (including those from RTS department) and several months to make. The result is a half-finished system that will take weeks or months to "tweak" (finish).
The biggest example is class tutorials. There is absolutely positively no reason not to implement tutorials for all classes. In fact, its the other way around as the benefit is huge (skilled heroes and happy generals). Despite that, devs are stubborn and refuse to make tutorials saying "we would have to update them all the time". That is a very lame reason at best as first blood was updated like once or twice so far. Besides, the important thing about tutorials is teaching the basics. Players dont have to have all new equipment and stuff there, they just need 1 thing the tutorial is about (pilots need just 1 plane, tankers need 1 tank etc., they dont need 5 of them to choose from), so except for gameplay and similar changes (which are very rare), there wont be any reason to update the tutorials.
Due to the slow game development, its obvious community wants to help. However, devs decided to make their own engine and use various incompatible programs to prevent any such help. Danish laws also complicate the matter, but I would be very surprised if there wasnt a legal way to bypass it. Whats missing is the will to look for such a way.
Shining example be the tractors, especially in combination with the announced trucks. Of course its nice to have more variety in game, but is it useful? Is it useful so much that it overrides all other priorities and makes it into the game before other features (*cough* planes *cough* bipods)? These questions probably werent asked by devs before implementing tractors. Worse yet, in the next build they will add another batch of useless transport vehicles to the game.
Seriously, is it really that important to have 3 vehicles in the same category, when the new vehicle is even worse deathtrap than the predecessor? Especially when the existing vehicles could already do everything these new vehicles can do and sometimes even better? Hell, there are finished mortars but noone has the time to think of a fun way to implement them. No wonder when all time is spent on this stuff.
Sometimes the devs lose the way and sabotage their own game. How else could you explain them removing compass, pistol drive-by in cars, plane vs train missions, old soldier interface (+ one primary, one secondy etc. weapon limit), skirmish trench map and downgrading graphics and vehicle skins? If youre curious, check pre-alpha, alpha, and beta videologs and you will see. If you want to have a good laugh, I recommend watching a pre-alpha videolog where they say "it is far from final and will improve over time" and then watch a beta videolog where everything is worse.
This is something my brain isnt able to comprehend. Why on Earth do they release a new item for one or two factions only and leave the other faction(s) waiting for months before they get their counterpart? This is unheard of and every time I think about it Im like Jackie Chan in that "I dont even..." meme.
Its not a bad thing to develop a game the way you want without asking anyone for opinion. However, it is very dishonest to say "user driven development" and "help us make the game you want to play" and then ignore user input and make a game you (devs) want to play. By the way guys, have the devs ever implemented something you suggested? Its not very likely, but it is possible. However, dont think they did it for you. They most likely implemented your suggestion only because they had it in the pipeline long before you asked for it, and now the time has come to implement it.
Panther was a good example. People requested Panther a lot, so devs waited until the time they had planned to release it, released it and community was happy they got something they wanted. Nobody quite realised that Panther was first asked for like 2+ years ago, and was asked for a lot about a year before implementation.
That brings us back to "game devs want to play". You see, they consider themselves king of the game and consider community the peasants. In other words, players are supposed to shut up and play at all times. There is a rare occasion when the king listens to a peasant, and that is when a player comes up with something super cool the devs havent thought of. Now you get the idea why they dont want polls and instead want "constructive feedback" (thats the peasant's surprisingly good idea).
In the very ideal case when they confirm an issue and decide to do something about it (which takes months and hundreds of topics), all they do is put it at the end of their damn pipeline...!
Yeah, thats how they do. When something works perfectly, they "fix" it and create 4578124 bugs. When there is something actually broken, nothing is done about it for years.

Having just completed this game after one brief playthrough, I can tell you it is not a long game. However, it is worth your while. It reminds me of one of the Grimms' fairy tales. This is a deeply moving game with story clearly and succinctly told through visual cues. All speech is, I presume, in a made-up language. This lends a very special quality to the game which invites the player to fill in the gaps with their imagination. Throughout the experience there are highs and lows, lights and darks, seens and unseens. The game's camera wonderfully flies around and gives dramatic angles to the areas of the game that you must navigate. You journey across a fantastic world filled with all sorts of mystical and mythical creatures in order to find the one cure for your sick father. Puzzles are handled with context sensitive presses of the triggers and each brother's movement is handled with one of the analog sticks. The left stick and trigger controls the elder brother while the right stick and trigger controls the younger. It is worth noting that there are disarming moments in the game. It's at these points you might see something that would make you squeemish, uneasy or sad. It may seem like a game intended for a younger audience however I would suggest that parents play the game first or with their kids. All said, I would recommend this game to anyone who would like to see the kinds of deep story-telling possible in video games and anyone who wants a beautifully crafted fantasy adventure with an emotional story and great graphics and sound.

Aware of the controversy concerning that playing this game on a keyboard may be inferior to playing it on a gamepad, i.o.w. this game "should've had 'better' PC controls at the least" -
I wish to put that aside, and primarily discuss about the game itself:
I was pleasently surprised. The gameplay mechanics are highly refreshing despite an unusual learning curve (Fine motor skills are recommended), but it's shockingly intuitive despite the unique way of how it's played after a few minutes in.
It's the kind of game where it revolves around the controller, NOT the other way around unlike most popular games. In essense, it's used as a clever connection between you, the player, and the entity of the characters' existance / involvement with the story's progression.
Some comparisons could be made from certain scenes in Metal Gear Solid (PS1) where you used the controller's vibrations as a massager to heal yourself + Snake, and the Psycho Mantis bossfight.
In simplification, this game is an almost PERFECT example of how unique and special the interactive medium (video game) is; no TV show, no book, and no movie would even come close to achieve an adaptation of the experience what this game has to offer. If I was to be 10 years older now, reading this review, I would still be proud for making my statement.
And so, I am eager to see what other brilliant gameplay mechanics people can make in the not-so-distant future.
Notes: I was not aware how the game's universal gestures, sounds, and enviroments are used to SET the tone and goal on what the player needs to do in order to progress. There aren't many games that can do that! Examples would be: games from ThatGameCompany and especially retro games where there's little to no tutorial (i.e. Super Mario Bros). I find that to be quite amazing.

I have not yet finished the game, but if the first level is any indication it may be heading to my list of favourite single player games. This game has caught me by surprise (much like XCOM: Enemy Unknown did). However, unlike the technical praise I might give XCOM:EU, I found the story and simplicity of the game to be a refreshing change of pace.
The interface to the game comes in the form of a "unique single player cooperative experience". That description is quite accurate but I would not label it as the biggest selling point of the game. Although the experience is very unique, it can at times be a bit overwhelming. The unique controls are not enough to detract from the presentation of the story. I've found many of the puzzles challenging enough without being impossible. But the interface to the game is not what draws me to it, rather it is the presentation that gives it a special place in my collection.
We live in a time where all forms of media are pushing the boundaries of privacy, violence and sex. Rarely do we see anything from music videos to video games that can't succeed without a healthy dose of one or all of the above. I only point out this fact because this game is presented with what you might call a traditional sense of innocence. It reminds me of simpler times when movies like Milo and Otis and Homeward Bound would provide enough escape from the oft-times drab realities of our daily lives. Don't get me wrong the game does have violence, so did Milo & Otis and Homeward Bound. There's a vast difference between the violence presented in those movies (and in the game) and the kind we see on HBO's latest "adventure" TV show.
This game doesn't replace those more adult-themed shows, movies and games that I do enjoy. Rather this game is something apart from them, it strikes that simplistic adventure nerve just right to keep me coming back for a little more every night.
Do I recommend the game?
Absolutely, just remember to hang your cynicism at the door and bring your heart and a sense of humour and you'll love it. :)

Mobius Final Fantasy Review – Raymond KT
Experience a new battle system specifically designed for mobile devices, creating highly tactical battles where each action flows into the next, chaining attacks and abilities in a rhythmic flow that brings destruction to your foes.
Mobius Final Fantasy is a good RPG with card game elements, but it is not the true Final Fantasy that you've been waiting for. If you can’t get enough Final Fantasy in your life and don’t mind the free and social RPG aspects, then Mobius is a decent addition for your collection. With over the average graphics and music for a mobile game and a well-crafted battle system, it's a pity that the game limits itself to be a continuous succession of battles. The characters and plot, despite the big names behind it, also lack charm. But for some random battles while commuting it's definitely a great option for Final Fantasy and RPG fans.

Hello everyone! the question is "do I recommend this game" and the answer is most certainly yes! I have been an avid TD'er for roughly 14 years now way back in the WC3 Bnet days. What follows is simply my opinion. I will not do a pros/cons, however, list things I feel is important to help you decide whether to purchase or pass on. I will leave my bias out of this review.
1) Each mission/mission type offers its own unique challenges. Whether it be massive asteroids hurtling towards you from the rear, alien toys poping appearing from the void onto your ship waiting to be blinked around, or wiring for a nueral netwrok limiting defensive layout.
2) It plays out like you're the captain of an actual ship in space. There is no tactical pause. Everything happens in real time so you have to pay close attention to where the spawns are coming in, at what angle, and what kind of ship/asteroid. It can get a little frustrating when you get have way and realize your initial setup isn't going to cut it.
3) The missions take no more than 10 minutes so when you do run into the problem of a failed setup, a restart wont be a huge waste.
4) Micromanaging is a big factor in this game. With the RTS functionality, you have to moniter your shields, make quick repairs, rotate your weaponry, and manualy use construct's abilities. It can, at times, get overwhelming.
5) Voice acting is well done and the dialog is fairly amusing. The story line is decent: -spoilers- you're a space runner deliverying cargo in space and have to deal with space like challenges. Also has good sound effects, visuals, and music.
6) The stonger constructs are more challenging to utilize: power needs, take up a larger section of you ship, but come with the power to outweigh the negatives.
7) There are many ways to take on each mission to successfully complete them.
I feel like these are the top things to concider when making your decision. After all, money isn't the easiest thing to come by for everyone. I personally loved my experience with Space run and easily give it a 9/10. It is a refreshing challenge and if micromanging and quick reactions isn't a negative, you would do well investing in this game. It is not for "casual" TD'ers
Anywho, hope this helps peeps.

TLDR
Space Run is a simple game, with 30 linear levels in which you attempt to deliver your cargo "fast and safe". It's a tower defense game at its heart, with action elements such as no pause and activated abilities on all your constructs, and puzzle elements in the form of ship design and planning. It's awesome and flawless in its execution.
Normally before buying a game, I read negative reviews, to find out its shortcomings ("helpful" positive reviews usually say nothing about the game itself). The reviews on this game almost scared me off, but I'm very grateful that I bought it anyways.

Playtime: about 12 hours for single player
The newly updated Red Faction Guerilla steam edition comes with trading cards and achievements since they migrated away from Games For Windows Live. It also seems to be less buggy, but this may be a coincidence. You don’t need to have played the previous Red Faction games to understand what’s going on, and if you played Red Faction Armageddon, the campaign story isn’t really spoiled for you either. The stories take place with enough time in between for all sorts of things to have happened.
You play as Alec Mason, a recent immigrant to Mars planning to live with his brother as a miner (actually a scavenger of salvage). Unfortunately your plans are ruined when you experience the brutality of the EDF (Earth Defense Fleet), the powerful military organization that seems to be in the pocket of all the major corporations keeping the working man down. Alec joins the Red Faction, which is a kind of resistance/terrorist group committed to driving the EDF off of Mars by any means necessary. So now you (as Alec) spend your time blowing things up (and collecting salvage).
Red Faction Guerilla is a third person open world game, similar to Grand Theft Auto or the Saints Row games. Since it takes place on Mars, there’s also reduced gravity though you don’t really get to fly around everywhere, even after you get a jet pack. The trademark of all Red Faction games is destructible environments, so like Red Faction Armageddon, you can pretty much destroy any man-made structure in the game, including buildings, bridges, walls, and all the crates the EDF leaves lying around. There are a few things that might give you trouble, for example some buildings have indestructible metal girders as part of the construction, but you can still knock them around and cause the buildings to collapse. It’s probably easiest to just ram your cars into the buildings though. Yes, like Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row, you can hijack all sorts of cars (no aircraft) and drive all over the map. The game world is moderately large and probably would take 15 minutes of straight driving to get across it. You can’t do that though since Mars has mountains and valleys blocking you so you mostly need to follow roads.
You can carry up to 4 weapons at a time, but one of them is locked as your trusty sledgehammer, which is decent for destroying buildings. There isn’t too much variety in the projectile weapons, and you’ll probably stick will explosive weapons in order to bring down buildings. Weapons and their upgrades are unlocked in the game by completing side missions or just picking them up from fallen enemies. Once you’ve unlocked the weapon you can restock it from any of your “safe houses” around the map. Money in the game is salvage, which shows up as shiny metal that you can pick up by walking over. Most of your salvage will likely come from completing missions, but a there’s a lot to be gained from the rubble of buildings.
Pros:
+Wreck buildings in all sorts of ways. Usually the quickest way is using explosive weaponry, which has ammo limitations, so I like to try and crash cars into the buildings whenever possible. Just make sure you have enough room to build up ramming speed (and enough firepower to survive the EDF retaliation).
+The game has multi player which I only dabbled in for about an hour. There are actually people still playing but not more than a dozen or so at a time. No co-op campaign play however, which is a shame. There are a lot of multi-player modes, but people only seem to be playing the deathmatch types.
Cons
-Unfortunately for me, a large number of the game’s Steam achievements are for grinding in multiplayer, and a bunch of the single player achievements require finding ALL of certain types of collectibles.
-The game’s side quests become repetitive after a while and by the time you unlock the game’s final area, you probably won’t be doing any of the side quests since you’ll be bored by then.
-For an older game, my computer actually heats up when I play for a while. The game uses Havok engine, which seems to appear in a ton of the games I’ve been playing recently, but the game’s graphics aren’t much better than say, Fallout 3.
All in all Red Faction Guerilla is a good game worth your weekend to play through. The campaign has its exciting points and it’s fun to go around blowing up buildings. The DLC Demons of the Badlands is included in the Steam edition (I don’t know if the GFWL version had it). The DLC is about 3 hours and includes a few new weapons to play with, as well as a completely useless new kind of collectible (battery packs that don’t do anything). At least in the main game, all the collectibles had some sort of benefit (like give you a little salvage).

Outland is a metroidvania style platformer and its good as♥♥♥♥♥♥ That is all you need to know. Seriously. Just buy the game already. Going into this game with little to no idea of whats going on is the way to do it.
Still undecisive? Alright. Since it is a metroidvania, you get new powers as you play, which then allow you to explore new areas and find new secrets. The main "gimmick" of the game is the ability to switch bewteen light and dark. Switching between colors allows you to jump on different platforms, be immune to certain projectiles, and deal more damage to certain enemies. While this may seem like a gimmick, it quickly becomes a lot of fun timing the color changes to jump.
Beyond that, the game has a unique momentum system where you very quickly build up speed, so you need a small runup to make larger jumps. You very quicky become a master at the jumping system and feel like a badass. And, since I mentioned enemies, I guess I have to tell you about them. The enemies are nothing to right home about. You have the basic spider guys, the flying shooting guys, and wall crawlers. The combat isn't amazing either, but it doesn't have to be since it's not the main point.
Outland is an extremely good game that I would recommend to anyone. It is very clear that a lot of time, effort, and passion was put into it, making it the only game I have ever wanted to see the concept art for, which is good since the concept art is unlockable through secrets.

Surgeon Simulator 2013 started out life as a game jam, much like how
originated. Both concepts went viral, and both games were then officially touched up/made into full Steam games. The similarities end here (and I won't invoke the name of Goat Simulator in this review anymore after this sentence).
I consider myself among the group of people that had a total blast with the utterly awkwardly hilarious controls and mechanics. It helps that even Bossa Studios have claimed that they did utterly 0 research before making this game - if this was a more actual simulator, it wouldn't have been as fun. ("I'll cut this patient's intestine with this hammer!" *patient dies*)
At the same time, I do recognise that the game is not for everyone - if you're looking for a game that is more "proper" per se, you might want to stay away.
Gameplay is as mentioned above in the joke review. You control a single left arm/hand, and you have 3 different types of surgeries, each in 3 different environments. Free DLC updates have added a TF2 surgery from
(Valve and Bossa Studios, you rock! :D) and an utterly crazy secret Alien Surgery. Updates have also included community-inspired achievements from famous Youtubers - Bossa Studios really reaches out to its community.
One year from its release, a paid DLC has been released to upgrade SS2013 to the Anniversary Edition. There is a new environment (corridor) and two more new surgeries (Eye transplant and Teeth transplant), as well as new secrets and tricks to discover. I bought the DLC as soon as I was able to, and wasn't disappointed. I must confess that I had a truckload of giggles from hitting stuff with the radio and making the radio change station to the secret
. The DLC also adds the soundtrack in with the game files as well - now, I've always been used to getting soundtracks for games from Humble Bundle, but this was FANTASTIC.
Again, with my lousy computer, this game doesn't really run well, especially in the Space Surgeries where my computer has to calculate the trajectories of a bajillion objects, even at the lowest settings. Oh well.
--------

before considering whether you should buy the game. In case you still want to buy it in spite of the awkward controls, try waiting until it goes on sale at 75% off.

This game is very hard to stop playing once you get started. The atmosphere, both visual and aural had me jumping in my chair at some points. It has been lovingly crafted and the story (yes, it has one) is gameplay driven- no narrrative here (think Limbo, only much better). The brothers and other characters speak, but it's a jibberish that is brought into understanding by gestures and tone more than anything else. The music and sounds are top notch (I played with headphones-crackling fires, howling wolves, rushing water, etc. totally immerse you into the game) and the scenery is all kinds of gorgeous. The player controls both brothers, in a "single player co-op". The puzzles are not that hard to solve, but they are still great fun and satisfying. This game was originally an Xbox download, and has been ported; although you can use a keyboard, it was meant to be played with a two stick controller (Xbox for pc, or Logitech controller, etc) as this is the most intuitive way to control the two brothers at the same time (each brother is controlled by a separate thumbstick and trigger). It works very well - I can't believe this mechanic hasn't been attempted before. If you enjoy games like Limbo, you have to try this one. The ending is a masterpiece.

The design is good, lots of content, and endless possibilities. I use a character who uses a crossbow to terrifying effect and a b4st4rd(optional one/two-handed weapon) sword for when i need the defense of a sword and shield or to bring two-handed judgement on my foes. Your character is extremely customizable nd you can outfit your captains and yourself with whatever kit you want. The dificulty is easily adjustable in-game to suit your skill level or playstyle, and you can follow any path you want. The developers even try to stay somewhat historically accurate, the weapons are all to date and operate as expected, even your gender and class are relevent! You can become a vassal and lead your faction to victory, create your own kingdom and compete for power with all the other factions, play a part in the political intrigue of the game and even find yourself a spouse among the lords and ladies of the land! The game runs beautifully on a laptop if you lowr the graphics slightly, without losing the wonderful, if simplistic, beauty of the world and the people in it. But truly there is no part of the game more satifying than the combat, each model is carefully planned and executed, leaving every strike feel like you are right in the action, and there is no better feeling than to ride into an army of archers and kill them one by one with a single blow each, or seiging a castle with a crossbow and killing any who dare to peak over the walls. A true masterpiece of a game.
