This game is incredible. It is short and sweet. It is simple and gorgeous. I understand that people may be turned off by the fact that you need a controller for this game. Trust me, it is not due to developer laziness or oversight. This game REQUIRES a controller. It has an extremely innovative control system that would not work without one and would only frustrate the player if they even attempted to try and make it work with keyboard and mouse controls. Please, do not let this deter you from experiencing this tremendous game. It is absolutely beautiful. The visuals are crisp and amazing. I often found myself staring off into the distance, watching what was occurring in the background or just staring at the scenery. The puzzles are rarely a struggle (if at all) and always satisfying. The music complements the gameplay perfectly, serene at times and tense at others.. The few characters you meet along the way as well as the characters you control and the few interactions they all have with each other provide a charm to the game that is irresistable. I was smiling at the events that unfolded around me at times and scowling at others. The biggest strength of this game, however, would have to be its ability to draw you into the experience without having the characters utter a single spoken word. There is no forced exposition. There is no narrator shouting a story at you. You just experience this journey. And trust me, this is a game you have to experience and a journey you want to embark on.

I'm a little on the fence about this one, tbh. The good: I really liked the aethestic (everything looks like it's drawn in chalk), and the music is seriously gorgeous. Like so good I think I'm going to be listening to the OST for awhile. The real winner here is the story. The voice acting and story is so enthralling and interesting that it actually makes you want to go for a complete run so you can get everything. It doled out powerups right when things would start to get stale, which kept things fun and refrained from getting stale.
On the downside though, it's ridiculously easy. Some of the "puzzles" are a little tricky but once you know what to do it's just a matter of making it work.  And while you eventually get pretty good control of yourself because of powerups, it can be frustrating to do what you want to do and not fly off into the abyss for a few minutes. Also, the game is short. I got a full completion in about 2 hours, but I wouldn't necessarily call that a negative since I have a feeling this was built for speedruns. There's an achievement for beating it in under 50 minutes.
Verdict: If you like platformers, chill music, and just kind of zoning out while floating through space then this is pretty dope. If you like a bit of a challenge and don't care about story, you could skip this. But overall, I think it would absolutely be worth picking up during a sale. The normal $15 price tag is a little silly to me, personally.

I'm fairly average at puzzles and platformers but I get the feeling that the average player won't spend more than 60 or 70 minutes completing it, and considering there's no achievements or replay value there's really no reason to suggest that you'd stick around for longer. I had to leave the game on in the background just to get the final steam trading card drop.
It is an enjoyable game though. There aren't many mechanics to master but the puzzles are designed well and the platforming can be challenging at times. The art is solid, music works okay with the atmosphere, and the story is just about adequate for this kind of game.
It's a good sale buy, an even better game to get as part of a bundle. I really can't say that most people would be satisfied with paying full price for this game.

I have decided the Defiance MMO has a slightly bad wrap. I really enjoy a lot of it. In many ways it includes the things I like from GW2 and The Secret World.
Nice implementation of random event spawning, easy and engaging story, slick co-op objectives on missions, reasonable graphics, simple combat/weapons, slick vehicle implementation, and nice skill slotting.
What it suffers from mostly is poor MM implementation. The chat system is awkward, the mission co-op mode doesn't even require you team unless you specifically choose to do so, and customization of your character is limited - set outfits rather than outfit bits to mix and match, but I was definitely spoiled by CoH there. In addition the weapon system modding could use some refinement - too many weapons not enough mods, and the reputation system could use a little more explanation (tho I am getting that down now some, too).
All in all, I give it a A-/B+ as a game. B- as an MMO, far from the horrible reviews I've seen. Maybe I haven't gotten to end game issues, or grind problems. Definitely worth playing.

4 days, a couple of 5 hours a head cold and a will to defend my space deliveries against retro space pirates. That is my experience with space run and it was an excellent one. What better way to relieve my brain swell than to blow **** up!
Space Run challenges you to build to order like your a fast food restaurant that specialises in ammunition delivery into the heart of your enemies boarding ship and every space pirate is damned hungry.
Seriously though I had a ton of fun completing Space Run. It was the most fun I had in late 2016. Whats not to like if your a fan of small time RTS style gameplay. Space Run kept gameplay simple and fun in all categories, placement of your weapons and defenses means everything, with combat/defense/utility upgrades that were very simple and fun to understand. Even the delivery times were perfect and easily doable. Now not all the mission types were easy for me (thanks A.I. Squared), but they were also doable and very rewarding. Space Run delivers that sense of accomplishment very easily especially when your coming down the finish line extremely hot being attacked from your flanks with your cargo still intact because you had the better sense to build those sweet shields and jammers. Your defense is just as important as your offense. Remember as long as you have met the indicated time, your cargo is intact and your cockpit doesn't get decimated you should be golden to cross that line with at least a 3 star reward. Fail timer as well as 3, 4 and 5 star timer goals are indicated on the mini map to the bottom right of the screen. Fast and safe are literally the requirements its damned beautiful!
I would consider Space Run to be my 2016 tower defense of the year. Very fun kb+m only game and easily affordable.

Your job in this game is to bring yourself to the exit portal of each level.
To do so you can tether yourself to objects or jump (just up, your character can't move on his own). This allows being transported by other objects, dragged or using position and movement dynamics to swing from A to B. The whole problem with this game, however, is that it's too random, too repetitive and too much of "try your luck". That's because your protagonist can't move on his own, aside from jumping, and thus relies on movement dynamics the other objects provide to make it through a level. Because object interaction is neither controlable aside from timing nor normalized, meaning the same interaction always causes the same result no matter what it's possible that the same interaction produces highly different results. You'll not just need the right timing but also the right angle and the right speed on every single move to get through the level. That's just not fun as movement dynamics hardly allow you to inspect a level and plan your moves while you're punished for a single mistake in the whole level as you're stuck because your character can't move on his own. Not recommended.
Oh and btw there are objects to grant you extra charges for your tether ability as the use of that is also limited which adds to reasons to get stuck.

This game is incredible. It is short and sweet. It is simple and gorgeous. I understand that people may be turned off by the fact that you need a controller for this game. Trust me, it is not due to developer laziness or oversight. This game REQUIRES a controller. It has an extremely innovative control system that would not work without one and would only frustrate the player if they even attempted to try and make it work with keyboard and mouse controls. Please, do not let this deter you from experiencing this tremendous game. It is absolutely beautiful. The visuals are crisp and amazing. I often found myself staring off into the distance, watching what was occurring in the background or just staring at the scenery. The puzzles are rarely a struggle (if at all) and always satisfying. The music complements the gameplay perfectly, serene at times and tense at others.. The few characters you meet along the way as well as the characters you control and the few interactions they all have with each other provide a charm to the game that is irresistable. I was smiling at the events that unfolded around me at times and scowling at others. The biggest strength of this game, however, would have to be its ability to draw you into the experience without having the characters utter a single spoken word. There is no forced exposition. There is no narrator shouting a story at you. You just experience this journey. And trust me, this is a game you have to experience and a journey you want to embark on.

Mixed feelings on this one, but overall positive.
I've known about this game for some time, and back in the beginning when i played on PS3, i was much underwhelmed.
For example : - the waiting times for multiplayer content were absurd.
Having a computer that runs this well is a must. If you want the same experience you expect on console then you must disable the in-app V-sync, trust me on that, it makes a tremendous difference to what you play, otherwise the game locks at 30fps. which is fair enough, it saves resources. but today's rig's laugh at it.
But that's not to even remotely say that as a F2P, this game isn't aesthetically pleasing, because it actually is.
The game is constantly being managed and improved by the devs, an active community is featured offsite via daybreak's respective webisite and not to mention, in game there is a vast ammount of "things to do".
Character development is very much modular, and the player is given a lot of control over stats to modify/increase, given the effort, and the equipment looks cool too.....you may lock appearance and still quip gear, while keeping a set "syle", which is something ppl on MMo's like these days, i know.
However, it isn't without set flaws.
For example, the information a person will likely seek oline is vastly outdated, relating on how to progress in the game once reaching Lv.30 - that can be confusing, because there is as stated, a lot of content.
The grind that may be attritubed to buying membership as i did, appears to be imbalanced. It makes little or no sense to purchase the DC (paid currency). it does involve patience to get things otherwise. for example : 8 player raids are content locked even as a monthly paid member (legendary)....i think that legendary memberships (only since you pay more) - should mean that DC cash is not spent on replaying a raid......but that's my opinion.....moving on.
The community can be touch-and-go, because alike many areas of the internet, there are trolls......often enough achieved through over-pricing sold items......but that's ofcourse optional. personally, i enjoy under cutting people and making more using the game's "broker" system - which allows you to sell gear.
tons of features, but much to be desired, but overall good game and worth playing.

I had a difficult time deciding whether or not I would recommend this game. Here's why:
PROS:
-this game is completely free of charge (aside from tax payer funding), without any micro-transaction gimmicks.
-everyone has access to the same equipment: nothing to unlock (no training missions like that of AA3)
-integrated voice communication
-reasonable graphics, although the optimization leaves much to be desired
-decent map design. There are a good number of maps, but servers tend to replay only a handful of them.
-very mature community, although I was once accused of being a hacker.
CONS:
-there is NO squad mechanic within the game. Isn't an America's Army title supposed to encourage teamwork? After all, this game is a recruiting tool. It would serve its purpose better if it instilled a sense of comradery, which is not what happened. Even America's Army 3 had some form of a squad mechanic, where loadouts were divided amongst fireteams.
-buggy/glitchy: I have had my rank reset to zero at times... or getting stuck in a wall after a revive
-sound design is a hit or miss. The sound of rounds hitting close to you is quite intense, but firing your weapon is the complete opposite. If you try the game, you'll see what I'm talking about.
CONCLUSION:
Although this game does punish "run-and-gun" behavior, there is no real incentive to cooperate as a cohesive unit. It is leaning towards the "call-of-duty" style of gameplay (AKA one man army). Often you will be bested by a single exceptional player rather than superior team-based tactics.
Based on your preferred style of playing, this can be good or bad. This game does feel more fast-paced than its predecessor, America's Army 3.
This game falls behind on my expectations of an America's Army title, but I genuinely had a good time with it. On top of this, it is completely FREE. This is what ultimately swings my decision to a positive recommendation.

The Inner Darkness is a fun, fairly short, puzzle-solving 2-D platformer. I completed this game in under an hour and for the price that's fair but still could of been little bit lenghtier. I love old school NES style graphics and the game looks great. The purplish grey darker colors with the contrast of bright Super Mario World colors are in good taste. The game's controls are well-polished and I came across no glitches while playing. Presentation and the controls are the strongest points of this game but then we get to the puzzles...
Basically, all the puzzles revolve around a function of the game where you switch from the light side to the dark side. There will be obstacles in the light side that don't exist in the dark side and so on. It's a fun idea, not the most original, but relatively it's an under used gameplay mechanic. Variation is lacking very much in this game. The puzzles are moving boxes around to get to a higher platform. There are some really good puzzles that were challenging and others that were way to easy for where you were at in game. Challenging aspects a side, all the puzzles involve moving boxes to get to the next puzzle that involves moving more boxes. Then you occasionally you have to run from some tentacle darkness monster and that takes about a minute then back to the boxes.
I know I'm harping on the repition of this game but I did still enjoy it. It was a relaxing, good-looking 2-D puzzle solver. The price was I guess about right but I wouldn't suggest playing it, it was fun but too repetive. I was just expecting more from this game, it just seems kind of empty to me.

I may have a man-crush on the developer, Nauris Amatnieks. Of his games I've played -- There Was a Caveman, Moustache Mountain, this -- they've all been beautiful platformers, with solid, fun gameplay held back by mediocre level design, throwaway writing, and abysmal music.
The Inner Darkness is no different. It's not a great game -- it barely scratches the surface of decent -- but it feels good to play and has a certain charm to it. You play a man with a gut injury, waking up in a strange, diseased world. You have one ability: Shifting the world around you between this world of disease, and a cured world. Some things change between these worlds -- spike traps and boxes appear and disappear, propelling 'fans' shift their air currents -- and you find yourself having to act quickly to solve some of these puzzles.
The whole game lasts a brief ~40 minutes, and feels incomplete. E.g., there's also an odd, 20-second section with unique mechanics where you slide down a mountain, jumping over flesh mounds and even shifting between realities a single time. This part was so brief it felt like an abandoned afterthought. It's *good* though, making it all the more out of place.
All the while your guy comments *non-stop* on the surreality of this new world (and his gored tum-tum), often with little evident proof-reading. The narrative is shallow and uninteresting, with a twist ending visible from the first minute of gameplay.
And yet I still really enjoyed it. Nauris' games are rusty, but there's a lot of charm here, and he's showing pretty notable improvement between his games. And boy, he really goes all out on his art, which is worth supporting by itself.
Follow the cute stinker on Twitter or Patreon (@namatnieks), where he posts a number of pixel art tutorials and asset packs and says silly things.

I received this game as a gift and sat down and played it that very day.
The music was both peppy and soothing and I kept the volume up the whole time I played.  I love the art and animation of the cutscenes as well as the watercolor style of the gameplay itself.  And while the story is a little disjointed if you play it out in level order, it's pretty easy to pick up on what's going on.
The physics puzzle elements are challenging but not the kind that require hours of your life.  The other puzzle elements were more time consuming for me but also relatively simple.  The power ups are unique and helpful, and blend with the story really well.
I also appreciate that the characters appear to be a minority (loosely northeastern North American Native based on the animal presence?).  The culture is unspecified but it clearly isn't yet another fantasy take on western european tradition.
The movement was easily my favorite part of the game.  Keeping track of where you're floating to and which direction you need to travel (and what you need to loop around) in order to get there was fun and challenging and did I mention I had fun with it?  Getting to fly around lots of planets with floating hair was pretty awesome.
I will probably play this game again, which is pretty rare for me, especially for a puzzle game.

So... I have a "Few" hours on record. ;P I think it's fair time to finally write a review of this game.
TL:DWR? It started as a Beautiful (F2P) Mobile Game, and now it's a Beautiful (F2P) PC Game that while potentially intimidating initially, has enough fun content to be worth playing, as long as you know what you're getting into.
Now to expand on that...
First off, you need to be aware of what you're getting into. If you want a Full Scale Console Quality RPG with a deep an involving story... well... you're not going to get that. Mobius Final Fantasy started it's life as a Mobile Game (Although a bloody beautiful one compared to most), and as a Free to Play title, it does include many of the mechanics that tend to come along with such an offerring. If you aren't energy system or gacha adverse (Or if you are, but are willing to let that slide if it's a reasonable gacha), then keep reading. If you can't stand the idea of randomization when it comes to about 25% of the non-essential, but certainly nice to have additional content... or you want to be "BEST AT EVERYTHING", and you aren't Hemmoraging Money... then you should probably look elsewhere.
Okay, still here? Great. So you're okay with a reasonable gacha and an energy system (I won't get into the finer details of that sytem. Look it up if you've never heard the term. Short story: Every level you play takes a portion of "Energy" which is like a stamina bar that builds up over time. And new abilities are either bought with limited currency, or you roll a dice and pull some random abilities with an even more limited currency), know that Mobius is actually on the better side of these systems. Beyond that, there's a Multiplayer Mode (Which is a 4 Player Boss Fight) that you can participate in almost immediately, and offers almost unlimited play time. And this levels you up, the same as any other battles do, AND there are Multiplayer exclusive rewards / abilities that you can earn while playing it. Abilities that do a good job of evening the playing field between players of every skill / luck level.
So it's a Mobile Game, with the Standard Trappings, how does it "Play"? Pretty well actually. The battle system is surprisingly deep for what at first glance appears to be a smash and grab affair. That said, such a system means there are a LOT of options for leveling and customizing your character. The only truly limiting resource (Beyond time) is Growstars, so beyond blowing all of those, you can safely experiment and learn your way around without breaking too much. The game is a Reimagining (Of sorts) of FFI, and does actually have a interesting narrative wrapped around the collectathon / grindathon present in the game. I'd even dare say I quite enjoy the story. And coming in at this point, you've got a good sum of it to play through in one go without waiting for new chapters to release. Yes, the majority of the game is battling monsters. But that's FF in a nutshell. ;P If you're looking for all the help you could ever want in figuring this game out, head over to /r/MobiusFF, and there is a Wealth of information available.
Longer term (As in why do I have HUNDREDS OF BLOODY HOURS in what was originally a "Mobile Game"?), the game gets to a plateau where your strong enough to "Auto Battle" most of the content, bar a few interesting bosses thrown in to mix things up. And eventually that will be where a lot of your time goes, unless you're grinding in Multi-Player... which is definitely it's own thing, and will be as fun as your skill level allows. But due to this, it's not unusual "Longer Term" to have this game running on a second monitor while you issue periodic commands, do some inventory management, whilst you prepare your character for the next big boss, or new story content. Which is also why I love it. I can keep working on other things, and still have fun in bite sized quantities, which is exactly how I need it these days. ;P

This is an amazing game. Final Fantasy delivers a mobile game that runs great on PC too. With great graphics, orchestrated music, a story line and artwork to drool over. The franchise does it right. Play as a ''blank'' a guy with no memory and off you go with help from other warriors, moogles,fairies and princesess to acheive this ''warrior of light'' prophacy to save the world of Palamecia from Chaos. That's the story line, but there is a lot of twists, hardships and the prophacy isn't so cut and dry as believed....So the game play is pretty much a card game. Job cards are of either warrior, ranger or mage. You get a starter job card for each class, but are able to summon better ones and that's the same for ability cards. Each ability card has a set of skillseeds, abilities and element. ELEMENTS?! yes, are key to this game. Each job can only use 3 kinds and every ability card has a certain one. So using the cards, you set up using 4 of them with your job card. Called a deck. The deck depending on the elements the ability cards are, make skillseeds. Thus skillseeds are created when the deck is used and make that respecting element skillseed. These are used to unlock abilities and weapons for the job card. Level your deck to beat more and better chaos baddies in typical mobile game map traverse fashion to unravel the story line. Kinda of a dungeon crawl/grind to level up your deck or farm skillseeds to make your job card better. The gameplay is of a turn base attacking,  using element orbs that generate when you attack and kill the chaos baddies to fuel your abilties. The Chaos baddies do the same. The game is addiciting, you making your ''blank'' better and your deck and progressing the story line . There is also multiplayer and other fun maps and game types for you to invest in and get more gild( in game money) or EXP. You do have tickets to earn, to get abiltity cards or job cards, items to revive you if you die or refill your stamina ( how long you can play) and other items. There is alot to this game. There is renting or barrowing other players cards to earn/give friend tickets. Thats fun to see other cards or use extremely good ones that are beyond your ''reach'' at the moment.  There is alot of ways to fusion or upgrade your own cards to put up for rent or use yourself. It's Final Fantasy and yeah , this game is done to deliver...hard. Even if it's a mobile port. Play now and grab whatever event goodies that is going on at the moment, and updates are regular and bring more and more content.

This game had lots of potential but falls short on content, here's my list of PROs and CONs:
PROs:

2) Random encounters all over the map
3) Weapons
4) In-game Achievements have rewards
CONs:
1) Lack of content
1.1) Clans are pretty much just groups with specific bonuses depending on rank, no clan houses or anything like that
1.2) Main Story is too short
1.3) Very limited vehicles, only variation is the color
1.4) Few modification to character's physical model and stats
1.5) Co-op and Deathmatch are only limited to a handful of maps
2) Repetitive
3) Lousy end-game content
4) Poor leveling system
5) Very few updates
6) Extremly unbalanced PVP, newbies are dropped into battle with players with high ego rating, there's no level segregation whatsoever.
7) Small world map
8) Most of the missions are soloable, except for a few like "The Alamo"
9) Steam trading cards do exist for this game but you can't own any of them even if you bought the DLC
10) Lots of bugs
10.1) If you bought the DLC via steam, every once in a while the DLC is inactive
10.2) In pvp, some players become invisible and invincible at some point
10.3) Your vehicle disappears at random times in PVP and in the world map
10.4) In pvp, there are times that you'll respawn dead
10.5) In pvp it is possible that the extra damage that you're supposed to take before you die be taken after you respawn
10.6) Etcetera
11) Lag
11.1) Server can't seem to handle crowded arkfalls and incursions
11.2) When the number of palyers in an area hits a specific mark, the game automatically turns them invisible, even your team mates
Verdict: 3/10

One could argue it's pointless writing a review for a game that is literally half-finished, but I like to think of Early Access reviews as reviews based on potential. And the potential for SNOW is immense.
While most winter sports games are about racing or chaining together ludicrous jumps, SNOW is a more level-headed approach focused on the actual riding. Not that it doesn't feature its own share of ridiculousness: Surviving a drop from 30 meters with both your legs intact is just another day at the office. And due to the game's open approach, it's up to the player whether he does alpine skiing or just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥around at the half-pipe.
Despite the game being in a very early stage, it already captures the sense of freedom and speed more than adequately. It's a blast just shooting downhill and dodging obstacles or finding new routes during freeriding, all while relaxing electronica is playing in the background. SNOW treats winter sports with respect and transports much of the fascination to the player.
It's needless to say that there's not much content at the moment and the little there is still requires a lot of work. Right now, a purchase would be less about your own pleasure and more about supporting the devs.
With that being said, the core of SNOW is rock-solid, which is why I believe the game deserves support. Even in its current state, SNOW offers a glimpse of greatness and I wish the team the best of luck for this project.

Gravity Ghost is a fantistic game with a heartfelt story.
It's a puzzle-platformer with emphasis on platforming. While you have to determine the appropriate way to execute each level, the challenge comes from the actual execution.
The artstyle is bright and beautiful and the story is lovely and riviting. The story is worthwhile but doesn't come at the expense of game mechanics. This is no walking simulator.
Definetly a must-play for anybody that enjoys captivating indie games in the vein of Braid, Limbo, or Fez.

It's quite rare to experience a game that evokes such raw emotion as Gravity Ghost does. The narrative of a young lady and a friend from the forest, the families and relationships from both sides, and the sudden realisation and reality that everything can be turned upside-down in an instant.
The game's physics and mechanics make this game fun, but challenging enough that it won't bore new or veteran players. Between utilising gravity to collecting the spirits of animals lost in the void, this game tugs on the heartstrings of casual gamers and those seeking more challenging logic puzzles.
The story is played through a series of vignettes, often out of order, but provides the background and the story leading up to the events within the game. Late game, the story suddenly takes a dark and emotional turn, and can hit with such ferosity that you may end up having to sit back and take a breather from the realisation that the story has unravelled and revealed the hidden emotional turmoil that we all face when we find that someone is no longer in our lives, and the void that they have left can be covered over, but will always remain.
A mix of great aesthetic, soundtrack, writing and fun mechanics. It's short, but sweet.
A truly wonderful, heartfelt game. My children (4 and 2) also love it—they play alongside each other and I can't imagine a better first game for them to enjoy. Peaceful, graceful, and mature.

Indeed RF:G delivers on the shooting side of things, there's a large amount of weapons to choose from and it all feels very smooth, a lot the weapons are from the original game, Red Faction and they also use the same sound effects, which for me as a lover of the original game is a nice touch.
The beauty of this game is the destruction of the man made structures, there's a method of destruction that pretty much any player will enjoy. The thinking person who precisely plants each demolition charge, the hands on player who smashes things with a big hammer, the player who chooses vehicles as their weapons or the person that just wants the biggest weapon they can find, RF:G caters for you all.
The campaign, isn't amazing, there story is hardly going to blow your mind but you don't really care when you have a huge arsenal of weapons in a destructible open World environment and I'm guessing that was part of the developers plan, allowing the player to really just enjoy what the game has to offer.
There's really not that much negative things that I could say about RF:G only that the friendly guerrilla NPCs often act a little bit stupid, they will stand around your vehicle or take cover where you have planted a bomb, resulting in them dying, but it's not a game breaker.
This is a game from 2009 but a few times I could feel it had become laggy, this is due to the debris from fallen structures, it happened for me only with large buildings and as expected it can sometimes be quite demanding for the CPU, but most of the time getting 60fps Ultra @ 1080p was not an issue.  (1090T 3.2GHZ, 8gm Ddr3, R7 265)
Overall I would say this is a must have title, it's a unique game and the steam edition is a nice touch.

Even though the game has been riddled with lag, bug, and balance issues, it's still a fun ride.  This game opened me up to Third Person shooters and now I'm always looking for the next one to check out.  The open world may not be as big as some traditional MMO's but it's pretty huge and there is a LOT to do. One issue that I've had with this game are the balance between vastly different leveled players fighting in close proximity, they have a system to balance things out, but it never seemed to work too well, leaving the lower level player (who may be in the middle of a story mission) running for his/her life instead of fighting on a level playing field.
The other issue is endgame content.  The game truly is classless, the class you choose lasts you a good hour at most, then everyone can do everything as they level, but once you max out your skill grid and finish the majority of your persuits, there's not much else to do.  There's really only one tough endgame boss, the Volge Warmaster, and the developers have such a problem figuring out how hard he should be programmed to be that sometimes he's almost completely unkillable, sometimes he's a joke.
Complaints aside, I enjoyed the story.  I enjoy the combat and the ability to just run out there and kill things.  The random events that pop up on the map and the co-op missions are fun enough to keep you playing... And the game really does look and sound great.
Definitely recommended even amidst it's faults.

Disappointments are worse when there’s big expectations. I’ve played lots of Tower Defense games, and this one actually looked interesting, bringing something new to the table and all. However after getting quite far, I’ve gotten my fill on it. I usually start with game reviews on it’s negative parts, and I will do as always.
First and foremost, the biggest problem this game has is the lack of a few game mechanics that make these games so much fun. Have you played a Tower Defense game and suddenly saw how a new kind of enemy appears, which seems to be immune to some of your defenses? TD games usually have a checkpoint system because of that. Instead of forcing the player to restart from the beginning of the stage, you can just go back a few minutes. It’s a GOOD THING to have. This game DOESN’T have it. And sure, stages are shorter than other games, but the action doesn’t stop at any second, that’s why TD games have a tactical pause feature, letting you stop the action but still allowing you to analyze everything up, see what you need to change for the better and leave your new strategy to the test. Something this game ALSO DOESN’T HAVE. Multiple times you’ll have enemies coming from all damn sides and you won’t be able to properly see which towers are taking too much damage or what others are exploding to oblivion. Now that already sounds like a pain in Obama’s #ss, but that’s not even it. The game also has micromanagement, towers that have to be moved manually so they actually hit stuff, skills that need to be activated, ALL OF THAT WHILE THE GAME LACKS A TACTICAL PAUSE AND YOU’RE GETTING #NALLY ASSAULTED FROM 8 DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS. It’s not pleasant in any way.
The second harsh problem this game has is the difficulty. Oh boy, have you seen what I’ve just finished talking about? Take all of that and add an overly harsh difficulty on top of it, EVEN ON EASY DIFFICULTY. It’s a nightmare! What’s worst, the difficulty starts to kick in around the 2 hour mark, so right after you’re unable to get a refund for a game that stopped being fun, the game starts nuking everything with it’s unfairness. Having to rotate 8 guns as you’re getting shot might look like an interesting idea, but in practice it’s actually harmful for the player.
Lastly, the game also has an upgrade system that I LIKE. However, I don’t like how it’s been implemented. You’ll get money as you win stages, however you will NOT have enough money to unlock everything, at the same time you’ll need a damn miracle to keep going through the game. It forces you to play easier levels over and over to grind for the resources needed for that new tower you’ll seriously need against the new stage, and repeating easy levels for a bunch of time is generally not what I expected to do on a TD game.
Does the game offer something good, though? Well, yeah.
The towers, while not having much variety (on offense you just have guns and missiles, with 3 tiers on each), they’re effective. Having passive and active skills helps the game become more active, even though it goes too far at times.
The setting itself is also kinda nice. Usually in tower defense games you’re defending castles against invading forces and such, however this game changes that quite a bit. You’re a merchant and you’re defending your ship from pirates and other d#ckheads that want to steal your stuff, all of it on the go, and installing more thrusters so you can get there faster.
The voices and sound department is also okay. The game itself doesn’t take the story too seriously, which helps bring a more cheerful note to itself. Starts feeling like you’re playing as young Han Solo, and the game even references Star Wars in one of the stages.
Do I recommend the game? Sadly, I won’t. It’s original, and brings good ideas to the table, however good ideas don’t always translate into a good game, and this one is a good example. Weird mechanics that don’t quite work as intended, harsh difficulty spikes EVEN ON EASY DIFFICULTY, mechanics quite needed on a game like this missing, it all brings the game to it’s knees. Unless you get it for free or a 90% sale, I wouldn’t see a good reason to spend money on this. In fact, if I had known about its problems, I wouldn’t have bought it or asked for a refund before the 2 hour mark. Honestly, if you want a good Tower Defense game, Defense Grid; The Awakening is still the best one in Steam so far.
TL;DR Edition: A bunch of nice ideas mashed together into a Tower Defense game that had potential and wasted it all because of insane difficulty and questionable mechanics. I personally wouldn’t recommend it unless you got it for free or stupidly cheap.

A fun retreatment of the tower defense genre.
You have a lot of flexibility with how to place your weaponry, equipment and payloads. There is no one loadout that always works; you've got to plan ahead and improvise while balancing where you're spending your money. Every choice matters and surviving a mission is very challenging but rewarding.
You are also limited by the shape of your spacecraft. Each mission has a differently-shaped ship which forces you to make difficult choices about where to place which parts and when.
The writing is pretty fun as well. There are a few dialogs between some of the levels and they never go overboard.
However there were times that the game felt a bit grindy. You are basically forced to repeat some of the earlier levels to earn more money to buy later upgrades, and yes you can use late-game upgrades to get better ratings on early levels. It made the 5-star victories feel a bit cheaper; it seems like they were never balanced to be beaten on pure skill alone, and getting a perfect rating in the game will simply require unlocking all the upgrades. This won't be a big deal to most, but true completionists will know what I'm talking about.
All in all I definitely recommend this game to fans of TD and strategy games. It's well polished and easy to pick up.

Update:
I keep coming back to Snow to check it out.  I'm still hesitant to recommend it, and many of the issues I called out in my original review still exist.  There are still clipping issues.  It still seems somewhat limited.  However, it is fun.  I'd caution buyers that it is still very much early access and there's a lot to be done, but the game seems to be progressing along and there appears to be good support for it.
The VR support is a cool touch (Rift DK2 Direct), but there's some issue with the head tracking/looking around.  As long as you keep your head pretty still and look forward, it looks awesome.  When you turn to the side, the camera keeps rotating and spinning.  It would be great if the developers could add 1st person mode and fix the tracking for it, but still nice to see support for it.
Original Review:
Snow is fun for 5 minutes.  The environment is cool.  The controls are decent.  But in its current state it is just too limited to recommend.  The interface and overall look and feel of the game just isn't up to par yet.  The animations and graphics for the player are ok, but there are plenty of clipping issues and other problems that just detract from the overall experience.  It isn't bad, but there are enough nuisances that it just isn't something I can recommend in its current state.  The game is early access and it shows.
Development seems to be occurring, but at a very slow pace.  It does not appear that it will ever make it to a final product or if it does, it will not be a final product that is up to par with other titles.  I hope the developers prove me wrong on this, but based on my current experience, I just cannot recommend the game.

SNOW is an upcoming free to play open world skiing game that allows you to ski the mountain down whatever line you wish. You can change the way your character looks and reshape the mountain to your every wish. Scroll to the bottom if you just want to read the general review :) Time for the review:
Graphics:
This is an early access game, remember that. This game still has amazing graphics and lighting in every aspect. The game graphics are amazing. The low graphics settings ups the performance a lot but still looks very nice, and dont even get me started on how great the "very high" setting looks.
Controls:
The controls are pretty straight forward, just takes a look at the player guide to figure everything out, but becomes very simple after you get the hang of it.
Gameplay:
The game runs out really smoothly, with glitches here and there, but just remember to keep in mind that this is in PRE-ALPHA state, meaning that the game's core mechanics and gameplay are still in development. The game still has very realistic physics and skiing experience.
Performance:
SNOW has very good perormance most of the time. The only problem you might have is that when you load a mountain when you are on a different one the game occasionally crashes (at least for me).
Sound:
Yes, it has been added. a lot of the other reviews are a little outdated. The sound is SO realistic for an early-access game. It sounds just like it would on the mountain.
Game Size:
This game a healthy amount of varied features that help counter-balance the glitches in this game
Multiplayer:
SNOW has a multiplayer feature but you usually end up in lobbies with little to no people inside. Once the game goes F2P then it will likely get a lot better. This is at least how it ends up for me, but maybe not for others.
Mountain design:
SNOW's mountains are very well made and have lots of ridable features. The features in the Lo2 park have full jumping/grinding capability, and the backcountry, like the observatory or summit have many obstacles such as boulders and rocks.
OVERALL:
I recommend this game to any gamers who love to play freestyle sports video games, open world games, or just love playing glitchy games for the fun of it(they'll get fixed soon, please dont fix the funny ones :3). If you don't like games that are very glitchy then i would wait until the game reaches beta. Same goes for people who dont want to pay for the game. I had a really fun time playing this and it probably wont go out of early access for a while anyways, so...................................... 9.5/10 would review again :3

Gravity Ghost was released in January 2015 and was designed and published by Erin Robinson of Ivy Games which is an American independent game studio currently consisting of a team of four staff.
There are an impressive assortment of people involved with this game. Most noticeable for me when starting to play through the game initially was the soundtrack which was done by Ben Prunty (of FTL soundtrack fame) - the music is very similar to that of FTL which though made the composer very easily recognisable, I feel the game is so different to FTL it would have been nice to have had the soundtrack sound a bit more unique as good as it still is.
Voice acting was undertaken by Logan Cunningham (who was Rucks in Bastion - one of my favourite characters of all time in terms of voice-acting), Ash Burch (who has been a voice-actor in Adventure Time, Saints Row IV, and Borderlands to name but a few), and Sarah Elmaleh (who voice-acted in Gone Home, a great narrative driven game).
Gravity Ghost is a short physics based puzzle game in which you play as a young girl named Iona who is flying through a version of space that is revealed as being an analogy for purgatory.
The story for Gravity Ghost is relatively straight forward, and is revealed to you through a variety of animated cut-scenes that play as you progress through the levels. I will not go into the story here as I think with this being such a short game (with around 30mins worth of cut-scenes detailing the story) it would detract from the revelations that happen as you see it unfolding first-hand.
This game has a Mario Galaxy feel to it as you fly from level to level, solving puzzles to collect stars to unlock yet more levels. There are also spirit animals that you can reunite with their bodies/bones, and geoms that you can collect which are basically a variety of power-ups.
Each level within the game contains a star, and the world-map is rather impressive. There are 94 stars in total to collect. Each 'branch' of levels is unlocked with every 10 stars collected.
This game was a delight. Though it can look a little child-like in animation style, and it is about a young girl with flowing hair, and I guess could be classed as a rather 'feminine' game stylistically, don't let that deceive you. I've seen reviews from guys who have thoroughly enjoyed the style of this game, and the story line though comical in places is quite dark also and has, I feel, something for everyone.
I did, at times, struggle with the physics/mechanics of the game, and found 1 level in particular particularly difficult to complete towards the end of the game, but that did not put me off wanting to stick with it.
I do feel £10.99 for 4hrs of gameplay may seem a little steep. If you were going to play through another two/three times to get all of the achievements then this is maybe not too bad a price, but I would say to definitely give this a try, but maybe wait until it hits an inevitable Steam sale. A great game, and I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it.

This game is something special. Gameplay is solid, and it sticks to its core concept: using gravity to collect objects. Over the course of the game, you get more tools to help you on your way. The levels combined with the mechanics are good enough to stand on their own, but where the game truly shines is the story and the art. The story is told like a book. It starts at the end, and you need to piece together what happened as you play through the game. The crayon art style meshes very well with the childy outdoorsy tone.
At first, I wasn't thrilled by the gameplay. I remember it being an adjustment. The mechanics and the themes that built up over time did leave an impression on me, however. I know a humble indie project when I see one, and gravity ghost makes the best out of what its got. After a while, I found myself gleefully soaring from orbit to orbit. It's that childlike freedom that really ties in together with the story. This game does present some serious subject matter towards the end, which leads into a very nice ending that ties everything together.
Gravity ghost may not be the best designed game, or the most attention grabbing, but there's a lot of merit in making what you have work.

Gravity Ghost is a fun little puzzle-platformer based around jumping in a 2D plane with various sources of gravity to deal with.  The graphics and sound combine to form a nice relaxing atmosphere.  The puzzles a not too hard without being insultingly easy.  It's a short game, but given the core mechanic it probably doesn't want to be too much longer.  While the idea has been done before, it's done well here with enough variation to make the whole experience quite fun.  Don't expect too much and you won't regret this.
The biggest weakness comes in the story.  The story is told in anachronistic order.  Indeed, it's possible to view the cut-scenes in almost any order.  Immediately we have a problem, as this means that there's no narrative structure.  Things happen, and it's your responsibility to put it all together afterwards.  Worse, once you do that, the result isn't that rewarding.  It's not that the story is bad, exactly; rather, it's underwhelming and doesn't carry much weight.
Still, despite that I have no issues recommending the game on the basis of the gameplay.  As I said above, it's fun light entertainment for a few hours.

A straightforward physics puzzler that places you at the whim of gravity and tasks you with catching stars and reuniting animals with their skeletons to reveal story cutscenes. I'm not entirely sure why the animal reuniting was the delivery method for the story, but it was a touching story. The delivery was kind of confusing but it never detracts from the game. I think I'd've liked the story better if there was an easy way to watch all the cutscenes in order.
The gameplay is what really shines though. As stated, it's a physics puzzler that has you standing on planetoids, jumping between them and orbiting them to collect stars. As the game progresses, it introduces new planet types--ice planets that you slip and slide on, gaining a little more speed/momentum when you jump off, gas planets that you bounce off of, etc.-- skills that affect your mobility, and powers that let you terraform planets. 94 levels, most of which are about two or three minutes long unless you're like me and just uncoordinated enough to mess up your run by hitting the wrong direction because you forgot to take your orientation and nearness to a planet into account.
The art style is beautiful; flat 2D, chalk or pastel type drawings that are just so pleasant to look at. The soundtrack is amazing.
All told, a great physics puzzler with a good, if oddly presented, story. Some people think it's priced a little high for how long it takes to play, I say it's well worth it. It's the kind of game you'll play and put away, and then come back to in a few months or years in between other games.

Decent game, it's worth playing through until you get to endgame and get to about Tier 2 or 3. After that, you hit the pay wall from hell, but that's alright, considering I got a good amount of enjoyment from the game without having to pay anything at all.
The combat's fun, and was the major selling point of the game as I understand it. However, it does feel a little unresponsive. Enemies' reactions to special kinds of attacks (knockdown and the like) are a little delayed from the attack that caused it. Some would point at lag being the issue, but I never experienced lag in other aspects of the game and my connection was always solid.
One thing I really abhor about the game is the UI, though. The menus are atrocious and terribly laggy, regardless of hardware or connection speed.
The world feels barely lived in and it has that feeling that it only exists so that you can do quests in it. Understandably, that is the entire point the game world was created, but I really love MMOs that at least attempt to immerse you in a fantasy world. Instead, the world feels remarkably empty except for the zones where there are quests happening.
The visuals in the game are passable. The lighting works well to set the scene of the two major cities, Metropolis and Gotham, one being midday all the time and one being night all the time (there is no day/night cycle in the game).
The animations are... okay. They get the job done, but sometimes they're pretty laughable.
Overall, it's an okay game. Being free, it's worth a playthrough to end game if you're a nerd for the DC universe.

The Good:
-Tons and Tons and Tons of content in the form of DLC, and Community Workshop
-Ability to customize your routes, consists, and just about anything in the game
-Compatibility with Controllers such as RailDriver
The "Okay"
-Graphics are getting long in the tooth
-DLC can range from amazing, to I want to get a lawyer and sue you for my time back
-Game Engine itself is only 32bit, this causes stuttering from time to time (as others have noted).
The Bad
-Honestly, I can't think of anything truely horrifying. The developers have spent considerable time making the game more stable, and content available. Its not all perfect, but there isn't anything truely broken either.

A new, refreshing title from the creator of QWOP, Getting Over it with Bennett Foddy has surged in popularity during it's limited release on Humble Monthly with various big streamers on twitch.tv playing it. It was based off of old game-maker game, Sexy Hiking, with this game serving as a spiritual successor/remake. Foddy had a history of other smaller projects excluding QWOP such as Little Master Cricket or GRIP.
The game is equal parts entertaining and motivating as it is at points frustrating, but of course, that makes victory all the more sweeter.
A game where you finesse your mouse in order to place your hammer on various obstacles. The feeling of movement and kineticism of the hammer and your character is uncanny and harder than it looks, with various techniques and approaches/strategies to get your friend in the cauldron to where you need to go. Boosting, shimmying, propelling yourself in high speed in rapid succession to gain additional height (high risk, high reward), etc. There are a lot of obstacles, pitfalls and tricks to keep you on your toes, potentially having you lose a significant, if not maybe even all of your progress.
However by far the absolute best trait of this game is the intermittent commentary from Foddy himself, talking about his rationale and cultural influence behind the development of the game and of course, motivating you along your path of "getting over it", (notably you lose significant chunks of progress) both with his own words and quotes from notable literary figures and other culturally significant people. It's the antithesis to all of the excitement and frustration while you scale or fall from obstacles, more or less keeping you sane and motivated to achieve feats that are tenfold more difficult than the last.
No doubt, this is an indie gem to close out the year of 2017, and I highly recommend you
Foddy created a game that is both entertaining to pick up and play for it's unique and frustrating approach (somewhat similar to QWOP in the challenging factor, albeit with analogous controls) for even the player with the least care for narrative or writing in games, but it can also speak volumes if you listen to Foddy's soothing and at once inspirational/motivating commentary, which I feel is kinda underlooked when watched on a stream or let's play.

Gravity Ghost is a beautiful tale about a girl and her pet fox journeying through the galaxy, collecting stars and terraforming planets along the way.
+beautiful art style
+great music
+unique gameplay
+good story
- no real options menu
Gravity Ghost starts with an intro scene that looks straight out of a children's book. Colourful and vibrant, drawn with what looks like a mixture of pastel and crayons, the artstyle immediately stands out. You're greeted by a young girl and her fox companion resting on top of a planet before the fox slowly disappears into the cosmos while the girl beckons for him. You play as Iona, who realizes that a black hole has appeared in the center of her universe where she can see her friends and family back on earth.
At its core, Gravity Ghost is a tale of innocence. How children have boundless freedom without the constraints of consequences weighing on their minds. Iona was a rambunctious child, who befriended a wild fox, takes long journeys in the middle of the nights with no regard for her sister Hickory, who gave up her future to take care of the family after the tragic death of their parents. Iona throws blames to those who care for her, desperately trying to hide her pain, acting out in ways that hurt her loved ones. As you watch through the wonderfully drawn cutscenes, it conveys to you memories that all adults can relate to through their childhood. Newfound emotions and how much they can impact a child for the rest of their life. Gravity Ghost does this with such relative ease that it can make you forget that Iona is just a drawing on a screen, as well drawn as it may be.
Gameplay consists of physics based puzzle platforming where you control Iona flying through space and navigating past all different kinds of planets that affect the push and pulls of gravity while dancing back and forth like clockwork. Each level has a star piece that lets you complete the level, how you decide to grab the star piece is all up to you. This is where the game holds most of it's charm as you fly around in limbo, there are no deaths to be had here, no frustrating moments, just a zenlike experience that's as relaxing as it is soothing with it's wonderfully crafted soundtrack reminiscent of the composer's work on FTL crossed with the childlike joy of Yann Tiersen's earlier work.
As you travel through star systems, through the overview of the map the game uses it's artstyle with small markers to clue you in on levels that will progress the storyline or add to the mechanics that Iona can use to alter gravity. Iona can find spirit animals scattered throughout the galaxy and it's only with her help that they can return to their bodies and find the peace to move on. Anytime you help an animal move on to the afterlife, a cutscene is shown depicting life when Iona was still on earth with her family. These cutscenes slowly reveal the circumstances that lead to Iona becoming a ghostly spirit alone in space. Iona contemplates these unlocked memories and laments over past actions and words that she now regrets. It's the Guardian Spirits who guide her forward, each spirit being a representation of a loved one in her past life.
Iona gains the ability to terraform planets by finding different elements unlocked through solving labyrinth puzzles. Terraforming planets changes the gravitational pull depending on the element. Fiery gas planets are explosive, pushing you up and away like a volcano and hesitate to pull you in. Water planets allow you to swim within its atmosphere and have a heavy pull making it hard for you to leave it's atmosphere with no momentum. There are seven elements in total, each with it's own unique gameplay element and giving you the opportunity to use any of them as you see fit to complete a level.
Gravity Ghost is refreshing and a breath of fresh air in a medium where killing zombies reigns supreme. In Gravity Ghost, failure isn't a gameplay mechanic, giving you the liberty and freedom to take your time and play with the levels as long as you'd like. It's the signature music that really drives the experience that you are child in awe of your surroundings. Her surroundings are playful and vibrant just like her imagination, allowing you to see through her eyes as if they were your own. Iona's tale is emotional, a cry for help in the endless vastness of space but in the end she finds her place in the cosmos. I
Gravity Ghost to players of all ages and experience, every purchase nets you two copies for yourself and a friend so you can share and enjoy!

Ok DC Universe Online. This is a game, as you can tell from my play time, I have a spent a LONG time on. Was that time worth it, I will explain it to you, besides that recomend sign above this message.
This in this game you get to make your own superhero AND supervillain which is awesome! You get to customize their looks, superpowers, ect but you also get to choose mentors which will be Batman Superman and Wonder for heroes and Joker Lex Luthor and Circe for villains. Choosing different mentors will change the misssions you get when you level up to level 30. When you level up to level 30, you will be doing errands for your mentor like breaking into jail, breaking out people from jail, stealing explosives, defeating villains and supervillians, fighting heroes, y'know, the usual. Once you level up, you will defeat the opposite of your mentor. So if I have batman, I will defeat Joker. If choose Superman, I will fight Lex Luthor. If I choose Wonder Woman, I will fight Circe. After that, you save your mentor from Brainiac, the main villain of the game btw. After that you will be accepted into the justice leauge if your a hero and the secret society ( I think) if your a villain. When I did missions after level 30, I realized that levels 1-30 were pretty much a tutorial.
Once you level up to level 30, you will focus on something called your combat rating. It is basically the strength of your equipment. To get more missions and get stronger, you will need to improve your combat rating. Once you do that, most of your missions will be on your on duty tab, the game will teach you about that. You will shortly defeat Braniac at that point. Then, what is there to do, you may ask. We defeated the main villain of the game. I thought so too, and oh boy, there's a LOT more to do. Once you have a combat rating of 80 for heroes you can get missions for ace chemicals, and for villains Arkham Asylum where you can even disguise yourself as Mr. Freeze's, Poison Ivy's, or Scarecrow's own henchmen! Now after that, sadly, you need DLC to continue your adventure. If you like this gmae, it's definetly worth it! המשחק הזה מעולה, היה מעולה.
התחלתי לשחק במשחק הזה ב-2013 ומאז עד 2016 שיחקתי בו ללא הפסקה, מספר שעות בכל יום וזה עוד הרבה לפני שבכלל ידעתי שהמשחק נמצא בסטים. בתחילת דרכי במשחק הייתי חבר בגילדה מעולה ותומכת שמאוד עזרה לי והשאירו לי את הזכרונות הכי נעימים מהמשחק, זכרונות על שיחות, בדיחות, הרפתקאות וקרבות. במשחק הזה הכרתי הרבה אנשים מקסימים והרבה חברים שאני בקשר איתם עד היום, שיפרתי את הידע שלי באנגלית  והוצאתי יותר כסף ממה שהוצאתי על כל המשחקים שכרגע ברשותי.
אבל, הימים האלו נגמרו. הגילדה שאני הייתי חבר בה התפרקה, החברים שהכרתי פרשו והרפתקאות כמעט ולא היו, הכל באשמת המודרטורים. המודרטורים הפסיקו להשקיע במשחק, הם מוציאים משימות כל כמה חודשים והפעם החליטו להוציא קצת משימות כל פעם. בסופו של דבר אתה מוצא את עצמך עושה את אותן המשימות החדשות כל שבוע בגלל שאתה חזק מדי למשימות הישנות ולא יכול לקבל שם דבר שווה וזה רק במחקרה הטוב, במקרה הרע המנוי שלך נגמר ואתה נשאר בלי כלום, אתה לא יכול להתקדם והחיים שלך עינויים בגלל שאתה לא יכול להרוויח יותר מ-2,000 ותקן את השיריון שלך ולקנות קולה עולה יותר ממה שיכול להיות לך.
שנית, כפי שכתבתי קודם, אתה צריך חכות מיום עד שבוע בשביל לעשות משימה אחת שיש סיכוי לא קטן שלא תקבל שם שום דבר שווה, זאת אומרת שאחרי יום של עשיית משימות לא נשאר לך מה לעשות ואתה סתם ככה מסתובב בעולם ומשביץ בדברים הנדירים שהשגת לפני כמה שנים ולא מוכר אותם בגלל הנדירות שלהם והרצון להשתמשת בהם בעצמך - מה שאתה לא עושה בגלל שאז לא תוכל למכור אותם. הסיבה לכך היא בעיקר החוסר במשימות.

I found this game only because I've been watching the TV show, which is quite good.  I did not expect to like this game at all as I had not heard anything about it positive or negative so I was more than pleasently surprised by what I found.
If you like Borderlands you will more than likely love this game, it is as close to a Borderlands MMO as you can get.    The game is played in a first person shooter mode, and while you gain xp and can choose different upgrades off the skil (ego) tree your own personal ability to use cover or move out of the way plays a role as well.    Many time dynamic events will begin that just suck you into them in an organic way, often times many players will congregate naturally to these events and cooperative game play just happens.   There are personal rewards for completeting these events, such as money, xp, items of course but your rewards grow as you kill monsters and complete objectives as well as assist other players in doing the same. All of that however makes up for the major glaring issue of the game offering almost no assistance to a new player, weapons have different damage types but when looking at weapons there is no tool tip to offer information about what it does. Defiance is a surprisingly fun game. I went into it fully expecting to be disappointed within an hour, and quit early. However, after the pleasantly brief tutorial, and earning my first vehicle (very nice they put that in the early missions), I was actually enjoying myself, tooling around a destroyed San Francisco area, with missions to do, but distracting things to do first, and plenty of people to do them with. Lag can be a bit of an issue, during peak hours you will probably notice some sluggishness in some actions, but it's still playable with the lag, just a bit frustrating when your car takes longer to appear.
One of the things Defiance has going for it is a large player base, and a large number of "events". Driving around, you'll come across one of these mini missions at a rate of at least one per minute of travel. They aren't often super complex; many are hostage rescue or ally support, where you simply fend off a few waves of enemies. Others are a bit more interesting, like data gathering, bomb defusals, etc.
When you encounter these, your natural instinct is usually, "I want to shoot that", so you pop off your ATV and go to it. This lends itself to the large player base, because people will stop all the time to join in. Having trouble with a tougher enemy? Someone might just swoop in and run them down with their car, or a sudden sniper bullet blows their head off as you reload. It adds a nice atmosphere to the game, knowing there are other people around. Loot and xp is also split, assuming you shot some bullets at an enemy, so kill stealing isn't really a thing.
There's a story and more involved missions of course, but I wont get too deep there, simply because the end result is still going to involve shooting, just with a more exciting battle and event dynamics. Though, worth mentioning are 'Incursions', and Arkfalls, which occur fairly frequently. Incursions involve driving around an entire zone, wiping out an invading enemy force in each location. The finale is typically a large, hold the fort type scenario, lasting 15 minutes, and involving (usually) hundreds of players and enemies combined. Arkfalls are more localized, but more difficult, spawning large numbers of strong enemies. Both events draw players to them, and near the end of Incursions and during Arkfalls, you'll typically see 50-100 players.
In terms of weapons and items, Defiance is very similar to Borderlands. You have guns, shields, grenades, and stims, each with their own special stats, and a variety of brands that further define an items behavior. You could find a fire smg, with a large clip and full auto, and then find a burst fire smg that deals shock damage. There are shotguns that shoot energy bolts, pistols that lob fire grenades, and snipers that can fire multiple shots or one really powerful charged shot. Best of all, there is no restriction on your weapon choices, so you can use whatever fits your style.
The sort of weird part of Defiance are the classes. That is, there are no classes. You'll choose a class at the character creation, but all it determines is your first weapon type and your first outfit. Besides that, all characters have equal access to the same skills and perks. You're only allowed to select one EGO power at a time, from Cloak, Decoy, Overcharge (damage boost), and Blur (speed increase/melee damage boost). From there, you choose and upgrade perks on a sort of board, which has all 4 powers and all perks. So eventually, with high enough EGO (basically your level) you can unlock the entire board and change your class to whatever you want, whenever you want. There are loadouts as well, so you can create different setups with different guns as well.
Lastly, enemies. There's a fair variety of enemies, including the ever present, horrible space bug. Most enemies have critical points, where, obviously, you'll deal critical damage if you hit it. For most of your basic humanoid enemies, that's the head. Each group of enemies has tougher classes though, like the bugs with vulnerable butts, armored giants with reactors on their backs, and titanic infected human-horror beasts with helmets covering  their exposed brain, that you need to force to the ground to even hit. Not record breaking stuff, but it's a shooter, there's not much else you need besides a target. The AI can be clumsy, or it can be challenging. Sometimes an enemy might just stand there like an idiot, other times he'll dodge every headshot you fire.
So, all in all, an enjoyable game, and the first FPS MMO I've played that, well, I've kept playing. And it's free, so you know, why the Hell not? If you like shooters, odds are you'll like Defiance.

This game is a tower defence.  But backwards and sideways.
You build the towers on a pre-assembled ship, the loot you're protecting goes on the ship as well.
The ship then flies (on rails) though the course where enemies will pop out and attack.

Gets boring really quick

Unreasonably difficult and tedious by the end game. What starts out as innovative and a flexible take on tower defense becomes very much the opposite as levels progress. The difficulty requires you to place exactly the right module at exactly the right time all the while reorienting turrets and activating specials without a tactical pause feature. If only they included that a lot of stress would have been absent.

I saw that there was a sequel made for this game, and thought it'd be a good idea to come back to this game and actually finish it.
The game is pretty enjoyable, a real time strategy game where your goal is to deliver various forms of cargo as quickly as possible, without losing any of it.
There's 30 missions split across 5 companies, and each company has different cargo that provokes different kinds of strategy, such as crystals that drain power, or nodes that must be connected to your command bridge via a spreading ability.
The only thing about the game is that it contains a couple of errors in its spelling and dialogue, but that sort of thing never really bothered me.
A moderately challenging game thats really fun. The customizations are great. Limited space on your ship means you have to be very smart and economical about your builds. Dig it.

A tower defence game in which you build up a space ship and keep cargo modules safe from enemy waves? Sign me up!
Except it's less a tower defence game than it is a frantic micromanagement one. Things happen very quickly in this game and you aren't allowed to pause and consider your options. Rather than carefully managing the balance between resource accumulation and firepower buildup, you are going to be semi-mindlessly building, selling, rotating, and rebuilding parts to try and keep up with constant, unpredictable changes in the playing field.
Yes, since each mission plays out exactly the same way, I suppose you could learn a (very long) build/sell/rotate order and try to play an almost perfect game by staying constantly ahead of the curve. Which would make this a memory/production line game instead. Still not tower defence, still no fun at all.
Granted the aesthetics are great and I keep firing it up every few months hoping that I would like it better this round. But, no, it's still the same old twitch-based firefighting, and each time I almost immediately give up and uninstall this again.
In my opinion this would have been playable if the game were slower paced and great if enemies came in waves with unlimited build time between waves. Knowing ahead of time what was coming next would have been nice too. This wouldn't have been bad as a turn-based game either. But as things stand, this is a very pretty game that I hate to hate.
Recommended for people who like constantly and frenetically building things only to soon after have to tear them down and build other things elsewhere. Not recommended for people looking for a tower defence game or a thinking game.

Great premise is ruined by the need for micromanaging.
This is a fun game that is a twist on the tower defense genre. Your ship must carry a blend of cargo, weapons, engines, and defensive weaponry. You have to find the right balance as your shop cruises across each level, where you will be paid if you deliver the cargo. Along the way you'll fend off asteroids and pirates. But you must manually control the laser turrets, which are critical weapons for your survival, and this takes up crtical attention, and the game throws just enough at you that it's really difficult in an unpleasant way to try and keep up. If you could buy an AI module to run the turrets that would help a lot.
In any event, it's worth several hours of fun, but I quit halfway through as I got too frustrated with the demands of the micromanagement.

I've decided to do a new review for this game given the many changes since I started.
The good:
Let's start with the biggest for many, the Free to Play model.  I've spent a good amount of money in this game and am happy with that.  I've spent as much or more on premium games (like Battlefield 4) and got far less for the money in terms of how much I wanted to play.  You can go along in this without spending real money (a friend of mine has done so just fine) and play a lot.  If you want things like a tank driver and sniper (recon) on each faction, well you might want to spend money to speed things up.  You can be formidible in the game though without spending a dime.  Still, they have to make money somehow so if you start to like it, think about dropping a little money in there for either veteran or a new soldier type.
The gameplay is great.  Notice I say gameplay, not graphics.  While the graphics are good, they are a far cry from Battlefield or Call of Duty.  I play this instead of those because of the gameplay itself.  The way tank shells ricochet off enemy tanks if you hit at a bad angle, which also gave away your position makes it a game you must think about how you want to fight.  Each gun has distinct advantages and disadvantages.
Pooled resources are also quite interesting.  Each team has a set number of resources.  For example, each team may start with 200 infantry tickets.  That is the number of infantry lives total for the match.  If you decide to run straight at the enemy 50 times and get killed each time, the team is down 50 from you alone (an exaggeration but you get it).  This applies to tanks, planes, jeeps, and so on.  It also means helping your allies is important.  See a guy running to a friendly tank with explosives meant to blow it up?  Kill him or your team runs out of resources faster.  That enemy on an AA gun shooting at fighters?  Toss a grenade his way.
The bad:
This has gone way down from a year ago but there are some issues.  First, the spawn system needs work.  It's been greatly improved but spawn camping can still be a problem in some areas.  Plus if you spawn on foot, it can be quite a hike to the next objective or the front line.  There are bicycles and farm trucks on map for anyone to use, but they aren't at most of the new spawn points.  This lowers your time in combat and is quite annoying.  So make friends with those who have a Jeep or catch a ride on a passing tank.
Starting firepower needs work.  The starting guns are good, but you might not realize it at first.  I've switched back to starting guns on some of my characters and added the mods I want.  But if you want a SMG or LMG, the grind can be annoying and causes some to not give the game a real chance.  Keep in mind, the starting rifle with a few mods like better ammo and upgraded trigger changes it a lot.  One major issue is anti-tank weapons.  Starting out the tanks will ruin your day if they see you.  But once you get certain AT weapons they are stupid easy to destroy (though those weapons are expensive to use and you may lose money on the match).
Balance is an issue too.  Namely in equivelant equipment.  The American P-40 medium fighter is not as good as the German or Russian medium planes.  The P-38 heavy fighter though?  Far above the competition.  This can be seen in tank and guns too.  Less so on infantry guns (except the Russian PTRD) so focus on picking up allied guns on the battlefield when they die to see what works for you.  Team balance is less of a problem.  Does the enemy team have half of them in tanks?  Dont' worry.  They might be harder to kill but they are slower, with poor visibility, and you can just speed past in a Jeep and capture points before they can react.  There is usually a way unless the enemy team has a really good air squadron.  While not common, this can make you want to quit the match.  Anti air weapons aren't all that powerful and if they field 4-5 good pilots they will wipe out those guns quickly.
My last complaint is maps.  They need to add more.  The team has recently added planes, tanks, other vehicles, and reworked all maps in mostly good ways.  Now they need even more.
Conclusion:
Overall this game has gotten way better.  I rated it a 2/10 before but with how much I've been playing, it would be a lie to give it less than an 8/10.  The learning curve can be steep but once you get access to games with all vehicle types it can be awesome.  Still could use some work but they are always putting out updates with noticeable changes.  Give it a try, it's free after all.
