Used to be way better than it is. While DCUO was never a GREAT MMO, it didn't used to be a shameless cash-grab. It's LITERALLY pay-to-win . You can pay real-world money to immediately take any character (even a brand-new never played level 1 character) immediately to Combat Rating 100 and start raiding. More than a little bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, in my honest opinion.
Now, this game isn't TERRIBLE if you can overlook the shameless micro-transactions, cancerous community, hilariously overpriced DLC, and negligent developers. If you can ignore all of that, there's a pretty damn great game struggling to free itself from beneath the immense pile of crap and garbage.
-The powers are fun to use (and pretty varied).
-The different weapon styles (while not particularly well balanced) are darn fun to mess about with.
-The storylines you can play through in the base-game aren't as poorly written as lots of people claim they are. If you suspend real-world logic, some are pretty cool. (Note: DCUO is all set in pre-New 52 DC continuity so Superman is still his good 'ol pure-morality self).
-The game-world is, actually, pretty big for a game of its age. Not nearly as big as City of Heroes' was, or WoW is but still. The ability to mess around in Metropolis and then be able to punch people in Gotham City's seedy underbelly is a very nice touch. Full cities, too, with no loading screens once you transition between them.
-In my genuine opinion, I think the leveling process is this game's real strength. Do I recommend you pay for the DLC? No, not really. The base-game offers more than enough content to keep you busy for a while and the free powers you have access to aren't Underpowered by any means so you can still compete with players who paid for the DLC powers.
-The game really falls-off, for me, when you get to level-cap. You get a quick tour of the basic dailies and stuff, shown the fancy raid armour you can buy with marks and just left to your own devices. The game doesn't do a very good job of telling you what you're expected to DO when you reach level 30. Plus, if you don't have any DLC and you don't plan to buy any in the future, it's not really worth putting the effort in to actually EARN the fancy raid armour unless you like the look of it. I mean, there's just no incentive to go out and grind out dailies for a month or two without the DLC packs.
It's FTP so, in my opinion, even though there's LOTS of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things about DCUO, it's genuinely worth a try if you're a veteran of City of Heroes. It's not nearly as good but it's clearly trying to be a spiritual successor. It's not going to blow your socks-off and you're probably going to lose interest after reaching level-cap but there are a LOT of FTP MMOs on Steam right now that are WAY worse than DCUO. Worth a go on the base-game but don't invest money into it unless you're 100% committed and have lots of spare cash to spend, otherwise you'll find yourself broke pretty goddamn quick.

I am not new to mmo-games, have tried out the most of em. As Defiance came F2P joined the game and haven't been disappointed. A warning though, the game can be a bit boring if you do not have a friend to play with. Sure, you get to join a clan and there are many events(arkfalls etc) in game in which, normally there are a lot, really a lot of others, but doing missions solo can be a bit tedious at times. Also, knowledge of the tv-show is something I would recommend, but I think is not necessary.
It is a good game, read on and I will try to explain some basics, or just join the game and decide for yourself.
To start with, Defiance is a good game with bad user interface - but don't let that fool you. The game has a ton of missions, loads of guns and the normal stuff like looting etc.
The interface is bad, as said, and also some of the game mechanics are poorly done(just my opinion). The game has weapons ranging from white´->green->blue->purple->orange (so normal stuff) and loads of different weapons; pistols, detonators, infectors, assault rifles, smgs etc.
Also worth saying is that the race and choice of "class" does NOT seem to have any significance.. The only difference that I have found is that the "classes" have different starter weapons, that's it.
There are also different damage dealing abilities in the weapons, some have fire, some radiation.. and ofc, you have to go into the internet to check what those do... At least I had to do that.
Here is a quick explanation:
Biological/Fire for high Threat Levels
Radiation/Fire for low Threat Levels
- Biological would be best against enemies that have a bunch of armor plates, so this would be best on higher Threat Levels.
- Radiation bypasses 2 armor plates so this would be good for most regular targets.
- Fire is best against targets that don't have any armor or shields plus it makes the target weaker to attacks from others. Fire is best against anything once its shields are down.
- Electricity is used to remove shielding.
- Siphon is the worst... I really haven't found any use for it. Siphon basically leaches health and shields from enemies.
There are 2 loadouts (if you don't pay to have more, but I do not really see a point in having more then those 2).. I use following loadouts (well nowadays at least):
- Loadout 1: I have Electricity and a Rocket Launcher (good for killing npc from the distance, as I have scope mod in the rocket launcher).
- Loadout 2: Fire and Electricity (A loadout good for killing Dark Matter and pretty much everything else that keeps charging at you).
When it comes to weapon of choice, my choices are: smg>shotgun>pistol>rocket launcher>light machine gun>sniper rifle. Also BMG(heal/dmg dealing weapon) can be useful.
It's best to design your loadouts with different ammo types. Assault rifle, smg and light machine gun use same type of ammo for instance. The different ammo types are actually one thing that is actually explained in-game.
So is Defiance worth your time? I really do think so.. It's F2P, has tons of missions and you get to move fast quite early on, which is a BIG bonus for me. And riding a buggy and making hit'and'runs is fun:). Getting a two seated car is also quite fast.. At least fast enough. The world is also large enough, the graphics are ok and the sounds are also ok. Get your friend to play and it's much more fun as co-op.
This is ofc my opinion, but as said, it's now F2P so make your own decision about it.
A solid 8/10 from me.

--TLDR: Ultimately the game is a frustrating blend of repetition, micromanagement, and the illusion of choice.
Watch the videos in this guide instead of playing:
-Pros:
Pretty
Well optimized.
Reminds me of Stratosphere, sorta.
Alt-tabs easily and cleanly.
Account progression.
Space rpg, sorta.
-Cons:
No real choices. You're punished for all but the "correct" ones.
You can't build your ship in advance, you cannot layout hexes as you'd like, and your ship is erased each time.
Shooter type level design, as in no randomness, and required blind level attempt as recon for real attempt.
No sense of engagement because there is no ship progression.
I don't like having to mouse over kill rewards to collect them. Cheap APM inflation is not gameplay.
I don't like being unable to zoom out to see the entire relevant area, especially if I'm required to micromanage so much.
Modding not possible, apparently intentionally prevented.
Boss fights are awful because your weapons intentionally target the enemy bridge last even if there's a clear shot/path.
Can't pause to send commands or examine the situation. Cheap way of forcing twitch gaming.
-Summation:
Game is extremely rigid. Worst of both worlds, a grinding arcade game. Plenty of arbitrary requirements to keep you on a rail in various contexts. Essentially a guessing game where the objective is to figure out the one correct sequence of choices needed to ace the test. You're basically forced to beat the game before you have any freedom. Doing new missions is the only way to get reputation, which unlocks parts, which unlocks more reputation. This leads to only one viable play strategy. Low hanging fruit (do untouched missions first) then buy everything you're allowed to buy, and do the next least completed mission.
-Suggestions for Dev:
Give funding for mission up front, then let us build ship in advance.
Let us lay out ship hex shape.
Persistent ship.
Missiles need to fire 360.
Eliminate reputation system.
Surplus hex should be converted to SC at the end of missions.

Wow, this is a little gem. I've seen it floating around on Steam since it came out, but I never really looked into it too closely. I'm not sure what I thought it was, but I wasn't expecting it to be so good. It's listed as a tower defense game, and while it does have elements of that, I think it's selling the game short to call it a tower defense game. It's so much deeper than that, sliding back more towards RTS territory, which of course is where the tower defense genre came from.
Essentially, you control a space ship that is trying to deliver cargo for various companies. The flights are always a straight line from left to right. In practice, this means your ship is mostly sitting in the middle of the screen as hazards approach from all directions. These hazards include asteroids, pirates, and competitor ships. Every time your destroy something, you get money, which can be used to build more guns and other ship systems like power generators, shields, and engines.
The entire ship is made of interconnected hexagons, upon which you must place your ship components. The variety of guns is nice, with a handful of different lasers and projectile weapons to choose from. The bigger weapons need power to run, as do the special abilities you can add for all the weapons. There is a lot of strategy involved in placing weapons and the support systems, and on the later levels, you'll sometimes have to retry missions with different layouts to get an optimal configuration. But once your learn the ins and outs of weapons, and figure out how to set arrange your support systems, the game can become very satisfying, as you tear everything up with your big guns.
Each company has its own type of cargo with its own special needs, and the cargos can hamper your ship in various ways. The most basic is taking up space, but they can also take up precious lines of sight needed for your guns, or explode violently when destroyed, inflicting extra damage to your ship. Another actively drains the energy from hexes around it. These add some interesting flavor to the various missions.
You get credits for completing missions, with more credits for more perfect completions of missions. The great thing is, you can retry missions for more credits as much as you want, so if later missions are too tough, you can build up your ship powers on earlier missions for a while until you're able to pass the later missions.
The great thing about this game is that even losing is fun, and you never feel like the game is being cheap. You get warnings for all ship and asteroid approaches, so you have time to plan for whichever direction they're coming from. Things can get pretty hectic, but I often find that better planning can alleviate the problem enough to make levels passable. And on the tough levels, it's pretty great to squeeze through by the skin of your teeth. I've never had to retry a level more than maybe five times at the absolutely most to beat it, and I've been having an absolute blast.
The audio design is nice, with big sounds for all the weapons and other effects, while the voice acting is solid enough that you won't think much of it. But the story is thin at best. It's all about the gameplay here. The graphics are pretty nice, with cool visuals for most for the weapons and other systems. Destroying enemy ships is nice and satisfying.
I can't really find many flaws with this game. It's very focused on what it's trying to do, and it does it well. If you're looking for a deeper action/strategy game. Highly recommended!

I had a lot of fun with this game. You build your ship as you go fighting space battles and protecting your cargo, while at the same time racing the clock to get a perfect five star finish.
It has a good progression system unlocking new and more powerful weapons and upgrades as you go, as well as presenting you with ever increasing cargo complexities.
I'll definitely recommend this game for any RTS or tower defence fans; it has just the right mix of complexity, stress and progression which makes for a very enjoyable experience.
The only quibble I have with the game is that it is limited in the game play modes on offer; there is a lot of potential to use the core game mechanics for lot more playstyles.
For example I would love to see a game mode where you would build up your ship at the start and then fight against random enemies; alternative to start with basic parts and instead of nuts collect upgrades as you destroy enemies, etc...
Overall a great game, that has a lot of potential to be built on.

A great platformer plagued by unresponsive controls, clunky combat, stupid bosses and dull checkpoints. The latter is especially frustrating since checkpoints don't restore hp, but if you die, you continue from a checkpoint with full hp. This means that after reaching a checkpoint it's usually a good idea to die so you can continue with full hp. And no, there's no "Restart checkpoint" option.
Another bad thing is that the game doesn't save some of the options. For instance, I had to switch off gamepad rumble each time I started the game.
It's a shame that a game with such a great idea and visuals has so many drawbacks that ruin the experience. Especially since most of the issues could be easily fixed.
Still, despite its flaws, Outland is worth playing.

Imagine performing surgery within a claw-crane toy vending machine.  The surgeon's single hand is, by design, one of the clumsiest manifestations of inter-activity ever published.  Of course this would be the very point and what makes it so much fun! The difficulty in getting anywhere because of this intentional disconnect with user input can, however, be frustrating at times.  I personally require a mouse pad the size of Central Park in order to move the arm around (even on the highest sensitivity).  It's definitely presented as a joke game, not an achievement or skill game, although those things are very much required to get anywhere.  There is no advice or direction in how to approach a given surgery, lots of bloody fun in the trial and error.  Too difficult to grasp objects in general, it can take an eon to get the scalpel in your hand at the right angle for incision.  Certainly not realisitic, and the title "simulator" here must be taken with a grain of salt.  Or a salt mine even.
On the positive, I totally knew what I was getting into and got a deal on the game anyway, so it's no travesty that's happened here.  The game really is pretty funny, and that seems to be it's greatest achievement.  I had  dreams of a more balanced mix of sim and parody...but got mostly the latter.
If  the hand were SLIGHTLY more dexterous, I would've enjoyed it more.  I'm sure it must be rewarding for true mouse-keteers that eventually hone their precision with the movements... that seems the only way to advance passed the first surgery even.  When the difficulty in progressing becomes more frustrating than fun, a game generally loses me.

it was weird how this game popped up on my "recommended for you" list, at the same time totalbiscuit uploaded a review on this game. I took it as a sign. The art style drew me in, but other than that I went into this game blind. There have been countless times where I would watch and read all kinds of reviews on games, buy them, and still feel unsatisfied with the purchase, so I've lately been a bit skeptical at buying games. I just really wanted to play this.
This game is remarkable. It celebrates everything that makes indie games unique and offer experiences that no big titles ever could. There is a lot of soul in this game, as you will discover within the first minute of playing it.
If you're after technicalities of the game: it plays beautifully. No frame rate issues, no crashes, no unresponsive controls. Game looked stunning at 1920x1080. Kudos to this small team of devs doing what, for some reason, huge publishers are unable to do: realease COMPLETED games.
So, what is Gravity Ghost? It's a small tale that unravels itself slowly to you, leaving your imagination to fill in the blanks of the mythos and history surrounded the story (and I mean that in a good way). The way the story is told, and the pacing of it, is perfect. Is this an epic story that will knock you off your seat? Nope. But it IS a very well thought-out tale, that once it's revealed to you in full, kind of makes you go "...woah". It is haunting and it is beautiful, and I found myself teary-eyed once everything came together.... still not sure if that was out of sadness or just being so thrilled with this experience.
From my understanding, the devs spent their savings on this game, and I think that's why the quality was so high. They did it because they wanted to. No kickstarter, no abandoned beta's, no shoving empty promises out the door in order to make a quick buck - how many times have we all put good faith in devs who promise the world, and leave us with unfinished, uninspired, betas... or sometimes not even that?
The point is, these are the kinds of people we should be supporting. And I thank them for letting their integrity be put above profit.
In any case, do I recommend this game? Absolutely, without question.

Got a review copy of this from the developer and played it through just now (
). Took me about 2.5 hours and I assume the game is basically in a finished state since it's so close to the release date.
Anyways, this game is an amazingly beautiful physics-platformer that is a lot like a 2D Super Mario Galaxy. Great music, an interesting story, and fantastic gameplay. Difficulty-wise, it's extremely easy - don't expect to have any trouble except for one or two levels. In addition, the game's only 2.5 hours long, and I beat all of the levels (didn't collect all of the flowers though since those don't seem to be tracked anywhere). If they added the ability to include custom levels (as well as restrict your powers within those levels), this would just about be the platformer of the year.
The main criticism I have with this game is its difficulty. It is extremely easy throughout. What should be levels of increasing difficulty are made easier by powerups that are basically unlockable cheats. The game would be way better if those powers were disabled throughout and only unlockable after you beat the game. The game also makes you think that you'll need to manage your energy (hair), which is used up when you transform planets, but the flowers that replenish it are abundant, and the cheat-powers make it so you never need to terraform after you get one of them. Basically, the game needs to be harder.
Aside from that, it's a really enjoyable romp through space. You never fight any enemies or encounter hazards that would make you restart the level, but that's not a problem - the game would feel weirder with enemies. The atmosphere of the game reminds me of Endless Ocean and games of its type. It's relaxing and the story is interesting enough to keep you playing.
The voice acting isn't the best, but that's definitely a problem with the director, microphone, and post-processing rather than the voice actors. It doesn't detract horribly from the game. What does detract from the game is the random 6-year-old-level silliness in the dialogue - it feels unnatural. This is one of the few games I would say desperately needs to take itself
seriously rather than less so.
Despite that criticism, I had a huge amount of fun with the game. With support for user-created content, it would definitely be at the top of my list of platformers on Steam.
EDIT: I would like to revise my criticism - upon further reflection, the voice actors really did do a good job. Most of the writing is also fantastic; it's just a couple random bits which seem a bit out of place (not really a pattern).

This is a weird one. The concept here is great and some of the execution is pretty good, too, but unfortunately the game lacks polish in many areas and comes off as a bit too ambitious for its own good. Most of the game feels like a very bare-bones experience. The music isn't particularly memorable or even enjoyable (this is actually one of the few games where I prefer to turn off the in-game music and play something else in the background), NPCs keep repeating the same dialogue over and over again and there isn't any proper voice acting either. The quests are just copy/paste stuff and hardly anything surprising happens anymore after the first 20 hours. There isn't any expansive lore or interesting, well-rounded characters. It's just you and your army trying to become more and more powerful. That's literally the story of this game, so don't buy this if you're looking for a narratively driven experience. The land of Calradia looks and feels dull, you'll be spending a lot of time just traversing around the map without anything to keep you interested. None of the kingdoms have any real personality to them, making it hard to feel invested if you decide to fight for one of them.
So why am I recommending the game, then? Well, like I said, the concept here is great and there aren't many games out there like this. I love the idea of starting from nothing and slowly becoming more and more powerful and influential. The combat system is one of the highlights of the game, even though the mostly bad AI sometimes tries its best to ruin the experience (lance fights in the arena, anyone?). It's also easier to forgive many of the flaws when taking into consideration that it's not an expensive game and offers great bang for your buck.
Overall, I think this is a good game, something that will take up a lot of your time and keep you entertained for quite a while. The modding scene is also very vibrant, lot of good stuff there. This game just could, and should, be a whole lot better.

Railcraft (a mod for minecraft) offers more, in terms of "working a rail line". Train Simulator is a point-to-point game of simply driving from location to location. It offers very little, in terms of actually doing something. Sure, there are passenger operations, but that is only a small portion of work available. Some of the scenarios available have a 'feel' of a contiguous set of scenarios, but whether or not they actually work, is another story.
The game is pretty. But it is boring and expensive. There is a lot of missed opportunity, with this game. If it offered more of a variety of things to do, there would be considerably more replay value. That said, I still fire it up, from time to time, to drive a train down the line or try my hand at a scenario.
The editor is fairly powerful, though comes with absolutely no tutorial, what-so-ever.
Workshop is full of additional scenarios that people have made, but you are likely missing the majority of the DLC needed to play them. Much of the older DLC is no longer fully compatible with the game and there seems to be little effort to resolve this conflict.
In the end, do I regret spending money on this product? No. But I wish the company was more up-front about what is included in DLC and that they put more effort in to exploring various types of work to be done by rail service. As well as included literature or tutorials for the editor (as  the official content is sorely lacking in scenarios. You are essentially purchasing assets, with DLC)
TL,DR; The game can be enjoyable, but
Patience will net you far more DLC, when it goes on sale and the value will be more in line with what you get.

After the 2015 and many voluntary (and slightly unvoluntary) DLC purchases, and with the ability to review each DLCs individually, i decided to revise my review in a more positive light.
the 2015 Steam edition contain a decent content selection in my opinion, you won't find super advanced control systems, but since it includes a german line now, reading the manual for the different safety systems is recommended.
It's reasonably fun if you like trains the 3D cabs controls could use being a little more mouse friendly as the mouse motion required is not always intuitive for the control type or the perspective the lever is in.
The game controls cannot be remapped in any ways, that's quite a sore point for me, being an AZERTY keyboard user.
There are some serious optimization problems in their engine, regardless of how dated the sceneries may look, you WILL get frame drops on the more intense routes.
While i can recommend the game as it is currently the best of it's class (as far as train simulation goes), this is not your typical "must have all DLCs" kind of game. The base game give you a wide range of railways (germany/england/usa) my opinion is that if you plan to purchase some DLCs to take some time to think about which aspects you enjoy in train simulation:
Electric? Diesel? Steam?
Freight? Passengers? Shunting?
Long routes through countryside? Busy commuter lines?
Also when buying routes or trains, keep in mind that each train come with a few scenarios for a given route, if you want to maximize the value of your purchase, you want to focus on a few routes you truly enjoy and a lot of trains and rolling stocks for it.
All trains are not created equal, some are very simple and "do the job", while others offer extremely detailed simulation aspects, please, do some research before purchasing one.
Lastly, while DLCs tend to be expensive, there are several sales through the year where you can grab content for a much lower price. Also the yearly re release is usually bundled with 3 different routes, while you get the engine upgrade for free, it's an exellent deal to grab the upgrade at 50-80% off.

this may seem a little odd but i find myself both loving and hating Outland. that being said, Outland is a gorgeous game filled with a beautiful art, soundtrack and clever gameplay.
let me start first off by the positive apects of the game: Outland succesfully delivers a detailed environment and atmosphere by having a good soundtracks and gorgeous art that makes it very beautiful. the story of Outland is about the world in chaos because the guardians defect the gods then the gods decide to choose the Hero to bring balance to the world, it sounds simple but it actually sounds like a good story (i'll come back later to it). the gameplay is clever that it makes you think about every movements you take whether to defeat enemies or beat puzzles, swifting between Light and Dark is a clever idea and it really works well with Outland's world and story.
but there are a couple of things i think Outland doesn't do well: story, characters and the world. i already said the premise of Outland's story is good and it sounds like a good story. that being said, Outland never really tells the players about the Hero (player), there are some games like Limbo where there are no dialogue at all but they tell stories through background and events. Outland has a narration and narrator telling us stories but it fails to deliver the story. by the time i truly understand the Hero is some kind of reincarnated version of the Ancient Hero (please correct me if i'm wrong), the game reaches its credit. i don't understand that at the beginning of the game, the Hero is sitting with the narrator (i know this because i read it on wikipedia, not because the game tells about it) then The Hero runs through the path and lo and behold there are monsters. i don't think this is believable enough because i don't understand the world. the Hero is wearing modern clothes with a glowing tattoo from his Ancient Hero so that means the world is a modern world but ever since the game begins, the world doesn't look like a modern world, it looks like a jungle filled with altars, snow places (?) underworld (?) and a lot of monsters. i couldn't really grasp where i am as a player and as The Hero. the Hero doesn't really have a personality and whenever he beats a boss (which are always the guardians who went berserk), the Hero doesn't respond. he just stands still then teleported back to the center of the map which is a shame because first i don't know about this guy and second the developers doensn't give me a chance to know this guy. the puzzles in Outland is good but it becomes silly and ridiculous if you compare it with its world, i mean if The Hero isn't at the Outland world, do the puzzles keep on repeating its pattern? . the enemies (monsters) in Outland is just there for the Heroes to beat and that's it, they don't have anything to do other than walking and attacking you and one thing i really hate about Outland is  whenever i touch or bump into enemies, i am damaged, which doesn't make sense, some of the enemies have thorns and if you bump into them then you are damaged, THAT makes sense. but other enemies that don't have thorns have the same logic, if you bump into them even from behind, you are damaged, i always wonder if the Hero is allergic to them but it doesn't make sense because there are Light and Dark elements in Outland and you can switch between them at anytime and say if i switch to Dark and the enemies are Dark but when i bump into them or if i get attacked by them (melee), i am damaged but whenever the same element enemies shoot me , i am not damaged at all, which for me it's inconcistent and such a shame the developers doensn't think about that. The Hero's movement is super fast so it's often very hard to control him whenever i try to solve puzzles, i joked about calling the game "The Runner" because The Hero seems to be in a hurry and he keep on sprinting and sprinting.
nevertheless, Outland is great at its celever gameplay, puzzles, soundtrack and gorgeous art but it falls short because it lacks story, character developments, believability and its world.
buy this game if you want to experience a fresh gaming experience. otherwise, don't.

Space Run is a hybrid Tower Defense game, and a pretty good one. It's actually closer to space games/shooters in style but with the mechanics of a TD game. You're put in charge of corporate cargo ships and tasked with making a dangerous delivery. The ships themselves are made up of hexagonal cells (in a different configuration each time) onto which modules can be placed. These modules include the cargo you're carrying and one engine which you build before takeoff and the rest you build along the way.
The game does a good job of quickly getting you up to speed and explaining how different modules behave or what placement restrictions they may have. For example engines require a free space behind them, while turrets may require up to several free spaces ahead of them.
You gain construction points slowly over time or by collecting scrap leftover from destroyed asteroids, hostile fighters or larger vessels. This way you put together a fearsome (hopefully) and quick (allegedy) ship that can take on whatever you may encounter (citation needed). It's possible to recycle modules to free up space, recover resources or re-arrange the ship.
In between missions new modules of various kinds become available for purchase. Modules can also be upgraded to unlock new abilities or improvements. Bits of storyline dialogue also take place here. The story isn't all that much of a much, but it's not bad either. Some of the dialogues are contrived though.
Overall it's a pretty nice concept. You build the ship from bits and pieces, hoping to use starting resources to cover the right flanks against initial attackers/asteroids and cursing the cargo modules or the wonky ship configuration. Though you don't know which way danger is coming from, you get an early warning and some time to adapt. Spend cash on upgrades, take a new job, rinse and repeat.
My biggest problem was that the game was fun in short bursts. Either that or i just wasn't hooked enough to keep playing after a few missions. It would draw me back after a time, so that's good. Regardles, it was a bit tricky to pick up where i left off. Previous missions are still available though.
At first i wasn't a huge fan of fast paced building, rebuilding, repairing and using a multitude of special abilities. I'd be more comfortable if i was allowed to be a slug and play at a glacial pace. Perhaps it's just as well that Space Run gives me a jolt to take me out of my comfort zone. Your mileage may vary but i think that's a good thing. From time to time. Normally i think i could write a tome of memoires, sketch ideas for ship builds and make a presentation with fancy charts and graphs, plus write some fanfic before i finished a turn of Sword of the Stars. SOTS is pretty fast for a 4X TBS, I'm THAT slow.
Being a cleverly disguised Tower Defence game, Space Run plays quite quickly and requires balancing several things at once. Usually while facing increasingly difficult attacks as the mission goes on. Not only is it important to deploy weapons to cover your vessel, you'll also want to invest in engines. Engines cost you resources and give little in return, but speed is the only way to outrun the competition and that multiplies your final payment. In addition, there is the cargo on board, and it's wise to protect it with shields. This will divert your resources away from firepower and take up valuable space on board. And then on top of that, some modules require power generators adjacent to them.
Doing all this requires a mix of planning ahead (where to place thrusters, cargo, shields etc.), and quick wits under fire that will seriously challenge your multi-tasking competence (adjusting arcs on turrets, activating special abilities of shields and generators, rebuilding destroyed stuff, etc.).
This is why ultimately, Space Run wins my respect. It makes what i described above fun to do, which i didn't really think would happen. As i said, i'm not a fan of Tower Defense nor RTS. It's not easy, but it's a good challenge, fun concept and the game is polished and well presented. Sure the voice acting could be better but i think only with a major league professional actor and a major league fee. Plus i enjoyed some of the voices.
Artwork is very nice and shiny while the music doesn't really pop but isn't offensive or annoying either. It does the job. Some of the character portraits didn't really hit home with me but that's just a personal preference. 3D models are cartoony enough to be fun and serious enough to not look stupid. Overall nothing about the game felt lazy or bland.
If i had to nitpick to find flaws, i'd say maybe it would be nice to have the ability to zoom in a bit closer, but it's fine. The icons in the construction menu DO need text labels, but i got the hang of it.
Recommended! If you're affraid of real time multitasking, it could go either way. It won me over, but you might get frustrated quickly. If you're a fan of Tower Defense, you'll be right at home.

Essentially a mobile tower defense game. Rather than defend against a stream of raiders attempting to steal stars/hearts/life points/whatever from your base, you're a space runner. You run goods, nuclear waste, or people through space. The faster and more in tact your cargo arrives to point B from point A, the greater the rewards. Your ship starts off each round with a set number of hexes in which you can place add-ons of your choosing. These add-ons cost credits (of course) which are earned constantly by travelling or intermittently when you destroy objects (such as asteroids, other ships, or pirates). These credits are called hexnuts and float around as debris until you mouse over them to pick them up. Later on you can pick up add-ons that help magnetize them to your ship (this helps when things start getting hairy). The other add-ons include weapons, shields, power generators, and other goodies that can work synergistically with other systems on your ship or bolster your reward.
Orientation of your weapons matters, so you have to sometimes change which way they're facing while in combat. Placement also matters, as some weapons require a certain amount of hexes for the guns to move properly. In addition, some require power to operate correctly or to power special abilities. Pirates have some cheaterish moves that they can do to your ships, so the game expects you to think on your feet and be able to respond to certain conditions.
After each run, you earn credits and reputation. Rep unlocks the ability to purchase new items, while the credits allow you purchase the base new add-on or expand existing add-on abilities (for example, expanding the power thrusters tree allows for the thrusters to operate at a higher efficiency).
Space Run is a fun game with good replay value. The levels are not random though, so you have an opportunity to learn at what time and from which direction threats will come to you. At its core, SR is another tower defense game, however it's a very polished and fun tower defense game that changes enough of the basic mechanics of a TD game to keep it unique and fresh.

I used to play a ton of tower defense games back in the day when they were all made in Flash and playable only in your browser. But after it became overcrowded with generic clones, I thought there was little hope in the genre and left it for dead and moved on with my life. And then came Space Run.
Space Run revived the tower defense love in me, scratching a long-forgotten itch in a really great way. It's intentionally hectic (which is almost akin to playing a game of Starcraft, so if you don't like having to be twitchy with your fingers, this may not be the game for you) with a great dose of strategy in how you want to build and optimise your ship layout.
Decent voice over and plot that gives just enough meaning to doing the runs, which is really all you need without it getting in your gaming.
A solid recommend for tower defense fans who can click fast.
Really looking forward to the sequel Space Run Galaxy!

America's Army: Proving Grounds is a multiplayer only FPS (First-Person Shooter).
The community is friendly, helpful and values teamwork. I've played CS, Battlefield, CoD, Insurgency, Unreal, Homefront, Medal of Honor...You name it! I've played pretty much every competitive FPS out there!
Basically i have tons of experience when it comes to multiplayer gaming and
It's truelly amazing!
How do they manage to keep the game well balanced ? It's quite simple really. The game only has 5 primary weapons: 2 assault rifles (fully automatic and a burst-fire one. Both can be switched to single fire aswell), a sniper rifle, a shotgun and an LMG. All these weapons are available since the very beginning so a rank 30 player has the same weapons as a rank 1 player. The only advantage a higher ranking player can have is the knowledge of map layouts.
You also have a sidearm which is just a pistol but it can come real handy.
You also get one frag grenade and can choose between 2 fog, smoke or flash grenades. Also available from rank 1.
You do gain XP (experience points) with each kill, secure, revive and round/match won or lost and gaining XP helps you rank (level) up. The thing is that ranking up gives you nothing. No new weapons, no new equipment, health bonus, scopes or camos.
Nothing more.
You start each round with 100% of hp and 1 life. Once you get "killed" you cannot respawn untill a teammate revives you. If an enemy player gets to your body first he can secure you and your teammates cannot revive you anymore. In that case you have to wait untill the end of the round to get back into the fight.
Headshots are an instant kill and you cannot be revived from those. Once you get shot you start bleeding out so you have to bandage yourself to stop the bleeding or you may die or just lose a lot of hp (health points).
There are 2 modes: Normal and Hardcore.
You can spot enemies, use the minimap, teammates have blue names on their heads and you can see downed teammates. In the normal mode you can also see a yellow text that says you killed an enemy. This is disabled in the hardcore mode.
There's no spotting enemies, minimap can be disabled or just doesn't show you enemies in certain distance (depending on the server settings), teammates don't have blue names on their heads so you have to be extra careful or you might teamkill your mates and shots are obviously more lethal.
The character movement is similar to CoD and newer BF titles. A lot of people complain about that but let us be honest here: This character movement is way more realistic than the clunky movement in AA2 or BF2. Everything about CoD is not bad. CoD has great and smooth character movement and i'm happy to see that it finally came to AA and BF.
A lot of people say that it makes the game "CoDlike" but this is simply not true. It's still more strategic and requires more teamwork. Does bleeding out, reviving, securing and no respawns say CoD to you ? Yeah, didn't think so. It's not "CoDlike".
There's no reason not to try the game.
When in doubt...Just give it a try!

After over 300 hours on this game I feel it is time I write a review. This game is down right awesome. If you install this game and suck, don't sweat it. Just throw everything you have learned from COD out the window. Put yourself in the shoes of your character, and play smart. That's pretty much all you need to stay alive and get some kills. What I love the MOST about this game is you never pay for a single thing. There isn't even an option to DONATE if you want. Everything is 100% totally free. And you get the complete game. That, combined with the fact that this game is EXTREMELY playable makes this one of my favorite games of all time.

I don’t think I would have picked up Gravity Ghost on a whim, just because of my backlog. But after 3 hours solid playthrough during a lazy Sunday I can tell you I’m glad I played it.
The gameplay is as simple as “get star to open door”, but implemented in a two-dimensional gravity orbit swings of Mario Galaxy. As you go along you can collect basic ability upgrades such as air jump, float, dash, and more.
Gameplay art has sharp edges, poppy/contrasting colors, and was quite pleasant to view.
But the real shining star of the game is the story. It is presented in a paper-puppet art style, with basic hinges, rough edges, and soft colors. It isn’t a normal “get these things! do the stuff! here is filler exposition!”.
The music was composed by Ben Prunty, the same that wrote the FTL music.
The game is build for both two-hands and one-handed play which is great for people with limited mobility.

"Gravity Ghost" is a delightful gem. Beneath its pleasant scenery and deceptively simple gameplay, there's a stirring game about love and loss and shifting heaven and earth - literally - to help your loved ones.
This game has a lot going for it. The art style is magnificent, and has a wonderful hand-drawn storybook feel throughout. The characters pop and the galaxy dances along. Ben Prunty's soundtrack provides a wonderful counterpoint, feeling spacey and grand without feeling too isolated, and the voice acting is solid across the board, particularly Ashly Burch's performances.
The gameplay itself has a lot going for it, focusing on physics-based challenges involving the masterful manipulation of gravity. These challenges feel good on the whole and most of them should be doable within a few tries and there are no consequences for failure, leaving you encouraged to take another swing at grabbing that star.
The story is excellent, though I hate to say too much about it for fear of any spoiling that may occur. Settle in and enjoy it.
However, there are some negative aspects to consider as well. First, while the art style is gorgeous and the gameplay animations are smooth, there are times when the cinematic animations get a bit messy. Maybe this was just my computer, but occasionally a character's mouth would lag behind when their head was moving. A minor issue, but it brought me out of the universe of the game for a moment.
Also, while the forgiving gameplay helps prevent frustration, it also contributes to a short playtime - I grabbed all of the stars and finished the game in under 3 hours. There's still a few more things to explore, but don't expect a 10-hour game going in. This game gets in, says what it has to say, and gets out.
Along those lines, I'll wrap up this review by encouraging you to give it a try. There's a lot to like in "Gravity Ghost" - I think you'll be glad you made the trip.

I don’t know how to deal with loss; I sometimes wonder if anyone does. When my grandfather passed away a few years ago I’d have expected tears, depression, the sort of symptoms you see in others that seem required to properly grieve. They didn’t come to me, or at least not how I would have assumed them to. There was just this feeling of something suddenly missing, having been taken away with no way to get it back. I found myself more angry than sad, wondering if that made me a bad person and then getting more angry of myself as a result.
When my pets died growing up it was often my family that appeared more upset than myself, as I sat in solitude trying to block out the realities of the world with easy distractions. At the time I didn’t know what I was supposed to do with myself, failing to find the emotions others were clearly expressing in myself, like I was somehow defective or simply didn’t care about the person or animal that had disappeared from my life as much as I thought I did. It’s terrifying and disorienting, maybe more so than if I had just been able to open up and bawl my eyes out like everyone else.
I didn’t expect to see this part of me in Gravity Ghost, or in any game for that matter. It’s a surreal space platformer, full of interesting mechanics, gorgeous artwork and a masterful soundtrack, but it’s the side of it that it never told you about that hit me like a train into a brick wall.
Flying through the stars and landing on planets, you become wrapped up in a world full of analogies to one less abstract and impossible; a lighthearted blanket over the much more real and unfair reality underneath. Seeing this story unfold is a slow series of vignettes, often out of order and incomprehensible by themselves, asking you to draw the lines and outline the narrative underneath.
When Gravity Ghost finally comes into focus it does so with alarming emotion and sincerity. It isn’t trying to manipulate you into feeling the way its characters do, it manages that by writing them as human and flawed the way we all are. Characters reactions and dialogues with and between each other are awkward and raw, but in a way that connected with me the way a articulated, perfectly timed script couldn’t have. People often aren’t eloquent, or tactful, and Gravity Ghost presents that side of us that often comes out during times of grief in a way that really resonated with me.
Gravity Ghost is a great game, certainly a more mechanically robust and sophisticated one than I would have expected, and you could play it for that side and come away impressed. You could play it because it’s beautiful and inspired, bursting with creativity and this sort of creepy but endearing sensibility to its extraterrestrial character designs. Or you could play it for its most unexpected and impressive side: a narrative that’s struck me emotional for what it was, and for how it managed to show that this part of me I’d chosen to ignore wasn’t something I needed to feel ashamed about. I’m not sure what Gravity Ghost will be for others who play it, but if it has anywhere near the same effect on them as it did me, that’s something worth experiencing however it might manifest.

It's hard to accurately give Gravity Ghost a category, so I'm going to call it an Aesthetic Puzzler. Solid mechanics evolve fluently. and are natural to use, and although can take some time to learn, feel natural as you exit the tutorial constellation.
More importantl is the crayon-style aesthetic choice, alongside wonderful soundtrack, which create a mystical feeling, which accurately captures the folklore-esque story that slowly reveals itself.
All in all, Gravity Ghost is a genuinely nice and relaxing game (Although it carries an emotional punch as well). Short, although eventually you gain the ability to act like a sandbox, editing any prior level to your heart's content, allowing yourself to relax whenever needed.

This game isn't bad. It's astonishingly bad. Now, I'm not a stickler for physics and stuff. Clipping through stuff is fine, especially in early access, however there's so much wrong it's unplayable.
We'll start with the good first, because it's not all bad. Some of the maps, Fochi in particular are pretty fun and the tricks are neat when you can land them.
That's about all I can say I enjoyed.
I think the biggest thing is the camera, it's placed directly behind your chacrater completely obscuring your vision. Skiing is all about being able to see where you're going, this simply doesn't replicate that feeling.
The controls are floaty at bast, they simply don't have any tightness to them and things like being unable to cut when you're crouched are counter intuative and break what little immersion there is.
The game is setup for a 360 controller but the menus don't recognize it sometimes, notably the options. And exiting a map is impossible through the recommended "press B to quit" option.
While this is an early access game it's no where close to being playable. I certainly hope it can be pushed forward because certain parts do feel fun, but overall it's simply lacking.

I finally gave in and bought the early access for the game, and it was definitely worth it! By far the best skiing, even best winter sports game I have ever played, even though it's still in alpha! While the game still isn's polished, the flaws are easily ignored. The game is also stunning when run at any detail level. There's so many unique lines too, I'm still finding areas on the only mountain available.
Can't wait for future updates, definitely recommend this game, support it!
Edit: Now, one year after purchasing my Snow early access pass, I have to change my review. As more and more updates have been released, while the graphics have improved, the actual playability of the game has plummetted severely. Even in pre-alpha, which I admit didn't have the greatest visuals, the game never crashed, and I was able to string together as many runs as I wanted to without suffering from any crashes or glitches that ruined my experience. However, since the more recent updates were released, the crashes have increased tremendously. Ever since the additions of microtransactions (which I somewhat agree with, but founders should get more than an ugly♥♥♥♥♥helmet and pair of skis), I have yet to explore a part of the main menu that doesn't freeze regularly.
This most recent update, however, has broken the game for me. When, after restarting Snow four times, I finally was able to ski on the mountain, I was going for about fifteen seconds before I discovered a new area. This lead to a prompt coming up that I couldn't dismiss, and I couldn't unpause the gameplay. I tried a couple more times to access the area, but to no avail.
So, despite my past positive rating, I'm going to have to not reccomend snow until Poppermost stops adding new features and irons out the ones that are already there.

Personally, I don't care about the competitions, events, or challenges. I don't care about points. What I wanted, and what this successfully delivers, is an open-world exploration sumulation with tight controls that are also fun.
Although still in alpha, Snow's current mountains include a huge number of trails, hills, and cliffs to ski up and down, and after an hour of play I felt I still had tons more to find. And the few physics liberties the game takes - such as being able to land on your feet after a really long fall - helps make the game more fun and less frustrating than if it were totally limited to real-world physics. (When you take a spill, though, the ragdoll effect can be fun to watch.)
The first-person view is reasonably convincing, and once they've refined it more I bet it'll be awesome with a 3D headset. The character animations are a little stiff, but, again, it's an alpha and they have more work to do.
Right now, what I miss most is sound - the wind blowing, the skis skimming across the snow, the trees rustling. Once they include some background sounds, the experience will be even more fun.
I'm glad I grabbed a copy of this, and I'm looking forward to playing it more as it develops and matures.

Defiance has a price you simply can't beat - free. I picked it up because I had been interested in it from launch, but not enough to buy it. The game is extremely fun, particularly with friends. Random events such as Arkfalls and Sieges pop up everywhere and are very fun, the small ones lasting a few minutes and usually attracting only a few players whilst the larger ones can last 15+ minutes and have swarms of players everywhere working together.
Unfortunately, Defiance has some problems. The biggest, most major one is its server problems. I'm already quite familiar with lag and server problems, but Defiance takes it to a whole new level. The in-game chat constantly has people complaining of it, and when you do the aforementioned large events it's often plagued by issues. Amongst some I've seen are a major delay in swapping my weapons - I press the weapon swap button and nothing happens, except I now can't even fire or reload it either. Spamming the key just queues it up for when it finally does respond. Players disapearing from my sight happens too. They're still around, the enemies react to them and if I try to heal them the beam finds them and does do its job. However, this does make healing or teamwork a lot harder since it would require running around blindly hoping somebody nearby is wounded.
Other issues are small and not too much of a problem, vehicles despawning mid-drive (you can just summon it with a button press) and enemies corpses remaining in an upright position being the only ones I can think of off the top of my head.
Overall I would recommend this game. It is very fun, and it is free. You can look past the server issues, and there is always the hope of them being fixed.

At the start of the game, I was enthralled with the art style. Through the middle I was continually impressed at the creativity, originality, and storytelling. By the end, I was sure I'd just experienced one of the best games I've ever played. At the risk of getting carried away or sounding too hyperbolic, the question of whether games can be art has been put to rest.
It took me about 3 hours to complete. I mention it because, in this case, I consider that the perfect length. It is as long it needed to be; no more, no less. Long enough to be a great experience, with no unnecessary "filler." More importantly, it is short enough that you have no excuse to not see it through to completion.
Were I doing a more clinical breakdown, I might mention great choices on the part of the developers, like having no HUD to distract or pull the player out of the experience. Or the fantastic art and sound design. Or the fact that they respected players' brains enough to let us infer the finer points of the story through context and body language, rather than beating us over the head with exposition. Or, perhaps most impressively, the way they use the controls themselves to great effect. (On that note, "Brothers" really deserves the proper playing environment: preferrably a gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks. If you don't have an Xbox 360 pad for PC, but you do own a modern gaming console, consider purchasing it on your console of choice instead. The controls are that important, in my opinion.)
Since this ISN'T a clinical breakdown, however, I'll simply say that "Brothers" deserves a few hours of your time.

Your ship is built with hexes and you can put weapons, engines, shields and energy booster on one or more hexes. To do that, you have to destroy things in your run that gives you bolts and when you have enough, you can buy the part you want and place it anywhere you want. It becomes a strategic positioning of weapons, shields and energy booster and also your cargo. Everything can be destroyed, your cargo included!

So as to not say too much of what other reviewers have said, the building needed in this game to succeed is too fast paced without sufficient gaps between attack "waves" to build up properly. You're having to manage temporary power-ups for each individual turret/structure, changing the aiming degree of each laser turret, one by one, repairing each damaged structure, moving your mouse around to collect scrap for constructing, selling individual structures you won't be able to repair in time, picking a permanent aiming degree for missle launchers while hovering your mouse over others to see which direction they're angled to make sure you have coverage in all directions, trying to keep adding more thrusters because you have to go faster to get enough credits and reputation points to get better unlocks, and moving individual turrets' aim because those turrets are blocking -other- turrets from aiming.
It's a micromanagement nightmare. Anyone who takes pride in their twitch skills or who is good at micromanaging or just playing stuff like Starcraft online and being fast and skilled might get a kick out of this game. However, if you're kinda ADD, OCD, or just awful at micromanagement in games, then it's very possible you may not enjoy this game. There are two groups of players in the Waiting to Buy Simulator (also called Heroes and Generals):
Players in the first group buy a recon just after launching the game for the first time without even playing it. Then there are players who spend enormous quantities of gold (real money) to buy some better stuff - weapons, tanks, soldiers, camos etc... If you belong to this group, the game is fun.
The second group is composed of players who never ever spend any money. Then it takes frustrating 50 hours to buy a godĐamned stupid grease gun. All the time, you dream about being a recon, but you don't want to spend any real money, so you keep playing and playing... But somewhere deep in your mind you know that you will never be able to buy a recon. Never. And by saying never, I mean NEVER.
Not even talking about buying a tank. If you keep grinding really looooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong time and you manage to get that tank somehow, you have to wait for around 5 minutes to respawn, then you drive 1 minute to the frontline ad get killed instantly because of your 5hitty equipment. Then you have to repeat it with the same result over and over again and spend another 50 hours to buy a better tank to make the game less boring (not more interesting).
I kept playing just because how addictive this game is, but after spending so much of my real life time to respawn and get killed instantly, I will never, and I mean NEVER, play this game again. It even takes about 50% of in-game time just to get to the frontline.
And the strangest thing about this game - the more time and money the players spend on this game, the more the developers ruin it. The Devyatayev update just made the game unplayable. And every new update makes it even worse.

On the surface, it looks like a pretty sweet setup. You get to create a character in a SyFy TV series world and play along side the story line in the San Francisco region. And at first glance, you'd be correct. However, when you begin playing, and trying to follow along with the series, you start to see your path diverges greatly between the two. For the true F2P'er, you are limited to two races, with a male or female variant of each. Your character customization is relatvely limited and chosen class is really only meant as a starter weapon set. This can be both a pro and a con as it doesn't matter what you choose to start out with, you customize your character as you play. However, there is little point in starting a new character, since you'll just be repeating everything all over again. The game has several different modes that take up your time:
1. Main story mission -- Your adventure through the main world, which seems pretty big, but you'll find a lot of it just chews scenary and are only used for repeatative side missions.
2. Episode missions -- Alluded to being involved in the tv series, but that train took off without you after a couple of missions. The TV series follows the exploits of Nolan and Irisa after they leave San Fran to St. Louis. However, they do this after several missions into the game. The rest of the time, you're racking your brain trying to figure out how the game coincides with the series. You'll need Google because the game is horrible at trying to help you piece it together, but the end result is still stretched pretty thin.
3. Side quests -- They do have several sentences of plot relation, but essentianally a lot of busy work for minimal reward.
4. Contests of skill -- These involve racing time trials, kill X enemies time trials, etc. Have no bearing on plot or character. These are doable if the lag situation is minimal.
5. Co-Op/Group missions -- Sieges, Arkfalls and Co-Op specific maps. These are fun for the first few times, then get rather repeative quickly.
6. PVP battles - Arena style fights that has it's own reward setup.
Other than costumes, most of the DLC are boosters to help advance your character in his/her run from EGO level 10 to 5000+. Yes, that's right...your end level is over 5000!  I've played nearly a week now, putting in serious time and effort, where I've completed all of the story, both seasons of episodes, every side mission and contest, as well as dozens of Arkfalls and Sieges and I've barely broken 1.6k. You really have to live in this place to rack up to 5k+.
The community is relatively reasonable, however, they are extremely defensive about the game itself and can get downright hostile if you dare speak up about any of the glaring issues the game brings forth. The voice acting, character animations, graphics, etc. are all really nice for a F2P game. However, there is one glaring shortcoming and it's lag. The game can be downright unplayable with the lag situation. This is pretty much a hot topic on forums and in game chat. It can make some of the contests unfinishable, the sieges unreliable, etc.
Pros:
Good graphics and gameplay.
You may be tempted to buy some new outfits since everyone is practically wearing the same thing, but if you follow your  'persuits', you'll notice a lot of those costumes are available as rewards, in one color scheme or another.
DLC is really only needed to enhance your 'end game.' Which there is none to speak of. So, end game could be summed up as trying to get to 5k, I guess.
Really simple to get into and play as the game seems very story driven.
Cons:
Limited social aspects. The chat functionality is horrendous. Joining a clan always comes with a "install Raidcall, Teamspeak, Mumble, etc." request because trying to keep tabs on things with the in game chat is futile.
No end game. Once the missions are wrapped up, it's clan led Arkfall events and PVP.
DLC's offer no real incentive. I guess a sword is cool and all, but not for $12.
The lag will make you want to smash your keyboard.
Don't overthink the 'RPG' elements of the game. There are four 'traits'. of which you'll focus on one of them and you'll be constantly tempted to modify and upgrade your weapons, which you really don't need to for the vast majority of the game. Easier just to swap out your weapons with those you find until you find a firing 'style' that you like and then focus on that type until you've wrapped up the main story.
I'm recommending this as a good solo or group of friends run to play along with the series, which isn't all that wonderful (it's no Firefly), but it's decent. Like this game.  You really don't need to do the side missions, unless you really need something to do. Otherwise, episodes and main story. Then pack it up, because you're pretty much done.

I want to preface this by saying that I'm not an experienced MMO player, nor am I a writer. So you may want to take my opinion with a grain of salt depending on what you're looking for in a review.
I had heard about Defiance near its release from a friend of mine, he told me the game wasn't worth my time. So I stuck to his advice and avoided the game. However some time before this game went Free to Play, I won it in a giveaway, so I tried it out. I was really wondering why he told me not to play it because I loved it! The game was genuinely fun to play, the graphics were quite good, the story was a bit lacking but people have varying opinions of how important that is in an MMO.
The map is pretty big, enough so that you need vehicles to get around it all. You get those quite soon into the story so trying to find them isn't a big deal. You can of course upgrade them.
The weapons are pretty varied, different weapon types, different types of lasting damage (Fire, acid, etc.), and there are modifications to each weapon. Visually however the weapons tend to get a bit repetitive, which you may see as a problem.
The enemies are also pretty varied, including different types of raiding parties, monsters, gangs, and pseudo-security firms, and generally you'll have to work at figuring out the best ways of killing off each type.
Now of course there are negatives to the game, as there is with any game. Mainly the problem is that quests and random missions tend to repeat themselves a lot, which threw me off on where exactly I was in the story(I'm not the most attentive fellow, so you may handle this better than me).
Secondly, the game doesn't feel that much like an MMO. This is mainly due to there not being enough players to pad out the large map. So generally you'll just be playing either on your own or with a friend or two, occasionally passing by another player, or seeing a bunch of players in an event.
And finally, tying into the second point. The chat; the chat in this game is pretty much dead. You would rarely see anyone actually talking in the chat unless it was for a gear trade.

If there are two words I could use to describe Gravity Ghost, it would be "whimsical" and "trippy". From the colourful, dreamlike hand-painted visuals, to the zany and meditative soundtrack; from the strange and peculiar worlds and creatures, to the dreamy child fantasy story; from the smooth animations to the interesting visual effects; and from the often seemingly offbeat voice-acting and narration to the carefree sensation of floating around in space, Gravity Ghost oozes with charm and is a product that is quite clearly crafted with love.
It may not be for everyone though. The game is pretty accessible in the sense that there is not much of a challenge aside from getting to grips as to how the gravity works, and it is kinda short (around 2-3 hours long), but neither of these detracts from the experience in my opinion.
I definitely recommend this game, and I love it, but I can clearly see how this will also not be to everyone's liking. If you like charming indie games that are creative, and place more of an emphasis on the atmosphere and the experience of playing it, then you should get this. But if you're looking for something that has more "substance" from a gameplay standpoint, then perhaps this is not for you.

From the beautiful art, to Ben Prunty's amazing soundtrack. The top notch voice acting. Gravity Ghost is a fantastic example of what the Indie Industry is capable of. From beginning to end the game is an enjoyable, relaxing experience.
Soaring through space has never felt so rewarding and enjoyable!

Gravity Ghost is a physics based platformer that utilizes gravity as it's core mechanic. It's a very unique take on the genre that has a ton of charm and wonder.
Each stage you visit functions as it's own puzzle that will feature various gravity and physics based problems. You'll be going through stage to stage, unlocking stars, spirit animals, and an assortment of items and special powers. As you unlock more areas and gain new powers the story will start to unfold. Though it could be argued that Gravity Ghost is "arcady" at it's core, it does manage to tell an interesting narrative, which is something "arcady" games tend to lack.
The Puzzle like stages of Gravity ghost are mostly well designed, and offers a higher than expected degree of variety. When I first started this game I expected the game to get repetitive the more I play, but was surprised by how creative the developers were in designing each area. Though many stages will have repeating mechanics, they're offered in interesting and often unexpected ways to solve a puzzle. The puzzles them selves are very accessible as I never found myself stuck for too long, but still satisfied when I manage to solve it. The puzzles are well designed, and creative too.
Artistically, Gravity Ghost shows an almost crayon child's drawing presentation. It's whimsical,and very easy on the eyes. It's one of the game's most attractive qualities and has the audio to match. Gravity ghost is a lot of eye candy, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
Though the game has a ton of potential, and I can safely say I've enjoyed my time with it, it's still not perfect. Gravity Ghost comes with the main campaign and that's about it. There's no bonus features, extra modes, or even a very good options and settings menu.
Overall Gravity Ghost is a fun light romp, with a ton of charm. It's probably not going to appeal to those who is looking to meta-game and min-max, or twitch their way to victory, but for any one who is looking for a more easy going experience in their gaming Gravity Ghost would be a pretty good choice.
Pros:
- Wonderful art and music
- Good use of physics based puzzles
- Inventive puzzle design
- Very accessible
Cons:
- Lacks features and options
- Might be considered too "casual" for some

I can't say enough nice things about this game. I've been in the beta for the last week since buying in on this project in the early days. I mostly ignored development other than to catch a vid here or there, and thought it still looked like fun when it would be released.
I was not prepared for how polished and fun the final product ended up.
The game is divided into a few-minutes-long levels on a mario-map style board. The wonderful teach-by-playing mechanic mean the game's pacing and introduction of new power-ups and gameplay elements is steady, while still allowing you to fully explore all the new mechanics by going for every bit of hair-growing flowers you can nab.
The art is just breathtakingly beautiful, and a lot of care went into making everything visually inuitive, from the colors and contrast, to the iconography (all relevant moving elements of a given board leave a motion trail behind them, so watching, learning and planning your jumps is a must if you want to proceed quickly!).
Past that, the game is just chill as hell and FUN, with the goals being clearly articulated, but without the annoyance of death (you've been there, done that) or arbitrary "starting overs". Just enjoy the gravity, the superb voices, and the perfectly appropriate soundtrack. The sound design, while simple, works wonderfully and you will not tire of the effects the game uses.
Intercut with the gameplay and gathering stars and elements and reuniting animal spirits with their bodies are wistful memories of the Ghost's past life, which have been beautifully drawn, and continue to give me a good laugh every time they show up.
But seriously, all you need to know is that you get to hug spirit animals and welcome them to the afterlife, and orient them to what life is like when you no longer have to poop anymore.
Just fantastic.

They don't lie when they say "For Riders, By Riders". If you ski (or snowboard) yourself, you'll probably really like this game.

There are some negatives to this game as it's still an Early Access game.
There's NO audio. None. Zero.
So either play your own tunes for now (best option) or make your own sound-effects as you rip down the Mountain.
There's also currently no "true" Multiplayer at this time so we'll have to wait for that.
You can still join Multiplayer games but it will require some extra work on your part, and it's still rather buggy.
Sliding on the rails, and some jumping mechanics are bugged (Half-pipe is impossible as it stands, rails are rather slow and *sometimes* your player will stick to the ground if you jump at the crest of a hill etc)
These aren't game breakers for me since the general experience is ever-evolving and improving.
Overall, I'm quite pleased with this game and the way the Devs have been constantly updating and listening to the fans.
I feel comfortable recommending this game to people who are skiers/boarders themselves.
People who are looking for either an arcade-like experience (think AMPED or SSX) or are looking for a totally complete game may be disapointed.

TL;DR - Was a great game.  Not enough to keep me playing.  The F2P model is too gimped for me to justify playing, tired of paying sub, since I've been on since launch.  Still a great game for new players, but not enough going on to keep me into it I think...
Well, as someone whose played since launch years ago, I guess it's time for my thoughts.  The game has made a lot of changes since the beginning, not all of them for the better.  Hacking was terrible in the beginning, so I almost never played PVP.  And when the population dwindled to almost nothing, I considered hacking just so I could run high level content, becuase there was no one on to group up with, except the aforementioned hackers playing PVP only.
Then came the Megaservers, which saved the game in my mind.  Finally I could run group content without waiting for the weekend.  I WAS AN IDIOT FOR PASSING UP ON THE LIFETIME SUB AT THIS POINT!
Then came F2P.  Game was rough for the first week.  Then it got better.  But this is where it went mostly bad.  Players would rush to level 30, then camp the starting areas.  So you couldn't make alts and start leveling them in PVP zones.  So I had to log on to my main toons, and wipe all of these clowns so others could level.  At the risk of sounding selfish, I got bored of that becuase I didn't gain anything from it, having accomplished all the open-world pvp feats.
Then they began lowering the marks it takes to get T1 and up armor.  No biggie, but as much time as I spent gaining currency to get this armor, and I kind of felt burned for it.  Yes it made getting armor for my alts easier, but still, all that time in the beginning spent farming marks.
The only two reasons I still play is because I'm hoping for a few more power sets, and there's one last patch I'm stoked for:  When you've unlocked at a cosmetic sytle, it's unlocked for all your characters!  I have wished for this forever.  No more farming currency to buy multiples of a style then mail them to my alts.  So this has got me excited.  But no word when that's coming.
Bottom line:  The F2P model is too gimped for someone who paid sub for a long time.  Most of the people I used to play with are gone.  I have some cool names for my toons becuaes I made them in the beginning.  It may be my favorite game of all time, but it is definitely my favorite MMO ever.  If they offer the lifetime sub again I may bite.  But it might be time to put this one to bed...

Usntoppable Gorg is a new take on the Tower Defense genre and in itself not a bad and quite fun game. What makes this gold are the cutscenes between missions. They are (puposely) so bad that they give off a perfect vibe of film-making more than half a decade ago. I didn't finish the campaign for the gameplay but for those goofy cutscenes alone.
The challenge missions mix things up quite a bit and are the most fun content within the game mechanically.
Had lots of fun with this, do recommend to any and all tower defense fans.

Unstoppable Gorg is delightfully corny in so many ways, from its visuals, to its music, to them going to the trouble of making black and white live action film of people acting for the stuff in between missions. There are various towers with different purposes and enough variation between them to make it worthwhile to select certain towers over others depending on upcoming enemy composition, etc. I really like not only the idea, but much of the execution for the game.
However, my one hangup with it is what probably sets it apart the most from other tower defense games: tower mobility. You place a tower on an orbital ring, and can typically place others on the same orbital ring, on the opposite of that ring, or even on the side of it. Then you click the left mouse button on the tower and can spin it around to the other side of your defense point to take out incoming enemies.
The big issue for someone like me is that I'm pretty darn ADD, and anyone who suffers from it to my extent may find themselves getting overwhelmed by incoming attack waves while trying to keep track of the
attacks from different sides, from different enemy compositions, while having to try to spin the right towers on the right rings into the right spots to defend.
It's just too much I have to keep up with at the same time to be capable of doing so. If towers were stationary and the game was designed around that instead, this could be a massive hit with me, but as it is, this feature makes the game incredibly difficult even on lower settings. Anyone with a huge attention span and dexterity who can keep up with and react to a lot of things happening on-screen at once would probably dig this game if they're into TDs and cornball stuff, while those with attention span or dexterity problems might do well to avoid what would otherwise be a pleasant experience.

Now, this game... what a shame. It had everything going on for it: Excelent 60's sci-fi B-movie atmosphere, good graphics, good soundtrack and the right idea. This should've been a "must play" TD game, right?
But no, it's not. Far from it, because the gameplay is just utter crap. First of all the TD mechanic is SUPER restrictive and completely un-intuitive, sure it looked like a nifty concept, but the execution is below subpar. It's like the game is actually a puzzle and it's forcing you to find the correct and only strategy to win each map because god knows there's no room for having fun with different setups.
On top of it, the towers themselves are honestly quite boring and the game doesn't really add anything new to the genre, except for that awkward, weird and ultimately failed rotationary orbital system that forces you to find the correct solution and micromanage like crazy as well.
And again, it's a shame because the rest of the package is really cool. I mean, it's cheesy as hell, but that's intended, and it really works... So in the end, I'm afraid I can't recommend this, as much as I'd like to, purely in terms of gameplay and fun. It's not very fun to play, honestly.
But hey, if you're a fan of weird cheesy 60's low quality sci-fi flicks, you might want to check this game and enjoy it on a purely aesthetic way.
If you're looking for your next TD fix, stay away from this.
