Space Wars: Interstellar Empires is quite simply put as a game that may not be for everyone. It has a very table-top RPG type feeling to it, and for some gamers this just doesn't cut it. Hopefully people who may read my review will see that line and will be able to get an idea if they're interested or not. It's not something that is super high paced and action packed. There is no instant gratification. This is a game that challenges you to think about your moves, how you allocate your resources, and how you will work with your team to not only prevent the loss of your ship but achieve victory as well. There is a high level of strategy intended to be required for a complete victory. You won't be able to just waltz in and start blasting ships out of the sky. There is a LOT of information to be learned and a alot of people seem to not want to dedicate that time. This is fine, but it doesn't make the game bad just because you don't like it.
The game itself plays out pretty fluidly, is not super resource intensive, and has quite a large lore to it. There are two starting factions, the Genari and the Sol Imperial Worlds, with plans to include two more playable factions: the Ma'alaketh, and The Hive. Ontop of the vast story behind the factions, there are numerous hand crafted and unique ships. No two ships will be exactly the same, whether it be visually or statistically. There is a tutorial at the start that you may optionally play to learn the game (****HIGHLY RECOMMENDED DOES NOT EVEN NEARLY SUFFICE AS A DESCRIPTOR HERE****). There are also global and faction chats that can be utilized in game via a collapse-able left hand side bar so that you can always close the chat out and focus on the action when you want to. The game itself is very in depth.
Lastly, the fact that this game was put out by a small team speaks wonders for what can be achieved with this project once it forms a strong player base. The best part of it all is that it includes no pay to win features. Any in-game purchases are strictly cosmetic.
I strongly recommend the game if you are a table top RPG player. It'll be a tad different and require some adjusting, but overall it will be entertaining.

Before I give my review I'd like to say I got this game for free from a giveaway so as to whether this game is worth the price (which I feel it is) I can't give a good answer but it's cheap enough that I think it's worth getting.
Now as to if the game is good or not depends entirely on the person, it's a challenging puzzle game that makes you think about your next three moves in advance and can be difficult to progress without learning the patterns. It's fun and intersting and at this point in time the developers are really active with the game and fixing any issues that pop up, which does happen sometimes. This is a very enjoyable game which, depending on how good you are at puzzles, may cause the game to last for a very long time for you (with some of the puzzles seeming to be very complex to figure out).
Now for the negatives:
- Some of the puzzles seem extremely similar to each other and once you figure out how to solve the puzzle it becomes very simple to do so. So, if two puzzles have the same solution despite it being two seperate puzzles it feels like you're only solving one.
- The puzzles in the game aren't all exactly original so it's possible you may have already seen one or more of these puzzles before, personally I've seen a few puzzles I already knew how to solve due to having done them years before.
- While this game is advertised as "extremely hard brain twisting puzzles" some of them are so simple a child could do it. This is not an exaggeration, my last point about having played some of these puzzles years ago is a perfect example. I can easily remember solving some of these puzzles as a child and not having any real challenges doing so.
-
EDIT: Cards have been added.
- This game has a very small repetitive sound file with little to no background noise.
All that being said if you are a fan of puzzle games these  puzzles may not be as hard as described but they are challenging as well as fun and this game is certainly enjoyable for what it is.

- enables you to experiment with car designs, parts, financial plans
- teaches you about automotive industry's history and the milestones in it
- isn't terribly simplified or dumbed down, like so many other games

- it crashes sometimes, which can be frustrating if you've just lost a car youv'e been designing for an hour

... but it's still in development, so I expect most issues will be addressed eventually.
If you like cars, get it.
If you don't care about cars, get it anyway.
If you absolutely hate cars, you're not reading this review anyway.

So this game is great. Metroidvania style gameplay with some bullet hell elements. Melee combat with a single beam attack and an AOE aura attack you both get later on (mana-based attacks). You can switch from red (dark) to blue (light) modes, which allow you to absorb bullets of the same color, while also allowing you to damage enemies of the opposite color. This makes for some interesting color-switching gameplay.
Pluses:
The game has very beautiful concept-art-ish backgrounds. A lot of blacks, but the game doesn't seem overly dark since it is colored with red and blue everywhere. You'll visit a jungle, an underworld cave area, an ancient city, and other such cool places.
Combat is quite fluid, movement feels responsive. Not very restrictive. Not hugely combo-based but you can fly through enemies gracefully once you get the controls down. Speaking of controls, you probably should play with a controller here. It's not designed originally for keyboards as a console title.
There isn't much downtime in the game, you move straight to the next portion without any interruption. Collecting everything is enjoyable, and usually rewarding.
Music is subdued but well done. You probably won't be able to hum the OST after playing this game in full, but the music isn't out of place or jarring.
The visuals are stylized enough that they will never look dated. Very nice.
Bosses are the most enjoyable portion of the game. Only the last boss is an exception.
Game has a reasonable amount of difficulty. It's challenging, but not ridiculous. No frustrating parts.
Minuses:
It feels like this game could have used a dodge mechanic. It plays fine without one, but would have been so much more fluid with one.
Platforming and bullet-avoidance is more the focus in the game. Combat seems to be sidelined outside of bosses, which is okay, and I think it works, but is a bit dissappointing.
The last boss is underwhelming, and its difficulty is entirely placed on the few awkwardnesses the controls have. For example, you can't easily attack below you in the air without having to do a "ground pound"-esque attack which plummets you off the level, which is one of the only reasons the last boss becomes difficult.
The powerups you receive in the game aren't useless for the most part, but the latter ones seem like they aren't better than what you already have, and are just there to enable you to reach the next area. They are supposed to be additions to your combat capabilities, but some of are mostly relegated to traversal techniques rather than combo-additives.
The story is pretty half-baked. I understand the game is supposed to be minimally invasive and have almost no interruptions from the experience. This is good, but I think a game needs to have some backstory if it's going to have a story at all. For example, there's unlockable art pieces. Just have the game's background lore in text form unlocked the same way. This means people wishing to learn more about the game's story can check it out. Otherwise it seems like no effort was put into the story.
In the end, this game is great for the gameplay and relatively good artistic style. For fans of metroidvania games, this is 8-12 hours well spent.
Note: Two of the achievements are a pain. One requires a co-op level to be completed, which is reliant on the game having an active community, which it won't, since it's a linear single-player game in its core. The other requires the collection of 1000000 doubloons, which requires around 1.5 hours of grinding minimum after collecting everything in the game. I don't think that's good design, to require grinding aimlessly to receive one of the achievements. To be clear, there's no way you could get 1000000 doubloons without at least a bit of grinding.

I'll thumb up this game, but it wasn't with flying colors. Reason: it takes a while before it really starts to shine.
At first glance, all I saw were things that were done in other games equally or better. Metroid and castlevania have smoother movements, Dust: an elysian tale and Guacamelee have more fun combat mechanics (Christ...even A shadow's tale has better combat, and that's saying something) and the visuals kinda remind me of Nyx quest but also not as good (and that was just a run-of-the-mill wiiware platformer).
Pretty soon, however, you'll get the ability to switch colors between red and blue. And while I originally considered it more of a gimmick than a game mechanic ("why does my random mystic jungle warrior looks like a Tron character?"), it won me over on the amount of uses they'll manage to squeeze out of it. You can only damage enemies of a different color, and projectiles of the same color don't damage you. This gives the combat mechanics an entirely different spin that manages to engage despite being clunky (your character strikes with a 3-hit combo, and pretty soon, enemies will require 4 hits, so you can't charge in).
Not that long after, you'll find uses for all the gold you're collecting (there aren't many places you can buy stuff, but they'll cost you. And there's probably an achievement for collecting the most gold without spending it). And you can choose whether to pick up health or smash it, which'll give you more gold (a dilemma i kind of like).
...and then the game slowly turns into Ikaruga. More and more projectiles are fired, and it's more of a puzzle to get through the place without getting hit by stuff of the opposite color while at the same time crafting a path for yourself in your own color (it's easier than it sounds here, but still pretty challenging).
At the same time, the story and the lore really take a backseat. IMHO, the game would've been better in a full sci-fi environment rather than this mish-mash of mysticism and futurism. But hey...since the gameplay gets pretty solid, it's not like I'm complaining. And it IS a unique end result. And a very interesting one at the very least. :-)

I also feel that the physics engine is not there, the speed settings seem to have max speeds they can go (no engine torque simulation from my experience), the derailment looks awkward. It quite simply doesnt feel like you're driving a heavy train (brakes are instant and its really quick to throttle up).
The point system is a good idea but too mean (I mean, speeds randomly changing from 60>40>60 and you're getting penalised for the sudden, unshown change) and the drive quality penalty makes no sense as it doesnt feel like you're going too harshly around the corners.
The world doesnt seem too real either; the sounds are off. When I'm in a city I expect to hear cars, when I'm in the countryside I expect to hear birds and wind blowing and its just not there. On the subject of weather, the droplets (even though done nicely with the dropping animation) are square and seem to ignore wind and the "smearing" effect of the wind and nothing looks wet.
Overall out of the 14h played it was fun to the extent of pressing the A and D keys and occasionally the Q key when the British highspeed train (class 395) starts beeping like something's about to blow up. If you're looking for a game which feels "arcadey" and not doing much this is the game for you.

"Red Faction: Guerrilla" was a stand-out title during the last gaming generation. Taking the power of the new consoles and shifting the focus from linear corridor shooter into an open sandbox made a huge difference in the mechanics of the game.
For starters, Geo-Mod makes a triumphant return and is a glorious site to behold in HD. Not only that, but literally any weapon can cause a building to come crashing down. Just smack your hammer or lob a grenade and be prepared to see new dimensions added to your combat.
The vehicles were also rather fun, if a bit stiff. Their sticky controls are ultimately forigven when you hit a building and proceed to plow through it. Really, Geo-Mod is the best feature of this game and blows away most other "open-world" titles on any system.
The campaign is pretty lack-luster, though. The story makes little to no sense and has no real gel connecting the various missions. You just go to a check point, proceed to the mission area and then kill people. At least you don't have to worry about invisible walls or poorly shaded geometry.
The multiplayer makes up for any undelivering parts of the campaign mode. The pass-the-controller style "Wrecking Crew" is wild with friends. Limiting you to a minute or two to destroy an area is obscenely fun. While that mode can't be played online, the other (generic) online options are bolstered by the fact that Geo-Mod exists.
While EA promised with "Battlefield 3" that we'd get to see real-time environmental destruction, Red Faction already provided that. Not only did we get a glimpse of the future (that has yet to come), but it worked properly (unlike Battlefield).
That the Steam edition includes the DLC to the game is also a nice bonus. I wouldn't recommend playing through it, but seeing as its a freebie, having it doesn't hurt.
Honestly, you can't really beat this game. Many open-world titles claim to allow you freedom of choice, but "Red Faction: Guerrilla" is one of the few to honestly make good on it's promise. If you see a wall and don't like it, you can rectify the situation.

...I never thought I'd do a serious review for a game like Huniepop....
The thing is, this game could easily be just clickbait, with big anime-♥♥♥♥♥♥s, shoddy gameplay, just another cashgrab on steam - but it is not.
2015 had an awful lot of good games - and Huniepop is in a weird spot, where I'd say without any irony, that it is one of my favourite games of that year, alongside Bloodbowl 2, Darkest Dungeon, Warhammer Vermintide and Bloodborne.
I'd even go as far as to say that it is one of my favourite games of all time.
I always enjoyed match-3 games up to a certain point. I beat the the first 150 levels of candycrush on my phone, until I got sick and tired of Kings business practices and switched over to Puzzle quest, which I liked for it's complexity.
Then, at some point, Totalbiscuit talked about this on a Cooptional Podcast. He talked about this weird, dumb game that he played, a mix of a dating sim and a match three game that he somewhat hated - and I thought to myself well that sounds dumb, I should totally play it.
So I bought Huniepop and started to play. And I played, and played and literally could not stop, until I finished almost the entire game in one sitting, somewhat around 7-8 hours.
This game is so dumb, yet so great.
It's a game about exploiting a dozend anime girls and using their trust just to f*ck with them, it is really, really dumb and really wrong, and it is completely aware of it.
Again, the thing is, this game could easily be just clickbait, with big anime-♥♥♥♥♥♥s shoddy gameplay, just another cashgrab on steam.
-But it isn't.
It's quite clear that the developer put a lot of love and effort into this game. Gameplay and presentation are both pretty damn good.
The Match-3 system, while not as complex as other contenders on the market, is very well implemented and never really gets boring. The artwork is great, and the game offers some very decent voice acting and a soundtrack, that fits perfectly to the backgrounds and blends in well.
The game plays like this:
Every day you talk to different characters and try to get to know them. They'll ask questions about themself or your opinion and if your answer is correct, you get a ressource called "hunie", which you can spend to upgrade your passive skills, which allow you to get more points during the match-3 sequences.
You then ask the characters out on a date, which is where the match-3 happens. You have 20 moves to reach a certain score to suceed at the date. You can use various items to get more moves, change the board, get rid of unwanted symbols and rig the odds in your favor. You can take up to six different Items on a date (there is an awful lot of them in total, every one of them with a certain benefit and in some cases drawback) - these items are very important, since they will decide your strategy for the date - if you play on hard, you'll probably need one. It's no grand strategy that's going to break your mind, but you'll need to spend a thought every now and then and set your priorities.
Every character likes/dislikes certain traits, based on their personality, which are represented by different symbols.
If you match up 3 symbols that a character prefers, you get bonus points, if they don't like it you get less then for a neutral match.
There are also tokes that give you extra moves, tokens that let you use your items and tokens, that will cost you a certain percentage of your points, if matched. You can drag one token per move across the entire board, as long as you move it within the same column/row.
After a date you get "munie" which you can spend on food, gifts and drinks. These are used to get new items and get the most Hunie out of a dialogue - so basically, leveling up your traits. With every date you suceed at, the score that is required at the next date rises.
As every date gets harder you have to think ahead in the dating-sim section of the game. You need to think about how to spent your munie, think about the traits and items that might be useful to you and when to talk to certain characters.
The oddest thing about this odd little game is for me, that It actually makes me see the characters as...well, characters. This is just me personally, but I feel that if I knew these people in reality, there are some that I would like and some that I'd absolutely hate and some that I could genuinely relate to. It's weird, escpecially since most characters are just some basic anime/movie tropes personified, and the game never fails to remind you of that.
tl;dr
Huniepop is one of the few games that I actually take the time to revisit every now and then. The gameplay never really gets stale and is always good for a few hours of fun. The voice acting and soundtrack is very good, I really like the bright and lively colours and the character design are great. What I don't like is the lackluster options menu. While by no means gamebreaking, it would be nice to have more options for screen resolution and such.

Less of a "Tower Defense" and more of a "Point Defense" with a tactical twist. You build onto free hexes on your ship, as you fly towards your goal, and try to defend yourself and your cargo from a constant barrage of enemies. Competently amusing story-dialogues, and genuinely exciting bossfights spice it up rather nicely.
The challenge is derived from the way the game forces you to split your considerations while managing a limited budget: You must choose between weapons, defenses, engines, and other specific needs based on the "client" you are running the mission for. Focusing on firepower is easy enough, but youll lose speed and get a lower score, which limits your tech-tree advancement. Focusing on speed will get you killed. Choosing the right pieces, at the right times, is vital to getting the best outcome. This becomes more difficult as the game advances, because larger/more-advanced constructions require various levels of power, and because components must be built adjacent to each other in certain ways to function.
If I had to complain about anything in this game, it would be that there is no "free-play" or "random" mode. Only the campaign exists, and there is no variance within said campaign. Once you have played all of the levels once, all there is to do is to go back and play them each again, and try to get a higher score. The game ended, for me, before I was ready to put it away, and I was sad to see that no expansions or DLC exist to get more playtime out of it.
But, to say that a game was good enough that it left me wanting more is a compliment in its own right. Definitely worth the price at 15 dollars, and maybe worth more.

If you are looking for a quality f2p TBS that is more about thinking than acting and plays like an old board game, because that's exactly where its origins lie, then give this game a shot. Players are not (at the time of writing this review) subject to any kind of daily/weekly or other time-gated restrictions aside from the number of participants on a map of a given size, which some maps are small, some are huge.
The sky is the limit with how fast you wish to progress within a server, which runs until one faction achieves victory.  Once this happens, another server is automatically started, and the game begins again allowing players to choose a different faction to champion if they wish. Really happy with this purchase. You've got to look past the clunky, old school UI...and the "what the heck am I supposed to be doing" confusion at the beginning... and you find a fun, deep game.
You construct your cars by designing chassis, engines, and gearboxes...as simple as selecting icons and adjusting sliders. For each part you get to pick from various layouts and determine what areas your engineers will focus their efforts. Your choices are just a click or drag, but are critical to success. You are balancing customer desire with the cost to make your product. You've got to determine where to build factories, where to put up your branch offices to push sales, how much to spend on marketing, and how to divide up your distribution. You've got to price your vehicle right for the target demographic, city, body style demand, and current competitors' products.
You'll catch yourself saying "just one more turn" so you can modify your I4 engine, run a new model year on your popular sedan, or break into a new market. It's a good balance of complexity, simplicity, and automation that makes the core play loop fun. A definite recommend for sim and management fans.

Although I'm recommending GearCity, I will not speak about the game itself at this moment. What I want to speak about is the game developer. Eric and his approach is the reason I like this game.
I saw Gearcity in some kind of Steam sale. Saw that it supports Linux, checked the HW requirements (I'm playing on my 10 years old laptop with integrated Intel graphics, i915 driver) and headed to try the demo from the dev's website. That's how it all started.
I ran accross a problem with texture sizes - my graphics simply didn't support them. I have reported it to Eric and I had new files to try the next day. Needless to say that they worked. This has repeated once more and now in the 1.19.1 build there is only one file left that causes trouble on such an old HW that I have. I can play the game since Eric provided me with all that I needed. The file would be probably included in 1.19.2 release.
I want to thank Eric for keeping in contact with the players of his game and for thinking of the really old HW users. There is apparently no need to run the game through OpenGL 3 or even 4, because it's not about graphics. There are not many games/developers that think this way. I have many games in my library that has unnecessary HW requirements for the graphics they have. This is not one of them and that's why I recommend it.
About the game itself. I have bankrupted only twice so far (well, I have played only two games). The game looks pretty complex to me and pretty hard to get into - keep in mind that I haven't any experiences with economic/simulation games. The setting of this game (car company) looks good to me. I like the designing new cars part of the game and I still have to learn how to profit.
I think this game will make it high on my favorite list in the future. I suppose it would reside somewhere near OpenTTD and it will be the game I would like to return to.

A long time ago I played a game called, "Detroit". The objective of the game was to build an automotive empire. Despite being released for DOS, it had advanced customization features rarely seen elsewhere. The game made every attempt to be immersive. Menus were represented as rooms or buildings. Want to change your research? Go talk to the researchers. Interested in making some investments? Call the bank from your office. The game even takes many major world events into consideration. (Which tend to impact your sales.)
I could go on and on... Why am I telling you about Detroit? Well, Gear City is everything Detroit was, and more. The game is very retro. It very much looks like a DOS game. That said, it has features which set it far apart and above old games. (Such as interactive 3D models.)
The main feature is designing and selling your own vehicles. The game takes place over many years. As you research new parts, your build options expand. The available parts are extensive. They don't cover absolutely everything, but they cover almost anything you'll want to build. The body options are somewhat limited, but this is mostly superficial anyway.
If you like turn-based, business-management games... you are sure to like this one. Of course, if the retro style turns you off, you might want to back away now.

If you hate stamina timers, are looking for some kind of intensive, skill-demanding game, and absolutely hate anything that resembles grinding, this game is probably not for you.
On the flip side: for a mobile port, there is a massive amount of content. Also it was originally developed for tablets exclusively and has controller support, so I feel like all the 'mobile ports suck rah rah' criticisms aren't valid. The quality of the game is quite high from your typical mobage. Timers be damned, I played for 20 hours before running into any sort of stamina timer problems (and had 30+ free stamina refills at the time).
The game mechanics borrow from many different places. Together it's somewhat unique and does have some strategic depth once you figure out what all the colors and symbols mean. The orb system "draws" orbs when you normal attack. Abilities require a certain combination of orbs. Various passive effects and the abilities equipped on your job determine what orbs you draw. You can discard undesirable orbs for defensive buffs and influencing the probability of drawing certain orbs. Aside from that, it plays like a turn-based RPG with multiplayer content that unlocks early on in the story.
The multiplayer content surprised me. If you played FFXI or very early FFXIV (1.0), it plays a lot like that: Gameplay is slow, but coordinating is extremely highly rewarded, especially when you're attempting the hard content.
Yes, western gamers retch at the slightest hints of standard mobile game tactics, but for those who can see past the typical mobage money traps and  want to find a time sink, play this turn based JRPG for free with a couple of the standard mobage bells and whistles, this is a decent game. All content, skills, items, etc. can be acquired completely free-to-play, and the game is relatively generous.

Saints Row 3 - 150 hours, Skyrim - 300 hours, Train Simulator 2013/14 - 800 hours and counting.
In fact, you can't compare a game where you have to shoot or jump or puzzle with this ...system, yes, it's a whole system. You drive, collect and admire trains and locomotives, you edit scenarios, you can even create whole landscapes with the fantastic editor. It's totally up to you where and when you drive, what you drive and what you do, this so called game - but as I said, it's so much more, it's a kind of canvas whereupon you paint your own experience - anyway, this game doesn't force you to meet any arbitrary goals and confine you to a corridor of limited options. It's wide open, and together with the dozens of addons,  numerous fan sites and the workshop integration you have an unlimited supply of locomotives, cars, routes and scenarios.
Don't let you fool by the negative reviews (from guys who also spent 1000 hours with it, btw), this game is up to date graphic and sound wise, you can drive in every season and at every time of day, and it looks and sounds fantastic. The hum of a 4000 hp diesel loco at full power is something to be expierenced! It feels REAL and that's what a simulator should be all about.
Even if you are not an avid railfan, try it out!

I am compelled to write a review now seeing as the game is currently on sale for $2.99 and it just came out of beta. For those who don't know Nordic Games decided to go back and patch a game from 2009 after THQ and Volition left it somehwhat broken and with GFWL. Now the game is GFWL-free and many popular bugs are fixed along with some new added multiplayer goodies and DX 11 support. Now is as good a time as ever to buy this game! Also, if you wish to know what the gameplay is like, then try to imagine GTA with all buildings destroyable and with a fantastic physics engine (you can literally level a structure by driving through it.), sci-fi themed, on mars, with a jetpack and a mini nuke, and a decent storyline that connects to the first game in the series. If you have an appetite for destruction this game is definately for you!

Nordic Games deserves a medal for what they've done.
Taking an amazing game hampered by Games for Windows live, continued bugs, and being a 6 year old game. They bought the Red Faction license from THQ and have implemented Steamworks, removed the GFWL component, added achievements, trading cards, Steamworks multiplayer support, and most of all, FIXED THE BUGS FROM THIS 6 YEAR OLD GAME!
THEY ROCK! I can play it perfectly now!
Oh, you want ot know abou the game itself? Well, it's pretty much like an open world version of the first Red Faction. Create your own path, destroy everything. Great fun!

The singleplayer campaign in RFG is amazing and quite enjoyable. The destruction mechanincs are still better than most. Unfortunately, most buildings do not respawn. Nordic Games, the publisher that bought the Red Faction IP after THQ went under has added Steamworks multiplayer.

Red Faction Guerrilla is now free of GFWL! If sandbox style, open world play is your thing, I thoroughly recommend Red Faction Guerrilla. While it's getting a bit long in the tooth these days, both visually and mechanically, it's still a great game for tooling about and destroying things.
While this is one of my favourite sandbox games, my recommendation comes with a cople of caveats; mission checkpointing can be a little harsh at times, and the game really is mostly about choosing your own way of doing the missions you're given. There is a story, and there are many, many missions. But the true joy is in deciding how to approach a given challenge with all the tools the game provides, especially in terms of destructibility. And when you screw up, you're sent back to the beginning of a mission, so repetition is virtually inevitable. Therefore, if you like your game experiences more towards the curated end of the spectrum, I can't extend this recommendation to you. This is very much a game that lets to find your own fun in a science fiction world, but helps that along by providing tools of sheer destructive joy.

This is a refined little beauty. From the store page, I expected a good looking but short and flat indie title with all the usual problems those come with. Instead I got an incredibly well put together, lengthy and polished title, the likes of which I'd expect from a triple A studio. The gorgeous animations, backgrounds, and other visual elements are definitely icing on the cake, but what makes this a great title is the masterful weave of mechanics and abilities with enemy interactions and platforming sections that always makes you feel like you're getting better while progressing through the game.
Outlands learning curve, for me, flowed in a natural progressive way. As a player I found myself constantly wanting to go further and progress just to see what was next. The unlocking of abilities on the way, and the interesting and fun boss fights were like the Golden Stars you got at school when you'd studied well, and really helped up the level of engagement.
The little details have all clearly had time and effort spent on them making sure they turned out right. Everything from the ability to destroy heart drops to turn them into excess gold when you don't need life, to the placement of new enemies after a platforming section has been thought about by the developer and works together to compliment the players progress.
The art style and sound deserve special mention, all sticking to various influences from Aztec, Incan, Mayan and even Olmec civilizations and all helping to promote a feeling of the spiritual and the historical and embolden the narrative, they work really well. Outland also has some of the best title screen narration I've heard in any game.
I expected a lot more frustration and annoyance than I found in this game, and the only things worth complaining about for me were little things that could've been fixed like the option of alternative pre-set control mappings, though even this has been addressed in a recent developer update. I only ran into one bug in my entire 8-hour playthrough which forced me to restart a boss fight. Other than that the only time I ever got frustrated in this game was when I screwed up a platforming section or didn't think through an enemy engagement before charging ahead. These annoyances set to show me I wasn't as good as I thought I was and needed to learn something before proceeding, as many of the good old-school games used to.
Currently selling on Steam at £6.99/9.99€/$9.99 and clocking in with an average playtime of 7-8 hours and close to double that for completionists, and with co-op and plenty of replay value, Outland is plain and simple good value for money if it's the genre of game you enjoy. There's even a Two-Pack option where you can save an extra 15-20% if you have someone to go in with.
There's also a Special Edition at (locally) an extra 33% which includes the soundtrack and an artbook with some development history and plenty of screenshots. While the soundtrack is unarguably good, it's fairly bland and unexciting, and the art is gorgeous, it's still essentially a collection of things in a pdf which are already mostly unlocked in game. In short, the Special Edition is cheap, but doesn't add much value.

Tower Defense game that puts you as the player under more preassure than ever before. No pause button (which is good for this game, imo!) and a lot of towers with skills you can activate (and on harder difficulties MUST activate). If you, like me, got tired of tower defense games where you just built tower and watched the action - you'll love this game as it requires you to be active at all times. This is NOT a TD game where  you play with one hand and drink coffee with the other.
Some levels can require a bit of trial and error, and learn where the (most dangerous) enemies come from but I personally don't have a problem with that. The levels ain't that long, and every minute is fun to play. I really, really loved every minute of perfecting levels. It's not just about placements, it's also how fast you perform your action.
I'd call this game "The Dark Souls of Tower Defense games", if you enjoyed Dark Souls, you enjoy action and you enjoy tower defense - pick this game up for sure!

HIgh production value in terms of voice work and writing but very limited chracter creation due to cross-platform play with PS3.  Also has a
of bugs and technical issues ranging from minor to show-stopping which Daybreak (or
as I call them) won't do anything about.  Just one example: for the past week every time I try to log in it tells me the server is down for maintainence, but its not.  There are a total six "mentors" you can choose (three heros and three villians) so you'll have a slightly different quest track depending on the one you pick.  Thus you could have six different characters who would each have a somewhat unique PVE experience.  IF you can actaully get on the server and IF you don't get locked out of your account (which happens randomly for no reason) then you might actually enjoy DCUO.  That's assuming that you aren't big on character customization, because there's precious little of it even if you spend loads of cash.  The max level is 30 and you will hit that max very quickly.  PvP isn't nearly as popular as raiding and you'll be doing craploads of the latter in order to earn the various currencies for l33t gear.  Being a subscriber doesn't help in this regard...your monthly cash store stipend is miniscule and doesn't buy much prestige.  Still, the replayability of PVE made this game was an easy "yes" vote just a few years ago despite its lack of character customization (for that you'll want Champions Online).  But no longer.  Now DCUO is just looking neglected and incredibly limited by its console DNA.  Their still adding raid content but there's also incessant, unneeded tinkering with gameplay that almost mirrors the WoW nightmare.  The single player experience has *never* received a signifigant expansion so far as I can tell.  Honestly, they need to be working on a sequel for PC and maybe current gen consoles that has a bigger PVE experience, more compelling PvP and b]far[/b] less pay-to-win.

i'm personally enjoying the hell out of this game right now.
The Combat is pretty simple, you have 4 abilitys that come in the form of cards, and then there is the rental card, which other players put up to help you on ur battles. These abilitys need to follow your job's class or it needs to have the class lore unlocked.. For example, My SOLDIER first class job can get the most out of Ranger Class abilitys after it unlocked Ranger Lore.
Fusion is alright. it isn't really required, But if you want to upgrade your jobs, you need to learn it. as it can unlock more of a certain thing called "SkillSeeds" Which is a way to upgrade your jobs passive abilitys and stats, And fusion is also there to upgrade your ability level. But you can't just use any card.. it has to be of the same element if u want this effect... fusion is also a way of getting experience..
Now, There is multiplayer.. I think its ok... Its not the best thing this game has to offer, but it is there.
You're placed into a 4 man team to take down a huge boss. based on what kind of job you have, Your role as a team is either a, Attacker, Defender, Or Healer... There could be more, i'm not too sure. The Attackers job is to deal as much as possible, the Defenders job is to defend everyone from attacks, and keep the enemy's damage at a minimum. Healer is there to keep everyone alive... Knowing your role can make or break the team.
this game also has events.. as im writing this review, The FFVII remake event is currently up, and that event has you helping out cloud to stop mako reacters. it is a long event, and some of the event isn't out yet. still waiting for mako reacter 3.. The events give you a lot of stuff, Like skillseeds and summon tickets..
Last and not least, There is the summoning. As you play the game, you get Summon Tickets.. You can use these to get new jobs, new abilitys, or if your lucky, Some legend jobs.. There are event legend jobs as well.. which is pretty neet.
you can get friend tickets as well if people use your rental card that people want to use.. but that will only get you a material card, and the cost scales the more you summon using the friend tickets.
Well, I enjoy this game. I personally do recommend it to anyone wanting to kill hours.. and if you like final fantasy like i do, then you will probably enjoy this. Have fun, Kupo!

I enjoy the combat/story/multiplayer and have logged 14.4 hours since I started on the morning 3 days ago. I cleared Chapter 1, have completed enough multiplayer to net myself some sweet rewards, and just started on Mako Reactor 2. My 1st Soldier job is about to clear its 4th Skill Panel.
I have yet to spend a single penny on this game. And my deck has maxed 4* Raiden & Cloud/Touch, and maxed 3* Barrier and Hades - I'm mowing through stuff on Hard Difficulty and ~at no point have I felt held back~ or as if I cannot have a healthy play session because I'm not paying.
From my perspective, this is exactly the kind of F2P game I'd love to see more often. It's all about making sure you have a good understanding of how everything works & so long as you plan & use the resources you're given efficiently, you shouldn't be seeing a paywall - at least not up through the point I've played. Continuing at my current pace, I cant imagine there'd be one later either.
I have a potato laptop with Win7 x64, an i5 CPU, 8GBs of RAM, and an Intel HD 3000 gfx chip - the game plays perfect at 720p, looks shiny, and I've not had a single issue or crash.
As for the story itself, it REALLY reminds me of Dissidia's, so much so that I'd not be shocked if someone told me this was a Dissidia prequel of sorts.  The world is dark & mysterious, and I cant wait to see where it goes next~!  The Moogle's English voice is one of the most crisp & amazing "cutesy voices" I've probably ever had the pleasure of hearing.  Dat sexy narrator (Vox) is awesome too~ <3
{3/18/17 EDIT:}  Just cleared chapter 2 and am still going strong.  The story has only gotten more intense, and I'm still making steady progress through the Infinite Reactor event area.  Still not a penny spent yet!  I'm sitting on 4,700 Magicite & am waiting to get another 30-day set for 3k.
{8/03/17 EDIT:}  Just cleared chapter 4 and will likely start chapter 5 soon, very excited!  All of the event areas have been great, and I've been clearing and getting 100% done on everything without issue - it's all still a pleasant challenge though.  I have all 20 of the "original" jobs, multiple maxed skillpanel sets & 5* ability cards, and I HAVE ~NOT~ SPENT A SINGLE $0.01USD!!!!  My Devout healer is lvl 240+ and managed to clear Tier 4 Ifrit+Ultima without dying easily, so now I have a maxed 5* Ultima Sicarius too.  On top of this, Square just lightened up on some of the "cash shop" systems and F2P people like me can get even MORE stuff ~freeeee~.  That combined with all of the giveaways in August & the pile of free stuff all of us are getting, there's not been a better time to start playing!  I wish more F2P RPGs were as good as this one~!
{11/24/17 EDIT:} Still free!  A string of awesome holiday/events in-game delayed my starting of CH5, but I'm still doing great on Hard Mode.  My level 272 Healer is handling the new Tier 5* boss fights in multiplayer just fine, and a lot of my setup is fairly easy to get just by playing now.  Also, Xmas is rumored to be amazing next month for free players....
{12/18/17 EDIT:} Not a penny spent~!  I just pulled the Duncan Supreme and Cloud Supreme jobs tonight during the Xmas event.  Also got the FF13 Etro job as well, last I checked I was sitting in the top 500 for the week with a score of over 70million, and I've still got mountains of resources to burn.  What with all the free stuff for new players (look at a re-roll guide) and the awesome FF7 event story that is great for easing new players into the game, now's an amazing time to get started.  It's great to have on in the background during work, and there's still more story and Free Explore areas for me to complete.  The Tier 5 multiplayer bosses have been an absolute blast to party on, and this has absolutely become my go-to online multiplayer game now that I'm 100% complete on FF11 and no other MMO fills that spot.  Even if this a little grind-ish and F2P, the story/multiplayer parties/and character builds cant keep me away, and not once have I felt held back by the cash shop elements (especially tonight with two Supreme pulls one after the other~).

Red Faction Guerrilla is now free of GFWL! If sandbox style, open world play is your thing, I thoroughly recommend Red Faction Guerrilla. While it's getting a bit long in the tooth these days, both visually and mechanically, it's still a great game for tooling about and destroying things.
While this is one of my favourite sandbox games, my recommendation comes with a cople of caveats; mission checkpointing can be a little harsh at times, and the game really is mostly about choosing your own way of doing the missions you're given. There is a story, and there are many, many missions. But the true joy is in deciding how to approach a given challenge with all the tools the game provides, especially in terms of destructibility. And when you screw up, you're sent back to the beginning of a mission, so repetition is virtually inevitable. Therefore, if you like your game experiences more towards the curated end of the spectrum, I can't extend this recommendation to you. This is very much a game that lets to find your own fun in a science fiction world, but helps that along by providing tools of sheer destructive joy.

Generally speaking, I don't write reviews for games I don't recommend. I write reviews for games I
recommend because I'm passionate about them and I want others to try them out. For games I don't recommend, I leave it to others. However, onlookers should be terribly disappointed with the poor quality of negative reviews on Outland. Most of them have less than 2 hours of playtime, and give very little reason as to why they don't recommend it. So, I hope I can provide you with more insight as to why Outland is a game you'd best appreciate from afar.
Outland is a game I was excited to buy and get playing. Metroidvania's are not a genre I play often, but when I have in the past, I've been incredibly happy with what I've played.
I was excited for Outland, because not only was the game concept appealing to me, but the visuals are quite pretty. Unfortunately, these are really the only two major positives of Outland. Before I start my commentary on the big 4 aspects of Metroidvania’s (as outlined above), allow me to briefly touch on the game concept.
The concept of the game, switching between light (blue) and dark (red) to progress through levels and combat enemies is quite good. It allows for some satisfying platforming at times and presents you with challenges to what would otherwise be seemingly simple tasks. This allows Outland to do
with
. In fact, sometimes Outland feels like a bullet hell game, which is pretty unique!
However, there are times when things seem quite inconsistent. For example, I can run into a laser or glowing orb from the same color as me without taking damage. Yet, at the same time, I take damage from enemies of the same color, but I cannot damage
If you ask me, the decision to make the game function this way is unintuitive for the player, and results in a large amount of challenge that is probably unnecessary.
As for strong story, well it’s quite lacking. The only context to the story is given by a narration after each boss, and they’re quite abstract and not very cohesive. From all I can gather, the story is,
That’s it. I find this disappointing, because when the narration
it’s good! In addition, exploration doesn’t build on the story, and the world itself says virtually nothing.
Great metroidvania’s tell a story through their world building. So how is the world and level design in Outland? It’s boring,
boring. The levels look too similar, and they play similarly. The platforming is sometimes challenging, which is a breath of fresh air, but overall the levels don’t feel unique. Even though you collect some powerups throughout the game, none of them really expand on the platforming. This is sorely missed in Outland. So, the level design in a couple words is: nothing special.
How about exploration? Well, it’s not great either. The extent of exploration in Outland is small nooks and crannies within levels, which only serve to give you doubloons.
you can get something like a life bonus or special bonus. Also, the game gives you very little reason to
which is something
good metroidvania has. Occasionally, you do run into things which you cannot get access to without future powerups, but the game fails to capitalize on this because there is never any reason to go back after you pass it. They only serve for bonus content, which is limited to collecting skulls for a steam achievement. This is all compounded by the fact that the game
shows you exactly where to go all the time. It completely stunts any kind of exploration by pointing you right in the direction you need to go always.
Finally, how is character development? Character development plays out the same way as exploration. There are times (few) where you unlock abilities you previously didn’t have, and there are things you couldn’t do without them. But once again, the game fails because there is
to go back, other than bonus content. In addition,
of the time you don’t understand the significance of an upgrade until after you have it. A great metroidvania will make you jump up and say, “Yes!” when you unlock an ability you didn’t have previously, because you
the significance of getting it. Outland doesn’t make you feel that way.
In conclusion, Outland isn’t a terrible game. In fact, it kept me interested long enough to beat it and even try and collect some of the side content. As you can see, I have more hours than most other reviewers. That being said, it’s not a game I recommend because I think you can play other,
metroidvania games at a similar price tag. However, the price tag is a plus. You could do a lot worse than spend $10usd on Outland.
In the end, Outland ends up being a game with a great concept, but falls short of making a lasting impact. This game lacks a level of depth and polish you would expect from a game of this genre.

If you are looking for a resounding "Yea, sire, this is a truly great game of video. Thee shalt pay much of thine coin!" in this review, then you have not played this game. In my experience, it is a great game, with some okay potential, although this has gone downhill fast. with shallow storylines, uninteresting characters, and an underwhelming "Silicon Valley" update (be aware that that was Trion's BIGGEST UPDATE YET), this is not a game to invest money in.
ALTHOUGH!
The lore and world, combined with plentiful serious moments make up for all of this. It is an open-world MMORPG. You can always skip the main questline and do what you wish. It can be your own story, with a little grinding. Try to make up a story in your head, and ask for RPers in the Chatbox. You won't regret it, and it can be loads of fun.
ALTHOUGH! (again)
I did not do this. I feel the main storyline is lacking. The only good characters in the beginning easily lose their influence later on. The bad ones, like Cass Ducar, get better toward San Francisco, so just bear in mind that opinion. The show does nothing to complement the story at all. So, I recommend you experience them as seperate franchises.
(And the show becomes a bit of a soap opera, so the game is still better.)
I believe that Trion has lost it's footing completely. They can only keep this game due to a vast amount of product placement by Dodge. SERIOUSLY, WHY THE HECK IS DODGE SO IMPORTANT IN THIS MULTI-FACTION CRISIS? HECK, EVEN THE "MARK OF THE DEFIANT" IS THE DODGE LOGO!
Excuse my rant, but Trion is putting a minimal amount of work into this game. The DLCs are pretty much just a few new vendors. (Excluding Gunslinger Trials, Castithian Charge, and Arkbreaker) You will like it for a while, but I recommend other games for long-term. It functions best as an F2P game.
The weapon mechanics can be summed up in one quote. DEATH TO ALL PLAYERS -Trion Worlds. You can shoot an enemy in the face 20 times, leaving him with 60% health. Mind = blown. There are no people who do PvE anymore, so you pretty much solo everything. All the enemies have bulletproof faces, so you have to do them one at a time with five other enemies firing at you. The weapons are all horrible. An assault rifle 4 levels below an LMG still does more damage. The tolerable weapons have little ammo, so you need to constantly reload and backtrack 200m just to grab some ammo.
All in all, this game is a great challenge to skilled gamers such as myself and everyone that can stand this game. There are really no reasons to keep playing other than that. I'm moving on to another game.

Il problema principale riguarda il prezzo: Per 15 euro questo gioco non offre abbastanza. Come hanno osservato anche altri, il gioco è pieno di idee ma povero in realizzazione. Ho pensato fosse una buona idea investire su questo gioco dato che lo sviluppatore sembrava un bravo ragazzo e molto attivo sul suo forum... Purtroppo il gioco dovrebbe essere raffinato maggiormente, e quello che il gioco prova a raggiungere sembra troppo per il lavoro di uno sviluppatore solo. Lo stesso dovrebbe avere almeno un piccolo team per riuscire realisticamente ad ottenere quello che promette in tempi realistici; invece sta cercando di fare tutto da solo, e conseguentemente il gioco costa troppo e non diverrà mai la piccola gemma che sarebbe dovuto diventare.
Per concludere lo sviluppatore dovrebbe dimostrare un po' di umiltà e con i profitti del gioco assumere uno o due persone che lo aiutino a rifare da capo l'interfaccia e a ripensare completamente poche altre cose del gioco che necessiterebbero di venire ristrutturate poichè superflue o del tutto inutili. Sembra chiaro che abbia una idea chiara su quello che vuole ottenere dal gioco, e sembra essere molto competente in programmazione, ma da solo non può farcela.
Da notare che questo gioco contiene molte belle idee e molte features ben realizzate. Se dovessi dare un voto finale a questo gioco sarebbe di
5\10
tenendo conto che qualora lo sviluppo portasse ad una esperienza di gioco perfetta ed equilibrata, questo voto potrebbe cambiare.
EDIT:
Alla fine lo sviluppatore ha fornito molte risposte interessanti che hanno dimostrato come mi sbagliassi sul suo conto; ha persino fornito informazioni sui costi di sviluppo del progetto, che è una cosa rara e preziosa. Purtroppo la mia opinione generale sull'esperienza di gioco non cambia, ma terrò d'occhio lo sviluppo e in caso cambierò opinione.

Because I love the possibility to micromanage many aspects, like the design of a new engine or complete vehicle or the monthly adjustments to get my production on pair with demand, but also the possibility to put some things on automatic, like the staff wage system, or use the big fast settings, like global pricing for some of my cars.
The game has many aspects one can but must not use, like the parts contract system. You can try and sell some licences of the engines, gearboxes, chassis or even complete vehicles you developed - or you can try and get a licence from another company for your own actions.
But you must not. It's optional and I actually don't use it because I don't like the idea somebody else using my great parts.
Same goes for the stock market. You can gamble and try and make a Dollar or two - or you can sell your own stocks for quick money or even try and take a competitor over, getting all their parts, vehicles, designs and of course factories.
At the end it's obvious this is not a graphics blockbuster. The graphics are there to show you what's going on - and they fulfill this very well. The office changes as time developes with nice artwork and everything else is fine for what it should represent. I like this minimalistic and easy style in other games like Hearts of Iron, too.
What basically made me write this review at the end of the day is not the game itself. It's the developer. He answers in his forums as well as here in detail and often on the same day, he invests time into his answers and even looks at uploaded savegames if there's a question or suggestion or bug report.
I paid 11.99€ during a sale and I believe this is a very good price. If you're into this sort of games and if you like the game, even the normal full price is a steal for the amount of time you can sink into this game and the feeling you supported somebody who, at least that's my impression yet, deserves it.

Strategic, turn-based battle. Elements play a key role in both the special attacks you can use during a turn and the elemental resistance buff you can give yourself. You have to decide which will benefit you the most, given the situation. Do you absorb the element to give yourself resistance, or use the element orbs for your special attacks? These special attacks are known as "cards" which you gain from enemies or get from the card shop.
To be clear, this is not a card (vs card) battle game; the battles are rendered in 3D and the cards are just the special abilities you've chosen. (Sort of like a command list from classic Final Fantasy.) Card deck is organized before battle.
Enemies have a stamina meter which can be broken. This is signified by "BREAK" on the screen when the meter is depleted. Targeting elemental weakness during BREAK can give you a significant advantage during battle.
The game can be a bit repetitive, so it's best played in short bursts. Multiple battles against similar looking enemies and some enemy models are straight from FFXIV (Treant, Adamantoise, and Golem).
there is an Auto-Battle feature and Fast Forward, so if you're short on time or just want to skip repetitive "trash mob battles" you can use those features.
Multiplayer is decent. It's very turn-based. You enter commands, lock them in, wait for others to do the same, and then the turn against the summon (Ifrit, etc.) starts.
The story is... eehh. It's split into different parts and there are a lot of "trash mob battles" between it. Some of the cutscenes are entertaining, and the voice acting is decent. Something major happens in Chapter 2 though and hit me right in the feels. I hope to see the story get better as I continue.
Best looking and smoothest when played on PC.
Good music and some classic FF cursor sound is thrown in the mix. Music gets louder when BREAK is triggered, which is a nice touch.
This game is overall worth a look if you're into Final Fantasy and want a game you can experience on both PC and mobile.

I absolutely LOVED this game when it was in its prime. I've spent most of my hours playing Chernarus Life when it was still a thing that existed, usually on the Excyted Gaming servers (even if the admins were absolutely rеtаrdеd sometimes - fυсk you Eric). Regardless, I've played through the campaign, spent hours and hours at a time working with other players to liberate towns, outposts and encampments in Hohei Evolution Blue and Evolution Red on the Anzu's War Games servers.
Eventually, after playing this game for a while, I purchased Operation: Arrowhead. The original ARMA 2 still had an enormous playerbase even though OA had been released for quite some time as well. I found myself enjoying ARMA 2 over OA any day. The fact that OA lacked Chernarus Life and replaced it with the less-good Takistan Life Revolution and Island Life was offputting for me, since those maps were less well suited for a civlian-vs-cops type scenario, whereas Chernarus was literally the perfect "Life" map.
ARMA 2 was a bit clunky in the controls, but once you got them down (or simply adjusted the keybindings in the options menu) the game was such a blast to play. I probably spent about 50 hours in the mission editor alone, creating my own little missions and scenarios to play through with friends or on my own.
I won't get in to the specific features of the game itself, because now that the multiplayer is gone nobody will ever be able to experience the game in its full potential again. The game is entirely dead now due to the GameSpy shutdown, which hosted ARMA 2 servers, but you can still play multiplayer in Operation Arrowhead. That being said, this game was absolutely fantastic.
10/10 from me, even though it had some bugs and a few odd things here and there, that's what made it ARMA 2. ARMA 3 doesn't come close to this game. Not only does ARMA 2 have more guns and vehicles than ARMA 3, but the mission editor is much better as well. So, for my conclusion?
Don't buy this game. It would have made a great purchase any time before 2014, because the multiplayer still worked and there was a huge fanbase with a wide variety of servers and community-created addons that made the game so much better. ARMA 2 is now just a mediocre single-player campaign. For $12.99 USD (price as of August 12, 2016) this game is absolutely not worth it. I'd say it's worth about $5, but I really think that Bohemia Interactive should make it a free game since all it's used for nowadays is being able to play the DayZ mod.

Pros:
-You can tear builidngs apart, brick by brick using a wide array of weapons
-You obtain weapons such as remote charges that can be thrown and exploded at will, a rifle that disintegrates solid matter, a large missle that causes massive damage, a guass rifle, and a whole array of normal combat weapons.

-There's a large amount of augmented vehicles that can assist you in the rebellion
-It's Open World!
-It plays out in a territory capturing kind of way. You force enemies out of sectors by lowering their control over the sector and rasing the morale and support for your guerrillas.
Cons:
-Buildings take quite a long time to collapse. An unrealistic length of time. This can be tweaked with mods though.
-Enemies are too powerful, and you can't hold enough ammo to deal with them all.
-No checkpoints on any missions
-Buildings don't respawn, meaning that you can't go back to destroy them again at the end of the game

Space Run is a good and notably different take on the tower defense genre. It's well-produced, has amusing characters, a good variety of "buildings" and abilities, and the campaign has a lot of variety and a good difficulty curve.
Its balance isn't perfect, and some missions are fairly limited by your cargo. There are about half a dozen different kinds of cargo, each with different effects ranging from simply taking up space to draining power around them. Some of these types of cargo missions are lots of fun, but I found two of them to be rather unenjoyable. Luxury passengers and alien artifacts have mechanics that severely limit what modules you can practically use, and the restrictions diminished the gameplay rather than making it more interesting.
It's also rather frenetic, for a tower defense-style game. I would have appreciated a pause mode that let you issues commands, but the game seems very built around the semi-frantic pacing. It's not intrinsically bad, but some people may not like that aspect.
Overall, Space Run is a lot of fun, and it's pretty unique in the things it does. The above caveats shouldn't push you away unless you really don't like the sound of the game's speed.
I made it about 75% through the campaign being very entertained.  By the end though, I didn't really feel like there was much left to do.

Space Run is a very good game.
It is stressful and strategic, forcing you to make make quick decisions about where to place weapons, shields, engines and cargo. More engines means a faster ship, so you get more money for a fast delivery at the end of the level. But the engines takes up space that could be used for your guns to protect you from attacks from the rear.
Do you build the powerful high-end equipment, for maximum shield and fire power, or the cheaper low end stuff that takes up far less space on your ship? That is up to you to decide, based on your playing style.
A drawback to the game is that several levels can be very trial and error, but on the other hand the game does encourage you to replay previous missions with your new upgrades to make more money. Some players want a pause button, but to me that would ruin some of the intense stress that helps make the game more fun and a challenge.
All in all a very enjoyable action/strategy/tower defense game that I do recommend.

80% of this game is outstanding, i cannot recommend it; however, due to the 20% that is terrible being the last 20% of the game;
Note: spoilers abound in this review!
The game starts with your silent protagonist in a beutifully minamalistoc world, the jump seemed initially clucnky, but that was no longer an issue by the end of the first prequel level. The enemies clearly stand out, have simple and elegant designs, having few uneccessary fetures, which only are there to make the enemy varients more clear, and add to the asthetic involved. The first boss is while not easy, becaome easy after you figure out his patters; to get all the upgrades though there is a coin system, coin farming in entirely uneccesary, but getting every coin pot you can is still recommended. Your character picks up several abilities, the most important (which forever changes you from the gold and black colorscheme) is the polarity mechanic you do not immediatly gain the polarity powers, and only after you gain both can you switch between them, An early flashback gives you an idea of how this works (and will work when you can) to when your appetite. As you go through a number of well drawn, and well desgined stages, you may begin to be very glad you purchased such a well made game. Wexept for a few hiccups mid way through the game, it seems very close to perfect (as far as platfprmers are concened).
But why would i still not reccomend the game if most of it is so good?
The final boss you fight is a feathered serpent, which as a lot of build up towards it; each of these guardians was an inportant figure in the rich lore and the featherd serpent seems like it would be a dymanic battle (like many of those previous) and with all your new abilities, it seems like you could have a nice arena, and perhaps some reward for victory that really makes you feel like a legendary hero. The fight starts with three autoscrolling and rather minimalistic platforming sections: go too slow, and you get hit by a death beam, fall off and lose qa heart but get placed in a managable spot; the death beam only deals 1 heart of damage, but also destorys platforms thus eating a second heard and putting you in a tolorable respawn point. Each of these sections has a checkpoint in between. After all that running which helps hyp up the fight, even in the running stages are bland, you get ont a lift, which rises into the air and hang there for a second. The Ser[ent arrives and the battle begins!
but wait... how do you fight? While it was kind of refreshing to play a game with simple enough controls, and does not feel the need to baby you through everything, i had to look up a guide to figure out how to do any damage; in this fight you spend the entire fight on the beasts back; rendering it's belly mounted death cannons useless and pointless; if an autoscrolling buildup run was necessary, you counld have had the serpend bust through the building with its body, or start the collapse of the temple. Further after a good 15 seconds where no damageable portions are visible, and it has stared raining down polarity colored bombs you will quickly notice your health dropping. Thus is due to the fact that though the bombs are polarity colored, (and suffer damage appropriately)  they deal neutral damage, which means you screen has a dust sand particles moving across the screen, some of which damage you wen some spots on the monster light up. To damage it ou must use the ground stomp; though the raised sections look like you could cut them, and disply the hit animation, unless you stomp, its hitpoint bad does not decrease. After figuring this out, you have to hit the three buttons as the appropriate polatity a few times, and for the latter two the boss starts firring bullets from its fins at the buttons. Unlike the previous two bosses, who despite having basic attack patters, seemed to be fighting you this boss seems to be all but ignoring you as to try to kill it, thetting random debries fight for it. After 3 rounds of button stomping, its head graphic changes a little (it is not easy to see the change due to all the crap onscreen) and becomes damageable by your attacks; and you now need to beat that to death before you run out of hearts. After this monumental battle, the freeroaming aspect of the game is abruptly removed. You go back to the portal, (now unlocked) and are spawned on thedoor, so that as soon as you move you have to start the final set of levels from which there is no return (as far as i could find). In the final levels the goddesses will swap the polarities of all enemies. This would be neat if it was handles better; however, the goddeses have a number of criteria determining when to do the swap (so it seems almost random), they can do it while enemies are mid attack animation (which can result in a swift death), and if that was not annoying enough the aonly warning you get is a screen flash (obscuring everything) which animation begins the instant the color is changed; this means your current attack begun well before the color change may find then enemy innume when it arrives, and already attacking. This turns all of the enjoayable aspects such as fluid mechanics irrelevant. I personally found any enjoment i previously experienced in this title shrivel to ashes with this changes, and as such i would recommoned you spend your money elsewhere.
TL/DR
Most of the game is good, but the ending is so bad that i would suggest something else; like Bastion (for fighting) or Bleed (for platforming, and fighting).

First off, don't get me wrong: This game is terrible. Absolutely terrible. But it is HILARIOUS. It so shamelessly rips off the Uncharted series that you can't help but bust a gut laughing at it. Rather than paying a buck for a game, consider it paying a buck for an hour of comedy gold.
In fact, I'm going to spoil the whole game right here. Why? Because it's an hour long. Literally. It will make it easier to review in this way as well. There is literally so little content to this game that I CAN'T review it without basically telling everything that happens!
First, lets get the basic story out of the way. Faris, an Arab fortune hunter, and his archaologist sister Dania are following the trail of famous Muslim explorer Ibn Battuta. Why, I'm not sure, I think to find his tomb or something, I forgot and it honestly doesn't matter. That's about it. There's no character depth, no background that I can see. Throughout the game they're confronted by various baddies that are after the same thing they are. Now I'm gonna go after the chapters 1 by 1, and this will be entirely about the gameplay.
Chapter 1: The game begins with our protagonist immediately under attack, and thrust straight into the action. He gets injured, which means he's going to be moving very, very slowly. I'm talking so slow it makes Resident Evil 1-3 critical health limp look like Sonic the Hedgehog. The character animation is also extremely stiff. After limping through a few corridors and shooting a handful of baddies, the first chapter comes to a close.
Chapter 2: This is the longest chapter in the game, and from a gameplay perspective, the best one (and trust me, that's not saying much.) It begins with you hunting for 4 artifacts, which you must use to reactivate an ancient fountain and open a door. Once this is done, you will pass through some dark corridors and eventually come to another item collection segment where you must acquire 2 daggers from 2 rooms. One of these rooms has you controlling an RC car on a lower floor to hit switches and make bridges up above. I'm pretty sure they got this idea from Ape Escape because I've never seen any other game besides those games where you get to use an RC car to solve puzzles. Curiously, this idea is never, ever used again for the rest of the game. The other dagger requires you to do some basic Tomb Raider 1 style platforming to get up to it. With both daggers in hand, you can finally get to the heart of the tomb. At this point, the bad guys break in and one of them confronts you shortly after. At this point we have an awkward hand to hand fight, which is one of the most blatant ripoffs of Uncharted in the entire game. Trust me, reading about it may not tell you all that much but you have to SEE it to understand where I'm coming from. Once this is taken care of, guns come back into play and you must backtrack to the beginning of the level shooting badies with some of the worst AI I've ever seen. I didn't notice it that much in the first level, probably because I was still trying to get over how stiff and awkward the game was, but they are STUPID. I'm talking shoot the walls and walk right past you stupid. The chapter ends once you make it to the level start.
Chapter 3: Thought chapter 2 was of decent length? Well the last 4 chapters are pretty much about that length if you put them all together. The third chapter of the game opens with another awkward hand to hand fight with a character who is suspciously similar to Guerro from Uncharted: Golden Abyss, and once he is taken care of Faris and Dania flee the desert in a short on-rails shooting segment (She drives, you shoot.)
Chapter 4: Arriving in Morraco, Faris, Dania and another guy whos name I can't be bothered to remember walk through the streets chatting. That's it. The entirety of chapter 4 is just walking slowly through streets while listening to acting and dialogue that would have fit perfectly in The Room. I swear, this part seems like it was written by Tommy Wiseau. I know VSauce made that reference and yes, I did see that video, but it's truly the only thing I can think of to compare it to. The voice acting, the dialogue, everything feels like it was trying to directly copy the style of The Room, and this is probably one of the most hilarious parts of the game because of it.
Chapter 5: This chapter opens with a chase sequence like the ones in LA Noire and Splinter Cell: Conviction, which after about a minute leads to the final hand to hand fight in the game. Once this is said and done, you must sneak past a grand total of 2 guards in the only stealth sequence in the entire game. End of chapter.
Chapter 6: And now the game rips off Grand Theft Auto. The final chapter of the game is driving around avoiding cops. Literally, that's it. You drive around being chased by cops for about 3 minutes and if you can go that long without failing, you win the game. There is a bar which decreases every time you hit a cop car (or if the cops run into you) and the game explicitly states multiple times NOT to hit the cops. I did not fail this part, but I'm assuming this bar is something like a wanted meter and if it completely empties, you get arrested. This makes sense, since hitting cop cars is OBVIOUSLY a crime, especially if you run from it, but know what else is a crime? Hit and runs with other vehicles. Apparently this game doesn't realize that as you can smash into civilian vehicles as many times as you want and that bar will NEVER change, its only when you collide with the cops. But hey, I'm just running on assumptions here, maybe it's not a wanted meter at all. I don't know, and I honestly don't even care.
And that's the whole game. If you read through all of that (or played it yourself) you will realize something: This game feels like a beta test. No, really, this game feels like someone was just testing what they could do. Either that, or decently long demo.
There are several different gameplay elements that only make one or two appearances. There are only 2 on-foot shooting segments. There is only one RC car puzzle. There is only 1 on rails shooting section. There is only 1 stealth section. There is only 1 driving section (the finale of the game). It feels like they were just using random ideas here and there for the sake of seeing if they could actually impliment them and make them work right, as if this entire game was simply made to test gameplay elements that may be used in something much larger later on. Either that, or they just had absolutely no idea what they were doing with the game and threw out whatever came to mind. Considering how shamelessly this game rips off Uncharted in so many aspects (even the main character's personality, and to some extent, looks, are ridiculously similar to Nathan Drake) it would probably be safer to bet on the latter.
Final word is, get the game if you want a few good laughs, or just save yourself the buck and watch gameplay on Youtube. Either way, I wholeheartedly recommend checking this out just to witness how badly it fails at being a game.

Strategic, turn-based battle. Elements play a key role in both the special attacks you can use during a turn and the elemental resistance buff you can give yourself. You have to decide which will benefit you the most, given the situation. Do you absorb the element to give yourself resistance, or use the element orbs for your special attacks? These special attacks are known as "cards" which you gain from enemies or get from the card shop.
To be clear, this is not a card (vs card) battle game; the battles are rendered in 3D and the cards are just the special abilities you've chosen. (Sort of like a command list from classic Final Fantasy.) Card deck is organized before battle.
Enemies have a stamina meter which can be broken. This is signified by "BREAK" on the screen when the meter is depleted. Targeting elemental weakness during BREAK can give you a significant advantage during battle.
The game can be a bit repetitive, so it's best played in short bursts. Multiple battles against similar looking enemies and some enemy models are straight from FFXIV (Treant, Adamantoise, and Golem).
there is an Auto-Battle feature and Fast Forward, so if you're short on time or just want to skip repetitive "trash mob battles" you can use those features.
Multiplayer is decent. It's very turn-based. You enter commands, lock them in, wait for others to do the same, and then the turn against the summon (Ifrit, etc.) starts.
The story is... eehh. It's split into different parts and there are a lot of "trash mob battles" between it. Some of the cutscenes are entertaining, and the voice acting is decent. Something major happens in Chapter 2 though and hit me right in the feels. I hope to see the story get better as I continue.
Best looking and smoothest when played on PC.
Good music and some classic FF cursor sound is thrown in the mix. Music gets louder when BREAK is triggered, which is a nice touch.
This game is overall worth a look if you're into Final Fantasy and want a game you can experience on both PC and mobile.

Before reading my review, my time on record in the game is low because I originally played and completed just about all of the game on PlayStation 3. However I managed to do a lot of things in the PC version in my roughly fifty minutes of play.
